docs.title: The grammar other apps skip, drilled until it comes without thinking.
docs.text:
Latin, Spanish and French, each a complete course in one app: every form of every verb, the grammar explained before it is drilled, and a look-up that tells you what any form is. Every answer is checked, not just shown, and the app comes back to what you got wrong. iPhone, iPad and Mac, with a companion app for Apple Watch.

Choose your language.

docs.title: Five ways to study
docs.text:
• Grammar lessons — a path in level order: one new thing per lesson, explained before it is drilled. For when you want the app to decide what comes next.
  • Theory — every theory page of the course in one list, by word type: the grammar, to read in order. For when you want to understand before you drill.
  • Practice Sets — ready-made sessions on one theme or tense, or sets you build and share yourself. For a fixed piece of work.
  • Self Study — every word type with its theory, word lists and drills; you decide what is in play. For working on exactly what you need.
  • Tests — every test for your level on one page. With Only new at this level, just what your level adds. The book button beside each test opens the theory. For finding out what you already know.

All five share one vocabulary catalogue and one adaptive engine: an answer given in any of them counts in all of them. Practice Sets and Grammar lessons appear only for a course that has them.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Every form LinguaMorpha produces for French is compared with an external source — the verbs with Wiktionary's conjugation tables. Every disagreement is recorded with its reason. Most are decided: a choice between grammars, a form the source lacks, a slip on our side that was fixed. The ones below are not. They are questions of French, not of software, and rather than settle them by guesswork they are listed here, for anyone who can answer them.

The questions are published as they stand in the register, in English.

docs.title: Verbs — against Wiktionary
docs.text:
Nothing open in this section.

Decided and recorded in this section (4) — open for the reasons

Each line is one recorded disagreement: what it concerns, the verdict the comparison gave, and the reason the register keeps — the maintainers' own note, in English.

  • valoir — imperatif_present · second · DIFFERS — vaux, not vaus. valoir writes -x in the first and second person singular (je vaux, tu vaux) and the impératif follows the présent tu, so vaux. Named in check_oracle_ratchet.py's header as one of the judgement calls that make the diff unsuitable as a gate; this is where it is written down. One cell, and the only French disagreement in 36,910.
  • absoudre, distraire, extraire … (5) · we suppress — The -aire verbs and two neighbours have no passé simple and no subjonctif imparfait — a defectiveness the catalogue declares and the engine honours at step 0.3, and the same fact that made five corpus rows teaching *tu soustrayis* a finding rather than a typo. Every suppressed cell of theirs is in those two tenses.
  • pleuvoir, grêler · we suppress — Impersonal: il pleut, il grêle, and no other person (the impersonal flag; tonner is not on it, because it thunders against a government too, and the oracle and we agree on its full table). Named in diff_paradigm_against_reference.py's own header as the canonical case — 'Wiktionary conjugates pleuvoir in full; we restrict it'.
  • devoir, décéder, résulter — imperatif_present · we suppress — No imperative, for the same reason as the Spanish group above: *décède!* and *résulte!* are not things one says, and devoir's imperative is unused in modern French. Three cells each — tu, nous, vous — and nothing outside the impératif.

If you can answer one of these, write to us through the Support page — a reference to a grammar or a text is enough. An answer changes the register, the register changes the app, and this page shortens.

docs.title: The choice drills
docs.text:
Être or avoir

A sentence with the auxiliary missing: est or a? The answer comes with the reason.

Passé composé or imparfait

Which tense does the sentence need — a eu or avait? The English hints at the aspect; you decide.

Indicatif or subjonctif

After à moins que: pleuve or pleut? The drill that settles the subjunctive.

docs.title: Nouns and adjectives
docs.text:
Noun gender

Every French noun has a gender and no rule covers them all; the endings give strong tendencies and the traps are famous. Read it, then drill it.

Which form of vieux goes with les jours? Gender and number, chosen against a real noun.

Which article?

Du, de la, des, or de — the article a whole sentence needs, countable or not.

docs.title: French hides its grammar in the spelling. Drill what you can't hear.
docs.text:
Parle, parles, parlent sound the same. The drills make you write them — and make you choose.

You can know the conjugations and still freeze the moment you have to build a sentence yourself. Reciting a form is a different act from choosing, in conversation or in a text, between passé composé and imparfait, between indicative and subjunctive, between être and avoir. Those are choices English does not make for you.

LinguaMorpha has you make the forms yourself. It builds every form of every verb it knows, across all sixteen tenses — the passé simple and the subjonctif imparfait included — and drills them in both directions. Not only "what is vinrent?" but also: "give the passé simple, ils, of venir". So you learn to recognise forms and to produce them.

A missing accent counts as correct, with the right spelling shown — unless the slip spells another form, and Exact spelling in Settings turns this off. The spellings of the 1990 reform count as correct too. And where a form has several readings, all of them count — parlais is je and tu.

Those three choices get drills of their own: passé composé or imparfait, indicative or subjunctive, être or avoir. Not only which one is right, but why.

Stuck while reading? Type the form into Look up. Vinrent gives you venir, passé simple, ils, with every reading of an ambiguous form.

Every form has been compared against an outside source. Every difference is documented in the open, on the site.

Try it free for 21 days — every feature, every language. Then unlock French on its own, or all languages, as a one-time purchase. No subscription, no account.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The learner on a course. Your course introduces a tense a chapter and never repeats it enough. Select the tenses and verb groups you have reached and drill them until the spelling of the form is automatic.

The reader. You want the literary tenses — the passé simple, the subjonctif imparfait — recognised on sight, and être or avoir settled without stopping to think.

The school pupil. French at secondary school: a tense per chapter, and the test asks for them all at once. Here you actually drill them — type the form for a verb, tense and person, choose être or avoir, passé composé or imparfait — and every answer is checked, accent and all, not just shown. Besides that, the agreement of adjectives and the article question — du, de la, des or de — asked the way the exam asks it. The app remembers what you got wrong and comes back to it.

How it compares. Duolingo, Babbel and Rosetta Stone give a broad experience — listening, speaking, everyday situations — and skip the depth. LinguaMorpha is the opposite: explicit grammar, the irregular part of every form made visible, and drills you choose yourself rather than a fixed curriculum. It has no speaking practice and no listening comprehension; it works well beside those apps, doing what they leave out.

The verb, in full

Conjugation · Regularity · Reference sheet — with the irregular parts marked where they depart from the verb's own group.

docs.title: Five ways to study
docs.text: Grammar lessons, Theory, Practice Sets, Self Study and Tests — the same five in every course, sharing one catalogue and one adaptive engine, so an answer given in any of them counts in all of them. What each one is for →

docs.title: What the app does
docs.text:
Type any form and see what it is. You read vécut, naquirent or eussent, or heard something that sounded like fasse, and are not sure which verb it is. Look up searches every conjugated form of every verb in the course — over 900 verbs in sixteen tenses — as well as every noun, adjective, phrase and word, and tells you the verb, the tense and the person, with every reading of an ambiguous form. Accents are optional, capitals are ignored, a word in your own language finds the French, and a misspelling still lands on the nearest headwords. Tap the result and the verb opens at that tense.

The marking scheme. In the conjugation tables, red falls on just the part of a form that departs from the verb's group — the è of j'achète, the stem of je ferai — and a form that is red from end to end, such as je suis, has to be learned as a whole. An underline marks the ending the pattern predicts. In the compound tenses the past participle carries the mark, so pris and ouvert are red wherever they appear.

Verb groups. Fourteen groups in five sections, each tickable in Select verb groups: the three classic groups and the pronominal verbs; the spelling changes (mangeons, commençons, essaie); the stem changes (achète, préfère, appelle); the auxiliary (avoir or être); and the fully irregular verbs and the verbs with an irregular subjonctif.

The verb detail. Tap any verb for a tabbed screen — Conjugation · Regularity · Reference sheet — with its translation in the header. Regularity names the stem behind each tense and shows in amber the stems you have to memorise; on Conjugation, a filter hides the tenses that follow the pattern. Reference sheet is a printable one-page PDF of the verb in every tense.

Choose what is in play. Sixteen tenses, each switchable on its own in Select tenses — the everyday ones first, the literary ones when your reading needs them — and the fourteen verb groups tickable one by one, so the drills follow the course you are on rather than running ahead of it.

Drills. Produce the conjugation and Recognise the conjugation, and three choice drills that ask what a sentence needs: Passé composé or imparfait, Indicatif or subjonctif and Être or avoir. When you answer a conjugation question correctly, the feedback can show a translation of the exact form you gave; where the app has no translation of its own, devices with Apple Intelligence (iOS 26 and macOS 26) can supply one.

Grammar lessons. If you would rather follow a path, over fifty step-by-step lessons take you through the same ground in order.

Sessions that work on what needs work. Every answer is recorded on your device. The words for each session are picked from your selection on the basis of your answer history and your Learning pace, and an Incorrect answers switch limits a session to what you got wrong before. Nouns and adjectives get the same treatment as verbs: gender, plural and agreement drills, so that le tour and la tour, bijoux and trous, stop being guesses.

docs.title: Speech and dictionaries
docs.text:
French forms are read aloud with the voices Apple provides on your device, in Standard, Enhanced and Premium quality, just as for Spanish. Verb and noun detail screens carry a Dictionaries row that looks the word up in Linguee, WordReference and Reverso — in a browser sheet inside the app on iPhone and iPad, and in your web browser on the Mac.

On Apple Watch, the companion app shows conjugation tables for the verbs you choose — the essential verbs at first, any verb in the course after that — in the tenses you choose.

docs.title: For the teacher
docs.text:
What a pupil does with it. The app does not replace the course book; it is what the pupil opens beside it. Sixteen tenses and fourteen verb groups each switch on and off separately, so the drills can be limited to what the chapter has introduced — this week's passé composé, not next year's subjonctif. Every session picks its words from the answer history, and the Incorrect answers switch keeps a session to what went wrong before. The reports show which tenses and words a pupil has practised, how well, and what has stuck.

The question the test asks. Knowing a conjugation is one thing; knowing which form a sentence needs is the other, and that is what the test asks. The choice drills do exactly that — être or avoir, passé composé or imparfait, indicatif or subjonctif, du / de la / des / de, the form of the adjective — with an explanation after every answer. And spelling counts: mangé is not manger, finissions not finissons.

A set for the class. A practice set is a session you put together yourself — these verbs, those tenses, this kind of exercise — and share as a file, by AirDrop, mail or the school's learning platform. The pupils import it and drill the same material. For next week's test, or for the irregular participles half the class still has not got. For a fixed route, the fifty-three grammar lessons in fourteen modules cover the same ground in order.

Hearing what you type. Every form is read aloud with the device's French voices, at an adjustable speed; a pupil who cannot tell parlé, parlait and parlez apart by ear hears them side by side. The detail screens link to Linguee, WordReference and Reverso — the teacher chooses which.

What it is not. No teacher dashboard, no accounts, no class administration, no results sent to the school. That is a choice: a pupil's answers stay on the pupil's own device, and there is no server for them to go to. To see how a pupil is doing, ask to see the report — or have it exported as a PDF. No speaking practice and no listening comprehension: that is what the lesson is for.

docs.title: How we know the forms are right
docs.text:
A conjugation app is as good as its forms. So they do not rest on the author but on comparison with a source a teacher knows, and on writing down every difference.

Every verb form against Wiktionary. All 36,872 forms the app produces for its 900-odd verbs — every person, tense and mood, the passé simple and the subjonctif imparfait included — have been compared with Wiktionary's conjugation tables. 36,871 agree letter for letter. One differs: je vaux, where Wiktionary writes vaus and the app follows the grammar. What the app deliberately leaves out — the passé simple of absoudre and frire, the personal forms of pleuvoir, the imperative of devoir — is in the register, with the reason.

Every difference is on paper. The register can be read on the Open questions page, with the decided differences. It also guards the future: a change to the app that moves one more form away from the source fails the check until someone has judged the difference.

What this does not prove. That a form is right says nothing about the translations, the example sentences and the explanations in the choice drills; those were written by the author and have not been read by a teacher of French. Anyone who finds a mistake in them helps the app most by reporting it — Support reads every message.

docs.title: For the school
docs.text:
One price per pupil, no subscription. French is a one-time purchase in the App Store, on the pupil's own iPhone, iPad or Mac; with the same Apple ID it is unlocked on all of them at once. No annual licence, no renewal.

21 days free first, for the whole class. Every pupil can use the complete French course for 21 days without paying. That is enough for a trial with a class before anyone buys.

No accounts, no data. The app asks for no name, no email address, no age. Answers, progress and settings stay on the device; there is no server, no analytics, no tracking. For the school's data-protection review that is the short answer: no personal data is processed. The long answer is the privacy policy.

One app for the modern and the classical languages. The same app holds Spanish — over 1,200 verbs in sixteen tenses, the subjuntivo included — and Latin — every declension, the classical verb system, a sentence parser — with the same drills, reports, practice sets and grammar lessons, and the same rule that nothing leaves the device. Each language unlocks on its own, or all three together as Unlock all languages.

iPhone, iPad and Mac. The same app on all three, with the same tables and drills: the school iPad in class, the pupil's own phone on the train, the Mac at the desk. One purchase covers every device on the same Apple ID; progress stays on each device, since there is no account to sync it through. Not for Android, Windows or Chromebook.

Three interface languages. The app, the guide and this site come in English, Dutch and Spanish; the pupil chooses, independently of the course. An international school or a bilingual stream runs the app in English.

Purchase by the school. A school edition that the school buys itself through Apple School Manager — licences the school owns, reassigned to the new class every year, with Apple's education discount from twenty copies — is possible, but does not exist yet. We will build it as soon as a school wants to buy it; if yours does, say so through the Support page. Until then the answer is: the pupil's own device, one purchase, and 21 days free for the whole class.

docs.title: The catalogue
docs.text:
• over 900 verbs across the three groups
  • over 1,400 nouns, with gender, plural and example sentences
  • over 250 adjectives, with all four forms for agreement in gender and number
  • adverbs, pronouns, numerals and prepositions, each with its own hub
  • over 200 set phrases, plus the example sentences of the verbs and nouns

docs.title: The grammar, in detail
docs.text: Exactly which tenses, groups and patterns the course covers — open for the reference

docs.title: Verb grammar
docs.text:
Full conjugation for the three groups — 1st (-er, parler), 2nd (-ir with the -iss- infix, finir) and 3rd (everything else: prendre, partir, mettre; the fully irregular verbs such as être, aller, faire and venir have a group of their own in Select verb groups).

Sixteen tenses, each switchable on its own in Select tenses — all four moods, including the literary tenses you will meet in reading.

Indicatif — simple

  • Présent
  • Imparfait
  • Futur Simple
  • Passé Simple — literary

Indicatif — compound

  • Passé Composé
  • Plus-que-parfait
  • Futur Antérieur
  • Passé Antérieur — literary (j'eus parlé), after quand, lorsque, dès que or après que

Conditionnel

  • Conditionnel Présent
  • Conditionnel Passé

Subjonctif

  • Subjonctif Présent
  • Subjonctif Passé
  • Subjonctif Imparfait — literary
  • Subjonctif Plus-que-parfait — literary (que j'eusse parlé)

Impératif

  • Impératif Présent — tu / nous / vous only
  • Impératif Passé — aie fini avant midi, the same three persons

docs.title: Noun grammar
docs.text:
Gender (le / la) and plural formation across the catalogue: the regular -s; the -x after -eau, -au and -eu, and on the seven -ou nouns that take it (bijoux, genoux, …) while every other -ou noun takes -s; the -al → -aux pattern and some -ail nouns; and compound nouns. The gender groups cover masculine/feminine pairs (chien / chienne), nouns with one form for both genders (un / une élève), and the nouns whose meaning changes with gender (le tour / la tour).

Meaning flashcards show each noun with its article, so gender is drilled alongside meaning rather than after it. Pick the correct article drills le or la; Which article? asks which article a whole sentence needs — definite, indefinite, partitive or bare de. Singular / Plural and Alternate gender pairs complete the set.

docs.title: Adjective and adverb grammar
docs.text:
Agreement across gender and number, sorted into seven agreement classes — including the irregular feminines -eux → -euse, -f → -ve and -er → -ère, the doubled consonants (bon → bonne) and the pairs to learn by heart (beau → belle). An Agreement drill asks for the form that goes with a given noun. The adverbs hub explains the -ment derivation and drills the meaning of derived, irregular and lexical adverbs.

Numerals include the counting-in-twenties pattern of soixante-dix, quatre-vingts and quatre-vingt-dix, with a drill on when vingt and cent take an -s. Prepositions have a contrast drill for the pairs learners confuse: pour / par, en / dans, à / de and depuis / pendant.

Pronouns have an Object pronoun drill — the direct, indirect or reflexive pronoun the sentence needs — and an Agreement drill that matches celui or le mien to a noun's gender and number.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Every form LinguaMorpha produces for Latin is compared with an external source — the verbs with Wiktionary's conjugation tables, the nouns, adjectives and pronouns with Collatinus. Every disagreement is recorded with its reason. Most are decided: a choice between grammars, a form the source lacks, a slip on our side that was fixed. The ones below are not. They are questions of Latin, not of software, and rather than settle them by guesswork they are listed here, for anyone who can answer them.

The questions are published as they stand in the register, in English.

docs.title: respondēre
docs.text: The app conjugates respondēre with a full personal passive (respondeor, respondēris …). Wiktionary gives it only the impersonal third person (respondētur). Does respondēre aliquid count as transitive enough for a personal passive, or should the app show the impersonal forms only?

docs.title: salvēre, pluere, stinguere … (4)
docs.text:
The app marks some tenses of salvēre, pluere, stinguere and fierī as defective and shows an empty row; Wiktionary's tables fill them (salvēbō, plūverō, stīnxerō, fītō). Which of these forms are attested in classical Latin? fītō, the future imperative of fīō, seems to be.

Decided and recorded in this section (7) — open for the reasons

Each line is one recorded disagreement: what it concerns, the verdict the comparison gave, and the reason the register keeps — the maintainers' own note, in English.

  • fluere, prōficere, vehere · accent-only — The oracle writes the AMBIGUOUS-LENGTH marker — macron over breve, flū̆xerō, vē̆xissēmus — where the quantity is disputed or varies by author. We commit to one length, because a learner reading a table needs a vowel to say and 'either' is not sayable. Not a spelling disagreement: it is a disagreement about whether to have an opinion. Named in ENGINE_QC_AND_CONFIDENCE.md as 'Wiktionary's variable-length macrons'.
  • nōlle — imperativus_futurum · accent-only — nōlītō / nōlītōte with the long ī, as the standard grammars print it; the oracle has nōlitō. Same class as the entry above — a quantity the oracle declines to commit to and we do.
  • plicāre · DIFFERS — Our perfect is plicāvī, the oracle's is plicuī. Both are attested and the dictionaries list both — Lewis & Short head the entry 'plĭco, āvi or ŭi'. We take the regular first-conjugation perfect because the verb is filed as a regular first-conjugation verb and a learner meeting it there should see the paradigm it is filed under. Thirty cells, all of them the perfect system built on that one stem.
  • revertere · DIFFERS — We conjugate it as the SEMI-DEPONENT — revertor, reverteris, revertitur in the present system, active revertī, reverteram in the perfect — which is how Classical Latin overwhelmingly uses it and how the grammars teach it. The oracle's lemma here is the plain active revertō, which also exists. Not a form disagreement but a choice of which of two real paradigms to file the word under; note the perfect system AGREES, which is what a semi-deponent predicts.
  • fundere, tribuere, īnstruere · INVENTED — The oracle gives these three a THIRD-PERSON-ONLY passive and we give the full one. Ours is right: all three are ordinary transitive verbs and fundor, tribuor, īnstruor are unremarkable Latin. The decisive evidence is in the reference file itself — adfundere, a compound of the very same verb, carries a complete personal passive there, so the restriction is not a fact about the stem. Twenty-one cells each: the four non-third persons of the five personal passive tenses, plus the future passive imperative.
  • * — *_passivum · we suppress — The intransitive carve-out, and it is deliberate: an intransitive verb has no PERSONAL passive in Latin, only the impersonal third singular (advenītur, 'there is an arriving'), so *adveniris and *advenīmur are not words. ENGINE_QC_AND_CONFIDENCE.md lists it among the invariants worth encoding — 'intransitives have only the impersonal 3sg passive'. The oracle generates the full six-person table for them. We emit the third person and suppress the rest, which is why every entry in this bucket is a non-third person.
  • meminisse, ōdisse · we suppress — Also taxonomy. These have only a perfect system, so the form that does duty as their future is the future perfect: we produce meminerō and ōderō under futurum_exactum and declare futurum defective, the oracle labels the same string futurum. Ours is the morphological label and the oracle's is the functional one. Both describe the same paradigm and the same form; nothing is missing on either side.

docs.title: Nouns, adjectives and pronouns — against Collatinus
propinquus
docs.text: For the degrees of propinquus the app forms propinquior, propinquissimus; Collatinus and the dictionaries give propior, proximus under the same headword. Which pair should a school course show?

docs.title: iners, simplex, memor — positivus
docs.text: For the one-ending adjectives iners, simplex and memor the app declines i-stems throughout (ablative inertī, genitive plural inertium, simplicium). Collatinus treats all three as consonant stems (inerte, inertum, simplicum); Allen & Greenough give iners and simplex as i-stems and memor as mixed (memorī but memorum). Which stem class should each follow?

docs.title: turris, puppis — singularis · accusativus
docs.text: For the accusative singular of turris and puppis the app prints turrem and puppem, treating -im as the rarer variant; Collatinus knows only turrim and puppim, and Allen & Greenough list both nouns among those that sometimes retain -im. Which form should a table print when it can print only one?

docs.title: aureus, caeruleus, continuus … (15) — positivus · masculinum · singularis · vocativus
docs.text: For the vocative masculine singular of adjectives in -eus and -uus (aureus, mortuus, tuus …) the app writes auree, mortue, tue by the second-declension rule; Collatinus keeps the nominative form. The grammars rule on nouns and on -ius, not on these. Which is right, or does the vocative of such adjectives simply not occur?

docs.title: clipeus — singularis · vocativus
docs.text: The same question for a noun: the app writes the vocative clipee, Collatinus clipeus.

docs.title: fīcus
docs.text:
The app declines fīcus as fourth declension throughout (fīcūs, fīcuī, fīcibus); the dictionaries and Collatinus make it second declension (fīcī, fīcō, fīcōs) with a few fourth-declension forms. Should the app file it as second declension?

Decided and recorded in this section (35) — open for the reasons

Each line is one recorded disagreement: what it concerns, the verdict the comparison gave, and the reason the register keeps — the maintainers' own note, in English.

  • niger — comparativus · DIFFERS — Collatinus's data bug, not a disagreement: its lemma line gives niger the radical nīgr- where its model expects nīgri-, so every comparative cell comes out *nīgrōr-. Ours is nigrior, nigrius — the regular formation every grammar gives.
  • gracilis — superlativus · DIFFERS — gracillimus. gracilis is one of the six -ilis adjectives that take -limus (facilis, difficilis, similis, dissimilis, gracilis, humilis; illimusLemmas in LatinAdjective.swift); Collatinus files it under the plain fortis model and writes gracilissimus.
  • multus — comparativus · ablativus · DIFFERS — plūre. The ablative singular of plūs is plūre in the grammars (plūrī is a rare variant); Collatinus's plus model gives only plūrī.
  • arx — pluralis · genitivus · DIFFERS — arcium: arx is a monosyllable with a stem in two consonants, the textbook i-stem class (urbs, urbium). Collatinus writes arcum.
  • canis — pluralis · genitivus · DIFFERS — canum: canis is one of the named exceptions to the parisyllabic i-stem rule (canis, iuvenis, pater, māter, frāter, senex take -um). Collatinus writes canium.
  • alius — singularis · genitivus · DIFFERS — The same word, spelled differently: our alīus (the long ī marking the contracted double i) against Collatinus's aliius / aliīus, which writes the two i's out. Not a disagreement about the form.
  • īdem — pluralis · genitivus · DIFFERS — eōrundem / eārundem, the assimilated spelling the grammars print; Collatinus writes eōrumdem, the unassimilated one. Both are attested; ours is the commoner.
  • socius — singularis · vocativus · DIFFERS — socī: nouns in -ius take the vocative in -ī (fīlī, Vergilī), the rule LatinNoun.declined applies to the whole class; Collatinus declines socius as a plain -us noun and writes socie.
  • īnferus — superlativus · DIFFERS — īnfimus, the superlative the school grammars give first; īmus (Collatinus's) is the other, both attested. Stored as superlative_lemma.
  • lacus — pluralis · dativus / ablativus · DIFFERS — lacubus: the grammars list lacus among the fourth-declension nouns that keep -ubus (with arcus, artus, quercus, tribus); Collatinus declines it as manus. Flagged ubus in the data.
  • domus — pluralis · accusativus / genitivus · DIFFERS — domus mixes the second and fourth declensions and both sets are attested: our domūs / domuum against Collatinus's domōs / domōrum. The textbook paradigm gives the fourth-declension forms first in these two cells and the second-declension domō, domōs elsewhere; the ablative domō is already stored. Whether to lead with domōs is the classicist's call.
  • parēns — pluralis · genitivus · DIFFERS — parentum and parentium are both attested (the grammars give parentum, 'also parentium'). Ours is the first.
  • cornū, genū — singularis · dativus · DIFFERS — The fourth-declension neuter dative singular is cornū in the paradigm the grammars print, with cornuī as the variant; Collatinus gives only the variant.
  • tigris · DIFFERS — tigris declines on two stems, tigr- (tigris, tigrem, tigrium) and tigrid- (tigridis, tigridem); both are attested and the dictionaries give both. Ours is the shorter; Collatinus generates the longer. For the classicist to prefer one.
  • quis — femininum · singularis · DIFFERS — quis as a substantive interrogative is masculine and feminine alike — quis, quem, quō for both — which is how the school grammars and our table have it; Collatinus gives the feminine the adjectival forms quae, quam, quā. A convention, recorded in LATIN_CONVENTIONS_AUDIT.md's spirit: say which tradition the table follows.
  • parēns · accent-only — Collatinus writes pārēns with a long a; the dictionaries (parēns, from pariō) have it short. Ours stands.
  • lac · accent-only — lac, short a (OLD, L&S); Collatinus writes lāc. Ours stands.
  • hērēs — singularis · nominativus / vocativus · accent-only — hērēs, hērēdis with both vowels long is the OLD's; Collatinus shortens the second in the nominative (hēres). Ours stands.
  • cornū, genū — singularis · nominativus / accusativus / vocativus · accent-only — The fourth-declension neuter nominative and accusative singular end in long -ū in the paradigm every grammar prints (cornū, genū); Collatinus marks them short. Ours stands.
  • hic · accent-only — hic (short i: the adverb hīc 'here' is the long one) and hoc; Collatinus writes hīc and hōc, the latter marking the length the doubled c gives the syllable (hocc). A notation difference, not a quantity we would print.
  • quis, quī — singularis · dativus · accent-only — cui, one syllable with the diphthong, as the classical grammars have it; Collatinus lists the disyllabic cuī and the archaic quoī as alternatives. Ours stands.
  • suī — dativus · accent-only — sibi with the short final i, the classical prose form; Collatinus lists sibī, the archaic and poetic long final, beside it. Ours stands.
  • multus — comparativus · singularis · we suppress — plūs has no masculine or feminine singular and no dative or vocative singular: the noun-like neuter plūs, plūris, plūre is the whole singular, which is what plusForms holds. Collatinus's multus model produces *plūror, plūrem, plūrī for the singular — a data bug on its side (plūror is not a word).
  • Iuppiter — pluralis · we suppress — Iuppiter has no plural in classical usage; the catalogue marks the plural defective. Collatinus generates Iovēs, Iovum, Iovibus from the Iov- stem, which is correct morphology for a word that does not occur in the plural.
  • spēs — pluralis · genitivus / dativus / ablativus · we suppress — spērum and spēbus are attested only in late Latin; the classical paradigm is defective in these three cells and the catalogue marks them so. Collatinus generates them.
  • vīs — singularis · dativus · we suppress — vīs has no genitive or dative singular in classical prose (the grammars mark both wanting); Collatinus supplies vī for the dative. The catalogue marks the cell defective.
  • uterque, quīdam, quīcumque … (5) · DIFFERS — The comparison's artefact, not a disagreement: Collatinus analyses the particle off (-que, -dam, -cumque, -quam) and lemmatises the rest as uter, quī or quis, so the oracle row holds utrum for our utrumque, quem for our quendam. Our forms are the whole pronoun, as the grammars print them; the base forms Collatinus returns agree with ours letter for letter once the particle is put back (quendam, quōrundam with the m assimilated to n before d).
  • aliquis — singularis · dativus · accent-only — alicui, one syllable with the diphthong, as for cui (see quis/quī above); Collatinus lists alicuī and the archaic aliquoī. Ours stands.
  • os · DIFFERS — A homograph in the oracle: Collatinus's lemmatiser folds os, ossis 'bone' onto ōs, ōris 'mouth' and returns ōris, ōre, ōra. Ours is os, ossis — the word the catalogue files (ōs 'mouth' is its own entry and agrees).
  • os · accent-only — The same homograph: ōs is 'mouth'; os 'bone' has a short o. Ours stands.
  • aes · accent-only — aes with the diphthong ae, which is long by nature and never takes a macron in the grammars; Collatinus writes aēs. A notation difference, not a quantity.
  • famēs — singularis · ablativus · accent-only — famē, the fifth-declension ablative the grammars give for famēs (famēs, famis, famē); Collatinus writes fame. Ours stands.
  • famēs — pluralis · we suppress — famēs has no classical plural; the catalogue marks it defective. Collatinus generates famium, famibus.
  • speciēs — pluralis · genitivus / dativus / ablativus · we suppress — speciēs, like rēs and diēs a fifth-declension noun, has no classical genitive, dative or ablative plural (speciērum and speciēbus are late); the catalogue marks the three cells defective, as for spēs. Collatinus generates them.
  • volucris — pluralis · genitivus · DIFFERS — volucrum, the genitive plural the grammars give (volucris is a consonant stem despite the parisyllabic nominative, like canis); volucrium is attested but rarer. Collatinus gives volucrium.

If you can answer one of these, write to us through the Support page — a reference to a grammar or a text is enough. An answer changes the register, the register changes the app, and this page shortens.

docs.title: Latin is morphology. Make it automatic.
docs.text:
Every ending, every macron, drilled until a sentence stops being a puzzle and becomes a text.

You can know every paradigm by heart and still come unstuck in a test. Reciting a paradigm is a different act from recognising rēbus in the middle of a sentence.

Vocabulary apps test a list someone typed in. Parsers give answers, but never ask anything. LinguaMorpha does both, and in two directions: "what is corporibus?" and "give the dative plural of corpus".

It can do that because it builds every form itself. It tests any form, marks your answer down to the macron — lenient or strict, you choose — and on a mistake shows the paradigm behind it. Where a form has several readings, all of them count: rosae is genitive and dative singular, nominative and vocative plural.

Stuck mid-translation? The parser is already there — plus ten passages, from a beginner's story to unaltered Cicero, translated line by line.

Every form has been compared against an outside source. Every difference is documented in the open, on the site.

Try it free for 21 days — every feature, every language. Then unlock Latin on its own, or all languages, as a one-time purchase. No subscription, no account.

iPhone & iPad Mac

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The self-learner. You are doing Latin without a teacher — Lingua Latina per se Illustrata under your own steam, or a textbook you work through yourself. Nobody tests you and nobody tells you it is nearly right. The app asks for the form instead of showing it, marks your answer down to the macron, and on a mistake names the paradigm behind it.

The reader. You can follow a text with a dictionary and a grammar but not without them. The parser checks your reading line by line, the readings put a parse behind every word, and the drills close the gaps the parser keeps finding.

The school pupil. Paradigms are not learned by reading them but by producing them, again and again, until they come by themselves. Scope the drills to the declensions, patterns and tenses your chapter has introduced — Wheelock, the school course, whichever it is — and drill until they stick: type the form for a case and number, conjugate in the tense asked, recognise what a form is. Every answer is checked, macron and all, not just shown. The app remembers what you got wrong and comes back to it. Besides that: the tables on your phone for the test, and the sentence parser for the homework.

How it compares. For Latin the alternatives are textbook companion sites, vocabulary lists and flashcard decks. LinguaMorpha puts the catalogue, the paradigm tables, the production and recognition drills, the parser, the readings and sessions that track what you get wrong into one app, instead of a collection of separate tools. It does not teach you to speak Latin, and it does not replace your textbook; it is what you use beside it.

docs.title: Five ways to study
docs.text: Grammar lessons, Theory, Practice Sets, Self Study and Tests — the same five in every course, sharing one catalogue and one adaptive engine, so an answer given in any of them counts in all of them. What each one is for →

docs.title: From paradigm to text
docs.text:
Every form, every macron. Every noun, adjective, pronoun and verb form in the course is stored with its macrons, and the typed drills check them. The check is lenient by default: rosis for rosīs still counts, and the feedback reads Correct — watch the macron and shows where the long vowel goes. Turn on Exact spelling (Settings → Study) and a missing macron is wrong — for when vowel length is what you are learning. Either way, the written form with its macrons is always the authority.

The five declensions, in one view and drilled both ways. The synopsis puts the endings of all five declensions side by side, singular and plural, and switches to a detailed grid with the neuter columns of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th. From there, Decline the noun asks you to produce the form a case and number call for, and Recognise the form asks what a form is — and in Latin the honest answer is often more than one, so every correct analysis of an ambiguous form counts. Select noun groups narrows the drills to the declensions you are working on, i-stems and the fourth-declension neuters included.

All five declensions, side by side

The endings of all five declensions in one grid, singular and plural. Switch to Detailed to add separate neuter columns for the 2nd, 3rd and 4th declensions.

Decline the noun

Produce the form that the case and number ask for — type it, or pick it from a list — with macron checking as lenient or as strict as you choose.

The agreement drill

The noun is already inflected and the adjective is missing. Pick the form that agrees; the explanation names the noun's gender, case and number.

Noun and adjective together. Paradigms are learned one word at a time, but Latin is read two words at a time. In the agreement drill a short sentence appears with a blank where an adjective belongs; the noun is already inflected, and you pick the adjective form that agrees with it in case, number and gender. After each answer a card explains the choice — pulchram agrees with rosam (f. Acc. sg.). All five adjective patterns take part.

The verb system in full. Indicative, subjunctive and imperative, active and passive, plus the six infinitives, all four participles, the gerund and the supine — every tense can be switched on or off in Select tenses, so the drills follow your textbook rather than running ahead of it. Tap any verb for a tabbed screen titled with the verb and its principal parts (amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum): Conjugation filtered by mood, tense, stem and voice; Regularity, which goes through the verb tense by tense, names the stem each tense is built on and shows in amber the stems you have to memorise; and a printable one-page Reference sheet. Then produce a form, recognise one, name the verb from its principal parts, or take the two choice drills — Perfectum or imperfectum and Indicativus or coniunctivus — that ask which tense or mood a sentence needs.

Type any form and see what it is. Look up takes whatever you met on the page — ferrent, rēbus, ductūrōs — and tells you what it is: the word it belongs to, its meaning, and its case and number or tense, person and voice, with every reading of an ambiguous form listed. It searches every form of every verb, noun and adjective in the course, not just the headwords. Macrons and capitals are optional, a word in your own language finds the Latin, and a form you half-remember or misspell still lands on the nearest headwords. A verb opens at the tense you typed; a noun opens with that form highlighted in its table.

From forms to sentences. Once the forms are there, the course turns them towards text. Nouns carry over 1,700 example sentences, each translated and labelled with the case and number the noun takes; adjectives show short sentences with the adjective agreeing with a noun; many verbs add tense examples and their separate senses. The sentence parser takes a whole sentence — a line of Caesar, a Vulgate verse, your homework — and returns every word as a chip with the lemma of its most likely reading and a badge when there are more; tap a chip for every possible parse, and nouns, adjectives and verbs open their full entry with the matching form highlighted. It ignores macrons and capitals, strips punctuation and splits enclitics such as -que and -cum, draws on more than 2,000 lemmas at the level of an introductory course, and marks what it does not know as unknown. A literal word-by-word gloss can be copied, and on devices with Apple Intelligence a Translate button asks for a machine translation. And the ten annotated readings — from a beginner's story through the Vulgate, Catullus and Phaedrus to unaltered Caesar and Cicero — put the parser under every word, an English and a Dutch translation under every line, and a teacher's note on the constructions worth noticing.

Sentence parser

Paste a Latin sentence; every word the catalogue knows comes back parsed, with a literal gloss you can copy.

Annotated readings

Ten passages, sorted by difficulty, with a translation under every line and a parse behind almost every word.

Beside your textbook. The course carries no chapter tags, so there is no per-chapter filter for Wheelock or Lingua Latina; instead you scope the drills by declension, adjective pattern, verb group and tense to match what the chapter has introduced, read the chapter, and drill the same material here until it is automatic. Every answer is recorded on your device, the words for each session are picked from your selection on the basis of your answer history, and an Incorrect answers switch limits a session to what you got wrong before. If you would rather be led, the Grammar lessons go through the same ground in order: twelve lessons in four modules, from the first declensions and the verb's present and perfect systems to the passive, pronouns, participles and the subjunctive. And when you meet Latin outside the app, the parser is the quickest way to check your reading.

What else does it look like? →

docs.title: For the teacher
docs.text:
What a pupil does with it. The app does not replace the course book; it is what the pupil opens beside it. Declensions, adjective patterns, verb groups and tenses each switch on and off separately, so the drills can be limited to what the chapter has introduced — this week's paradigms, not next month's. Every session picks its words from the answer history, and the Incorrect answers switch keeps a session to what went wrong before. The reports show which tenses and words a pupil has practised, how well, and what has stuck.

A set for the class. A practice set is a session you put together yourself — these words, those tenses, this kind of exercise — and share as a file, by AirDrop, mail or the school's learning platform. The pupils import it and drill the same material. For next week's test, or for the paradigm half the class still has not got.

Checking homework. Paste a sentence into the sentence parser and every word comes back analysed, with every reading of an ambiguous form. It is the fastest check on a reading that does not work: rēbus is not an accusative, whatever the pupil thought. The readings — from a beginner's story through the Vulgate, Catullus and Phaedrus to unadapted Caesar and Cicero — carry a parse behind every word, an English and a Dutch translation under every line and, at the constructions worth a pause, a teacher note: the jussive subjunctive in the Pater Noster, the ablative of respect in Caesar, the accusative and infinitive in Cicero.

The words of the classroom. The app names tenses and moods in Latin (Praesens, Perfectum, Coniunctivus) in every interface language; names a verb by its first person (amō) in the English interface and by its infinitive (amāre) in the Dutch one, with the principal parts after it; orders the cases nominative – genitive – dative – accusative – ablative – vocative, as the Dutch and German school grammars do; and labels the rows of a conjugation 1 sg … 3 pl, without a pronoun. Macrons follow the Oxford Latin Dictionary and Ørberg's Familia Romana. Every one of these choices is stated in one place in the guide, so a pupil who sees something other than in the book knows why.

What it is not. No teacher dashboard, no accounts, no class administration, no results sent to the school. That is a choice: a pupil's answers stay on the pupil's own device, and there is no server for them to go to. To see how a pupil is doing, ask to see the report — or have it exported as a PDF.

docs.title: How we know the forms are right
docs.text:
The app's author is not a classicist. So the correctness of the forms does not rest on his judgement but on comparison with sources a classicist does trust, and on writing down every difference.

Every verb form against Wiktionary. All 66,290 forms the app produces for all its verbs — every person, tense and mood, active and passive, infinitives, participles, gerund and supine — have been compared with Wiktionary's conjugation tables. 66,048 agree letter for letter; 93 differ only in a vowel length, where Wiktionary leaves the length open and the app commits to one; 65 differ outright; and 84 are forms the app produces that Wiktionary does not list — the full passives of verbs for which Wiktionary gives only the third person. Every difference is written down, with what it is and why the app keeps its form or does not — and the register is there to read, on the Open questions page.

Every declined form against Collatinus. All 42,096 forms of the nouns, the adjectives in three degrees and the pronouns have been compared with Collatinus, the lemmatiser by Yves Ouvrard and Philippe Verkerk that Biblissima distributes. 41,629 agree, the positional lengths before ns and nf included; 43 differ only in a vowel length; 394 differ outright, and every one has been judged and recorded: a choice between grammars, a form Collatinus lacks or writes differently, or an open question. The rest are forms the app leaves out, such as the plural of Iuppiter and the genitive plural of spēs. The slips the comparison found on our side were fixed before anything was counted.

Every disagreement is on paper. The differences that remain live in a register with their reasons — turrim or turrem for the accusative of turris, the vocative of aureus, the stem of simplex. Some are decided; a handful are open, and those go to a classicist rather than being settled by us — they are listed on a page of their own. The register also guards the future: a change to the app that moves one more form away from the source fails the check until someone has judged the difference.

What this does not prove. That a form is right says nothing about the translations, the example sentences and the teacher notes; those were written by the author and have not been read by anyone with a degree in classics. A teacher who finds a mistake in them helps the app most by reporting it — support reads every message.

docs.title: For the school
docs.text:
One price per pupil, no subscription. Latin is a one-time purchase in the App Store, on the pupil's own iPhone, iPad or Mac; with the same Apple ID it is unlocked on all of them at once. No annual licence, no renewal.

21 days free first, for the whole class. Every pupil can use the complete Latin course for 21 days without paying. That is enough for a trial with a class before anyone buys.

No accounts, no data. The app asks for no name, no email address, no age. Answers, progress and settings stay on the device; there is no server, no analytics, no tracking. For the school's data-protection review that is the short answer: no personal data is processed. The long answer is the privacy policy.

One app for the modern and the classical languages. The same app holds Spanish — over 1,200 verbs in sixteen tenses, the subjuntivo included — and French — over 900 verbs, the passé simple included — with the same drills, reports, practice sets and grammar lessons, and the same rule that nothing leaves the device. A pupil taking Latin and French learns both the same way; a school teaching all three has one app to assess. Each language unlocks on its own, or all three together as Unlock all languages.

iPhone, iPad and Mac. The same app on all three, with the same tables and drills: the school iPad in class, the pupil's own phone on the train, the Mac at the desk. One purchase covers every device on the same Apple ID; progress stays on each device, since there is no account to sync it through. Not for Android, Windows or Chromebook.

Three interface languages. The app, the guide and this site come in English, Dutch and Spanish; the pupil chooses, independently of the course. An international school or a bilingual stream runs the app in English, with the same Latin terms and the same tables.

Purchase by the school. A school edition that the school buys itself through Apple School Manager — licences the school owns, reassigned to the new class every year, with Apple's education discount from twenty copies — is possible, but does not exist yet. We will build it as soon as a school wants to buy it; if yours does, say so through the Support page. Until then the answer is: the pupil's own device, one purchase, and 21 days free for the whole class.

docs.title: The catalogue
docs.text:
• over 600 verbs in six verb groups: the five conjugations and the fully irregular verbs
  • over 650 nouns across all five declensions, plus two irregular nouns
  • over 350 adjectives across all five patterns
  • the core pronouns — personal, demonstrative, relative, interrogative and indefinite — each with its full paradigm
  • the cardinal numbers from 1 to 20, the tens up to 100, and mīlle
  • prepositions, adverbs, conjunctions, interjections and set phrases, each with its own hub

docs.title: The grammar, in detail
docs.text: Exactly which forms, groups and patterns the course covers — open for the reference

docs.title: Verb grammar
docs.text:
The full classical tense system: indicative, subjunctive and imperative, active and passive, plus the non-finite forms. Each tense can be switched on or off in Select tenses.

Indicative — present system (active and passive)

  • Praesens
  • Imperfectum
  • Futurum

Indicative — perfect system (active and passive — the passive built with the perfect participle and esse)

  • Perfectum
  • Plusquamperfectum
  • Futurum Exactum

Subjunctive — four tenses (active and passive)

  • Coniunctivus Praesens
  • Coniunctivus Imperfectum
  • Coniunctivus Perfectum
  • Coniunctivus Plusquamperfectum

Imperative

  • Present (the everyday "do this!")
  • Future (formal register — laws, prayers, maxims)
  • Their passive forms

Non-finite forms

  • Six infinitives (three tenses × two voices)
  • All four participles: present active, perfect passive, future active, and the future passive or gerundive
  • Gerund (the verbal noun)
  • Supine (accusative in -um for purpose, ablative in -ū for respect)

Verb groups. The verbs are filed in six groups: the 1st (-āre), 2nd (-ēre), 3rd (-ere), 3rd-iō and 4th (-īre) conjugations, and the fully irregular verbs (sum, possum, eō, fīō and their compounds). Ferō, volō, nōlō and mālō sit in the 3rd conjugation with their irregular forms stored one by one.

The verb detail. Tap any verb for a tabbed screen — Conjugation · Regularity · Reference sheet — titled with the verb and its principal parts. Conjugation can be filtered by mood, tense, stem and voice. Regularity goes through the verb tense by tense, names the stem each tense is built on and shows in amber the stems you have to memorise. Reference sheet is a printable one-page PDF of the active voice.

Drills. Produce a form or recognise one — every analysis of an ambiguous form counts — name the verb from its perfect or supine in Principal parts, and two choice drills, Perfectum or imperfectum and Indicativus or coniunctivus, that ask which tense or mood a sentence needs.

docs.title: Noun grammar
docs.text:
All five declensions:

  • First (gen. -ae, almost all feminine): puella, aqua, rosa
  • Second (gen. -ī, masculine -us or neuter -um, plus the -er nouns): servus, bellum, puer
  • Third (gen. -is, all genders) — including the i-stems (urbs, cīvis, mare) and nouns in -or, usually masculine, with feminine exceptions such as arbor
  • Fourth (gen. -ūs, mostly masculine, with the feminines manus and domus and the neuters cornū and genū): exercitus, frūctus
  • Fifth (gen. -ēī or -eī, almost all feminine, with diēs usually masculine): diēs, rēs

Choosing what to practise. Select noun groups narrows the drills to the declensions you want. The two nouns whose paradigms are stored form by form rather than generated, vīs and Iuppiter, have an Irregular row of their own and are drilled like any other noun. Drill a noun both ways: Decline the noun asks for a form, Recognise the form asks what a form is.

docs.title: Adjective grammar
docs.text:
All five textbook patterns:

  • 1st/2nd-declension (-us / -a / -um): bonus, magnus
  • 1st/2nd-declension -er (-er / -a / -um): pulcher, miser, sacer — the same endings, but the masculine nominative singular ends in -er
  • 3rd-declension two-ending (fortis / forte): masculine and feminine share a form, the neuter has its own
  • 3rd-declension one-ending (ingēns, gen. ingentis): one nominative for all three genders, with the stem shown by the genitive
  • 3rd-declension three-ending (ācer / ācris / ācre): three different nominative singulars

Comparative and superlative are formed for the adjectives that have them in classical Latin (-ior / -ius, then -issimus, with -rimus for -er adjectives and -limus for facilis and its family), and not for adjectives in -eus, -ius and -uus (aureus, arduus), the possessives or the ordinals. The irregulars — bonus → melior → optimus, magnus → maior → maximus, malus → peior → pessimus, parvus → minor → minimus — are stored explicitly. The sentence parser recognises all of these forms; the drills work with the positive degree: Decline the adjective asks for a form, Recognise the form asks for its case, number and gender, and the Agreement drill matches it to a noun.

docs.title: Pronouns, prepositions and numerals
docs.text:
Pronouns — every form stored individually, grouped by class: personal (ego, tū, reflexive suī), demonstrative (is, hic, ille, iste, ipse, īdem), relative (quī), interrogative (quis) and indefinite (aliquis, quīdam, quisque, nēmō, alius …). The form drill asks for a case, number and gender and offers the same pronoun's other forms as the wrong options.

Prepositions — the Case-government drill asks which case each preposition governs.

Numerals — the cardinal numbers. Ūnus, duo and trēs decline and get a full table; the others, from quattuor to centum and mīlle, are indeclinable and show a card with their single form.

docs.title: Privacy Policy
docs.text:
Last updated: July 30, 2026

This Privacy Policy describes how LinguaMorpha ("we", "us", or "our") handles information when you use the LinguaMorpha application for iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch (the "App").

The short version: LinguaMorpha is a local-first app. All your data — answers, progress, settings — stays on your device. There is no account, no cloud sync, and no analytics tracking.

docs.title: What you provide
docs.text:
• Your answers and study activity — Every answer you give in a flashcard or drill is stored locally on your device, along with the date, time, word, question type and whether you were right. This data is used by the App's adaptive learning system to decide which words to show you next. It is never sent off the device by the App; it leaves the device only if you export it yourself (see below).
  • Your practice sets — Practice sets you create or import are stored locally on your device.
  • Your preferences — App language, learning language, appearance, session size, learning pace, voice and speech speed, dictionary choices, report thresholds, and word-selection filters are stored locally on your device. The Apple Watch app keeps its own settings on the watch and does not exchange data with your iPhone.
  • Trial and purchase status — The date your free trial started, and a record of which languages you have unlocked, are stored in your device's keychain so the App can tell whether the trial is running and which languages are unlocked.

docs.title: What we don't collect
docs.text:
• We do not collect any personal information such as your name, email address, or date of birth.
  • We do not require, create, or maintain user accounts.
  • We do not collect your precise or approximate location.
  • We do not access your contacts, camera, microphone, or photos. The App does not include speaking exercises, audio recording, or any feature that uses the microphone.
  • We do not run any analytics, telemetry, or crash-reporting service against your use of the App. There is no Google Analytics, Firebase, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Sentry, Crashlytics, or equivalent in the App.
  • We do not store or transmit your answer history, progress, or any other study data to our servers. We do not have a server for this data.

docs.title: When the app uses the internet
docs.text:
The App is designed to work fully offline. There are a few specific situations where it may make a network connection:

  • In-app purchases. If you purchase or restore a LinguaMorpha one-time purchase, the App communicates with Apple's App Store and StoreKit servers. This is handled entirely by Apple — we do not see your payment information.
  • External dictionary lookups. In the Spanish and French courses, verb and noun detail screens include optional buttons that open an external dictionary (Linguee, WordReference, Reverso, or RAE) for the word shown. On iPhone and iPad the page opens in an in-app Safari view; on the Mac it opens in your default web browser. This action is user-initiated, and Safari or your browser (not LinguaMorpha) is what loads the page.
  • Bug reports and feedback. If you email us feedback or a bug report, it goes through your own mail account directly to the developer and contains only what you choose to write and attach. When you start a report from inside the App, the App opens your mail app with the App's version number and the name of the screen already filled in as the subject; nothing is sent until you send the email yourself. The App itself does not collect or transmit anything in the background.
  • Exporting your own data. If you export your study history or practice sets, the App writes them to a file and hands it to the share sheet or save panel; where it goes from there (for example AirDrop, Files or email) is your choice.

Some optional translation features on devices with Apple Intelligence (iOS 26 or macOS 26) use Apple's on-device language model on your device. The App does not send that text to us.

docs.title: How we use information
docs.text:
Because we don't collect personal information, there's very little to use. The on-device data described above is used for:

  • Powering the adaptive learning system inside the App.
  • Restoring your session state, preferences, and study history between launches.
  • Responding to support requests that you send us by email — only the information you choose to include in the email.

docs.title: Data sharing
docs.text: We do not share any of your data with third parties, because there is no data on our side to share. Communication with the App Store for purchases is handled by Apple under Apple's own privacy policy.

docs.title: Data retention and deletion
docs.text: Your study data lives on your device until you delete it. You can reset your progress at any time from inside the App: open Settings and, under Reports, choose Reset Data — you can reset verb, noun, word or phrase progress individually, or all progress at once. Erase all data and settings, in the same Settings screen, deletes all your progress and preferences. Uninstalling the App removes its study data and preferences from your device. The trial and purchase record kept in the device keychain is not part of the App's own storage and may remain on the device after the App is uninstalled.

docs.title: Your rights
docs.text: Because we do not hold any personal data about you, requests to access, correct, or delete your data are best handled directly on your device using the reset and uninstall mechanisms described above. If you have questions, contact us at privacy@linguamorpha.nl.

docs.title: Children's privacy
docs.text: LinguaMorpha is not directed at children under the age of 13, but the App does not collect personal information from anyone, so children's privacy is not put at risk by using it.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Your study data lives in the App's sandboxed storage on your device. The iOS and macOS app sandbox prevents other apps from reading it.

When you send a bug report email, the email is transmitted using your own mail account's normal security (typically TLS/HTTPS).

docs.title: Changes to this policy
docs.text: We may update this Privacy Policy if the App's behaviour changes. When we do, we will update the "Last updated" date at the top of this page.

docs.title: Contact us
docs.text:
If you have questions about this Privacy Policy, please contact us:

Email: privacy@linguamorpha.nl

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
Every form LinguaMorpha produces for Spanish is compared with an external source — the verbs with Wiktionary's conjugation tables. Every disagreement is recorded with its reason. Most are decided: a choice between grammars, a form the source lacks, a slip on our side that was fixed. The ones below are not. They are questions of Spanish, not of software, and rather than settle them by guesswork they are listed here, for anyone who can answer them.

The questions are published as they stand in the register, in English.

docs.title: haber — imperativoAfirmativo · second
docs.text:
The app gives haber a second-person imperative, ha; Wiktionary offers habe, he, hete or hábete. In living Spanish haber has effectively no imperative — what survives is the fossilised he in he aquí. Should the app show a form at all, and if so which, or should the cell be left empty?

Decided and recorded in this section (6) — open for the reasons

Each line is one recorded disagreement: what it concerns, the verdict the comparison gave, and the reason the register keeps — the maintainers' own note, in English.

  • acontecer, ocurrir, atardecer … (8) · we suppress — Impersonal verbs — the weather verbs and the two 'to happen' verbs. Llueve, nieva, acontece: there is no subject to be first or second person, and *lluevo* is not Spanish. We emit the third person only. Wiktionary's template fills all six because it fills all six for everything, which is why this bucket is reported and not counted against us.
  • agradar, apetecer, corresponder … (18) — imperativo* · we suppress — Verbs the catalogue declares to have no imperative, and every suppressed cell of theirs is an imperative — you cannot order someone to gustar, doler, faltar, fallecer or suceder. A semantic claim rather than a morphological one, which is precisely why the oracle disagrees: the forms are formable and Wiktionary forms them. Listed by lemma rather than matched by tense so that adding a verb to the claim takes an edit here.
  • crujir, ladrar, latir … (4) · we suppress — Sound verbs — a floor creaks, a dog barks, a heart beats, a cat miaows. The catalogue marks them third_person_only (d128e873): third singular and plural, los perros ladran, and no yo ladro or tú maúllas offered as a form to learn. A usage claim rather than a morphological one — the forms are formable, and turn up in figurative use — which is why Wiktionary fills all six persons and why the four verbs are named here rather than matched by rule. 136 cells: the first and second persons of every tense, imperatives included.
  • soler · we suppress — Defective, and famously so: soler has no future, no conditional and no imperative — *soleré* is not said. Twenty-two cells, all in those three tenses.
  • criar, fluir, freír … (6) · accent-only — The RAE's 2010 Ortografía ruled these monosyllabic for accentuation — guio, crio, fluis, riais — and the oracle follows it. We keep the traditional accent (guió, crié, fluís, riáis), which is what Spanish speakers and Spanish textbooks overwhelmingly still write, and what a learner will meet in print. A deliberate choice of one live norm over another, not a spelling error, and it is recorded here so that changing our mind is an edit rather than an argument. Twenty cells across six verbs, all of them the -io/-ie/-ais shapes the rule touches.
  • despertarse, reírse — imperativoAfirmativo · DIFFERS — Ours is right and the oracle is wrong, which is rare enough to say plainly. despiértate, ríete, riámonos: the stem change is obligatory under stress, and the oracle's despértate, réete, reámonos are built from the unchanged stem. The signature identifies it as a template defect rather than a variant — it hits ONLY the reflexive imperative, only for stem-changing verbs, and the same verbs' non-reflexive imperatives (despierta, ríe) agree with us.

If you can answer one of these, write to us through the Support page — a reference to a grammar or a text is enough. An answer changes the register, the register changes the app, and this page shortens.

docs.title: Easy to start. Hard to get right. This is for the hard part.
docs.text:
Sixteen tenses, the subjunctive, the irregulars and the choices no vocabulary settles for you — drilled until they come without thinking.

You can know the conjugations and still freeze the moment you have to build a sentence yourself. Reciting a form is a different act from choosing, in conversation or in a text, between indefinido and imperfecto, between ser and estar, between indicative and subjunctive — choices English does not make for you.

LinguaMorpha builds every form of every verb it knows, across all sixteen tenses, and tests them in both directions. It asks not only "what is anduvieron?" but also: "give the pretérito indefinido, ellos, of andar". So you practise recognising forms and producing them.

A missing accent counts as correct, with the right spelling shown; so does a typo in the stem, because the ending is the grammatical part — unless the slip spells another form (hablo for habló is wrong), and Exact spelling in Settings turns this off. And where a form has several readings, every one of them counts: comía is yo and él.

The choices get drills of their own: ser or estar, indefinido or imperfecto, indicative or subjunctive — with the reason given.

Look at a verb and the irregular part is marked for you: red on the letters that change, an underline on the ending the pattern predicts. Tengo, puedo, tendré — at a glance.

And the traps get closed decks of their own: la mano, el mapa, the false friends, the words that change meaning. Nothing to set up.

Stuck while reading? Type the form into Look up. Anduvieron gives you andar, pretérito, ellos, with every reading of an ambiguous form.

Every form has been compared against an outside source. Every difference is documented in the open, on the site.

Try it free for 21 days — every feature, every language. Then unlock Spanish on its own, or all languages, as a one-time purchase. No subscription, no account.

iPhone & iPad Mac

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The learner on a course. Evening classes, an online course, a textbook: they introduce the tenses and move on. Select the tenses and verb groups your course has reached and drill them until the forms come without thinking.

The learner in Spain or Latin America. You get by, and you know the verbs are what keep you at "getting by". Sixteen tenses, the subjunctive, the irregulars and the ser/estar and preterite/imperfect choices, drilled with feedback that explains — and a look-up that tells you which verb that form on the menu, in the paper or in the conversation came from.

The app-course graduate. You have finished the tree and still cannot produce the pretérito of poner on demand. This is the drill the conversation apps deliberately leave out.

The school pupil. Spanish at secondary school: the tenses arrive chapter by chapter and the test asks for them all at once. Here you actually drill them — type the form for a verb, tense and person, choose between ser and estar, between indefinido and imperfecto — and every answer is checked, accent and all, not just shown. The app remembers what you got wrong and comes back to it.

How it compares. Duolingo, Babbel and Rosetta Stone give a broad experience — listening, speaking, everyday situations — and skip the depth. LinguaMorpha is the opposite: explicit grammar, the pattern of every form made visible, and drills you choose yourself rather than a fixed curriculum. It has no speaking practice and no listening comprehension; it works well beside those apps, doing what they leave out.

Irregulars marked, not just listed

Red falls only on the part of a form that departs from the regular pattern — so you see exactly where a verb is irregular, and by how much.

The traps, in their own decks

False friends, nouns whose ending points to the wrong gender, and more — small, closed decks that need no setup.

docs.title: Five ways to study
docs.text: Grammar lessons, Theory, Practice Sets, Self Study and Tests — the same five in every course, sharing one catalogue and one adaptive engine, so an answer given in any of them counts in all of them. What each one is for →

docs.title: What the app does
docs.text:
Type any form and see what it is. You heard quepo, read anduvieron, saw dimos and are not sure which verb it is. Look up searches every conjugated form of every verb in the course — over 1,200 verbs in sixteen tenses — as well as every noun, adjective, phrase and word, and tells you the verb, the tense and the person, with every reading of an ambiguous form. Accents are optional, capitals are ignored, a word in your own language finds the Spanish, and a misspelling still lands on the nearest headwords: tiner finds tener. Tap the result and the verb opens at that tense.

The marking scheme. Conjugation tables use three marks. Red falls on just the part of a form that departs from the regular pattern — the changed vowel of puedo, the g of tengo, the shortened stem of tendré — while the rest stays in the normal colour. A form that is red from end to end (soy, voy, era) has to be learned as a whole. An underline marks the ending the pattern predicts, so even on an irregular form you can see which half follows the rule. Blue is used for one thing only: the endings of the strong preterite (-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron), whose stems are irregular but whose endings form a consistent set of their own.

The shape of the marking tells you what you are looking at: a red letter in the yo form alone points to a yo irregular such as tengo or conozco; a red stem vowel in every present form except nosotros and vosotros is a classic stem change.

Regularity, tense by tense. Each verb's Regularity tab gives every tense a verdict — from Regular to Irregular — and shows in amber the stems you have to memorise; on the Conjugation tab, a filter hides the tenses that follow the pattern.

Choice drills. Most drills ask for a form; these ask which form the sentence needs — ser or estar, preterite or imperfect, indicative or subjunctive, por or para. That is where knowing the forms stops being enough. An explanation follows every answer.

Traps. Closed decks of things that actively mislead: false friends (the deck follows your app language, because the traps for an English speaker are not the traps for a Dutch one), the nouns whose meaning changes with the article (el capital / la capital), the gender traps whose ending points the wrong way, and the adjectives whose meaning shifts between ser and estar. Each deck brings its own words, so there is nothing to select first.

Choose what is in play. Sixteen tenses, each switchable on its own in Select tenses, and twenty-three verb groups, each tickable in Select verb groups — every stem change in one tap, or just the yo irregulars, or the strong preterites. Verbs can also be filtered by CEFR level and topic, so the drills follow the course you are on rather than running ahead of it.

Drills aimed at the weak spots.

  • Verb meaning — flashcards, Spanish ↔ your language, in either direction
  • Produce the conjugation — give the form for a verb, tense and person, typed or picked
  • Recognise the conjugation — given a form, identify verb, tense and person
  • Past participle — recall the participio, irregulars included
  • Gerund — recall the gerundio
  • Preterite — the yo and él forms of the indefinido, where the strong preterites show
  • Future stem — the one stem the futuro and the condicional are both built on, fifty-one verbs
  • Yo-form stem and Preterite stem — build the subjunctive on the yo form (tengo → tenga) and the imperfect subjunctive on the indefinido (tuvieron → tuviera)
  • Stem changes, -ir stem change and Spelling changes — the whole presente of a stem-changing verb, the -ir change outside it (pidió, pidiendo), and -car / -gar / -zar keeping their sound (busqué)
  • Short tú commands — the eight short commands and their negatives: ten / no tengas
  • Ser or estar, Preterite or imperfect, Indicative or subjunctive, Which past tense? (perfecto or indefinido), Gustar and verbs like it and Ir a, tener que, acabar de — the choice drills

Sessions that work on what needs work. Every answer is recorded on your device. The words for each session are picked from your selection on the basis of your answer history and your Learning pace, and an Incorrect answers switch limits a session to what you got wrong before. Nouns get the same treatment as verbs: gender and plural drills, and closed decks for the traps, so that el mapa and la mano stop being guesses.
