docs.title: Speech and dictionaries
docs.text:
Spanish forms are read aloud with the voices Apple provides on your device, in Standard, Enhanced and Premium quality — the Enhanced and Premium voices are free to download and sound far more natural. A speed slider slows speech down for listening practice.

Verb and noun detail screens carry a Dictionaries row that looks the word up in Linguee, WordReference, Reverso and the RAE — in a browser sheet inside the app on iPhone and iPad, and in your web browser on the Mac. Choose which appear in Settings → Spanish → Dictionary services.

On Apple Watch, the companion app shows conjugation tables for the verbs you choose — the essential verbs at first, any verb in the course after that — in the tenses you choose.

docs.title: For the teacher
docs.text:
What a pupil does with it. The app does not replace the course book; it is what the pupil opens beside it. Sixteen tenses and twenty-three verb groups each switch on and off separately, and verbs filter by CEFR level, so the drills can be limited to what the chapter has introduced — this week's indefinido, not next year's subjuntivo. Every session picks its words from the answer history, and the Incorrect answers switch keeps a session to what went wrong before. The reports show which tenses and words a pupil has practised, how well, and what has stuck.

The question the test asks. Knowing a conjugation is one thing; knowing which form a sentence needs is the other, and that is what the test asks. The choice drills do exactly that — ser or estar, indefinido or imperfecto, indicative or subjuntivo, por or para — with an explanation after every answer. The Traps decks are written for the pupil's own language: the false friends a Dutch speaker falls for are not an English speaker's, and the deck follows the app's language.

A set for the class. A practice set is a session you put together yourself — these verbs, those tenses, this kind of exercise — and share as a file, by AirDrop, mail or the school's learning platform. The pupils import it and drill the same material. For next week's test, or for the strong preterites half the class still has not got. For a fixed route, the grammar lessons in four level sections, A1 to B2, cover the same ground in order.

Hearing what you type. Every form is read aloud with the device's Spanish voices, at an adjustable speed; a pupil who confuses hablé and hable hears the difference. The detail screens link to the RAE, Linguee, WordReference and Reverso — the teacher chooses which.

What it is not. No teacher dashboard, no accounts, no class administration, no results sent to the school. That is a choice: a pupil's answers stay on the pupil's own device, and there is no server for them to go to. To see how a pupil is doing, ask to see the report — or have it exported as a PDF. No speaking practice and no listening comprehension: that is what the lesson is for.

docs.title: How we know the forms are right
docs.text:
A conjugation app is as good as its forms. So they do not rest on the author but on comparison with a source a teacher knows, and on writing down every difference.

Every verb form against Wiktionary. All 47,292 forms the app produces for its 1,200-odd verbs — every person, tense and mood, participle and gerundio — have been compared with Wiktionary's conjugation tables. 47,264 agree letter for letter. 20 differ only in an accent, where the app follows the RAE's Ortografía of 2010 — guio, crio, riais without the accent — and Wiktionary writes the old one. 8 differ outright, and for each the register says what it is and why the app keeps its form or does not: the imperative despiértate, where Wiktionary is wrong, and the imperative of haber, where nobody is sure. What the app deliberately leaves out — the personal forms of llover and nevar, the imperative of gustar and soler — is recorded too, with the reason.

Every difference is on paper. The register can be read on the Open questions page, with the decided differences and the open question. It also guards the future: a change to the app that moves one more form away from the source fails the check until someone has judged the difference.

What this does not prove. That a form is right says nothing about the translations, the example sentences and the explanations in the choice drills; those were written by the author and have not been read by a teacher of Spanish. Anyone who finds a mistake in them helps the app most by reporting it — Support reads every message.

docs.title: For the school
docs.text:
One price per pupil, no subscription. Spanish is a one-time purchase in the App Store, on the pupil's own iPhone, iPad or Mac; with the same Apple ID it is unlocked on all of them at once. No annual licence, no renewal.

21 days free first, for the whole class. Every pupil can use the complete Spanish course for 21 days without paying. That is enough for a trial with a class before anyone buys.

No accounts, no data. The app asks for no name, no email address, no age. Answers, progress and settings stay on the device; there is no server, no analytics, no tracking. For the school's data-protection review that is the short answer: no personal data is processed. The long answer is the privacy policy.

One app for the modern and the classical languages. The same app holds French — over 900 verbs, the passé simple included — and Latin — every declension, the classical verb system, a sentence parser — with the same drills, reports, practice sets and grammar lessons, and the same rule that nothing leaves the device. Each language unlocks on its own, or all three together as Unlock all languages.

iPhone, iPad and Mac. The same app on all three, with the same tables and drills: the school iPad in class, the pupil's own phone on the train, the Mac at the desk. One purchase covers every device on the same Apple ID; progress stays on each device, since there is no account to sync it through. Not for Android, Windows or Chromebook.

Two interface languages for Spanish. The app, the guide and this site come in English, Dutch and Spanish, but a pupil learning Spanish runs the app in English or Dutch — a Spanish interface on a Spanish course would hand the pupil the answers, and the app does not allow that pairing. An international school or a bilingual stream runs the app in English.

Purchase by the school. A school edition that the school buys itself through Apple School Manager — licences the school owns, reassigned to the new class every year, with Apple's education discount from twenty copies — is possible, but does not exist yet. We will build it as soon as a school wants to buy it; if yours does, say so through the Support page. Until then the answer is: the pupil's own device, one purchase, and 21 days free for the whole class.

docs.title: The catalogue
docs.text:
• over 1,200 verbs, filterable by CEFR level, topic and verb group
  • over 1,600 nouns, each with its article and its plural, nearly all with three example sentences
  • over 270 set phrases, plus the example sentences of the verbs and nouns — thousands of sentences, each one drillable
  • adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, numerals and prepositions, each with its own hub

docs.title: The grammar, in detail
docs.text: Exactly which tenses, verb groups and noun groups the course covers — open for the reference

docs.title: Verb grammar
docs.text:
Sixteen tenses, each switchable on its own in Select tenses — from the present to the pluperfect subjunctive.

Indicative — simple

  • Presente
  • Pretérito Indefinido
  • Pretérito Imperfecto
  • Futuro
  • Condicional

Indicative — compound

  • Pretérito Perfecto
  • Pluscuamperfecto
  • Futuro Perfecto
  • Condicional Perfecto

Subjunctive

  • Presente de Subjuntivo
  • Imperfecto de Subjuntivo
  • Pretérito Perfecto Subjuntivo
  • Pluscuamperfecto Subjuntivo

Imperative

  • Imperativo Afirmativo
  • Imperativo Negativo

Formas no Personales (progressive)

  • Gerundio — conjugated through all six persons (estoy hablando, estás hablando, …), not just the bare -ando / -iendo form

The past participle and the bare gerundio sit at the top of each verb's Conjugation tab, marked where they are irregular; the full six-person progressive appears among the tenses below them.

docs.title: Verb groups
docs.text:
Most Spanish verbs are regular — but the irregular ones cluster into recognisable groups, and drilling them by group rather than one at a time is a fast way to internalise the pattern.

Twenty-three groups, each tickable on its own in Select verb groups, in nine sections. Each section header has an All button, so one tap selects, for example, every stem change for a single focused session. A second view sorts the verbs by how many exceptions they have — none, one, two and so on.

Fully regular

  • Regular — the predictable -ar / -er / -ir endings

Stem-changing verbs — the vowel changes where it carries the stress: in the present, every person but nosotros and vosotros

  • e → ie — pensar, querer, preferir
  • o → ue — poder, dormir
  • e → i — pedir (-ir verbs only)
  • u → ue — jugar
  • i → ie — adquirir
  • Accent shift í / ú — enviar → envío, actuar → actúo

Yo-form irregularities

  • Irregular yo: -go — tener, poner, salir, hacer, decir
  • Irregular yo: -zco — conocer → conozco
  • Consonant + -cer / -cir: c → z — vencer → venzo
  • Spelling shift -ger / -gir — escoger → escojo
  • Verbs ending in -guir — seguir → sigo

Spelling-change verbs

  • Y-insertion — leer, creer, oír, caer, where the y appears between vowels (leyó)
  • Verbs ending in -uir — construir → construyo
  • Spelling shift -car / -gar / -zar — buscar → busqué, llegar → llegué, empezar → empecé

An irregular stem in one tense

  • Strong preterite — tener → tuve, hacer → hice, poder → pude, decir → dije
  • Irregular future stem — tener → tendré, poder → podré, decir → diré: one shortened stem carries both the future and the conditional
  • Irregular participle — abrir → abierto, escribir → escrito, romper → roto: regular in every simple tense, with one participle to learn

Irregulars that fit no pattern

  • Irregular — ser, ir, estar, dar, haber, ver: irregular in ways no other group names

The last three sections change no ending; they say how the verb is built into a sentence, so a verb there can be perfectly regular as well.

Reflexive verbs

  • Reflexive — lavarse, vestirse

Impersonal and gusto-type verbs

  • Impersonal — llover, nevar, third person singular only
  • Me gusta pattern — gustar, encantar, doler: the thing that pleases is the subject

Stative verbs

  • Stative — states rather than actions, so not normally used with estar + gerundio

docs.title: Noun grammar
docs.text:
Nouns are what learners most often try to brute-force, and where pattern recognition pays off most. The noun groups sort nouns by their grammatical character, and a noun can belong to several groups at once (canción has a predictable feminine suffix and loses its accent in the plural), so the group filter can target very specific patterns:

  • Gender traps — mano and foto end in -o but are feminine; día and mapa end in -a but are masculine
  • Greek -ma masculines — el problema, el idioma
  • Predictable feminine suffixes — -a, -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -umbre
  • Predictable masculine suffixes — -o, -or, -aje, -ón, -án, -ín
  • Stressed-á feminines — el agua, las aguas: el in the singular, feminine all the same
  • Different meaning by article — el capital (money) and la capital (city)
  • Gender pairs — el tío / la tía, heteronymous pairs such as el padre / la madre, and one-form nouns such as el / la dentista
  • Invariable plural — el lunes / los lunes
  • Plurale tantum — los pantalones
  • Plural formation — lápiz → lápices, canción → canciones, consonant + -es
  • False cognates — words that look like a word in your own language but mean something else

Six drills: Noun meaning, Pick the correct article, Singular / Plural, Alternate gender pairs, Meaning changes with gender and One article for both sexes (Juan es una persona amable).

Gender and plural rules, stated

The endings that predict gender, the nouns that break the rule, and how plurals are formed.

Pick the correct article

el or la, drilled until the ending stops fooling you.

Phrases and example sentences

Set phrases plus the verb and noun example sentences, each drillable in its own right.

Speech sounds robotic

docs.title: General
docs.text:
What is LinguaMorpha?

A morphology-first language app for Latin (every declension and adjective pattern, the full classical verb system, macron-accurate checking, a sentence parser and an agreement drill), Spanish and French (full verb conjugation in sixteen tenses, noun gender and plurals, set phrases and vocabulary). All three mark irregular forms with the same colour code. It is not a full language course; it is a structured, grammar-first drill tool for mastering what you have been taught elsewhere. See the Features page for what's inside.

Do I need to learn Latin first to get value out of Spanish or French?

No. The courses share machinery (the adaptive engine, the drill screens, the help system), not a learning path; each course stands on its own.

That said, taking more than one is rewarding in its own right: with the same colour code in all three, the differences stand out — where two languages kept the same Latin ending differently, or how a Latin case turns into word order and prepositions.

Which languages can I learn?

Latin, Spanish, and French, all in the same app, in no required order.

Is LinguaMorpha free?

It's a free download with a free trial — no subscriptions, no ads. A 21-day trial of every course and every feature starts when you finish the first-launch setup; after that, you unlock the courses you want with a one-time in-app purchase. Purchases belong to your Apple ID, and thanks to Universal Purchase, unlocking a language on your iPhone unlocks it on your Mac too (and the other way round).

You unlock each language — Spanish, French, or Latin — individually, or buy Unlock all languages, which unlocks every course, including any course added to the app later, at no additional charge. The App Store listing in your country is the source of truth for the current prices; we don't restate them here so they can't go stale.

What devices does LinguaMorpha support?

iPhone, iPad and Mac, with a companion app for Apple Watch that is only a reference for the conjugation tables of Spanish and French verbs. The App Store listing shows the minimum system version for each. Two optional extras use Apple Intelligence and need iOS 26 or macOS 26 on a device that supports it: the idiomatic sentence translation in the Latin sentence parser, and a translation of the exact form in the conjugation drills where the app has none of its own. See Where you study.

Do I need an internet connection to use the app?

No. All word data is bundled with the app, your answers are stored on your device, and speech uses the voices installed on your device. You only need a connection to buy or restore a purchase, and to open the online dictionaries in the Spanish and French courses.

Which Spanish dialect does the app teach?

Peninsular Spanish — the Spanish of Spain. The conjugation tables include vosotros and the drills ask for it, and the example sentences mostly use the vocabulary of Spain — ordenador rather than computadora, coche rather than carro. For speech, you can still choose any regional Spanish voice installed on your device.

What variety of Latin does the app teach?

Classical Latin, with every form stored with its macrons; typed answers are checked leniently on macrons by default, strictly if you prefer. Vocabulary is chosen at the level of an introductory course, so sentences from a beginner's textbook — Ørberg's Familia Romana, Wheelock — usually parse in the sentence parser.

Which languages can the app itself be shown in?

English, Dutch, or Spanish. That choice (App language in Settings) sets the language of the menus, labels and help, and the language translations are shown in. Spanish is not offered as the app language while you study Spanish, because a translation into the language you are learning would only repeat the word — except with the Spanish Lengua castellana scheme for native speakers, which shows no translations.

docs.title: Accounts, sync, and data
docs.text:
Do I need to create an account?

No. There is no account system. Open the app and start using it.

Can several people use the app on one device?

Yes. Tap the flag to open Scheme and level, and choose Add learner. Each learner has their own progress, scheme and level; everything else is shared.

Does my progress sync between my devices?

There's no automatic sync — each device keeps its own answer history and nothing is uploaded. But you can move it yourself: export your study history under Settings → Progress → Study History and import it on the other device; importing adds answers and never removes any. Practice Sets move separately, as a backup of your set library from the Practice Sets screen (on the Mac, in the File menu).

Where is my data stored?

In the app's own private storage on your device — a database that iOS and macOS keep walled off from other apps. Nothing is sent to a server.

How do I reset my progress?

Open Settings, go to the Progress tab and choose Reset Progress. You can reset verb, noun, word or phrase progress on its own, or Reset all progress at once; only the learner in use is reset. (Erase all data and settings is a separate factory reset of every learner and all settings.)

docs.title: Using the app
docs.text:
What are Theory, Study and Practice?

The three sections every Self Study hub is built from: Theory explains the rules, Study lets you browse without anything being recorded, and Practice is where every answer is recorded. See The Theory / Study / Practice pattern.

What's the difference between word pool and session size?

Your word pool is everything eligible to appear — a hub's Select groups choices, your level and your topics — and your session size is how many questions one sitting asks (Questions per session in Settings → Study). See Choosing what is in play.

How do I answer a flashcard?

Tap the card to turn it over, then swipe right if you knew it, left if you didn't — or tap Correct or Wrong (on the Mac, and on iPhone and iPad when VoiceOver is on). See Flashcard sessions.

What is the sentence parser?

A Latin-only mode of Look up: type or paste a Latin sentence and every word comes back with its lemma, its form and its translation. See Sentence parser.

What is the concordance drill?

A Latin drill, called Agreement drill in the Adjectives and Nouns hubs: you pick the form of an adjective that agrees with its noun in case, number and gender. See Adjectives and the concordance drill.

What is the Dictionaries button?

The book button on a verb, noun or word page in the Spanish and French courses, which opens online dictionaries for the word — Linguee, WordReference and Reverso, plus RAE for Spanish. You choose which ones appear under Dictionary services in Settings.

Why is part of a verb form shown in red?

Red marks the part of a form that departs from its pattern; a fully red form has to be learned whole. See Conjugation tables for the full key.

How does the adaptive learning work?

Every answer is recorded on your device; words you got wrong last time come first, then new words and your weakest words, in a mix set by Learning pace. See Adaptive learning — how it works.

docs.title: Speech
docs.text:
Why does the speech sound robotic?

Your device comes with Standard voices, and they sound mechanical. Better ones are free to download — choose Enhanced: Spanish for the Spanish course, French for the French course, and Italian if you study Latin. The Support page shows how, step by step.

Which voice reads Latin?

An Italian voice installed on your device, at about half the normal speed — no system has a Latin voice. Treat it as an approximation; the written form with its macrons remains the authority on pronunciation. See Latin speech.

Can I slow the speech down?

Yes, for Spanish and French: use the Speed slider on your course's tab in Settings (on iPhone and iPad, on the Voice screen). Latin always plays at its own slow speed.

docs.title: Feedback and bugs
docs.text:
How do I report a problem or suggest something?

Email feedback@linguamorpha.nl — it goes straight to the developer. Inside the app, press and hold a Help button or ? to start an email about that screen, with the app version and the screen's name already in the subject.

Something isn't working — what should I try?

Try these in order:

  1. Force-quit and reopen the app.
  2. Check for an app update in the App Store.
  3. Restart your device.
  4. As a last resort, reinstall the app. Export first: reinstalling deletes your answer history and practice sets, so export them (see above) and import them afterwards.

If the issue persists, email support@linguamorpha.nl with your device model, your system version, and the LinguaMorpha version and build — a line like 1.4 (102), found under ⋯ → About on iPhone or iPad, or LinguaMorpha → About LinguaMorpha in the Mac menu bar.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
What data does LinguaMorpha collect?

Nothing personal. See the Privacy Policy for the full statement.

Does LinguaMorpha share my data with third parties?

No — there is no server to share data with. Your study data stays on your device unless you export it yourself.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
LinguaMorpha was built around a simple conviction: the grammar of these languages is knowable. There are rules, the irregular forms group into patterns, and once you can see those patterns, the language stops feeling arbitrary.

LinguaMorpha is a morphology-first study app. Latin covers every declension, every adjective pattern, the degrees of comparison where classical Latin has them, macron-accurate checking, plus a sentence parser that labels every word of a Latin sentence. Spanish covers verb conjugation in sixteen tenses, noun gender and plurals, set phrases and thousands of example sentences, and single-word vocabulary. French covers verb conjugation in sixteen tenses, noun gender and plurals, and phrases. All three languages share one marking scheme.

Each course is a complete study system in its own right — pick the one you actually want to learn and ignore the rest. They share machinery (the adaptive engine, the drill screens, the help system), not a learning path. The differences are the size of the catalogue and the grammar specific to each language.

docs.title: What's in each course
docs.text:
What each course covers, in full, is on its own page: Latin (over 600 verbs, over 650 nouns, the sentence parser and the agreement drill), Spanish (over 1,200 verbs, over 1,600 nouns, over 270 set phrases, the Traps decks) and French (over 900 verbs, over 1,400 nouns, sixteen tenses including the literary ones).

The rest of this page is what they all share.

docs.title: How the patterns are made visible
docs.text:
In all three languages, conjugation tables mark each form so you can see where it departs from its pattern, and by how much. A form that follows its pattern gets no colour, so the marking tells you something real.

The marks mean the same thing everywhere. Red falls on just the part that departs; a form that is red throughout has to be learned as a whole. An underline marks the ending the pattern predicts, on regular and irregular forms alike — the part you do not have to learn separately. Blue is used only in Spanish, for the separate ending set of the strong preterites (tuve, pude).

The full key, with worked examples, is in the Spanish conjugation tables guide.

docs.title: How you study
docs.text: There are five ways in, and all of them share one vocabulary catalogue and one adaptive engine, so an answer given in any of them counts in all of them. Grammar lessons take you through verb, noun and adjective morphology in a fixed order. Theory gathers every theory page of the course in one place: the rules, explained, in grammar text and paradigms you read rather than answer. Practice Sets are ready-made sessions you launch as a unit; run the bundled ones, or build and share your own. Self Study puts you in full control: you choose the words, the groups and tenses, and which drill to run. Tests put every test for your level on one page, with the theory one tap away. And at any time outside a drill, Look up takes any form you type and tells you what it is; in Latin, a second mode parses a whole sentence.

docs.title: Where you study
docs.text:
iPhone, iPad and Mac are all full study platforms — every drill, Self Study, Practice Sets, Grammar lessons, the reference tables and your progress reports are on each. LinguaMorpha runs natively on all three, with a companion app for Apple Watch. With Universal Purchase, the iPhone/iPad and Mac apps share one purchase, so a language you unlock on one is unlocked on the other. See The app for the platforms and languages.

On the Mac, the app is built for the desktop rather than scaled up from the phone: a sidebar, Settings in its own window, import and export in the File menu, the User Guide in the Help menu, keyboard shortcuts, and a verb's reference sheet you can save as a PDF — made for studying at a desk, with a keyboard.

Apple Watch is deliberately small — a reference, not a place to study: choose verbs and tenses, then read their conjugation. No drills, no progress, no lessons. Spanish and French only.

docs.title: Adaptive learning
docs.text:
Every answer you give is recorded in a database on your device. Each session's words are chosen in this order:

  1. Words you got wrong last time come first. Answering one correctly removes the flag.
  2. New words and review words fill the remaining places. New words come in order of importance — a combination of CEFR level and frequency, so common A1 words come before rare C2 words. Review words come weakest first, adjusted for how recently you saw them, so the review rotates.

A Learning pace setting (Relaxed / Balanced / Intensive) sets the mix of review and new words. In a flashcard session, a card you get wrong can come round again, but never twice in a row. (Every course is adaptive in the same way — Latin, Spanish and French alike.)

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
Everything stays on your device — no account, no cloud sync, no tracking or analytics. See the full Privacy Policy.

Because nothing syncs through a server, moving your data is always something you do yourself: export your study history and your Practice Sets as files, and import them on another device. Nothing leaves your device unless you export it.

docs.title: Getting Started with LinguaMorpha
docs.text: The shortest path from "just installed" to "running a drill that teaches me something". Each step links to the full explanation, so this page stays a route rather than a manual — the detail lives in Using the app.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
iPhone & iPad Mac

There is no account and no sign-in — you can start as soon as it is installed. A 21-day trial of every language starts when you finish the first-launch setup. See The app for platforms, requirements and what unlocking costs.

docs.title: 2. Pick a language
docs.text: On iPhone and iPad, tap the flag at the top left of the main screen; on the Mac, click it at the top of the sidebar. In Scheme and level, choose a scheme of the language you want, and a level in it. Each language is complete on its own, so start with the one you actually want: Latin, Spanish or French. You can switch at any time; your answers stay recorded.

docs.title: 3. Turn on a better voice
docs.text:
The default voices sound robotic and the better ones are free. Download an Enhanced voice for your language — Italian if you study Latin. For Spanish or French, then pick it in LinguaMorpha: open Settings, switch to the tab for your course, and choose Voice. For Latin the app picks the Italian voice itself.

How to do it →

docs.title: 4. Run your first session
docs.text: Each course's tips suggest a first session that is hard to get wrong — the declension paradigms for Latin, the A1 nouns for Spanish and French.

docs.title: 5. Look up a form you don't recognise
docs.text: Tap the magnifying glass at the bottom right (on the Mac: Edit ▸ Look up…, ⇧⌘F) and type the form — dije, viendo, ceperat — and Look up names the word and the form.

docs.title: 6. Try the sentence parser (Latin)
docs.text: In Look up, switch from Word to Sentence, paste a Latin sentence and tap Parse to see every word labelled — see Sentence parser.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
Once the first sessions feel routine:

  • Select word scope — choose the topics Self Study draws on.
  • Practice Sets and Tests — ready-made sessions, and every test for your level on one page.
  • My Progress — the heatmap, coverage, accuracy and your weakest words.
  • Using the app — the full tour of every screen.

Help inside the app

Most screens have a Help button or a ? icon that opens a short help sheet about that screen, and the User Guide — under ⋯ → Help on iPhone and iPad, under Help in the Mac sidebar — is the same guide as this website, bundled into the app.

docs.title: How LinguaMorpha Compares
docs.text: LinguaMorpha is a focused study tool for vocabulary and morphology, and what it should be compared with depends on the language. For Spanish and French the alternatives are the big conversational apps; for Latin they are the word-list apps and the tools around a school method. In both cases LinguaMorpha has no speaking practice, no listening comprehension beyond a Listen mode on the flashcards, and no social features — it goes further into the things those tools skip.

docs.title: Duolingo
docs.text: Duolingo is built around short lessons with game elements such as streaks and points, and a strong emphasis on bringing you back every day. It is excellent for building a habit. It does not explain grammar in much depth — you pick up patterns implicitly. LinguaMorpha works well alongside Duolingo by providing what Duolingo deliberately leaves out: explicit grammar and a clear view of how the forms are built.

docs.title: Babbel
docs.text: Babbel is more structured than Duolingo and more oriented towards adults. Lessons are based on conversations; grammar is briefly explained alongside the vocabulary. LinguaMorpha adds depth and repetition. Instead of following a fixed curriculum, you can stop at any point, select exactly the verbs and tenses you are working on, and practise them until the forms come automatically.

docs.title: Rosetta Stone
docs.text: Rosetta Stone takes a pure immersion approach — no translations, no grammar explanations. LinguaMorpha is the opposite: it is explicit and analytical. It gives you the rules and tests your understanding directly.

docs.title: For Latin
docs.text: The alternatives are different — the word-list app every pupil has, textbook companion websites, flashcard decks, and the free parsers and dictionaries classicists use. LinguaMorpha differs by bringing the whole chain into one app: the catalogue, paradigm tables, production drills, recognition drills, a sentence parser, reading passages and adaptive sessions, instead of a collection of separate tools.

docs.title: StudyGo (formerly WRTS)
docs.text: The app every Dutch pupil already has. StudyGo drills word lists — the official lists per chapter of the school's own method, so a pupil learns exactly the words the test asks for, and its paid tiers add practice tests per chapter, explanation videos and tutors. What it drills is the list: rosa means rose. It does not generate the forms, so it cannot ask for rosīs and check the macron, and it does not read a sentence. LinguaMorpha is the other half: it does not know your method's chapter word list, but every form of every word it does know, and it checks what you produce. In one sentence: StudyGo helps a pupil memorise forms; LinguaMorpha helps them recognise and produce forms. A pupil who learns the chapter's words in StudyGo and drills the chapter's paradigms here has covered the test from both sides.

docs.title: Parsers and dictionaries
docs.text: For looking up a form, the classicist's free tools are hard to beat: Whitaker's Words, Collatinus, the online Lewis & Short. They know far more words than LinguaMorpha's catalogue of some 2,000 lemmas, and they are the right place for a rare form in Tacitus. What they do not do is drill: they tell you what rēbus is and leave you there. LinguaMorpha's parser knows fewer words but every word it knows opens onto its full table with the form marked, and from the table you are one tap from producing the same form yourself.

docs.title: Using them together
docs.text:
For Spanish and French:

  • Use Duolingo or Babbel for daily exposure, listening practice and broad vocabulary.
  • Use LinguaMorpha to consolidate specific vocabulary and drill the grammar points those apps introduce but do not cover in depth.

For Latin:

  • Use StudyGo for the chapter's word list, as the school expects.
  • Use your textbook (the school's method, or Lingua Latina per se Illustrata on your own) for reading.
  • Use LinguaMorpha for the paradigms the textbook exercises do not repeat often enough, and its parser to check a reading.

LinguaMorpha does not try to teach you to speak a language. Its Grammar lessons can take you through the grammar from the start, but it is above all the tool you use when you want to master something specific.

docs.title: The app
docs.text:
LinguaMorpha is one app, not a family of downloads. It holds three independent modules in one place — Latin, Spanish and French — with a language switcher between them. Each module follows its own language: Latin has declensions, cases and a sentence parser, Spanish and French have their tense systems, gender and agreement. You download the app free, try everything for 21 days, then unlock the modules you want: each one on its own, or all of them as a bundle.

Language Teaches App language available Status Spanish Spanish English, Dutch Available now French French English, Dutch, Spanish Available now Latin Latin English, Dutch, Spanish Available now

docs.title: One app, three languages
docs.text:
Each language inside LinguaMorpha is a complete study system for one language — the verb system, nouns and gender (declensions and cases for Latin), adjectives, pronouns, prepositions, numerals, adverbs and phrases, with drills, Grammar lessons and progress reports. Pick a language and it works from start to finish on its own.

On iPhone and iPad, tap the flag at the top left of the main screen; on the Mac, click it at the top of the sidebar. It opens Scheme and level, where you choose a language by choosing one of its level schemes, and your level in it; a lock marks a language you have not unlocked. The same screen holds the learners: several people can share one device, each with their own progress, scheme and level. Switching back and forth loses nothing: My Progress always reports on the language you are studying.

docs.title: Five ways to study
docs.text:
• Grammar lessons — a path in level order: one new thing per lesson, explained before it is drilled. For when you want the app to decide what comes next.
  • Theory — every theory page of the course in one list, by word type: the grammar, to read in order. For when you want to understand before you drill.
  • Practice Sets — ready-made sessions on one theme or tense, or sets you build and share yourself. For a fixed piece of work.
  • Self Study — every word type with its theory, word lists and drills; you decide what is in play. For working on exactly what you need.
  • Tests — every test for your level on one page. With Only new at this level, just what your level adds. The book button beside each test opens the theory. For finding out what you already know.

All five share one vocabulary catalogue and one adaptive engine: an answer given in any of them counts in all of them. Practice Sets and Grammar lessons appear only for a course that has them.

More in the user guide: What is LinguaMorpha?

docs.title: Download and unlock
docs.text:
iPhone & iPad Mac

The app is free to try for 21 days with every feature and every language unlocked; the trial starts when you finish the first-launch setup, and a banner shows how many days are left. After the trial, you unlock the languages you want as in-app purchases — Spanish, French or Latin individually, or Unlock all languages, which unlocks every language in the app. No subscription, no advertising, no accounts. Restore Previous Purchase is in the store screen.

Why the bundle rather than one language. Not because you plan to study three at once. Because the languages are built to be read against each other, and the bundle lets you do that.

All three languages run on one engine and are marked with one scheme, so learning to read a conjugation table in Spanish teaches you to read one in French and Latin at a glance. That shared notation makes the comparison easy to see: red marks the part of a form that departs from the pattern in all three, so which verbs are irregular everywhere and which only in one language becomes something you see instead of something you have to work out. Spanish hacer, French faire and Latin facere are one verb; the Spanish hice and the French je fis both continue the Latin perfect fēcī, changed in different ways. With only one language unlocked, you cannot compare them.

Everything else is shared too: the same drills, the same screens, the same Practice Sets — so a second language brings no new interface to learn, only new words.

A single language is the right choice if you know which one you want and the family connection does not interest you. It is not a reduced version: one language unlocked is that language complete, every drill and every screen.

One purchase covers both platforms. The iPhone/iPad and Mac apps share a single App Store listing under Universal Purchase, so a language you unlock on one is unlocked on the other — same Apple ID, no second payment. There is also a small Apple Watch companion: a verb-conjugation reference for Spanish and French.

Everything runs on your device and works offline; your answers and progress never leave it unless you export them yourself.

docs.title: App languages
docs.text:
"App language available" is the language the app's own text — menus, labels, help and translations — is shown in. It is separate from the language you are learning. For example, the French course can be used with the app in English, Dutch or Spanish.

The language you are studying is not offered as the app language, because a translation into the language you are learning would only repeat the word. That is why the Spanish course is offered with the app in English or Dutch, while French and Latin can also be used with the app in Spanish. The exception is the Spanish Lengua castellana scheme for native speakers: it shows no translations, so with it the app can be in Spanish too.

docs.title: What is LinguaMorpha?
docs.text: LinguaMorpha is for adults who want to master the structural grammar of a language — declension, conjugation, agreement, plural formation — the parts other apps tend to gloss over. It is morphology-first: every feature in the app is designed to make the rules visible, not to leave you to absorb them by osmosis.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
• Home — where you start. On iPhone and iPad it is the main screen, titled LinguaMorpha; on the Mac it is the Home row near the top of the sidebar, and the app always opens there (⇧⌘H brings you back). From Home you choose one of the ways to study below.
  • Look up — type any form you meet, dije, viendo, ceperat, and it tells you which word it is and what form: for a verb its tense and person, for a noun its number. On iPhone and iPad it is the round magnifying glass at the bottom right of every screen; on the Mac, the Look up a form field at the top of the sidebar. See Look up.

docs.title: Ways to study
docs.text:
• Grammar lessons — a path in level order: one new thing per lesson, explained before it is drilled. For when you want the app to decide what comes next.
  • Theory — every theory page of the course in one list, by word type: the grammar, to read in order. For when you want to understand before you drill.
  • Practice Sets — ready-made sessions on one theme or tense, or sets you build and share yourself. For a fixed piece of work.
  • Self Study — every word type with its theory, word lists and drills; you decide what is in play. For working on exactly what you need.
  • Tests — every test for your level on one page. With Only new at this level, just what your level adds. The book button beside each test opens the theory. For finding out what you already know.

They all share one vocabulary catalogue and one adaptive engine: an answer given in any of them counts in all of them. Practice Sets and Grammar lessons appear only for a course that has them, and the level scheme in use can hide a way in or a tool as well — some built-in schemes have no Traps or Linguistic analysis, for example.

docs.title: One network of cards
docs.text:
Everything in LinguaMorpha is a card: a verb with its conjugation, a tense with its theory, a list of irregular verbs, a drill. The cards are linked wherever there is a connection between them, so most can be reached from several directions, and you never need to know where something "lives". Start from the side you know — a form you met, a verb, a tense or a drill — and the rest is a tap away.

Take the indefinido in Spanish. Its card is on the Tenses page under Theory. The ⓘ beside the tense, when you choose your tenses, opens that page at its card, and Look up finds it when you type indefinido. From the card, Irregular verbs opens the verbs that depart from it, grouped by pattern, and the graduation cap at the top of that list offers every drill about the tense. A verb in the list opens its conjugation at the indefinido, with why it departs; typing dije in Look up lands on the same page. In a drill, the book on the card opens the verb's conjugation again.

docs.title: The platform shape
docs.text:
LinguaMorpha is one app for iPhone, iPad and Mac, with a companion app for Apple Watch. It holds three courses: Spanish, French and Latin. You switch between them with the chip that shows the course's flag and your level — in the toolbar on iPhone and iPad, at the top of the sidebar on the Mac: it opens Scheme and level, where you choose a course by choosing one of its schemes (see Levels). On the Mac, ⌘1, ⌘2 and ⌘3 in the Study menu switch course too. The app itself can be shown in English, Dutch or Spanish; Spanish is not offered as the app language while you are studying Spanish, because a translation into the language you are learning would only repeat the word.

Each course is a complete study system in its own right. The courses share the same machinery — the adaptive engine, the drill screens, the help system — but not a learning path: each stands on its own. This guide covers the parts of the app that work the same whatever you study; the course guide for the language you are studying covers the rest.

Buying. A 21-day free trial of every course starts when you finish the first-launch setup. After that, you unlock a course with a one-time in-app purchase, or buy Unlock all languages, which unlocks every course. There is no subscription and no auto-renewal. A banner at the top of the main screen shows how many trial days are left — Trial — 12 days left — and opens the store (on the Mac the countdown sits at the foot of the sidebar, above an Unlock button that opens it), where you can also Restore Previous Purchase or Redeem Code — a code you received, for example for a discount or a free copy, is entered in Apple's own window and applies to the product it was made for. After the trial the banner reads Unlock more languages, or Purchases once you own everything. A course you have not unlocked shows a lock in Scheme and level, and on iPhone and iPad its study screens open the store instead.

No subscriptions, no advertising, no accounts. Your answers stay on your device.

docs.title: The app-wide screens
docs.text:
• Home — your starting point: the main screen on iPhone and iPad, the Home row near the top of the sidebar on the Mac.
  • Getting started — a short orientation page that says which way in suits you; on the Mac it is Home itself.
  • My Progress — the reports on what you have practised and what stuck.
  • Settings — app language, appearance, questions per session, pace and grading, level schemes, speech, dictionaries and your study data.
  • Select word scope — the topic filter that narrows which words Self Study draws on, within your level.
  • Level schemes — which level everything in the course first appears at; your own level is chosen in Scheme and level.
  • Look up — type any form and see what it is.
  • User Guide — this guide, and the guide for the course you are studying.

docs.title: Adjectives
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Adjectives hub from the Adjectives tile on the Self Study screen. The Spanish catalogue has over 290 adjectives, each with its four forms (masculine and feminine, singular and plural). The hub covers agreement, shortening, position, comparison and how an adjective becomes an adverb. It has the usual Theory / Study / Practice layout.

Under the title, a badge shows how many adjectives you are working with. It counts the agreement classes you ticked in Select adjective groups, narrowed by your level and the topics in Select word scope. The badge turns red when nothing is left to drill.

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select adjective groups: tick the agreement classes you want.
  • Adjective grammar (Theory): agreement, plurals, shortening, position and comparison.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Adjective reference: the selected adjectives.
  • Ser/estar shifts reference (Study): adjectives whose meaning changes with ser or estar, both senses side by side. This is the same list as in Traps.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Adjective meaning.
  • Agreement drill, Shortening drill and Comparisons (Practice).

Nothing you do on the selection, Theory and Study screens is recorded. Every answer in a drill is recorded.

docs.title: Select adjective groups
docs.text:
Spanish adjectives fall into three agreement classes:

Class Example Variable (-o / -a) rápido / rápida / rápidos / rápidas Invariant (-e) grande / grandes Invariant (consonant) fácil / fáciles

Tap a class to switch it on or off. Tap ⓘ for an explanation of the class and a Browse all adjectives row that lists its members. Adjectives of nationality and those in -or, -án, -ón, -ín end in a consonant but count as variable, because they have a feminine in -a: español → española, trabajador → trabajadora.

The line at the top shows how many adjectives you selected and how many of those are left within your level and Select word scope. The Select word scope row takes you there.

docs.title: Adjective grammar
docs.text:
This Theory page has five sections:

  • Agreement: an adjective takes the gender and number of its noun. Una casa alta, un edificio alto, casas altas, edificios altos: one adjective, four forms, all decided by the noun.
  • Forming plurals: add -s after an unstressed vowel (alto → altos, grande → grandes) and -es after a consonant (fácil → fáciles). A final -z becomes -ces (feliz → felices). A written accent on a final -án, -ón, -ín disappears in the plural (alemán → alemanes, común → comunes). Joven gains one: jóvenes.
  • Shortening (apócope): a few adjectives lose their ending directly before a masculine singular noun: bueno → buen, malo → mal, primero → primer, tercero → tercer, alguno → algún, ninguno → ningún. Grande → gran and cualquiera → cualquier shorten before a singular noun of either gender: una gran ciudad, cualquier persona. Santo → san before most masculine names (san Pedro), but santo Tomás, santo Domingo. After the noun, and after ser or estar, the full form is used: un hombre bueno, el día es bueno.
  • Position: most adjectives follow the noun (una casa blanca). Some change meaning when they come first: un gran hombre (a great man) and un hombre grande (a big man), un viejo amigo (an old friend, of long standing) and un amigo viejo (an elderly friend), el pobre niño (the unfortunate child) and el niño pobre (the child without money).
  • Comparison: más … que, menos … que, tan … como. The superlative puts the article in front: la más rápida. Four adjectives have an irregular comparative: bueno → mejor, malo → peor, grande → mayor, pequeño → menor. Mayor and menor are used mainly for age (mi hermano mayor). The suffix -ísimo means "very": altísimo.

docs.title: Adjective reference
docs.text: A list of the selected adjectives with their translations, in alphabetical order, with an A–Z index and a search field. Search matches the adjective or its translation and ignores accents. Tap an adjective to open its page. The page shows the four forms, the agreement class, the short form if there is one, and the irregular comparative if there is one.

docs.title: Adjective meaning
docs.text: Flashcards for the meaning of each adjective. The card shows the masculine singular form (rápido), and you recall the translation, or the other way round. See Word meaning for how the flashcards work.

docs.title: How the choice drills work
docs.text:
The Agreement drill, Shortening drill and Comparisons here, and the choice drills in the Pronouns, Numerals and Prepositions hubs, all work the same way:

  • At the top is the Incorrect answers switch. Turn it on to practise only the items you have got wrong and have not yet mastered.
  • The header shows Question 3 of 20 and your score so far.
  • The screen says what to do (for example "Which form of bueno goes with this noun?"), shows the material and lists the options. Tap an option. The correct answer turns green with a tick. If you chose wrong, your answer turns red with a cross. In the sentence drills, the option you tap fills the gap, so you can read the whole sentence.
  • Tap Next, and after the last question See results. At the end, tap New session for a new round.

The number of questions comes from Questions per session in Settings → Study. Which items come up depends on your earlier answers. Learning pace in the same place sets the mix of new and weak items.

docs.title: Agreement drill
docs.text: You see a noun with its gender and number, for example casas (houses (f.pl)), and the task "Which form of alto goes with this noun?". Pick the form that agrees with the noun. The options are the adjective's different forms, so an invariant adjective such as fácil has only two. Opened from a Practice set that contains adjectives, the drill uses the set's adjectives instead of your selection; the nouns are the drill's own, and the session is recorded under the set.

docs.title: Shortening drill
docs.text:
This drill uses the adjectives that have a short form: bueno (buen), malo (mal) and grande (gran). You see a short phrase with a gap, and the task "Which form of bueno completes the phrase?". There are always two options: the short form and a full form. The phrase takes one of four shapes, and the drill cycles through them:

Phrase Answer un ___ libro buen, mal, gran: shortening applies un libro ___ bueno, malo, grande: the adjective comes after the noun una ___ idea buena, mala, but gran unos ___ libros buenos, malos, grandes: shortening only applies in the singular

The feminine phrase tests the difference between the two rules: grande shortens before any singular noun, bueno and malo only before a masculine one.

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text: A sentence drill for comparing: más, menos, tan and tanto, and the irregular mejor, peor, mayor and menor. You see a sentence in your language, such as "Madrid is bigger than Toledo.", and the Spanish sentence with a gap: Madrid es ___ grande que Toledo. Choose the word (más). It does not use your adjective selection: the sentences are the drill's own. See The choice drills.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Start with all agreement classes switched on and a low level in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag).
  2. Run Meaning until the common adjectives are familiar.
  3. Add the Agreement drill to practise gender and number.
  4. When agreement is automatic, add the Shortening drill.

docs.title: Adverbs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Adverbs hub from the Adverbs tile on the Self Study screen. The Spanish catalogue has over 230 adverbs of three kinds:

  • Derived: built from an adjective with -mente: rápidamente, fácilmente.
  • Irregular: built from an adjective, but not by the rule: bien (from bueno) and mal (from malo).
  • Lexical: not built from an adjective. These include place words (aquí, allí, cerca), time words (ahora, ayer, siempre, nunca, ya), degree words (muy, casi, bastante) and words like también and tampoco.

The derived adverbs in the catalogue are a chosen list. The app does not make an adverb from every adjective, because many adjectives have none (see Adverb grammar below).

The badge under the title shows how many adverbs your selected kinds contain within your level. The topics in Select word scope do not narrow it.

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select adverb groups: tick the kinds you want. Tap ⓘ on a kind for an explanation and a list of its adverbs. Tap an adverb to open its page.
  • Adverb grammar (Theory): the rule, its limits, the adverbs of their own, and comparison.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Adverb reference: the selected adverbs.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Adverb meaning: flashcards for the meaning of each adverb. See Word meaning for how the flashcards work.

There is no form drill for adverbs. Once you know the rule, derived adverbs are predictable, so the drill tests meaning only.

docs.title: Adverb grammar
docs.text:
Adverb grammar has five cards that open and close when you tap their heading:

  • Adding -mente — add -mente to the feminine singular of the adjective: rápida → rápidamente, cuidadosa → cuidadosamente. An adjective with one form for both genders uses that form: fácil → fácilmente, triste → tristemente. The adjective keeps its written accent. With two adverbs in a row, only the last one takes -mente: lenta y cuidadosamente.
  • Two irregulars — bueno → bien, malo → mal.
  • Adjectives without -mente — adjectives that classify have no -mente form: colours (no rojamente), nationality (no españolamente; say a la española), states such as muerto or casado, and categories such as ferroviario (railway). A test: if muy fits the adjective, there is usually an adverb.
  • Adverbs of their own — adverbs that do not come from an adjective: time (ahora, siempre), place (aquí), amount (muy) and manner (así).
  • Comparison — adverbs are compared like adjectives: más rápidamente que, tan rápidamente como. Bien and mal become mejor and peor. Mucho and poco take -ísimo: muchísimo, poquísimo.

docs.title: Adverb reference
docs.text:
The selected adverbs in three sections, Derived, Irregular and Lexical. Only the first section is open when you arrive. Tap a heading to open or close it. A search opens all sections. Irregular adverbs carry an irr. badge and lexical adverbs a lex. badge. The search matches the start of the adverb (so rapid finds rápidamente) or any part of its translation.

Tap an adverb to open its page. It shows the kind (Derived (regular), Derived (irregular) or Lexical) and, for a derived adverb, the adjective it comes from.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Run Meaning on the Lexical adverbs first. These are the ones you have to memorise.
  2. For the derived adverbs, learn the rule in Adverb grammar rather than drilling each one.

docs.title: French module
docs.text:
The French module is a complete course in its own right. It covers over 900 verbs conjugated in sixteen tenses, over 1,400 nouns with their gender and plurals, about 280 adjectives with their agreement, and the smaller word classes around them. You don't need to know another language first. Irregular forms are marked in the conjugation tables down to the letters that depart from the pattern.

The ways to study it are described under Ways to study in the User Guide. This guide describes what is in the course, word type by word type.

Each word type has its own tile on Self Study, and each tile opens a hub with the same three sections: Theory, Study and Practice. Level and topic are not set per hub. Your level is chosen by tapping the flag (Scheme and level), the topics in Self Study → Select word scope, and every hub uses both. There is no frequency filter in Self Study.

  • Verbs — over 900 verbs in the three French groups, with fourteen verb groups to choose from and sixteen tenses across the indicatif, conditionnel, subjonctif and impératif. Choose verb groups and tenses, read the theory, look up any verb's full conjugation, then drill meaning, production and recognition, and three choice drills: Passé composé or imparfait, Indicatif or subjonctif and Être or avoir. See Verbs.
  • Nouns — over 1,400 nouns with gender, plurals and translations. The drills are Noun meaning, Pick the correct article, Which article? (the article a whole sentence needs), Singular / Plural and Alternate gender pairs.
  • Adjectives — about 280 adjectives: agreement in gender and number, the irregular feminines and plurals, and position. The drills are Adjective meaning and an Agreement drill.
  • Adverbs — about 170 adverbs: the ones derived with -ment, the irregular forms and the plain lexical adverbs, with an Adverb meaning drill.
  • Pronouns — around 45 pronouns: personal, demonstrative, relative, interrogative and more. The drills are Pronoun meaning, Which pronoun? and an Agreement drill (celui, le mien).
  • Prepositions — about 20 prepositions, with a Preposition meaning drill and a Contrast drill (pour or par, en or dans, à or de).
  • Numerals — cardinals, ordinals, fractions, multiples and collectives, including the vigesimal soixante-dix and quatre-vingts. The drills are Numeral meaning and Does it take an -s?
  • Other Vocabulary — the remaining single words: conjunctions, articles, determiners, interjections and similar.
  • Phrases — over 240 set phrases and common expressions.

Under Tools on Self Study (on the Mac, in the sidebar), Look up finds any conjugated form, plural or vocabulary item. French also has Grammar lessons on the home screen: over fifty step-by-step lessons grouped into modules.

docs.title: Level schemes
docs.text: The French course has one level scheme, CEFR: six levels, A1 to C2. To arrange the course differently, duplicate it and make your own (see Level schemes in the User Guide).

docs.title: Adjectives
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Adjectives hub covers agreement in gender and number: every adjective has four forms (masculine and feminine, singular and plural). The catalogue has about 280 adjectives, each with its four forms, a translation, a level and a topic.

Open Self Study → Adjectives. The hub has:

  • Theory — Adjective grammar: feminine and plural forms, irregulars, and position.
  • Study — Reference (Adjective reference): the selected adjectives with all four forms.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select adjective groups): choose which agreement classes appear in the catalogue and the drills. Then the drills:
  • Meaning (Adjective meaning) — flashcards for the meaning of the selected adjectives.
  • Agreement drill — pick the form that agrees with a given noun.

The line under the hub title shows how many adjectives are in your selection, out of the whole catalogue; it turns red when there are none. The selection is the agreement classes you tick, narrowed by your level and the topics in Self Study → Select word scope. The reference list, the meaning deck and the agreement drill all use this same selection.

A recommended workflow

  1. Tick all classes and set your level to A1 under Scheme and level (tap the flag).
  2. Run Meaning until the meanings are familiar.
  3. Use the Agreement drill to fix the forms, one or two classes at a time — start with Regular (+e) and Invariable, then add the others.

docs.title: Select adjective groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The adjectives are sorted into seven agreement classes, worked out from each adjective's own forms:

  • Regular (+e) — add -e for the feminine: grand → grande, petit → petite, français → française. The largest class.
  • Invariable — the masculine already ends in -e, so the feminine is the same word: jeune, rouge, facile. Only the plural changes.
  • Doubling (double consonant + e) — bon → bonne, gentil → gentille, gros → grosse, ancien → ancienne.
  • -eux → -euse — heureux → heureuse, sérieux → sérieuse.
  • -er → -ère — premier → première, cher → chère, léger → légère.
  • -f → -ve — neuf → neuve, actif → active, sportif → sportive.
  • Irregular — pairs to learn by heart: beau → belle, vieux → vieille, blanc → blanche, long → longue, frais → fraîche, doux → douce.

Tap a class to switch it on or off; each row shows its size and a few examples. Tap ⓘ for an explanation of the class and a list of its adjectives (tap one to open it). The line at the top shows how many adjectives you selected and how many remain within your word scope; the Select word scope row below it takes you to the topic filter.

docs.title: Adjective grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A reference page; nothing is recorded.

The agreement rule. An adjective takes the gender and number of its noun: un grand jardin, une grande maison, de grands jardins, de grandes maisons. A group of mixed gender takes the masculine plural: un frère et une sœur intelligents. Agreement often lives only in the spelling — grand and grands sound the same — but a feminine -e after a consonant makes that consonant heard: petit → petite.

Making the feminine. The default is to add -e (grand → grande, joli → jolie). An adjective that already ends in -e doesn't change (jeune, rouge, facile). Some double the final consonant (bon → bonne), some rewrite the ending (heureux → heureuse, actif → active, premier → première), and a few change the consonant altogether (blanc → blanche, long → longue, sec → sèche).

Making the plural. The default is to add -s to the singular of the right gender (grande → grandes). A masculine ending in -s or -x doesn't change (gris, heureux). -eau becomes -eaux (beau → beaux), and -al becomes -aux (principal → principaux), just as with nouns.

The famous three. Beau, nouveau and vieux have a third masculine form before a vowel or mute h: un bel homme, un nouvel ami, un vieil arbre (feminine belle, nouvelle, vieille). In the plural the extra form disappears: de beaux hommes.

Position. Most adjectives go after the noun: une voiture rouge, un livre intéressant. A small, frequent set goes before it — the BAGS adjectives: Beauty (beau, joli), Age (jeune, vieux, nouveau), Goodness (bon, mauvais) and Size (grand, petit, gros). A few change meaning with position: un homme grand (a tall man) against un grand homme (a great man); ma propre chambre (my own room) against ma chambre propre (my clean room); un ancien collègue (a former colleague) against une maison ancienne (an old house).

Tap one of the adjective's forms (an invariable adjective offers fewer, because some forms are the same). The right answer is marked with a tick, a wrong choice with a cross; tap Next to go on. Opened from a Practice set that contains adjectives, the drill uses the set's adjectives instead of your selection; the nouns are the drill's own, and the session is recorded under the set.

docs.title: Adverbs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Adverbs hub covers French adverbs of three kinds: the derived adverbs built from an adjective with -ment, the irregular ones that come from an adjective but not by the plain rule, and the lexical adverbs that have no adjective behind them. The catalogue has about 170 adverbs.

Open Self Study → Adverbs. The hub has:

  • Theory — Adverb grammar: the -ment rule and its other endings, the adverbs of their own, and comparison.
  • Study — Reference (Adverb reference): the selected adverbs, with a badge for the kind.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select adverb groups): choose which kinds appear. Then the drills: flashcards for the meaning of the selected adverbs.

The line under the hub title shows how many adverbs your kind selection gives you, out of the whole catalogue. The selection is the kinds you tick, within your level; the topics in Select word scope are not applied.

A recommended workflow. Read Adverb grammar once — the -ment rule is mechanical and needs no drilling. Then spend your time on Meaning with Lexical and Irregular ticked: those are the adverbs you have to learn as words.

docs.title: Select adverb groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Three kinds:

  • Derived — the feminine of the adjective plus -ment: lent → lente → lentement, heureux → heureuse → heureusement. The largest group.
  • Irregular — from an adjective, but not by the plain rule: constant → constamment, évident → évidemment, and vrai → vraiment, absolu → absolument.
  • Lexical — no visible adjective behind them: bien, mal, vite, très, souvent, toujours, déjà, ici, là.

Tap a kind to switch it on or off; each row shows its size and a few examples. Tap ⓘ for an explanation and the list of adverbs of that kind. The line at the top shows how many adverbs you selected.

docs.title: Adverb grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A reference page; nothing is recorded. Tap a card to open or close it.

  • Adding -ment — -ment goes on the feminine singular: lent → lente → lentement, heureux → heureuse → heureusement, doux → douce → doucement. An adjective ending in a vowel takes it on the masculine: rapide → rapidement, vrai → vraiment, poli → poliment.
  • Other endings — -ant becomes -amment (constant → constamment, courant → couramment) and -ent becomes -emment (récent → récemment, évident → évidemment). Both sound the same. lent → lentement is the exception. A few take -ément: précis → précisément, énorme → énormément, profond → profondément. Bon and mauvais have adverbs of their own: bien and mal.
  • Adjectives without -ment — only adjectives that describe a manner or a degree have a -ment form. Colours, nationalities and category adjectives have none.
  • Adverbs of their own — many common adverbs come from no adjective and are learned as words: time (maintenant, déjà, encore, souvent, toujours, jamais), place (ici, là), amount (très, trop, beaucoup, peu) and manner (bien, mal, vite).
  • Comparison — plus … que, moins … que and aussi … que: plus lentement que, moins souvent que, aussi vite que. Bien becomes mieux; mal becomes plus mal.
