docs.title: Tips for getting started with French
Tips for getting started with French
docs.text:
1. Set up speech first. Install an Enhanced or Premium French voice in Apple's settings, then choose it in LinguaMorpha under Settings → French → Voice. Standard voices sound robotic, and the better voices make a real difference. See Setting up French speech.

  2. Start with A1 nouns. Tap the flag and choose A1 under Scheme and level. Set Questions per session to 20 in Settings → Study. Then open Nouns and run a few Meaning sessions until the basic vocabulary feels solid. Follow up with Pick the correct article, so that le or la is learned along with each noun.

  3. Add verbs gradually. Once the A1 nouns feel comfortable, open Self Study → Verbs. In Select groups, choose only 1st group (-er). In Select tenses, choose only Présent. Run Produce the conjugation until the regular present tense is automatic, before you touch anything irregular.

  4. Use the conjugation tables actively. Before you drill, open Reference on the verbs hub, tap a verb you are about to practise and look at its Conjugation tab. Red marks the parts of a form that depart from the regular pattern. Once you understand the pattern, the drill sticks faster.

  5. Broaden in steps. Move your level up to A2. Add verb groups one at a time, for example 2nd group (-ir / -iss-), then Auxiliary être. Add one tense at a time: Imparfait and Passé Composé are the most useful after Présent. Never widen your selection so far that sessions feel overwhelming.

  6. Watch the numbers from 70 to 99. When you reach Numerals, spend extra time on soixante-dix (70), quatre-vingts (80) and quatre-vingt-dix (90). They count in twenties, unlike anything in English.

  7. Try the false friends. Under Practice Sets, in the Topics folder, the False friends set drills nouns that look like English words but mean something else: librairie is a bookshop, monnaie is change, lecture is reading. It is a short set, and it runs as Noun meaning cards.

  8. Check your progress. Tap the chart icon at the top of the Home screen (on the Mac, choose My Progress in the sidebar) and look under Weakest words: the words you have practised often enough to rank and still get wrong most. Tap a verb there to drill just that verb, or tap Practise all to drill every verb on the list.

docs.title: Nouns
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The French course has over 1,400 nouns. Every noun has its gender, its plural (where it has one) and a translation and three example sentences. The Nouns hub is where you practise the parts of noun vocabulary that cause the most mistakes: gender (le or la), plurals, and the nouns that have a masculine and a feminine form.

Open Self Study → Nouns to reach the hub. It has three sections:

  • Theory — Noun grammar: how gender, plurals and compounds work.
  • Study — Reference (Noun reference): browse every noun with its translation.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select noun groups): choose the kinds of noun to practise. Then the drills:
  • Meaning (Noun meaning) — flashcards: recall what each noun means.
  • Pick the correct article — choose le or la for each noun.
  • Which article? — choose the article a sentence needs: definite, indefinite, partitive or bare de.
  • Singular / Plural — form the plural (or the singular) of the selected nouns.
  • Alternate gender pairs — give the masculine or feminine form of a noun.

The line under the hub title shows how many nouns your selection gives you, out of the whole catalogue. The Select groups row shows how many of the noun groups in your level you have ticked; the count turns red when none are ticked. Touch and hold most rows for a short explanation, or use the Help button at the top of the hub.

Which drills follow your selection. Noun meaning, Pick the correct article and Singular / Plural use the nouns in your selected groups, narrowed by your level and the topics you set in Self Study → Select word scope. Alternate gender pairs always uses every noun that has both a masculine and a feminine form. Which article? uses its own fixed set of sentences. Noun reference always lists the whole catalogue.

A recommended workflow

  1. In Select groups, start with Regular, and set your level to A1 under Scheme and level (tap the flag). Set Questions per session to 20 in Settings → Study.
  2. Run Meaning until the core vocabulary and its articles are solid.
  3. Add Pick the correct article to fix le and la in memory, and Which article? once you meet the partitive.
  4. Move on to Singular / Plural, then add the plural-formation groups in Select groups.
  5. Leave Alternate gender pairs until the ordinary genders are secure.

docs.title: Select noun groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select noun groups decides which nouns can appear in Noun meaning, Pick the correct article and Singular / Plural. Nouns are grouped by their grammatical behaviour, not by vocabulary. Level and topic apply to every word type: the level under Scheme and level (tap the flag), the topics in Self Study → Select word scope; there is no frequency filter in Self Study.

The ten groups are arranged in four sections:

  • Basic — Regular: one gender, a plural in -s, nothing else to learn. This is by far the largest group; a noun is only here when it belongs to no other group.
  • Gender patterns — M/F pair (a masculine and a feminine form: boulanger / boulangère, chien / chienne), Epicene (one form for both genders, only the article changes: un élève / une élève) and Different meaning by gender (the gender picks the meaning: le tour is a turn, la tour is a tower).
  • Plural class — Mass / uncountable (no plural in normal use: le lait, le courage), Plurale tantum (only plural: les affaires, les gens) and Invariable singular/plural (the same form in both numbers: le bras / les bras, le choix / les choix).
  • Plural formation — Plural -x (bateau → bateaux, jeu → jeux, genou → genoux), Plural -al/-ail → -aux (animal → animaux, travail → travaux) and Compound (nouns of several words or with a hyphen: salle de bains → salles de bains).

A noun can belong to several groups at once, and it is in your selection when any of its groups is ticked.

Using the screen

  • Tap a group's row to include or exclude it. Each row shows how many nouns it contains.
  • Tap ⓘ on a row to open the group's info page: what the group covers and an example. For the smaller groups it also lists the nouns that belong to it.
  • All and None at the top select or clear every group at once; each section header has its own All / None button.
  • An unticked group can show a note such as "12 still in scope via Regular": those nouns are already in your selection through another group you have ticked.
  • The line at the top shows how many groups you have ticked and how many nouns that gives you within your word scope. The Select word scope row takes you to the topic filter.
  • If you leave the screen with no group ticked, the app warns you that the noun drills will be empty. Choose Stay and select or Go back anyway.

Selection and session size are two separate things. Your selection is the set of nouns that can appear in a drill. Your session size is how many questions one session asks: Questions per session in Settings → Study (10, 20, 30, 50, or ∞ to keep going until you stop).

docs.title: Noun grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Noun grammar is a reference page: nothing is tested and nothing is recorded. Each section matches one or more groups in Select noun groups, so you can read about a pattern and then narrow the drills to exactly that group.

Gender. French has no neuter: every noun is masculine (le) or feminine (la), and no rule covers them all, so learn the article with the word — la maison, never just maison. Endings give strong tendencies, not guarantees:

  • Usually feminine: -tion / -sion (la nation), -té (la liberté), -ure (la voiture), -ette (la baguette), -ance / -ence (la chance).
  • Usually masculine: -age (le fromage), -ment (le moment), -eau (le bateau), -isme (le tourisme), -oir (le miroir).

The exceptions are famous precisely because the tendencies are good: le problème, le système (masculine despite -e), la plage (feminine despite -age), l'eau (feminine). Treat the ending as a first guess and the article as the truth.

People and animals. M/F pairs usually derive the feminine with a suffix (boulanger → boulangère, chien → chienne, acteur → actrice), and occasionally use a different word. Epicenes use one form for both genders, and the article does all the work: un artiste / une artiste. A small set changes meaning with gender: le tour (turn) and la tour (tower), le voile (veil) and la voile (sail). Getting the article wrong there changes what you said.

Nouns without a normal plural. Mass nouns stay singular and take the partitive (du lait, du courage) rather than a number. Plurale tantum nouns exist only in the plural (les gens). Nouns that already end in -s, -x or -z don't change (le nez / les nez); only the article shows the number.

Plurals beyond -s.

  • -eau, -au and -eu take -x: bateau → bateaux, jeu → jeux. Seven nouns in -ou do too — bijoux, cailloux, choux, genoux, hiboux, joujoux, poux; every other -ou noun takes -s (trou → trous).
  • -al and some -ail nouns rebuild the ending as -aux: animal → animaux, travail → travaux. Exceptions such as bal → bals and festival → festivals take a plain -s.

In speech none of this is audible — bateau and bateaux sound the same. The plural is heard in the article: le / les.

Compound nouns. The plural goes on the parts that are nouns or adjectives, not simply on the end: salle de bains → salles de bains, arrière-grand-père → arrière-grands-pères, chef-d'œuvre → chefs-d'œuvre. Verbs and invariable words inside the compound don't change: un porte-monnaie → des porte-monnaie.

docs.title: Noun reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Noun reference is a browse-only list: nothing is tested and nothing is recorded. It lists the whole noun catalogue, not just your selection, so a noun never disappears from it because of a filter. Use it to check a translation before a session, or to look up a noun you got wrong.

The list is alphabetical with a search field; on iPhone and iPad an A–Z index runs down the side. Each row shows the noun with its article and its translation. A masculine/feminine pair such as chien / chienne appears as two separate rows, each with its own article and meaning.

The noun's page. Tap a noun to open it:

iPhoneiPadMac

  • the noun with its article and its translation
  • its singular and plural forms
  • its Level and Topics
  • Examples: French sentences, each with a translation and a speaker button to hear it
  • the book icon in the toolbar, for online dictionaries (see External dictionary lookups)

docs.title: Noun meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the meaning of the nouns in your selection. Each noun is shown with its article, so you learn its gender along with its meaning. Every answer is recorded, and nouns you get wrong come back more often. The other meaning decks in the French course (adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, numerals, prepositions, phrases and other vocabulary) work in the same way.

How a card works. The card shows a word; you recall its translation, then tap the card to turn it (Tap to reveal). On iPhone and iPad, swipe right if you knew it and left if you didn't. On a Mac (and with VoiceOver) you use the Correct and Wrong buttons instead. The next card follows automatically.

The controls at the top:

  • Direction — French → your language, your language → French, or a random mix of both.
  • Incorrect answers — only show the cards you have answered wrongly. If there are none, the app tells you and switches the filter off.
  • Listen — when a French voice is available, the French side is spoken instead of shown; turn the card to see how it is spelt.

The speaker button on the card reads the visible side aloud. After a run of seven correct answers the app offers to end the session early: choose Stop — session complete or Continue. At the end, New session starts another round.

docs.title: Pick the correct article
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A noun is shown without its article. Tap le or la. The card flashes green or red and turns round to show the noun with its article and its translation. After a right answer the next noun appears by itself, unless Auto-advance after correct answer is off in Settings → Study; after a wrong one the card stays until you tap Next. The speaker button reads the noun aloud.

  • The nouns come from your selection. Nouns of more than one word, and nouns ending in -s, are left out.
  • For a noun that takes both genders (élève), either answer is right, and the card says so.
  • Each noun is asked once per session. The line at the top shows your score so far ("6 out of 8 correct") and how many nouns are candidates.
  • Incorrect answers limits the session to the nouns whose gender you have got wrong.

docs.title: Which article?
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Which article? asks a different question from Pick the correct article. That drill asks which article a noun takes. This one asks which article a sentence needs — and the noun alone can't tell you: le café and du café are both correct French.

Each question shows an English sentence with a label naming the rule, and the French sentence with a gap. Tap one of two articles; the gap fills in, the right answer is marked, and a Why …? card explains the rule. Tap Next to go on (See results after the last one).

The sentences cover six rules:

  • After a negation — the partitive and the indefinite article become bare de: je ne mange pas de pain, nous n'avons pas d'enfants. After être they don't: ce n'est pas la réponse.
  • After a quantity — beaucoup de, un kilo de, un peu de take bare de: un peu de lait, but ajoute du lait.
  • The verb decides — verbs of liking take the definite article (j'aime le café); verbs of eating, drinking and buying take the partitive (je bois du café).
  • Countable or not — j'ai mangé un gâteau (a whole cake) against j'ai mangé du gâteau (some cake).
  • Plural — j'achète des pommes (some apples) against j'aime les pommes (apples in general).
  • A specific thing — the definite article's ordinary job: ferme la porte, la France.

The drill has its own fixed set of sentences and ignores your noun selection. Your answers are recorded per rule, so the rule you miss most comes back more often. The session length follows Questions per session (with ∞, a session has at most 50 questions).

docs.title: Singular / Plural
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard drill for plurals. The card shows a noun with its article and translation, and asks Give the plural (le cheval → les chevaux) or Give the singular; the direction is chosen at random for each card. Turn the card, then mark yourself right or wrong as in Noun meaning.

The nouns come from your selection, but only nouns with a normal singular and plural are used: mass nouns, plurale tantum and invariable nouns are left out. If none are left, the drill says so and offers Select scope.

docs.title: Alternate gender pairs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard drill for the nouns that have both a masculine and a feminine form. The card shows one form with its article and translation and asks Give the feminine form (le boulanger → la boulangère) or Give the masculine form. Turn the card and mark yourself as in Noun meaning.

The drill uses all such nouns — the M/F pairs and the nouns whose meaning changes with gender (le tour → la tour, where the translation on each side shows the change) — whatever you have selected. The article is elided where needed: l'ami → l'amie.

docs.title: Numerals
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Numerals hub covers French numbers of five kinds — cardinals, ordinals, fractionals, multiplicatives and collectives — with particular attention to the numbers from 70 to 99 and to the rules for the plural -s.

Open Self Study → Numerals. The hub has:

  • Theory — Numeral grammar: the counting system from 1 to 1000.
  • Study — Reference (Numeral reference): the selected numerals with their translations.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select numeral groups): choose which kinds appear. Then the drills:
  • Meaning (Numeral meaning) — flashcards for the meaning of the selected numerals.
  • Does it take an -s? — quatre-vingts or quatre-vingt-deux: the position decides.

The line under the hub title shows how many numerals your kind selection gives you, out of the whole catalogue. Only the kinds you tick decide the selection: your level decides whether the hub appears, not which numerals it holds, and the topics in Select word scope are not applied here.

A recommended workflow

  1. Tick Cardinal only and run Meaning. Pay special attention to soixante-dix, quatre-vingts and quatre-vingt-dix.
  2. Use Does it take an -s? to fix the spelling rules.
  3. Add the other kinds.

docs.title: Select numeral groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The five kinds:

  • Cardinal — the counting numbers: un, deux, trois … vingt, trente … soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix, cent, mille.
  • Ordinal — premier, deuxième, troisième … vingtième, centième, millième.
  • Fractional — demi, moitié, tiers, quart.
  • Multiplicative — double, triple, quadruple, quintuple.
  • Collective — paire, dizaine, douzaine, quinzaine, vingtaine, centaine, millier.

Tap a kind to switch it on or off; each row shows its size and the first few numerals. Tap ⓘ for an explanation of the kind and its numerals:

  • Ordinals add -ième to the cardinal, dropping a final -e (quatre → quatrième), with two spelling changes: cinq → cinquième, neuf → neuvième. Only premier / première and second / seconde agree in gender.
  • Fractionals: demi doesn't change before its noun and takes a hyphen (une demi-heure), but agrees after it (une heure et demie). La moitié is the noun for half of something. From a fifth onwards the ordinal is used: un cinquième.
  • Multiplicatives are adjectives (un double espresso) and nouns (le double de).
  • Collectives are nouns — feminine, except millier — and take de: une douzaine d'œufs. Apart from douzaine and paire they mean "about": une vingtaine de personnes is twenty or so.

docs.title: Numeral grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A reference page on the cardinal numbers; nothing is recorded.

1 to 19. Un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize are sixteen words to memorise. 17 to 19 are compounds with a hyphen: dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf. Un is the only number that agrees in gender: un livre, une table.

The tens. Vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante. Units join with a hyphen (vingt-deux, trente-cinq), except the 1, which takes et: vingt et un, trente et un … soixante et un.

70, 80, 90. Above 69, French counts in twenties:

  • soixante-dix = 60 + 10 → 70, continuing soixante et onze (71), soixante-douze (72) … soixante-dix-neuf (79).
  • quatre-vingts = 4 × 20 → 80. The -s drops when another number follows: quatre-vingt-un (81) — with no et.
  • quatre-vingt-dix = 4 × 20 + 10 → 90, continuing quatre-vingt-onze (91) … quatre-vingt-dix-neuf (99).

Belgium and Switzerland use septante (70) and nonante (90), and parts of Switzerland huitante (80). They are worth recognising, but the app teaches the forms used in France.

Cent and mille. Cent (100) and mille (1000) stand without un: cent euros. Cent takes an -s in round hundreds (deux cents) but not when a number follows (deux cent un). Mille never changes: deux mille.

docs.title: Numeral reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A browse-only list of the selected numerals with their translations, in sections by kind, with a search field. Search also finds a numeral by its value (80). Use the By value / Alphabetical switch at the top to change the order. Nothing is recorded.

Tap a numeral to open its page:

iPhoneiPadMac

  • the numeral and its translation, with its kind and value (Value: 80; a fraction shows as 1/4, a multiple as ×3)
  • for some numerals, a note on Agreement and use — for example that vingt takes -s only when multiplied and final
  • Built on, Built on it or Same family: chips linking an ordinal, fraction or collective to its cardinal and the other way round. Tap a chip to open that numeral.
  • its level and frequency

docs.title: Numeral meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the meaning of the selected numerals, in either direction. It works like Noun meaning. Every answer is recorded.

docs.title: Does it take an -s?
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Each question shows an English sentence with the number in digits and a label naming the rule, and the French sentence with a gap at the end of the numeral: Il a quatre-vingt___ ans. ("He is 80 years old.") Tap the ending — usually s or the empty option for no ending. The gap fills in, the right answer is marked and a card explains the rule. Tap Next to go on.

The sentences come in pairs, because each rule is only visible against its opposite:

  • Multiplied and final — vingt and cent take -s: quatre-vingts ans, deux cents euros.
  • Followed by another — another number follows, so the -s goes: quatre-vingt-deux ans, deux cent cinq euros.
  • Not multiplied — a bare cent or vingt has no -s: cent ans, vingt invités.
  • Invariable — mille never changes: deux mille euros.
  • Counter noun — million and milliard are nouns: they take -s and are followed by de: deux millions d'habitants.
  • Gender — un agrees with its noun, also inside a compound: vingt et une pages, trente et un jours.

The drill has its own fixed set of sentences and ignores your kind selection. Answers are recorded per rule.

docs.title: Phrases
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Phrases hub from the Phrases tile on the Self Study screen. The line under the title ("… of … phrases") shows how many phrases your selection leaves. The phrases are of two kinds:

  1. Set phrases — about 240 fixed expressions to learn as a whole: greetings and social phrases (s'il vous plaît, de rien, à bientôt), time expressions (tout de suite, à tout à l'heure) and connecting phrases (à cause de, bien sûr, tout à fait). Some are built around a verb (avoir faim, avoir besoin de, faire attention).
  2. Example sentences — the sentences written for the verbs and nouns, each practised as a phrase: the tense examples of the verbs (Tu abandonnes toujours tes projets à mi-chemin.) and the example sentences of the nouns (Le chien dort dans le jardin.). A verb's tense example is only included when its tense is switched on in Select tenses.

The hub has these screens:

  • Phrases or sentences (Practice) — choose which kinds count.
  • Select tenses (Practice) — the tenses the verbs' tense examples may use.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Phrase reference, the selected phrases.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Phrase meaning, flashcards.

There is no Theory page for French phrases. Phrases work best alongside the Verbs and Nouns hubs, not instead of them. For single words that have no hub, see Other Vocabulary.

Phrases or sentences. Tap Set phrases or Example sentences to switch the kind on or off; tick both for both. Each row shows its size and a few samples; tap ⓘ for a short explanation with more examples. The line at the top shows how many phrases you selected and how many are left after the rest of your scope. The pool is also narrowed by:

  • Select tenses — a verb's tense example only counts when its tense is selected. This is the same tense choice as on the Verbs hub, which the Select tenses row in this hub opens: a change here changes the verb drills too.
  • Your level and Select word scope — an example sentence takes the level and topic of its verb or noun, and a tense example also needs its tense in your level. Its level is the later of the two.

Set phrases alone is a small, focused pool; with Example sentences on, many thousands of sentences are included. Learn set phrases as a whole: don't translate tout de suite word by word.

Phrase reference. A list of the phrases in your selection with their translations, with a search field that matches the phrase or its translation. Nothing is recorded here.

  • Touch and hold a row to hear the phrase.
  • The toolbar button hides or shows the translations (Hide translation / Show translation), so you can test yourself on the list.
  • Tap a phrase to open its page. A set phrase shows its translation and type (Expression or Verbal expression), its Level, Frequency and Topics, and the book icon in the toolbar for online dictionaries.
  • An example sentence's page is marked Example sentence. It shows its Level, for a tense example with where it comes from (the verb's level and the tense's); for a tense example its tense under Tenses, which you tap for the tense's ⓘ; its Topics; and an Illustrates card with the verb or noun it belongs to, which you tap to open that word.

Phrase meaning. A flashcard deck for the meaning of the selected phrases. It works like Noun meaning: the phrase is on the card and you recall its translation, or the other way round. On a card for a verb example sentence, the verb appears as a chip on the French side; tap it to open that verb. The speaker button is especially useful here — hearing a whole phrase helps you remember its rhythm.

docs.title: Prepositions
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Prepositions hub covers twenty common French prepositions. French prepositions don't change form, so instead of tables the hub concentrates on meaning, on the forced contractions of à and de, and on the pairs learners confuse: pour and par, en and dans, à and de, depuis and pendant.

Open Self Study → Prepositions. The hub has:

  • Theory — Preposition grammar: à / de contractions, en against dans, and place against time.
  • Study — Reference (Preposition reference): the selected prepositions with their translations.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select preposition groups): choose which senses appear. Then the drills:
  • Meaning (Preposition meaning) — flashcards for the meaning of the selected prepositions.
  • Contrast drill — pick the right preposition (pour or par, en or dans, à or de, depuis or pendant).

The line under the hub title shows how many prepositions your sense selection gives you, out of the whole catalogue. Only the senses you tick decide the selection: your level decides whether the hub appears, not which prepositions it holds, and the topics in Select word scope are not applied here.

A recommended workflow

  1. Tick all senses and run Meaning to learn the twenty prepositions.
  2. Spend most of your time on the Contrast drill.
  3. To focus on one pair, narrow the senses: Time alone, for example, keeps the en / dans and depuis / pendant questions.

docs.title: Select preposition groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Each preposition is tagged with one or more senses, and a preposition is in your selection when any of its senses is ticked. The screen shows four senses:

  • Location — where something is: dans, sur, sous, devant, derrière, entre, chez, contre, and à and en for towns and countries.
  • Motion — the path: à (destination), de (origin), vers (direction), par (the way through), depuis (starting point).
  • Time — when and how long: à, en, dans, depuis, pendant, pour, vers, avant, après.
  • Manner — how: avec, sans, par.

Tap a sense to switch it on or off; each row shows its size and the first few prepositions. Tap ⓘ for an explanation of the sense and its prepositions. The line at the top shows how many prepositions you selected.

docs.title: Preposition grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A reference page; nothing is recorded.

À and de. À points towards: a place (à Paris), a time (à midi), a person you give or speak to (je parle à Marie). De points from or means "of": origin (je viens de Lyon), possession (le livre de Marie) and many fixed pairings (avoir besoin de). Before le and les both contract, always:

  • à + le → au (au cinéma), à + les → aux (aux États-Unis)
  • de + le → du, de + les → des

À la, à l', de la and de l' don't contract. Writing à le is one of the surest beginner mistakes.

En and dans. Both mean "in":

  • dans — physically inside (dans la boîte, dans la maison), and "in … from now": je pars dans une heure.
  • en — states, materials, months, years, and feminine countries (en France, en été, en 2026), and how long something took: j'ai fait le trajet en une heure.

Place and direction. Sur / sous (on / under), devant / derrière (in front of / behind), entre (between), vers (towards, and "around" a time: vers midi), contre (against). Chez means "at the place of": chez moi, chez le médecin. It takes a person, not a place name.

Time. Avant / après (before / after) and pendant (during, or for a completed stretch: pendant deux heures). Depuis ("since / for") takes the present for something still going on, where English uses the perfect: j'habite ici depuis trois ans — "I have lived here for three years".

Pour and par. Pour marks purpose, destination and benefit: un cadeau pour toi, le train pour Paris, pour apprendre. Par marks the route, the means, the agent and distribution: par la fenêtre, par le train, écrit par Hugo, trois fois par semaine. Avec and sans (with / without) complete the set; sans usually takes no article: sans argent.

docs.title: Preposition reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A browse-only list of the selected prepositions with their translations, with a search field. Nothing is recorded.

Tap a preposition to open its page: the preposition and its translation, its kind and how many senses it has, its Senses, and — for the eight contrast prepositions — Often confused with, naming its partner (pour ↔ par, en ↔ dans, à ↔ de, depuis ↔ pendant). Its level and frequency are shown at the bottom.

iPhoneiPadMac

docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the meaning of the selected prepositions, in either direction. It works like Noun meaning. Every answer is recorded.

docs.title: Contrast drill
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Each question shows an English sentence with a label naming the use, and the French sentence with a gap. You choose between the two prepositions of a pair:

  • pour / par — J'étudie ___ apprendre le français (Purpose → pour); Écrit ___ Victor Hugo (Agent → par); Trois fois ___ semaine (Per → par).
  • en / dans — J'habite ___ France (→ en); Les clés sont ___ la boîte (→ dans); Je pars ___ une heure (Time from now → dans) against J'ai fait le trajet ___ une heure (Time taken → en).
  • à / de — Je vais ___ Lyon (Destination → à); Je viens ___ Lyon (Origin → de); Un verre ___ vin (→ de).
  • depuis / pendant — J'habite ici ___ trois ans (Ongoing (since) → depuis); J'ai travaillé ___ deux heures (Completed duration → pendant).

Some sentences vary from question to question: the city, the length of time, the month or the activity changes. After you answer, the right preposition is marked and a card explains the difference. Tap Next to go on.

A question is included only when its answer is among the prepositions in your selection. Answers are recorded per preposition and use, so the uses you miss come back more often. If none of the eight contrast prepositions is selected, the drill asks you to add senses in Select preposition groups.

docs.title: Pronouns
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Pronouns hub covers the French pronoun catalogue in six classes: personal, demonstrative, possessive, indefinite, relative and interrogative.

Open Self Study → Pronouns. The hub has:

  • Theory — Pronoun grammar: subject and object forms, qui / que / dont, and question words.
  • Study — Reference (Pronoun reference): the selected pronouns with translations.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select pronoun groups): choose which classes appear in the catalogue and the meaning deck. Then the drills:
  • Meaning (Pronoun meaning) — flashcards for the meaning of the selected pronouns.
  • Which pronoun? — pick the right object pronoun: direct object, indirect object or reflexive.
  • Agreement drill — match celui, le mien and similar pronouns to a noun's gender and number.

The line under the hub title shows how many pronouns your class selection gives you, out of the whole catalogue. Only the classes you tick decide the selection: your level decides whether the hub appears, not which pronouns it holds, and the topics in Select word scope are not applied here.

A recommended workflow

  1. Start with the Personal class and run Meaning.
  2. Add Which pronoun? — le or lui, les or leur is where most mistakes are.
  3. Add Demonstrative and Possessive and use the Agreement drill.

docs.title: Select pronoun groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The six classes:

  • Personal — the subject pronouns je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles, the object pronouns me, te, le, la, les, lui, leur and the reflexive se.
  • Demonstrative — ce, ceci, cela, ça and celui with its -ci and -là forms.
  • Possessive — le mien, le tien, le sien, le nôtre, le vôtre, le leur.
  • Indefinite — quelqu'un, quelque chose, personne, rien, tout, aucun.
  • Relative — qui, que, dont, où.
  • Interrogative — qui, que, quoi, quel, lequel, où.

Tap a class to switch it on or off; each row shows its size and the first few pronouns. Tap ⓘ to read about the class and see all its pronouns; tap one to open it.

iPhoneiPadMac

docs.title: Pronoun grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A reference page; nothing is recorded.

Subject pronouns — je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles. French verb endings are mostly silent, so the subject pronoun is required: parle on its own doesn't say who is speaking.

  • tu is informal singular; vous is plural, or formal singular. When in doubt, use vous.
  • on literally means "one", but in everyday French it usually means "we": on y va ("let's go"). It always takes a third-person singular verb.
  • il / ils and elle / elles follow grammatical gender, not only people: la table… elle est grande. A mixed group is ils.
  • je becomes j' before a vowel: j'aime.

Object and reflexive pronouns go before the conjugated verb: je le vois, elle me parle.

  • Direct object: me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les. Le and la become l' before a vowel: je l'aime.
  • Indirect object ("to …"): me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur. Lui means both "to him" and "to her".
  • Reflexive: me, te, se, nous, vous, se — se serves every third person: il se lave, elles se lavent.

Watch out: le, la, les are also articles and leur is also a possessive. Before a verb they are pronouns (je les vois); before a noun they are not (les livres, leur maison).

Ce, ceci, cela, ça. Ce is the neutral pronoun of c'est / ce sont. Ceci and cela point at an idea or a situation; ça is the everyday spoken form of cela (ça va ?). Celui, celle, ceux, celles replace a noun already mentioned and agree with it; they never stand alone but take -ci, -là, de or a relative clause: celui de mon frère.

Indefinites. quelqu'un / personne (someone / no one), quelque chose / rien (something / nothing), tout (everything). Personne and rien go with ne: je ne vois personne. In a short answer they stand alone: Qui est là ? — Personne.

Possessive pronouns replace a noun and carry the article: le mien, la tienne, les nôtres. They agree with the thing owned, not with the owner. Don't confuse them with the possessive determiners mon / ma / mes, which go with a noun.

Relative pronouns. The choice between qui and que depends on the pronoun's role, not on people or things:

  • qui is the subject of the relative clause: le livre qui est sur la table.
  • que is the object: le livre que je lis. It becomes qu' before a vowel.
  • dont replaces de + something: l'ami dont je parle, le livre dont j'ai besoin (from avoir besoin de).
  • où covers place and time: la ville où j'habite, le jour où il est arrivé.

Asking. Qui asks about people (Qui vient ?), que about things (Que fais-tu ?), and quoi is used after a preposition or on its own (De quoi parles-tu ?). Quel agrees with its noun (quelle heure) and lequel replaces one (laquelle préfères-tu ?). Everyday French often uses est-ce que: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?

docs.text:

A browse-only list of the selected pronouns with their translations, in sections by class, with a search field. Nothing is recorded.

Tap a pronoun to open its page: the pronoun and its translation, its Class, and its Level (with its frequency).

docs.title: Pronoun meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the meaning of the selected pronouns, in either direction. It works like Noun meaning. Every answer is recorded.

docs.title: Which pronoun?
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Each question shows an English sentence with the pronoun in bold and a label — Direct object, Indirect object or Reflexive — and the French sentence with a gap before the verb. Tap one of four pronouns — the right form and three other object forms from your pool:

  • Elle ___ voit. — "She sees me." → me
  • Elle ___ donne un cadeau. — "She gives him a gift." → lui
  • Nous ___ donnons les clés. — "We give them the keys." → leur
  • Ils ___ lavent. — "They wash themselves." → se

After you answer, the right pronoun is marked and a card explains why — for example that téléphoner à quelqu'un takes an indirect object, so "I telephone her" is je lui téléphone. Tap Next to go on.

Every sentence has a single pronoun before a verb that starts with a consonant, so you never have to elide in the gap; the explanations mention m', t', l' and s' where they apply. Answers are recorded per slot and person, so the combinations you miss come back more often. The drill needs the Personal class to be ticked in Select pronoun groups; without it the drill tells you to add it.

docs.title: Agreement drill
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Each question shows a noun with its article, its gender and number, and its translation — for example les voitures (f.pl), "cars" — and asks Which form of celui goes with this noun? Tap the form that agrees: here celles. The pronouns drilled are the ones that change for gender and number: celui, celui-ci, celui-là, the six possessives (le mien … le leur), quel, lequel and aucun. Where two forms are the same, as in les nôtres, the drill shows the form once. Aucun is only asked with a singular noun.

The drill follows your class selection: only the ticked classes that agree with a noun — demonstratives, possessives, interrogatives, indefinites — feed it, and with none of them ticked it says so. Answers are recorded per pronoun.

docs.title: A. French verb groups
docs.text:
Every French verb belongs to one of three classic groups, set by its infinitive: the regular -er verbs (1st group), the regular -ir verbs with -iss- (2nd group), and everything else (3rd group). LinguaMorpha builds on those three with groups for spelling changes, stem changes, the auxiliary and irregularity. The groups decide what you drill (Self Study → Verbs → Select groups) and appear as coloured badges on each verb. A verb can belong to more than one group: manger is in 1st group (-er), Spelling -ger (mangeons) and Auxiliary avoir.

Select verb groups shows the groups below in five sections. Each row shows how many verbs it holds, and the ⓘ button opens an explanation with the verbs in that group. The catalogue holds over 900 verbs.

docs.title: 1st group (-er)
docs.text: The regular -er verbs: parler, aimer, donner. By far the largest family, and almost every newly coined French verb joins it. The stem is the infinitive minus -er (parler → parl-). An -er verb with a stem change, such as acheter or préférer, is not in this row but only in its own group below. A verb with only a spelling adjustment, such as manger or commencer, is in this row and in its spelling group as well. Aller looks like an -er verb, but it belongs to the 3rd group, and in the app it is under Fully irregular.

docs.title: 2nd group (-ir / -iss-)
docs.text: The regular -ir verbs that insert -iss- between stem and ending in the plural of the present, throughout the imparfait, in the present subjonctif and in the present participle: finir → nous finissons, je finissais, que je finisse, finissant. Other examples: choisir, réussir, grandir.

docs.title: 3rd group (-re / -ir / -oir)
docs.text: Everything that fits neither of the first two groups: the -re verbs (prendre, vendre, mettre), the -oir verbs (recevoir, prévoir, émouvoir) and the -ir verbs without -iss- (partir, dormir, ouvrir). The verbs in Fully irregular (être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, venir and the others) belong to the 3rd group too, but this row leaves them out. There is no single present-tense pattern: each verb has its own present forms. What the 3rd group shares with the other two is the endings of the imparfait, the futur simple and the conditionnel présent.

docs.title: Pronominal
docs.text: Verbs used with a reflexive pronoun: se laver, se lever, s'asseoir. Pronominal is not a fourth group. The verb keeps its own group and conjugates as it would without the pronoun: se laver → je me lave (1st group), se réjouir → je me réjouis (2nd group), se battre → je me bats (3rd group). All pronominal verbs take être in the compound tenses.

docs.title: Spelling
docs.text: 1st-group verbs whose spelling changes in some forms, while the sound stays the same.

docs.title: Spelling -ger (mangeons)
docs.text: -ger verbs keep an e before an ending that begins with a or o, so that the g stays soft: nous mangeons, je mangeais, il mangea, en mangeant. Other examples: voyager, changer, nager.

docs.title: Spelling -cer (commençons)
docs.text: -cer verbs write ç before a or o, so that the c stays soft: nous commençons, je commençais, il commença. Before e and i nothing changes: nous commencions. Other examples: lancer, placer, avancer.

docs.title: Spelling -yer (essaie)
docs.text: -yer verbs change y to i before a silent e: j'essaie, tu essaies, il essaie, ils essaient, but nous essayons, vous essayez. The i runs through the futur and the conditionnel (j'essaierai). -ayer verbs allow both spellings (je paie and je paye); -oyer and -uyer verbs always take the i (j'emploie, j'appuie).

docs.title: Stem Changes
docs.text: 1st-group verbs whose stem changes in the forms with a silent ending: je, tu, il, ils in the present, and the same persons of the present subjonctif. Nous and vous keep the stem of the infinitive.

docs.title: Stem e → è (achète)
docs.text: An e in the last syllable of the stem becomes è: lever → je lève, nous levons. Other examples: mener, peser, se promener. The è also appears throughout the futur and the conditionnel: je lèverai.

docs.title: Stem é → è (préfère)
docs.text: An é in the last syllable of the stem becomes è: préférer → je préfère, nous préférons. Other examples: espérer, répéter, céder.

docs.title: Doubled consonant (appelle, jette)
docs.text: The -eler and -eter verbs. Most double the l or t instead of writing an accent: appeler → j'appelle, nous appelons; jeter → je jette, nous jetons. This group holds only the -eler and -eter verbs that double the consonant. The few that take è instead, such as acheter → j'achète and geler → je gèle, are in Stem e → è (achète). The conjugation tables show each verb's actual forms.

docs.title: Auxiliary
docs.text: Which auxiliary the verb takes in the compound tenses (passé composé, plus-que-parfait, futur antérieur, conditionnel passé, …).

docs.title: Auxiliary avoir
docs.text: Most verbs form their compound tenses with avoir: j'ai parlé, j'avais parlé, j'aurai parlé. The past participle does not agree with the subject (elle a parlé). It agrees only with a direct object that comes before the verb: je l'ai vue, les lettres que j'ai écrites.

docs.title: Auxiliary être
docs.text:
A closed set of verbs of movement and change of state take être: aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, rester, tomber, naître, mourir, devenir and compounds such as revenir. So do all pronominal verbs. With être, the past participle agrees with the subject: il est parti, elle est partie, ils sont partis. With a pronominal verb, the participle agrees with the reflexive pronoun when that pronoun is the direct object: elle s'est lavée, but elle s'est lavé les mains.

Six verbs take either auxiliary, depending on the sentence: monter, descendre, sortir, ressortir, passer, retourner. Without a direct object they take être (elle est sortie); with one they take avoir (elle a sorti la voiture). These six appear in both auxiliary groups. The conjugation tables show the être forms, and the verb's details carry the note with a direct object → avoir.

docs.title: Fully irregular
docs.text: The 3rd-group verbs that follow no pattern and have to be learned verb by verb: être, avoir, aller, faire, dire, pouvoir, vouloir, savoir, valoir, devoir, voir, mourir, s'asseoir and the impersonal falloir and pleuvoir. The verbs conjugated like faire (défaire, satisfaire), venir (devenir, revenir, se souvenir) and tenir (obtenir, maintenir) are here too, and so are the expressions built on any of them (avoir besoin de, faire partie de). About fifty verbs in all. They are not in 3rd group (-re / -ir / -oir).

docs.title: Subjonctif irrégulier
docs.text: For almost every French verb, the present subjonctif is built from the ils form of the present: ils finissent → que je finisse. The verbs in this group have a subjonctif stem of their own, which you have to learn: être (que je sois), avoir (que j'aie), aller (que j'aille), faire (que je fasse), pouvoir (que je puisse), savoir (que je sache), vouloir (que je veuille), valoir (que je vaille), falloir (qu'il faille). The group also includes défaire, refaire, pleuvoir and se souvenir de.

docs.title: B. French verb tenses
docs.text: LinguaMorpha offers sixteen tenses, grouped by mood in Self Study → Verbs → Select tenses. You can switch each one on or off, and the Tenses page under Theory explains when each is used and how it is built.

docs.title: Présent
docs.text: Current or general actions: je parle, tu parles, il parle.

docs.title: Imparfait
docs.text: Ongoing or habitual past, descriptions and background: je parlais. Built on the stem of the nous form of the present, plus -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient (nous finissons → je finissais). The only exception is être: j'étais.

docs.title: Futur Simple
docs.text: Future actions, predictions and promises: je parlerai. The endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont go on the infinitive (the -re verbs drop their final e: prendre → je prendrai). Some 3rd-group verbs have an irregular future stem: aller → j'irai, venir → je viendrai, être → je serai, avoir → j'aurai, faire → je ferai.

docs.title: Passé Simple
docs.text: The literary simple past: il parla, il finit, il vint. It is found in novels, formal essays and historical texts, but hardly ever in spoken French, where the passé composé takes its place. You need it for reading.

docs.title: Passé Composé
docs.text: The everyday spoken past, for completed actions: avoir or être in the present + past participle (j'ai parlé, elle est allée).

docs.title: Plus-que-parfait
docs.text: The past before the past: auxiliary in the imparfait + past participle (j'avais parlé, elle était partie).

docs.title: Futur Antérieur
docs.text: An action that will be completed before another future event: auxiliary in the futur simple + past participle (j'aurai parlé).

docs.title: Passé Antérieur
docs.text: Auxiliary in the passé simple + past participle (j'eus parlé, il fut parti). A literary tense that goes with the passé simple: it appears after quand, lorsque, dès que or après que in a narrative whose main verb is in the passé simple. You will mostly meet it in reading.

docs.title: Conditionnel Présent
docs.text: Hypothetical actions, polite requests, and the consequence in an if-sentence: je parlerais. The future stem + the imparfait endings. Si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais.

docs.title: Conditionnel Passé
docs.text: What would have happened: auxiliary in the conditionnel présent + past participle (j'aurais parlé). Si j'avais su, je l'aurais dit.

docs.title: Impératif Présent
docs.text: Commands, instructions and invitations: parle ! parlons ! parlez ! There are only three forms (tu, nous, vous), and no subject pronoun. The forms come from the present, but 1st-group verbs drop the final -s of the tu form (parle, not parles). Être (sois, soyons, soyez), avoir (aie, ayons, ayez) and aller (va, allons, allez) have their own forms.

docs.title: Impératif Passé
docs.text: Auxiliary in the impératif + past participle (aie parlé, sois parti). It orders something to be finished by a given moment: Aie fini avant midi (have it done before noon). Rare, and like the impératif présent it has only the tu, nous and vous forms.

docs.title: Subjonctif
docs.text: The subjonctif expresses what is wished, feared, needed or uncertain, and nearly always follows que.

docs.title: Subjonctif Présent
docs.text: Il faut que tu parles, bien qu'elle soit fatiguée.

docs.title: Subjonctif Passé
docs.text: Auxiliary in the subjonctif présent + past participle, when the action in the que clause is completed: je doute qu'elle soit arrivée, bien qu'il ait travaillé.

docs.title: Subjonctif Imparfait
docs.text: The literary counterpart of the subjonctif présent, found in formal writing and classic literature: il voulait qu'elle parlât, que je parlasse.

docs.title: Subjonctif Plus-que-parfait
docs.text: Auxiliary in the subjonctif imparfait + past participle: que j'eusse parlé. Rarer still, and literary. In formal style it can also replace the conditionnel passé: j'eusse préféré for j'aurais préféré.

docs.title: Setting up French speech
docs.text: iPhoneiPadMac

docs.title: Why this matters (French)
docs.text:
The voices are Apple's, not LinguaMorpha's. The app speaks through the text-to-speech engine built into iOS, iPadOS and macOS. It can only use voices already installed on your device. It has no voices of its own and cannot improve Apple's.

Apple offers French voices at three quality levels: Standard, Enhanced and Premium. Standard voices sound robotic. Enhanced and Premium voices sound far more natural and are strongly recommended for language learning. They are free, and once you download one, every app on the device can use it.

docs.title: Downloading a better French voice
docs.text:
You do this in Apple's settings, not in LinguaMorpha:

  1. On iPhone or iPad, open the Settings app and go to Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices → French. On the Mac, open System Settings and go to Accessibility → Spoken Content → System Voice → Manage Voices.
  2. Choose the region whose accent you want to learn (France, Canada, and so on).
  3. Download a voice marked Enhanced or Premium. These are large downloads, so use Wi-Fi.

Apple sometimes moves these settings between OS versions. If the path above doesn't match your device, search its settings for "Voices".

docs.title: Choosing the voice and speed in LinguaMorpha
docs.text:
• iPhone and iPad — open the ⋯ menu on the Home screen, choose Settings, and switch to the French tab. Under Voice & Conjugation, tap Voice. The French Voice screen lists the voices, and below them is the Speaking Speed slider, from Slowest to Fastest.
  • Mac — open LinguaMorpha's Settings and choose the French tab. The Voice menu and the Speed slider are right there.

Only voices already installed on your device appear. Each one shows its region's flag, its name and its quality (Premium, Enhanced or Standard). Voices for France come first, then the other French-speaking regions, with the best quality first in each group. Until you choose a voice, the app uses the best-quality voice for France on your device. If no French voice is installed, the screen tells you where to download one.

Speed is one setting for all spoken languages; Latin is the exception and always plays at its own slower pace. The slider goes slightly faster than normal at the top end. On the Mac, the speed starts a little slower than on iPhone and iPad, because Mac voices speak faster.

Include pronoun, in the same section, adds je / tu / il… before each form when a conjugation table is read aloud. The pronoun follows the form, so you hear j'ouvre, not je ouvre. It is on by default.

LinguaMorpha reads the French side with the voice you choose here. The English, Dutch or Spanish side of a flashcard is read by your device's standard voice for that language.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Traps holds closed decks of things that mislead — not vocabulary you select, but a hazard list you work through once and revisit. In French the hub has one deck so far: Meaning changes with gender, the nouns that are two words sharing a spelling — le tour is a turn, la tour a tower; le voile a veil, la voile a sail. The Study row Meaning-changers reference lists them with both senses side by side; the Practice row drills each form as its own card, the article on the front and the sense of that exact form on the back. The deck brings its own nouns: nothing is selected first, and your level is the only filter. Open it from Self Study → Traps (iPhone, iPad) or the Traps item in the Mac sidebar.

The same nouns also appear in Alternate gender pairs under Nouns, as pairs; here they are drilled sense by sense.

docs.title: Verbs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open Self Study → Verbs to reach the verbs hub. The card at the top reads "Conjugations, meanings, and translations" and shows how many verbs your current selection gives you out of the whole catalogue. Its Help button explains the hub. A long press on a row (on the Mac, press and hold) explains that row.

If your verb groups select verbs but your level and topics remove all of them, a warning appears at the top of Practice: "No verbs match once your topic scope is applied." Widen your topics or clear the topic filter to get the verbs back.

The hub has three sections.

Theory

  • Verb groups — how the three French groups differ, a card for each verb group, the compound families and how the conjugation tables mark irregular forms, and Regular patterns to print. See Verb groups.
  • Tenses — when each tense is used, how it is built and what it looks like. See Tenses.

Study

  • Reference (Verb reference) — every verb in your selection with its translation. Tap a verb for its full conjugation, usage and structure. See Verb reference and Conjugation tables.

Practice

  • Select groups (Select verb groups) — pick the conjugation patterns to drill, and with them the verbs in your pool. The badge shows how many of the groups in your level are ticked, e.g. "14 of 14", and turns red at zero. See Select verb groups.
  • Select tenses — pick which of the tenses in your level to study, e.g. "16 of 16". See Select tenses.

Groups and tenses above your level are not offered, so at a low level these counts are smaller.

  • Meaning (Verb meaning)
  • Produce the conjugation
  • Recognise the conjugation
  • Passé composé or imparfait
  • Indicatif or subjonctif
  • Être or avoir

Each drill has its own section in this guide.

docs.title: Studying verbs goes in three steps
docs.text:
1. Choose what to study. In Select groups, tick the patterns you want. In Select tenses, narrow to the tenses you are learning: the conjugation tables and the drills then show only those. Your level comes from Scheme and level (tap the flag) and the topics from Self Study → Select word scope; set your level to A1 to start with the most common verbs.
  2. Study. Read Verb groups and Tenses under Theory, then open verbs in Reference to see their tables before you drill them.
  3. Drill. Warm up with Meaning so you know what the verbs mean, then move to Produce the conjugation and Recognise the conjugation. Add tenses one at a time as each becomes solid; imparfait and passé composé are the most useful after présent. For the forms that break the pattern, see Irregularity by tense; use the choice drills once the forms are secure.

docs.title: The three verb groups
docs.text:
Every French verb belongs to one of three groups, set by its infinitive and how it conjugates.

  • 1st group — -er (parler, aimer, travailler) — by far the largest and most regular group. Aller looks like a member but belongs to the 3rd group.
  • 2nd group — -ir with the -iss- infix (finir, choisir, réussir) — regular -ir verbs that insert -iss- in the plural of the present and throughout the imperfect (nous finissons, je finissais).
  • 3rd group — everything else (aller, faire, prendre, venir, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, voir) — the -re and -oir verbs and the -ir verbs that take no -iss-. Many follow a pattern of their own; this is where most of the memorising is.

The three groups take different endings in only two tenses, the présent and the passé simple. In the imparfait, futur simple and conditionnel présent all three take the same endings.

Compound tenses (passé composé, plus-que-parfait, …) are built with an auxiliary: avoir for most verbs, être for a short list of verbs of movement and change of state (aller, venir, arriver, partir, naître, mourir, devenir, …) and for all pronominal verbs. A few verbs, such as monter, descendre, sortir and passer, take avoir when they have a direct object. With être, the past participle agrees with the subject.

docs.title: The conjugation colour code (French)
docs.text:
The conjugation tables mark each form so you can see where a verb departs from its group's pattern, and by how much. French uses the same three marks as the other courses, and each mark means one thing.

Underline — the regular ending. The ending is underlined where it is the one the pattern predicts: parlons. It appears on irregular forms too, because most irregular forms are irregular only in the stem.

Red on part of a form — something changed. Only the part that departs is red, and a regular ending is still underlined. For example:

  • Stem changes and spelling adjustments: in acheter, the present j'achète has the è in red, while nous achetons has no red because its stem does not change. Manger → nous mangeons and commencer → nous commençons show the adjusted letter in red.
  • Irregular future stems: faire → je ferai has the e in red, and the ending -ai is underlined.
  • Group-3 présent: only the part of the stem that changes is red. Pouvoir → nous pouvons has no red at all: pouv- is the stem the infinitive gives, and -ons is underlined.
  • Strong passé simple stems: the stem is red and the ending underlined, as in boire → je bus.

Red across the whole form — completely irregular. The form has no systematic connection to the pattern and must be learned as a whole: the présent of être (je suis, nous sommes), avoir (ils ont) and aller (je vais, ils vont).

Compound tenses. The auxiliary is never marked; the past participle carries the mark. An irregular participle such as pris, mis or ouvert is red in every compound tense. A regular one (parlé, fini, entendu) has its last letter underlined.

Blue marks an ending from a second set of endings in the other courses. French has one set per group, so blue never appears in French tables.

docs.title: Passé composé or imparfait
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Spoken French has two everyday past tenses, the passé composé and the imparfait. The choice between them is not about when something happened but about how you look at it: as a completed event, or as something ongoing, habitual or in the background. The conjugation drills tell you which tense to use; this drill asks you to choose it.

How a question looks. Under the instruction "Choose the tense", the card shows the sentence in your language, with a badge naming the principle at work. Below it comes the French sentence with a gap:

While I was reading, the telephone rang. Interruption French: Pendant que je lisais, le téléphone ___.

The two options are the same verb in the two tenses (a sonné / sonnait). Tap one: it fills the gap, the right answer gets a tick, and a card explains the choice ("Why a sonné?"). Read it even when you were right. Then tap Next; after the last one, See results.

The three kinds of question.

  • A time marker points the way. Hier, l'été dernier, tout à coup and a counted number of times (trois fois) go with the passé composé (Completed event). Quand j'étais enfant, toujours, tous les matins and English "used to" go with the imparfait (Habitual / ongoing). Descriptions, the weather, clock time and age in the past take the imparfait (Description).
  • A scene and an event. Pendant que je lisais, le téléphone a sonné. The imparfait sets the scene (Backdrop); the passé composé is the event that cuts into it (Interruption). A series of events is told in the passé composé (Chain of events). A period with clear limits is still a completed event: J'ai habité à Paris pendant trois ans (Closed duration).
  • The verb changes meaning (Meaning changes). A few verbs mean something different in each tense. The French sentence is the same for both options, so the sentence in your language is your only clue:
Passé composé Imparfait j'ai connu — I met je connaissais — I knew j'ai su — I found out je savais — I knew il a voulu — he tried il voulait — he wanted elle n'a pas voulu — she refused elle ne voulait pas — she didn't want to j'ai pu — I managed to je pouvais — I was able to j'ai dû — I had to (and did) je devais — I was supposed to j'ai eu — I got, received j'avais — I had il y a eu — there was (it happened) il y avait — there was (it existed)

What's recorded. Each principle is recorded separately, so a principle you keep missing, such as Backdrop, comes back more often. The Incorrect answers switch limits a session to the principles you have got wrong before.

docs.title: Être or avoir
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Every compound tense needs an auxiliary, and in French it is either avoir or être. The conjugation drills supply the whole compound form, auxiliary included; this drill asks you to choose the auxiliary.

How a question looks. Under the instruction "Choose the auxiliary", the card shows the sentence in your language, with a badge naming the rule at work. Below it comes the French sentence with a gap:

She came at eight o'clock. Movement French: Elle ___ venue à huit heures.

The two options are the two auxiliaries in the right person (est / a, sommes / avons). The participle is already written, and already agrees where it must (venue), so the auxiliary is the only thing asked. Tap one to answer; a card then explains the choice.

The four rules in the deck.

  • Movement — the short list of verbs of movement and change of state that take être: aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester, tomber, naître, mourir and their relatives (revenir, devenir). J'ai allé is the most common auxiliary mistake in French.
  • Pronominal — every verb with me, te, se … takes être, with no exceptions: je me suis levé, elle s'est lavé les mains, even though laver on its own takes avoir. The pronoun is the clue.
  • Takes an object — monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer and passer take être on their own and avoir with a direct object, and the meaning shifts: il est sorti (he went out), il a sorti la poubelle (he took out the bin); elle est montée (she went up), elle a monté la valise (she carried the suitcase up). The French sentences look almost the same, so the object and the sentence in your language decide.
  • Ordinary verb — everything else takes avoir: j'ai mangé, elle a fini, nous avons dormi. It also covers verbs of movement that are not on the list: il a marché, elle a voyagé, j'ai couru.

Almost half the answers are avoir. A deck where être was always right would teach you to answer être by default.

What's recorded. Each rule is recorded separately, so a rule you keep missing, such as Takes an object, comes back more often.

docs.title: Produce the conjugation
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The production drill. You get a verb, a tense and a person, and you give the conjugated form.

How a question looks. The card reads "Type the correct form for" (or "Pick the correct form for"), then the infinitive in large type, then two rows, Tense and Person.

Type the correct form for venir Tense: Futur Simple Person: nous

The questions come from the verbs and tenses in your selection (Select verb groups and Select tenses). Narrowing the selection is how you work on one thing: one tense across many verbs, or one verb group in a single tense.

The two icons on the card.

  • The book appears once your answer is graded. It opens the verb's table for the tense that was asked — in a sheet on iPhone and iPad, in a window of its own on the Mac that you can move aside — and closes when you go on to the next question.
  • The speaker pronounces the infinitive.

Type and Pick. Switch with the Type / Pick control above the card. You can switch at any time; the current answer is cleared when you do.

  • Type — type the form without the subject pronoun and tap Check (or press Return, or tap the arrow in the field). Pressing Return with an empty field moves on to a new question.
  • Pick — choose the form from a wheel of up to ten options, then tap Check. The wrong options are the same verb in other persons and in your other selected tenses, forms of similar-looking verbs from your selection, and the form the verb would have if it were regular. When the answer has two words (avons parlé), most options share the auxiliary, so you have to judge the participle itself.

Feedback. After Check, a feedback card appears and the button becomes Next.

  • Correct (green) — shows the verb's translation, or a translation of the exact form you were asked for ("we will come").
  • Accent: … (green) — the right letters, but an accent or cedilla is missing, extra or wrong. This counts as correct; the card shows the correct spelling.
  • The answer is … (red) — wrong. If what you gave is a real form of some verb, the card also says what it was and shows two tables: the tense your answer belongs to, with your form in red, and the tense that was asked, with the right form in blue. Otherwise it shows only the table with the right form.

Accent applies only in Type mode and only while Exact spelling is off (Settings → Study → Grading; off by default). It never applies when what you typed is another form of the same verb: parle for parlé is a different form, so it is wrong. With Exact spelling on, only the exact form counts.

French has no typo allowance: a wrong letter other than an accent is wrong. The spellings of the 1990 reform count as plain correct in the futur simple and conditionnel présent, with no correction: je cèderai is accepted as well as je céderai.

The translation of the exact form comes from the app's own translations. Where there is none, devices with Apple Intelligence (iOS 26 and macOS 26) can supply one.

Skip. The Skip button always moves to a new question without recording anything.

Production settings.

iPhoneiPadMac

The gear button opens Production settings, where you can restrict the drill to chosen values of Verb, Tense and Person. Leave an axis empty to let it vary freely; Clear all restrictions undoes them all.

The session. The line at the top counts your answers ("7 out of 9 correct"), and the bar under it shows your success rate. The Incorrect answers switch limits the session to questions you have got wrong before. A session ends after Settings → Study → Questions per session. The verbs are picked from your selection, based on your answer history and your Learning pace. After seven correct answers in a row, the app offers to stop there: Continue or Stop — session complete.

What's recorded. Every checked answer is recorded on your device. Answers with only an accent wrong count as correct. Skipped questions are not recorded.

Suggested workflow.

  1. Start in Pick mode while a tense is new.
  2. Switch to Type once the endings look familiar: Pick lets you eliminate options, Type makes you recall the form.
  3. Alternate sessions with Recognise the conjugation. Here you produce a form; there you name the form you are given.

docs.title: Conjugation tables
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Tap any verb in Verb reference to open its page. The same page opens from a verb group's Browse all verbs list and from Look up. The verb's infinitive is the title.

The header

Above the tabs you see what the verb means and what kind of verb it is:

  • the translation of the infinitive (on the Mac, beside the infinitive in the title bar);
  • Extended meaning, folded away — for a verb with several distinct senses, a numbered list of them. It goes with the translations: a scheme that shows none hides it too;
  • the verb's level, beside the group badges: the verb groups it belongs to, such as 1st group (-er), Stem e → è (achète) or Auxiliary être. They are coloured by section: grey for Basic, blue for Spelling, red for Stem Changes, purple for Auxiliary, orange for Fully irregular and mint for Subjonctif irrégulier. Tap a badge to open the group's card, with its explanation, a worked example and Browse all verbs with the number of verbs in the group. In that list a verb family is one row — prendre with +N for apprendre, comprendre and the others built on it; tap the row to see the family.
  • for a verb built on another — revenir on venir, prédire on dire — a family note: "Belongs to the family of dire, with interdire, maudire". Where the verb departs from its base the note says so, form by form: prédire follows dire except in vous prédisez, not vous prédites. On the base verb the note lists the members, and adds "Learn this verb and you have them all" when none of them departs, as on venir.

Below that are three tabs: Conjugation · Regularity · Reference sheet. The page opens on Conjugation.

Conjugation

The Conjugation tab starts with a card of the non-finite forms: Present participle, Past participle, Past infinitive and Perfect participle (parlant, parlé, avoir parlé, ayant parlé). Below it comes one table per tense, for the tenses of your level. If your level has none, the tab tells you so. Each table is headed by its tense and mood and lists the persons with their forms. Under the tense's name a line says what the tense is for, and under the table is the verb's own sentence in that tense, with its translation and a speaker button. On its header, the book icon opens that tense's theory — when it is used, how it is formed, its endings — and the speaker icon reads the whole tense aloud. The forms are marked as described in The conjugation colour code (French).

By Tense / By Person. A picker above the tables switches the view. By Tense shows one table per tense, as above. By Person turns them around: one panel per person — je, tu, … — listing that person's form in every tense, with the tense name above each form, so you can follow how one person's ending changes from tense to tense. The mood is named where it changes. The speaker on a panel reads that person through all the tenses. The choice is remembered across verbs.

Only irregular tenses. The filter button in the toolbar shows only the tenses where this verb departs from the pattern. The choice is remembered across verbs, and per device. While it hides tenses, a note above the tables says so — "Only irregular tenses: 4 of 16 shown." — with Show all tenses to switch it off.

Why a tense departs. Under the table of a tense where the verb departs is a fold-out, labelled with the verdict — Partly irregular, Regular endings, changed stem. Open, it gives the reason in a sentence, the stems the tense is built on (a stem to learn in amber), and for each person that departs the form the pattern predicts, struck through, beside the real one.

Pronominal verbs are shown with their pronoun (je me lève). In the affirmative impératif the pronoun follows the verb (lève-toi). Impersonal verbs such as falloir and pleuvoir are conjugated only in the il form.

The eye button in the toolbar shows a translation under every conjugated form. French has written translations for almost every verb. For verbs with a second meaning, a second button switches all the translations on the page to that meaning. The book icon in the toolbar looks the verb up in online dictionaries.

Regularity

The tab starts with a card of facts about how the verb is built: its Auxiliary (avoir, être, or avoir / être with the note "with a direct object → avoir") and, for a verb with se, its Form (pronominal).

Regularity answers one question: where does this verb depart from the regular pattern? It lists only the tenses where it does, in the usual tense order. Each row has a coloured dot and a verdict: Regular endings, changed stem, Regular endings, learned form, Partly irregular, Irregular or No regular pattern. Under a partly irregular tense, the persons that depart are listed.

Under each tense is the stem it is built on. A stem you have to learn, such as viendr- for the future of venir, is in amber. So is a single form that carries a whole tense, such as the participle pris for the compound tenses of prendre. That is why those compound tenses read Regular endings, learned form: the auxiliary is regular, and the participle is the thing to learn. The two colours answer different questions. Amber on Regularity names a whole stem or form to memorise; red on Conjugation marks the letters of one form that departed.

A last line names the tenses that follow the pattern (Regular in the other tenses: …); a verb with nothing to learn shows only Regular in all tenses. Tap a tense to go to it on Conjugation, with its explanation open under the table.

Reference sheet

iPhoneiPadMac

Reference sheet is a printable one-page PDF of the verb in every tense, whatever you have selected, with the same marks as the tables. Its header gives the verb's group and auxiliary. The sheet lists the non-finite forms, the simple and compound tenses of the indicatif, and the subjonctif and impératif side by side. The compound tenses show the auxiliary's forms with the participle once beside them. On iPhone and iPad, the share button sends, saves or prints the sheet; on the Mac, the toolbar menu offers Copy and Save as….

Regular patterns

iPhoneiPadMac

Regular patterns, at the bottom of the Verb groups page under To print, is the other printable page: the regular endings of all sixteen tenses at once, grouped by mood — indicatif, conditionnel, subjonctif, impératif — with the simple tenses before the compound ones. A simple tense gives its endings per group, -er, -ir and -re where they differ and one column where they agree; a compound tense gives the auxiliary, avoir or être, with the participle.

It is the regular pattern only. An irregular verb keeps most of these endings on a stem of its own; its Reference sheet shows where. The tables are the ones in the tense cards on Tenses — one tense at a time there, all sixteen here.

Tip: In Produce the conjugation and Recognise the conjugation, once your answer is graded a book icon on the card shows the verb's table for that tense. This is useful right after a wrong answer.

docs.title: Irregularity by tense
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The verbs that break the pattern, tense by tense. This screen is Irregularity by tense: open Linguistic analysis on the Home screen and tap Irregularity by tense. It is also where the drill for a single tense starts.

One row per tense: how many things there are to learn there — a family of verbs that share one stem counts once, and so does a verb on its own — and the share of its verbs that are not fully predictable. Tenses that hold exactly the same verbs are folded into one row, and the row says what they share — the compound tenses all rest on the same past participles. A cap beside the number means there is a drill behind the row.

Opening a row lists those verbs. From there:

  • tapping a verb opens its page at that tense, with the explanation of why it departs open under the table (for a folded row, at the first of its tenses);
  • Practise starts Produce the conjugation over exactly the irregular verbs on the list, in that tense;
  • Cycle through randomly shows one verb's conjugation at a time in that tense and walks every verb on the list, in the order shown.

The order menu in the toolbar sets the order of the list:

  • By pattern — the default. The verbs are grouped under the patterns that explain how the tense is formed.
  • By reason — the verbs are grouped by what departs: The stem differs, The ending differs, and The stem and the ending differ for a verb that departs in both. Each row shows the stem the verb takes in that tense, such as viendr- for the futur of venir, and beside it, as a + number, how many more verbs of its family share that stem. At the top, the box Fewer than the numbers suggest shows how much there really is to learn: a family of verbs that share one stem counts once, and so does a verb on its own.
  • Alphabetical — the verbs from A to Z.

The filter button in the toolbar is on when the list opens: it shows the irregular verbs only. Switch it off with Show all verbs and the list shows every verb in your level, from A to Z, each opening at that tense; only the irregular verbs show the explanation of why they depart. Show irregular verbs only switches the filter back on. Practise and the drills keep to the irregular verbs. With all verbs shown, the order menu is hidden.

What the list shows.

  • The rows follow the order of the tenses in the app.
  • A tense needs at least three irregular verbs before the cap appears; the row itself is always there.
  • The verbs come from the whole catalogue, not from your verb selection.

The first time you open the screen it scans the catalogue, which takes a moment ("Scanning the catalogue…").

docs.title: Indicatif or subjonctif
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

French uses the subjonctif after certain words and in certain kinds of clause. The conjugation drills give you the mood; this drill asks you when it is needed.

How a question looks. Under the instruction "Choose the mood", the card shows the sentence in your language, with a badge naming the trigger at work (Belief, Doubt / denial, Volition, Emotion, …). Below it comes the French sentence with a gap. The two options are the same verb in the indicatif and in the subjonctif (vient / vienne). Tap one to answer; a card then explains the choice.

A que is not a trigger. About a third of the answers in this drill are the indicatif, on purpose. A drill where the answer is always the subjonctif only teaches you to spot que. The questions are built from minimal pairs: the same sentence with one thing changed, and a different mood.

Indicatif Subjonctif Je pense qu'il vient Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne Il est vrai qu'elle est malade Il n'est pas vrai qu'elle soit malade Parce qu'il est tard Bien qu'il soit tard Il est probable qu'il le sait Il est possible qu'il le sache Je cherche l'homme qui sait le russe Je cherche un homme qui sache le russe

What moves the mood is negation, the kind of judgement, and whether the thing referred to is known.

The trigger classes.

  • Always subjonctif: wanting (je veux que, elle voudrait que), emotion (je suis content que, j'ai peur que, c'est dommage que), doubt and denial (je doute que, je ne pense pas que), necessity (il faut que), and the conjunctions bien que, pour que, avant que and à moins que. A superlative takes it too: c'est le meilleur film que je connaisse.
  • Indicatif: statements of belief and fact, such as je pense que, il est vrai que, and j'espère que: French espérer takes the indicatif.
  • It depends: impersonal expressions split (il est possible que + subjonctif, but il est probable que and il paraît que + indicatif), and so do relative clauses (a known thing takes the indicatif, any thing that fits takes the subjonctif).
