A future event does not bring the subjonctif. Quand takes the indicatif, with the future for a future event: Appelle-moi quand tu partiras. Avant que takes the subjonctif whatever the time: Appelle-moi avant que tu partes. In the same way, a condition with si takes the indicatif (S'il pleut, nous resterons), while à moins que takes the subjonctif (Nous irons à moins qu'il ne pleuve).

What's recorded. Each trigger class is recorded separately, so a class you keep missing comes back more often.

docs.title: Recognise the conjugation
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The recognition drill, the reverse of Produce the conjugation. You see a conjugated form and say what it is: which verb, which tense and which person.

How a question looks. The form is shown in large type, with a speaker that pronounces it. Once you have checked, a book appears beside the form: it opens the table of the form's tense for its verb — in a window of its own on the Mac — and closes when you go on. Below the form are three pickers: VERB, TENSE and PERSON.

  • VERB offers the right verb among verbs whose spelling is similar. These come from the whole catalogue, not only from your selection.
  • TENSE offers the tenses you have selected in Select tenses.
  • PERSON offers all six persons.

The form is always a real form of a verb in your selection. Pronominal verbs are shown with their pronoun, so they can't be confused with the plain verb.

The action button changes with what you have done:

  • Skip — nothing picked yet. Moves to a new question without recording anything.
  • Check — all three pickers set. The button is disabled while only some of them are set.
  • Next — after checking.

Ambiguous forms. Many French forms have more than one reading. Parle is the je and the il/elle form of the présent, and also of the subjonctif présent. Finis is both présent and passé simple. Any valid reading counts as correct. After a correct answer, the feedback says Correct and lists Other valid analyses:, each with its table. After a wrong one, it says Not quite, marks which of your three picks were wrong, and shows Your answer: (the table your picks point to, in red) and then the Valid analyses: (in blue). The feedback also gives a translation of the form, where one is available.

Recognition settings.

iPhoneiPadMac

The gear button opens the settings:

  • Picker style — Chips (the default) or Wheel. Wheels take more room but are easier to scroll; chips are denser.
  • Multi-answer mode — instead of naming one reading, you collect every reading the form has. Set the pickers and tap Add this analysis for each one; your claims are listed and can be removed. Check then grades the whole set, and only the complete set counts as fully correct.
  • Test me on — switch Verb, Tense and Person on or off. A dimension you switch off is shown as a hint above the form, so you can start with the tense alone and add person and verb later. At least one must stay on.
  • Verb options (shown while Verb is tested) — how many verbs the VERB picker offers.

The session. The line at the top counts your answers ("7 / 9 correct"), with a bar showing your success rate. The Incorrect answers switch, the session length and the choice of verbs work as in Produce the conjugation. Each checked answer is recorded on your device; skipped questions are not.

When to use it. Recognition is the drill for reading: use it when you can produce the common forms but stumble over them in a text. It is also the way to meet the literary tenses, passé simple and subjonctif imparfait, which you will read far more often than you write. If it feels too hard, run Produce the conjugation in Pick mode first, then come back.

docs.title: Select tenses
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select tenses chooses which of the sixteen tenses you study. The choice applies everywhere verbs are practised: the conjugation tables show only the selected tenses, the example sentence under each tense on a verb's page follows it, and the conjugation drills ask only about those tenses.

The card at the top shows how many tenses are active, e.g. "16 of 16". Tap a row to include or exclude that tense. Each section header has an All / None button, and All | None at the top right selects or clears every tense at once. If you leave the screen with nothing selected, the app warns you ("No tenses selected").

By Section

The tenses are grouped by mood:

  • Indicatif – Temps Simples — Présent, Imparfait, Futur Simple.
  • Indicatif – Passé Simple — Passé Simple.
  • Indicatif – Temps Composés — Passé Composé, Plus-que-parfait, Futur Antérieur, Passé Antérieur.
  • Conditionnel — Conditionnel Présent, Conditionnel Passé.
  • Impératif — Impératif Présent, Impératif Passé.
  • Subjonctif — Subjonctif Présent, Subjonctif Passé, Subjonctif Imparfait, Subjonctif Plus-que-parfait.

Long-press a section header (on the Mac, press and hold) to read what that group of tenses is for.

By Level

The second view groups the same tenses by the level at which each first appears in the scheme you use:

Level Tenses A1 Présent, Passé Composé, Impératif Présent A2 Imparfait, Futur Simple B1 Plus-que-parfait, Conditionnel Présent, Subjonctif Présent B2 Futur Antérieur, Conditionnel Passé, Subjonctif Passé C1 Passé Simple, Passé Antérieur, Impératif Passé C2 Subjonctif Imparfait, Subjonctif Plus-que-parfait

The ⓘ on each tense

iPhoneiPadMac

Every tense row has an ⓘ. It opens the Tenses page, the same page as Tenses under Theory on the verbs hub, scrolled to that tense with its card open: an overview, when the tense is used, an example conjugation, example sentences and how the tense is formed. The other tenses are one tap away. On iPhone and iPad the page opens with a back button. On the Mac it opens in a window of its own, which can stay open beside the list; another ⓘ moves it to that tense.

Tip: Start with Présent alone. Add the others one at a time; Imparfait and Passé Composé are usually the next ones worth learning.

docs.title: Select verb groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select verb groups chooses which verbs you practise, by their grammatical character rather than one by one. The screen does not set level or topic: those are global. Your level is under Scheme and level (tap the flag), and the Select word scope row near the top takes you to the topics. Its second line says All topics or Filtered by topic.

The card at the top keeps a running count of what you have chosen, e.g. "14 of 14 groups · … · 212 in scope", with the number of selected verbs in the middle: how many groups are ticked, how many verbs those groups cover in the whole catalogue, and how many of those are left within your level and word scope. The last number is what the drills draw from.

Tap a row to tick or untick it. Each row shows how many verbs are in the group, and its ⓘ opens the group's card, with an explanation, a worked example and Browse all verbs. Each section header has an All / None button, and All | None at the top right ticks or clears every group at once.

If you leave the screen with nothing ticked, the app warns you ("No verb groups selected") and offers Stay and select or Go back anyway.

The groups

The 14 groups are listed under five sections. Only the groups in your level are shown: at A1 that is 1st group (-er) and Auxiliary avoir, and Fully irregular joins at B2.

Section Groups Basic 1st group (-er), 2nd group (-ir / -iss-), 3rd group (-re / -ir / -oir), Pronominal Spelling Spelling -ger (mangeons), Spelling -cer (commençons), Spelling -yer (essaie) Stem Changes Stem e → è (achète), Stem é → è (préfère), Doubled consonant (appelle, jette) Auxiliary Auxiliary avoir, Auxiliary être Irregular Fully irregular, Subjonctif irrégulier iPhoneiPadMac

Long-press a section header (on the Mac, press and hold) for an explanation of the whole section.

Some things to know about the groups:

  • 1st group (-er) and 2nd group (-ir / -iss-) hold the verbs that follow their group's pattern without stored exceptions. A 1st-group verb with a stem change, such as acheter, is in its stem-change group instead. A verb with only a spelling adjustment, such as manger, is in both 1st group (-er) and its spelling group.
  • 3rd group (-re / -ir / -oir) holds every 3rd-group verb except the ones in Fully irregular.
  • Pronominal holds the verbs listed with se (se lever, se souvenir).
  • Auxiliary avoir and Auxiliary être sort verbs by the auxiliary they take in the compound tenses. Every verb is in at least one of them, and the few verbs that take either (monter, descendre, sortir, passer, retourner, ressortir) are in both.
  • Subjonctif irrégulier holds the verbs whose subjonctif présent cannot be built from their present tense (aller → que j'aille).

A verb usually belongs to more than one group, and it is in your pool when any of its groups is ticked. Parler, for example, is in 1st group (-er) and in Auxiliary avoir. So ticking Auxiliary avoir on its own already selects almost the whole catalogue. To study one pattern, untick the two auxiliary groups.

Seeing which verbs you ended up with

This screen chooses patterns; it does not list the verbs they match. To see the resulting pool, open Reference on the verbs hub.

docs.title: Tenses
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Tenses, under Theory on the verbs hub, explains how the French tenses divide the work between them. Nothing is recorded. The introduction is folded away when the page opens, so the tenses come first.

The tenses are listed under the same headings as Select tenses: Indicatif – Temps Simples, Indicatif – Passé Simple, Indicatif – Temps Composés, Conditionnel, Impératif and Subjonctif. Each tense has a card that opens to show when it is used, an example conjugation, example sentences and how it is formed. The ⓘ beside a tense, for example on Select tenses, opens this page at that tense, with its card open.

A few points worth knowing before you choose tenses:

  • The Passé Simple is the literary past. You meet it in novels and history books, but spoken French uses the Passé Composé in its place. The Passé Antérieur and the Subjonctif Imparfait and Plus-que-parfait are literary too.
  • Every compound tense is an auxiliary (avoir or être) in a simple tense plus the past participle: j'ai parlé, j'avais parlé, j'aurai parlé, j'eus parlé, j'aurais parlé, que j'aie parlé, que j'eusse parlé, aie parlé.
  • The two imperatives have only the tu, nous and vous forms.
  • In the conjugation tables, every subjunctive form is shown after que (que je parle, qu'il parle).

docs.title: Verb groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Verb groups, under Theory on the verbs hub, is reference reading: nothing is recorded. Read it before you choose groups, because Select verb groups is only as useful as your sense of what the groups are.

The page opens with the three French groups side by side. The tables show the only two tenses where their endings differ, the présent and the passé simple, and then the endings all three share in the imparfait, futur and conditionnel:

présent 1 (-er) présent 2 (-ir / -iss-) shared imparfait je -e -is -ais tu -es -is -ais il -e -it -ait nous -ons -issons -ions vous -ez -issez -iez ils -ent -issent -aient

The 3rd group has no column of its own in the présent or passé simple: each of its verbs has its own forms there. The imparfait endings go on the stem of the nous form of the present (nous parlons → je parlais). The futur and conditionnel endings go on the whole infinitive (parler → je parlerai).

Below the intro, the groups are listed under their five sections (Basic, Spelling, Stem Changes, Auxiliary, Irregular), which fold open. Each group has a card with a short description. Open it for the full explanation, with endings tables for the group where it has its own pattern, and a worked example. These are the same cards the ⓘ buttons on Select verb groups and the group badges on a verb's page open.

After the groups comes Beyond the groups. Compound families lists the verbs built on another verb with a prefix — apprendre and comprendre are prendre — with, after a member's name, where it departs from its base. How irregularities are shown explains the three marks used in the conjugation tables (see The conjugation colour code (French)). At the bottom, To print holds Regular patterns.

docs.title: Verb meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck of the verbs in your selection: the infinitive on one side, its translation on the other. The deck is about meaning only, with no tense or person. It is the fastest way through a new verb group before the conjugation drills ask you to conjugate it.

Direction. The control at the top sets which side you see first:

  • French → your language — you see the verb and recall its meaning.
  • Your language → French — you see the meaning and recall the verb.
  • ⇄ — both directions, mixed.

The card. It shows one side and "Tap to reveal". Think of the answer, then tap the card: it flips to show the other side. Two icons sit on the card:

  • The book opens the verb's conjugation in the tenses you selected, without leaving the deck.
  • The speaker reads out the side you are looking at.

Grading. Grade yourself once the card is turned. On iPhone and iPad, swipe right if you knew it and left if you didn't. On the Mac, and on iPhone and iPad with VoiceOver, use the Wrong and Correct buttons instead. The card then moves on by itself.

Listen. If a French voice is installed, a Listen switch appears next to Incorrect answers. With it on, French cards are spoken instead of written ("Listen, then turn the card"). The back then shows the written word as well, so you can check what you heard. The switch is hidden in the your language → French direction.

The session. The line above the card counts your answers ("5 out of 6 correct"). The Incorrect answers switch limits the deck to verbs you have got wrong before. If there are no wrong answers yet, the app says so and switches the filter off. A session ends after the number of questions set in Settings → Study → Questions per session. After seven correct answers in a row, the app offers to stop there. The verbs for each session are picked from your selection, based on your answer history and your Learning pace.

What's recorded. Each graded card is recorded on your device against the verb.

docs.title: Verb reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Verb reference, under Study on the verbs hub, is the browse list of your verbs: no testing, nothing recorded. Use it to review translations before a drill, to look up a verb you met in a drill, or to see which verbs your groups and word scope have selected.

The list contains every verb your current selection gives you: the ticked verb groups, filtered by your level and the topics set in Select word scope. Each row shows the infinitive with its translation. The list is alphabetical, with an A–Z index down the right edge for jumping. The search field matches both the French infinitive and the translation, and ignores accents, so preferer finds préférer.

If your selection contains no verbs, the screen says "No verbs selected" and offers Select scope to change your topic filter.

Tap a verb to open its page, with the tables, usage, structure and reference sheet described under Conjugation tables.

Verb reference or Verb meaning?

  • Verb reference — this screen. Browse only; nothing is recorded. Use it for a quick warm-up, or to dig into a verb you keep getting wrong.
  • Verb meaning — the flashcard drill under Practice, where every answer is recorded and your weak verbs come back more often.

A good loop is to look through Verb reference for a minute to bring the vocabulary back, then run Meaning on the same selection.

docs.title: Other Vocabulary
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open this hub from the Other Vocabulary tile on the Self Study screen. It holds the small single words that have no hub of their own. In French there are 27:

  • Articles (4): le / la / l' / les, un / une, des, du / de la / de l'
  • Determiners (6): ce / cet / cette / ces, chaque, tout / toute / tous / toutes, beaucoup de, quelque / quelques, plusieurs
  • Conjunctions (10): et, ou, mais, donc, car, parce que, quand, pendant que, comme, si
  • Interjections (7): bonjour, au revoir, merci, oui, non, félicitations !, incroyable !

Adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions and numerals have their own hubs. For expressions of several words, such as s'il vous plaît, see Phrases.

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select word groups, to choose the categories.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Word reference, the selected words.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Word meaning, flashcards.

There is no Theory page for this hub in French; the explanations are in the category info sheets instead.

Select word groups. Tap Article, Conjunction, Determiner or Interjection to switch it on or off; each row shows how many words it has. Tap ⓘ for an explanation of the category and a list of its words:

  • Articles — definite le, la, l', les, indefinite un, une, des, and the partitive du, de la, de l' for an unmeasured amount: je bois du café. After a negation the partitive and indefinite become de: je n'ai pas de café.
  • Determiners — the demonstratives ce, cet (before a vowel or mute h: cet homme), cette, ces; chaque and plusieurs, which never change; tout, which agrees; quelques; and beaucoup de, whose de never contracts with an article.
  • Conjunctions — et, ou, mais, donc, car join equal parts; parce que, quand, si, comme, pendant que start a subordinate clause. Si becomes s' before il (s'il), but never before elle.
  • Interjections — words that are a whole utterance on their own. French puts a space before ! and ?: incroyable !

The line at the top shows how many words you selected, and how many are left within your level; topics don't apply to this hub. If you tick nothing, the screen warns you that the drill will be empty, with the choices Stay and select and Go back anyway.

Word reference. A list of the selected words with their translations and a search field that matches the word or its translation. Nothing is recorded here. Tap a word to open its page: the word, its translation and category, its Level, Frequency and Topics, and the book icon in the toolbar for online dictionaries.

Word meaning. A flashcard deck for the meaning of the selected words, in either direction. It works like Noun meaning. Every answer is recorded.

docs.title: Words and phrases
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Two tiles on the Self Study screen cover the vocabulary that has no hub of its own:

  • Phrases — set phrases, and the example sentences of the verbs and nouns. This is the largest pool in the French course: many thousands of sentences, depending on the tenses you study. See Phrases.
  • Other Vocabulary — the small single words that are not verbs, nouns, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions or numerals. In French these are articles, determiners, conjunctions and interjections. See Other Vocabulary.

Both hubs have Study and Practice sections. The drill is a flashcard deck for meaning, in either direction.

docs.title: External dictionary lookups
docs.text:
The pages of French verbs, nouns, phrases and other words have a book icon in the toolbar. Tap it for a menu of three online dictionaries: Linguee, WordReference and Reverso. Choose one to look the word up. On iPhone and iPad the page opens in a Safari sheet inside the app; on the Mac it opens in your browser. Linguee and Reverso translate into Dutch when Dutch is your app language, and into English otherwise; WordReference always uses English.

Which dictionaries appear is set under Settings → French → Dictionary services. The switches are shared with the Spanish course: turning one off there turns it off here too. If you switch off Linguee, WordReference and Reverso, the book disappears.

docs.title: Grammar lessons
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Grammar lessons are the curriculum side of LinguaMorpha: a fixed sequence of lessons that introduces grammar and vocabulary step by step, with no decisions to make about scope. Use them when you would rather follow a path than build one.

Tap Grammar lessons on the main screen, or choose it under Study in the Mac sidebar. It appears for courses that have lessons; the header says how many there are. The screen offers a catalogue per kind of lesson the course has:

  • Verbs — a structured path through conjugation, one tense at a time.
  • Nouns — gender, plural formation and the patterns nouns follow.
  • Adjectives — agreement in gender and number, and where adjectives go.

A course whose curriculum is one continuous path shows its lesson list straight away instead. The course guide says what its lessons cover and how far they go.

The catalogues are independent, so you can work through them side by side.

docs.title: The lesson list
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The lessons are grouped into modules. Each module heading shows its name, how many of its lessons you have completed (for example 3 / 10) and a chevron. Tap the heading to open or close the module; the app remembers which modules you left open. All modules start closed. A module that lies wholly above your level (see Your level) says Above this level under its name.

Inside an open module, each lesson shows its number — a green circle once it is done — ringed by how well you master it (see How well you master a lesson), with its title and description, the opening lines of its explanation, and two summary lines: New: what it adds (for example 20 verbs · New tense: Presente) and Practise: its exercises. Every lesson is open to you at any time; the numbers show the intended order, and a lesson above your level is dimmed.

iPhoneiPadMac

Where a module has an introduction, it is the first row of the module, marked with a book. It explains what the module is about, usually with a reference table, and stays available to reread at any time.

At the foot of the catalogue, Reset all progress clears every completion mark so you can start the curriculum again.

docs.title: Inside a lesson
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The top card shows the lesson's CEFR level, sometimes a tag for the pattern it teaches, its number, title and description, and — when the lesson brings in a tense no earlier lesson covered — a New tense badge. About this lesson explains the grammar.

iPhoneiPadMac

Study aids. Where the module has a reference card — an endings table, for example — it appears at the top of each lesson it applies to, so the reference is always where you need it.

The rest of the lesson has two phases.

1 Words in this lesson. The material, on the page:

  • the verbs as a list, each with its meaning. Tap a verb to lay its card over the list, beside the names: its conjugation, a speaker button and — for verbs that have them — a button to show translations. The card shows one tense at a time; with more than one, tabs above the table choose it. It shows the lesson's tenses; a lesson that teaches no tense of its own, such as a theme lesson, shows every tense the path has taught so far — the present at first, more later on. The card sits level with its verb and moves when you tap another; the open verb's row is tinted. On the Mac, ↑ and ↓ move through the list. Close the card with ✕ (on the Mac also Esc), or tap the name again;
  • an ⓘ beside a tense opens the Tenses page at that tense, with its card open and the other tenses a tap away; Back returns to the lesson. On the Mac the page opens in a window of its own, which can stay open beside the lesson; another ⓘ moves it to that tense;
  • nouns and phrases in a Vocabulary card, and adjectives in an Adjectives card, where the lesson has them;
  • a speaker in the heading of each list reads the whole list, with a pause after each item to repeat it.

Examples. After the words come the lesson's example sentences: each in the language you study with its translation below and a speaker of its own, and a speaker in the heading that reads them all. Every word the lesson teaches appears in at least one of them. A sentence that needs a word — why this tense, where a form comes from — carries a lamp: tap the sentence or the lamp for that line, and again to close it.

Words above this level. Some lessons offer words one level up that belong with their subject — in a lesson at CEFR A1 about food, desayuno and cena. Switch on Also words above A1 (the lesson's CEFR level) at the top of the words: they join the lists with their level beside them, get a card of examples of their own, and are practised in the exercises too. They never count towards the lesson's mastery. The switch is remembered from lesson to lesson.

Previous and next lesson. At the end of every lesson there is a card for the lesson before it and one for the lesson after it on the path; tap one to go there without returning to the list — Back still takes you to it. On a Mac, Previous lesson (⌘[) and Next lesson (⌘]) in the Study menu do the same; on an iPad with a keyboard, so do ⌘[ and ⌘].

2 Practice. Under Once you feel ready, test yourself, the lesson's exercises — for example verb meaning, conjugation, noun and phrase flashcards. A lesson that drills the meaning of more than one kind of word, such as a theme lesson with nouns and verbs, has one Meaning deck for all of them. Tap one to start. On the Mac an exercise opens in a sheet over the lesson.

This lesson / All. The meaning exercises and the verb exercises — conjugation and recognition — carry a This lesson / All switch. This lesson practises the words the lesson lists; All adds every word from the earlier lessons, which keeps older material warm. Each exercise has its own switch, and the choice carries over to other lessons. Where a lesson lists no words of a kind, the switch stands on All. The other exercises — pairs, the missing form, agreement — always use the lesson's own words.

docs.title: How well you master a lesson
docs.text:
The top card shows a ring with a percentage: how well you know the lesson's new words. Each word counts both ways — recognising it, and coming up with it from its meaning — and in a lesson about a tense, each verb in that tense counts too. All your answers on these words count, wherever you practise them, but a typed answer weighs most, a flashcard you mark yourself a little less, and an answer picked from a list least. The lesson becomes Mastered when your answers show that you reliably know every part of it, not after a few right. The ▲ beside the percentage is what you added since you opened the lesson. Tap the ring for the full explanation. The same ring surrounds the lesson's number in the list.

The lesson report. The list button beside the ring opens the lesson's report. Under What the ring counts, each word of the lesson with where it stands, part by part — recognise: known · produce: learning, or per tense for a verb — and how many of all its parts are known; tap a word for its page. Under Past sessions, the sessions you opened from this lesson, with their scores.

docs.title: Marking a lesson done
docs.text: Tap Mark done in the top card when you have finished. If you master less than half of the lesson, the app says so and offers Keep practicing or Mark complete anyway. On a completed lesson the button reads Mark not done, to take the mark off again.

docs.title: When to switch to Self Study
docs.text:
Grammar lessons are a good starting point and a good checkpoint. But when you want to:

  • spend longer on one tense or verb group,
  • drill a topic (food, travel, the body…) until it is automatic,
  • work on the noun gender of your elementary vocabulary,

Self Study gives you the controls. Many learners switch between the two from week to week.

docs.title: Latin module
docs.text:
The Latin module covers every declension, every adjective pattern, the full classical verb system, twenty-four pronouns, twenty-nine numerals, and a closed-class lexicon of prepositions, conjunctions, particles, adverbs, and indefinite pronouns. The sentence parser draws on the whole catalogue — more than 2,000 lemmas, the great majority of them at CEFR A1–B1. Vocabulary is chosen at the level of an introductory course, so sentences from a beginner's textbook — Ørberg's Familia Romana, Wheelock — usually parse, though not every word will be in the catalogue.

The ways to study it are described under Ways to study in the User Guide. This guide describes what is in the course, word type by word type.

Every form is stored with its macrons. Typed answers are checked leniently on macrons by default; you can make the check strict (see Macron-accurate checking).

docs.title: How the app writes Latin
docs.text:
The app follows the conventions of the classroom rather than those of any one dictionary, so that what you see on screen matches what a teacher writes on the board. The choices, in one place:

  • The verb's headword follows the interface language. In the Dutch interface a verb is named by its infinitive (amāre), as Dutch schools do; in the English and Spanish interfaces by its first person singular (amō), as English and Spanish grammars do. The citation line under the title gives the principal parts in the same order — amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum or amāre, amō, amāvī, amātum — with the supine in -um as the fourth part and, for a deponent, the perfect with sum (sequor, sequī, secūtus sum).
  • Tense and mood names are Latin, in every interface: Praesens, Imperfectum, Futurum, Perfectum, Plusquamperfectum, Futurum Exactum, and the moods Indicativus, Coniunctivus, Imperativus. The names are written without macrons; the forms always with them.
  • Macrons follow the Oxford Latin Dictionary and Ørberg's Familia Romana, including the hidden lengths before ns and nf (mōns, cōnsul, īnferus).
  • Cases come in the order nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative, vocative — the order of the Dutch and German school grammars. British and American books order them nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, ablative; the forms are the same. The vocative is shown in every table.
  • Conjugation rows are labelled by person and number — 1 sg, 2 sg, 3 sg, 1 pl, 2 pl, 3 pl — never by a pronoun, since Latin normally leaves the subject pronoun out.
  • Degrees of comparison are formed only for adjectives that have them in classical Latin. Adjectives in -eus, -ius, -uus (aureus, ēgregius, arduus), the possessives (meus, noster) and the ordinals (prīmus, secundus) form none; the irregular degrees (bonus — melior — optimus) are stored, not derived.

docs.title: What's in the Latin module
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Each part of speech has its own tile on Self Study, and each tile opens a hub with the same Theory / Study / Practice sections as the rest of the app. In a hub the rows carry short names (Select groups, Reference, Meaning); the screens they open name the word type (Select noun groups, Noun reference, Noun meaning), and this guide names the row when it tells you what to tap and the screen when it describes the screen. The group selection is a card of its own at the top of Practice, above the drills.

  • Nouns — over 650 nouns across the five declensions, plus two irregular nouns. Pick declensions, read the paradigms, browse the nouns, then drill production and recognition. See Declensions.
  • Adjectives — over 350 adjectives across the five textbook patterns, with comparative and superlative forms and the agreement drill.
  • Verbs — over 600 verbs across the conjugations, with the indicative, subjunctive and imperative, active and passive, plus participles, infinitives, gerundive and supine.
  • Pronouns — twenty-four pronouns (personal, reflexive, demonstrative, intensive, relative, interrogative and indefinite), each with its own stored paradigm.
  • Numerals — twenty-nine numerals.
  • Prepositions, Adverbs, Other Vocabulary (conjunctions, interjections and a few other small words) and Phrases — the smaller word classes, each with its own hub.

Alongside the hubs, several features are specific to Latin:

  • Sentence parser — enter a Latin sentence and every word is parsed.
  • Reading texts — ten curated passages, from a beginner's story to Caesar and Cicero, with every word tappable.
  • Macron-accurate checking — how macrons are graded, and how to type them.
  • Latin and speech — how Latin is read aloud.

docs.title: Level schemes
docs.text:
The Latin course has two level schemes. Choose one under Level schemes in the course tab of Settings (see Level schemes in the User Guide). Both show translations and leave the app language as it is.

  • Gymnasium — the standard scheme: one level per year of the Dutch gymnasium, Klas 1 to Klas 6, with the grammar in the usual school order.
  • Mature — for an adult working alone: four stages, Beginner to Advanced. The grammar comes earlier, in the order of the usual adult courses: all declensions and the indicative first, then the subjunctive and the participle constructions, then the rare forms.

docs.title: Macron-accurate checking
docs.text: Macrons are the bars over long vowels: ā ē ī ō ū. They change meaning: rosa (nominative singular, "rose") and rosā (ablative singular, "with/by a rose") differ only in the length of the final a. The app's word lists, tables and drill answers are spelled with macrons (amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum).

docs.title: How typed answers are checked
docs.text:
In the typed drills (Produce the conjugation, Decline the noun and Decline the adjective, in Type mode), what counts as right depends on Exact spelling. You'll find it in Settings → Study → Grading; it is one setting for every course. It is off by default.

  • Exact spelling off (default) — an answer that matches except for macrons counts as correct. The feedback reads Correct — watch the macron (in the verb drill, Accent: with the correct form) and shows the expected form, so rosis for rosīs scores as right and you see where the long vowel goes. This check also ignores capitals. The exception is an answer that is another form of the same word: rosa for rosā is the nominative, not the ablative, so it is wrong.
  • Exact spelling on — the answer must match exactly, macrons included. Rosis for rosīs is marked Not quite and counts as wrong, and the feedback shows the expected form.

Pick mode is unaffected: the options already carry their macrons, so you are right only if you choose the right one.

docs.title: Typing macrons
docs.text:
• iPhone and iPad — touch and hold a vowel key on the keyboard, then slide to the vowel with the bar (ā ē ī ō ū) and let go.
  • Mac — press and hold a vowel key. A menu of accented letters appears. Choose the one with the bar with the mouse or by typing the number shown under it. If you type a lot of Latin, the ABC – Extended input source (System Settings → Keyboard → Input Sources) lets you type Option-A and then the vowel.

The app has no macron keyboard of its own. Because the default check ignores macrons, you can practise without typing them and turn Exact spelling on when you want vowel length to count.

docs.title: Sentence parser
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The sentence parser reads a whole Latin sentence and tells you what every word in it is. Open Self Study → Look up (on the Mac, Look up in the sidebar) and switch the toggle at the top from Word to Sentence. The toggle only appears when Latin is your learning language.

Type or paste a sentence (a line of Caesar, a Vulgate verse, a sentence from your homework) into the box and tap Parse. If you have nothing to hand, tap the suggestion under the box ("Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres") to fill it in. The × button clears the box.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
• A count — how many words the sentence has and how many were recognised.
  • Literal gloss — a word-by-word rendering built from the first parse of each word. It is not a proper translation: it keeps the Latin word order and picks one meaning per word, but it shows quickly what the sentence is about. Copy puts it on the clipboard.
  • Translate — on devices with Apple Intelligence (iOS 26 or macOS 26 and later), this asks the on-device language model for an Idiomatic translation, in Dutch if Dutch is your app language and in English otherwise. If the model can't run, a short message says why (for example that Apple Intelligence is switched off). The translation is machine-made, so check it against the parse.
  • Word chips — one chip per word. Each chip shows the word as you typed it and, underneath, the lemma of its most likely parse. A +2-style badge means the word has more possible parses. Words the parser doesn't know show unknown and can't be tapped.

Tap a chip to open the Parse sheet, which lists every possible parse of that word: the lemma, what the form is (for example Noun — case, number, gender and the declension, or Verb — person and tense) and the translation. Parses that differ only in case share one row, so rosa shows one row for nominative, vocative and ablative singular rather than three. Latin forms are often ambiguous: eō is both "I go" (from īre) and the dative or ablative of the pronoun is, and both appear.

The parses are ordered by a fixed rule of thumb, not by the sentence: verbs first, then pronouns, small words, numerals, nouns, adjectives and participles, and within those the commoner case, number and tense first. Treat the top parse as a hint, not a verdict.

Rows with a chevron open more detail:

  • a noun opens the noun's page, with the matching form highlighted in its declension table;
  • an adjective opens the adjective's page;
  • a verb opens its conjugation at the tense that matched; a participle opens the conjugation of its verb.

Pronouns, numerals and small words (prepositions, conjunctions, adverbs, particles) show their parse but don't open anything.

docs.title: What the parser handles
docs.text:
• Macrons and capitals — matching ignores both, so gallia est omnis divisa finds dīvīsa. The chip keeps what you typed; the lemmas and forms in the Parse sheet carry the catalogue's macrons.
  • Punctuation — punctuation and symbols at the start or end of a word (commas, full stops, question marks, quotation marks, brackets) are removed before lookup.
  • Enclitics — when a word isn't found as it stands and ends in -que, -ve, -ne or -cum, the parser removes the ending and tries again. Filiusque then shows the parses of filius plus a separate row for -que ("and"); mēcum shows mē plus -cum ("with"). Words that are complete in themselves, such as neque or itaque, are not split.
  • Adverbs — besides the common ones, adverbs formed from adjectives in the catalogue (fortiter, clārē) are recognised and show the adjective they come from.

docs.title: What the parser does not do
docs.text:
• It parses one word at a time. It says what each word is, not what it is doing in the sentence (subject, object, agent), and it does not combine words: in amātus est you get the participle amātus and the verb est separately.
  • It does not choose between readings. Every parse is listed; deciding which one fits the sentence is up to you.
  • It does not restore elided vowels in verse (atqu' ego for atque ego). Paste the full form.
  • It only knows the words in the app's catalogue. Rarer words, most names and words that aren't there show unknown. The screen itself suggests sentences from a beginner's course such as Ørberg's Familia Romana or Wheelock: most of their words are in the catalogue.
  • It keeps no history. Each parse replaces the last.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Reading — paste a sentence you are stuck on, get the morphology, then work out the syntax yourself.
  • Checking your own translation — if you're unsure of a form, see what the parser makes of it.
  • Sight reading — identify each word yourself first, then parse the sentence to check.

docs.title: Adjectives and the concordance drill
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Latin Adjectives hub from the Adjectives tile on the Self Study screen. The catalogue holds over 350 adjectives across the five textbook patterns, and every one of them has a full case × number × gender paradigm. The hub has the usual Theory / Study / Practice layout. Under the title, a badge shows how many adjectives your current selection leaves, out of every adjective in the catalogue. The badge turns red when nothing is left to drill.

The five patterns, with the number of adjectives in each:

Pattern Example Adjectives 1st/2nd-decl. -us / -a / -um bonus, -a, -um over 220 1st/2nd-decl. -er variant pulcher, pulchra, pulchrum; miser, misera, miserum 18 3rd-decl. two-ending fortis, -e over 60 3rd-decl. one-ending ingens, ingentis over 40 3rd-decl. three-ending ācer, ācris, ācre 8

For the grammar of each pattern, see Appendix D.

docs.title: Select adjective groups (Practice)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The only selection row in Practice is Select groups. Its screen lists the five patterns under Declension pattern, with the number of adjectives in each. Tap a pattern to switch it on or off. Tap ⓘ to open a sheet with the pattern's worked paradigm and notes, followed by the list of Adjectives in this pattern. Tap any adjective in that list to open its detail screen.

Pattern is the only choice on this screen, and the comparative is not offered as a pattern. Your level and topics still apply, though. Every adjective screen and drill uses your pattern selection within your level and word scope. The picker's Select word scope row opens that screen, and when the scope leaves fewer adjectives the count line shows how many are in scope.

docs.title: Adjective patterns (Theory)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A reference page with a short introduction and one card per pattern, in the order of the table above. The first card is open when you arrive and the others are closed. Tap a card's header to open or close it. An open card shows how the pattern is formed, a full paradigm for its model adjective (pulcher and miser side by side for the -er pattern), and a More link.

docs.title: Pattern detail
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

More opens the full write-up for one pattern:

  • Paradigm — singular and plural tables, six cases down and m / f / n across.
  • Formation — how the stem is found and which ending sets each gender borrows.
  • More examples — further adjectives of the pattern in citation form, for example magnus, parvus, longus… for -us / -a / -um.
  • Agreement — how the three gender columns relate in this pattern.
  • Pitfalls — common confusions, such as the masculine vocative in -e (bone!).

docs.title: Adjective reference (Study)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac iPhoneiPadMac

A searchable A–Z list of the adjectives in your selection. Each row shows the citation form and its translation. You can search by Latin lemma or by translation. Tap an adjective to open its detail screen:

  • the citation form and translation;
  • the full paradigm (singular and plural, m / f / n);
  • Level and Topics chips;
  • up to three Examples marked auto: short sentences generated by the app. In each one the adjective agrees with a noun and appears in bold, and a label below gives the case and number.

docs.title: Adjective meaning (Practice)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Self-judged flashcards: tap the card to see the other side, the adjective or its translation. Swipe right if you knew it and left if you didn't. This drill uses the same pattern selection as the other drills.

docs.title: Decline the adjective (Practice)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The production drill. The card shows the adjective's citation form and translation, followed by a case · number · gender target such as Accusativus · Singularis · Femininum. The vocative is never asked.

  • Type mode — type the form and tap Check.
  • Pick mode — choose the form from a wheel of up to ten options. The distractors are other forms of the same adjective, topped up with the same cell of other adjectives in your pool when needed.

After you check, the feedback reads Correct, Not quite (with the expected form), or Correct — watch the macron. That last verdict appears when you typed the right letters without the macrons. To make missing macrons count as wrong, turn on Exact spelling (Settings → Study → Grading) (see Macron-accurate checking).

docs.title: Recognise the form (Practice)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The recognition drill. The card shows an inflected form, with the adjective's citation form and translation below it. Pick Case, Number and Gender, then tap Check. If you set nothing, the button reads Skip. The vocative is never the form asked, but vocative analyses count when they match.

Many forms fit several cells. bonōrum, for example, is genitive plural masculine and neuter. Any valid analysis counts as correct, and the feedback lists the Other valid answers. A wrong answer lists all the Valid answers. Every feedback card has a Show all forms link, which opens the full paradigm with the asked form highlighted.

The gear button opens Recognition settings:

  • Picker style — Wheel or Chips.
  • Multi-answer mode — you claim each analysis with Add this analysis before you check. Only the complete set counts as correct, and a partial set shows "N of M found" along with the analyses you missed.

Each answer is recorded as a single right-or-wrong result. There is no partial credit for getting some of the three axes right.

All the drills record answers against the adjective. They take their session length and learning pace from Settings → Study. The Incorrect answers toggle at the top of a drill limits the session to adjectives you have been getting wrong.

docs.title: Comparative and superlative
docs.text: The comparative (-ior / -ius) and superlative (-issimus; -rimus after -er) are not a separate screen or drill, and the comparative is not a selectable pattern. The app derives them from each adjective, and they are stored explicitly for the irregulars bonus → melior → optimus, magnus → maior → maximus, malus → peior → pessimus and parvus → minor → minimus. The Sentence parser recognises these forms. For the rules, see Appendix D.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Start with only the -us / -a / -um pattern. It is by far the largest group and the textbook starting point.
  2. Keep Adjective patterns open as a reference while you drill.
  3. Alternate between Decline the adjective and Recognise the form, as you do for nouns.
  4. Add the 3rd-declension two-ending pattern next. Its i-stem endings (ablative singular -ī, genitive plural -ium, neuter plural -ia) need practice of their own.
  5. Once you can produce noun and adjective forms separately, move on to the Agreement drill.

docs.title: The Concordance Drill
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

In the hub this drill is called Agreement drill. It shows a short Latin sentence with a blank where an adjective belongs. The noun is already in its inflected form. Your task is to pick the form of the adjective that agrees with the noun in case, number and gender. That agreement is the concordance the drill is named after.

What a question shows. Here is an example:

Choose the form of pulcher, pulchra, pulchrum

Latin

___ rosam amō.

agrees with rosam (f. Acc. sg.)

  • pulcher
  • pulchram
  • pulchrārum
  • pulchrīs

The instruction gives the adjective in its citation form. Under the sentence, a hint names the noun and its gender, case and number, so the task is to turn those three features into the right form of the adjective. There are always four options. One is correct, and the other three are different forms of the same adjective, picked at random from its paradigm.

Answering. A single tap answers. Your pick fills the blank, the correct option gets a green tick, and a wrong pick gets a red cross. An explanation card then gives the reason:

Why pulchram?

pulchram agrees with rosam (f. Acc. sg.).

The card shows the same text whether you picked right or wrong. It does not say which axis you missed. Tap Next to continue, or See results after the last question.

Where the sentences come from. Each question combines a random noun from your noun selection, an adjective from your adjective selection, and a random case and number. The case is nominative, genitive, dative, accusative or ablative. The vocative is never asked. The app then picks a short sentence frame for that case from a small built-in set. Nominative frames put the noun in subject position (… cantat), genitive frames make it a possessor (Liber … in mēnsā est), dative frames make it an indirect object (… dōnum dō), accusative frames make it a direct object (… videō), and ablative frames use a preposition (Cum … ambulō). The frames don't change with number, so a plural noun can end up with a singular verb. That makes the sentence odd Latin, but the agreement being tested is still correct. In every frame the adjective sits right next to its noun, so the drill practises attributive agreement only.

Your pool. The drill draws on both group selections: Select groups in the Nouns hub and Select groups in the Adjectives hub, each within your level and word scope. To focus on one noun declension or one adjective pattern, narrow the matching selection. If either selection leaves nothing to draw from, the drill shows Nothing to drill and asks you to check both selections.

From a practice set. Opened from a Practice set, the drill uses the set's nouns and adjectives instead of the group selections. A set that has only nouns is matched against every adjective in the catalogue, and a set with only adjectives against every noun — so a chapter's nouns can be drilled in agreement with adjectives you already know. The session is recorded under the set.

Session and recording. The Incorrect answers toggle at the top limits the session to adjectives you have been getting wrong. The number of questions comes from Questions per session in Settings → Study. Each answer is recorded as right or wrong against the adjective, so it counts towards that adjective's progress. The noun in the sentence is not recorded.

When to use it. Use this drill once you can produce noun forms and adjective forms reliably on their own. It is the integration drill: it has you put the two together in a sentence.

docs.title: Adverbs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Adverbs hub has over 440 Latin adverbs of three kinds:

  • Derived: built from an adjective. Adjectives of the 1st/2nd declension take -ē (longus → longē, pulcher → pulchrē). 3rd-declension adjectives take -iter (fortis → fortiter). Stems ending in -nt- take -nter (prūdēns → prūdenter). Over 300 adverbs are of this kind.
  • Irregular: built from an adjective, but not by the rule: bene, male, magnopere, multum, paulum.
  • Lexical: not built from an adjective. These include place words (hīc, ibi), time words (nunc, semper, crās), degree words (valdē, paene) and connecting words (etiam, autem). There are over 100.

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select adverb groups: tick the kinds you want. Tap ⓘ on a kind for an explanation and the adverbs of that kind.
  • Adverb grammar (Theory): cards for Regular adverbs (the -ē / -iter / -nter rules), Irregular adverbs, Comparison (fortius, fortissimē; bene → melius → optimē) and Adverbs of their own.
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Reference (Study) — opens Adverb reference: the selected adverbs, each marked with its kind. The detail screen for a derived adverb shows the adjective it comes from.
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Adverb meaning: flashcards for the meaning of each adverb.
iPhoneiPadMac

There is no form drill for adverbs. Once you know the rule, derived adverbs are predictable, so the drill tests meaning only.

docs.title: Declensions
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Every Latin noun belongs to one of five declensions, identified by the genitive singular ending. LinguaMorpha uses the declension as the main way to choose which nouns you practise.

Declension Gen. sg. Typical gender Examples Nouns in the app 1st -ae feminine (a few masculines: agricola, nauta, poēta) rosa, puella, aqua over 150 2nd -ī masculine or neuter (with an -er sub-pattern) servus, bellum, puer over 190 3rd -is (the nominative varies) all three genders rēx, urbs, mare over 250 4th -ūs mostly masculine (manus, domus feminine; cornū, genū neuter) exercitus, frūctus 40 5th -ēī (-eī after a consonant) almost all feminine (diēs masculine) diēs, rēs, fidēs 8

Two further nouns, vīs and Iuppiter, have their own Irregular group (see Selecting Declensions). That makes over 650 nouns in total.

The engine generates the forms of the regular nouns from the lemma, the genitive and the gender. That includes the i-stem variants of the 3rd declension (genitive plural -ium, as in urbium; neuter ablative singular -ī and plural -ia, as in marī, maria), the 2nd-declension -er nouns (puer, ager, magister), and the 4th-declension neuters (cornū, genū). Nouns with irregular cells, such as deus, domus and bōs, have those forms stored individually.

Open Self Study → Nouns to reach the nouns hub. It has three sections:

  • Theory — Declension paradigms: the five declensions with worked examples. See Declension Paradigms.
  • Study — Reference (Noun reference): browse the nouns you have selected, with their translations, full paradigms and example sentences.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select noun groups): choose the declensions to practise. See Selecting Declensions. Then the drills:
  • Meaning (Noun meaning) — flashcards: recall what each noun means. Then Decline the noun and Recognise the form, below, and last the Agreement drill, which pairs nouns with adjectives (see The Concordance Drill).
iPhoneiPadMac

The line under the hub title shows how many nouns your current selection gives you, out of every noun in the catalogue. It turns red when the selection is empty.

docs.title: Decline the Noun
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The production drill. You get a noun and a case and number, and you give the matching form.

How a question looks. The card at the top shows the noun's citation and meaning, then the form to produce:

rosa, rosae (f.) rose

Dativus · Pluralis

The genitive is always given, so you can find the stem even for 3rd-declension nouns whose nominative doesn't show it.

Type and Pick. Switch with the Type / Pick control above the question. You can switch at any time; the current answer is cleared when you do.

  • Type — type the form and tap Check (or press Return, or tap the arrow in the field).
  • Pick — choose the form from a wheel of up to ten options, then tap Check. The wrong options are mostly the same noun's other forms (is it the genitive or the dative singular?), topped up with the same case and number of other nouns in your selection.

Feedback. After Check, a feedback card appears, and the button becomes Next. After a correct answer the next question loads by itself after a moment, unless Auto-advance after correct answer is off in Settings → Study; after a wrong answer it waits until you tap Next.

  • Correct (green) — shows the answer.
  • Correct — watch the macron (orange) — you typed the right letters but left out or misplaced a macron. This counts as correct. The card shows the expected form with its macrons.
  • Not quite (red) — shows the expected form.

Macrons. In Type mode, macrons are checked leniently by default: rosis for rosīs gets Correct — watch the macron. To make a missing macron count as wrong, turn on Exact spelling in Settings → Study → Grading. Pick mode always compares the exact form, because the options already carry their macrons. See Macron-accurate checking.

Which forms are asked. Any case and number the noun has, except the vocative, which is never asked. (For most nouns it is the same as the nominative; the vocative still appears among the Pick options.) Cells a noun doesn't have are skipped: plural-only nouns are only asked for plural forms, and Iuppiter only for singular ones. The locative is not part of the drill.

The session. The line above the question counts your answers ("7 / 9 correct"). The Incorrect answers switch at the top limits the session to nouns you have got wrong before. A session ends after the number of questions set in Settings → Study → Questions per session (∞ keeps it going until you stop). The nouns for each session are picked from your selection, based on your answer history and your Learning pace.

From a practice set. The same drill opens from a Practice set that contains nouns — the bundled First declension: every form, or one you built yourself with Decline the noun switched on. There the pool is the set's nouns, not your Select noun groups selection, and the session is recorded under the set, so the set's own report shows it. This is how a set for one chapter of a course book drills exactly that chapter's nouns.

What's recorded. Each checked answer is recorded on your device against the noun (not the individual form). Correct — watch the macron counts as correct. Recognise the form records to the same noun history, so both drills use it when picking nouns.

Suggested workflow.

  1. Start in Pick mode until the endings look familiar.
  2. Switch to Type mode: Pick lets you eliminate options, Type makes you recall the form.
  3. Keep Exact spelling off at first, then turn it on once the forms are solid.
  4. Alternate sessions with Recognise the form — production and recognition train different skills.

docs.title: Declension Paradigms
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Pure reference: no testing and no scoring. Tap Declension paradigms in the hub's Theory section to open an overview of the five declensions. From there you can go to a side-by-side table or to a detail screen for each declension.

The overview. A short introduction is followed by one card per declension. The first card is open when you arrive; tap a card's header to open or close it. An open card shows:

  • a note on how to recognise the declension and which genders it has;
  • a worked paradigm for each example noun, headed by its citation (puella, puellae (f.)). The 2nd declension shows amīcus and templum, the 3rd rēx and tempus;
  • a More link to that declension's detail screen.

Each paradigm is a six-by-two table. The rows are the six cases, with full Latin names (Nominativus, Genitivus, Dativus, Accusativus, Ablativus, Vocativus), and the columns are Singularis and Pluralis. All six rows are always shown, so the vocative row appears even when it matches the nominative. A form that does not exist, such as the singular of a plural-only noun, is shown as a faded dash (—).

iPhoneiPadMac

All declensions side by side. The card above the declensions opens the Synoptic table, which shows the endings of all five declensions in one grid, with a singular table and a plural table. Choose the layout at the top:

  • Basic — one column per declension (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th), with the masculine or feminine endings.
  • Detailed — separate neuter columns for the 2nd, 3rd and 4th declensions (1st, 2nd m, 2nd n, 3rd, 3rd n, 4th, 4th n, 5th). The table scrolls sideways if it doesn't fit.

The app remembers your choice. In the 3rd declension the nominative singular (and the vocative, and for neuters the accusative) cannot be predicted from an ending, so those cells say varies. Tap one to see example 3rd-declension nouns, each with its nominative, genitive and meaning. The genitive shows the stem that the rest of the paradigm is built on. Blue varies cells draw masculine/feminine examples; purple ones draw neuter examples.

The declension detail screen. More opens a full write-up of one declension:

  • Paradigm — the worked tables again;
  • Formation — how the stem and endings combine;
  • More examples — further nouns of the declension, each shown with its genitive;
  • Gender — which genders occur and the main exceptions;
  • Pitfalls — common confusions, highlighted as warnings.
iPhoneiPadMac

iPhoneiPadMac

Paradigms of individual nouns. For the paradigm of any one noun, use Reference in the Study section. It lists the nouns in your current selection alphabetically, with a search field and an A–Z index. Search ignores macrons. Tap a noun to open its detail screen:

  • the lemma and translation, with a citation line: lemma, genitive, gender and declension (puella, puellae (f.) · 1st declension (-ae));
  • the full case × number table. Plural-only nouns (arma, castra, līberī, tenebrae, dīvitiae, īnsidiae, hīberna, moenia, superī, māiōrēs) show dashes in the singular column;
  • the noun's level and topic;
  • Examples — example sentences for the noun, each with a translation and a tag naming the case and number the noun takes in that sentence (Accusativus · Singularis).

When you reach a noun from a parsed word in the Sentence parser, the table highlights every cell with that form, so you can see at a glance all the cases it could be.

The tables have no tap-to-hear.

docs.title: Recognise the Form
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The recognition drill, the reverse of Decline the Noun. You see a declined form and say which case and number it is.

How a question looks. The form is shown large. Below it, the noun's citation and meaning are given as a hint:

puellārum puella, puellae (f.) girl

Answer with two pickers, Case and Number, then tap Check. Gender is not asked, because the hint already gives it. The action button changes with what you have done:

  • Skip — nothing picked yet. Moves to a new question without recording anything.
  • Check — both pickers set. The button is disabled while only one of them is set.
  • Next — after checking. After a correct answer the drill moves on by itself while Auto-advance after correct answer is on.

The form is always a real form of a noun in your selection. The vocative is never asked, and cells a noun doesn't have are skipped (plural-only nouns only appear in the plural).

Ambiguous forms. Latin forms are often ambiguous: puellae can be genitive singular, dative singular, nominative plural or vocative plural. When a form has several valid analyses, any of them counts as correct. After a correct answer, the feedback lists the Other valid answers. After a wrong one, the card says Not quite and lists the Valid answers. Under the feedback, Show all forms opens the noun's full paradigm with every cell that matches the shown form highlighted.

Recognition settings. The gear button in the toolbar opens the settings:

  • Picker style — Chips (the default) or Wheel. This choice is shared with the other recognition drills.
  • Multi-answer mode — instead of naming one analysis, you collect every analysis the form has. Set the pickers and tap Add this analysis for each one. Your picks appear under Claimed: (tap the × to remove one). Then tap Check to grade the whole set:
  • Correct! All N found (green) — you found every analysis and nothing wrong.
  • N of M found (orange) — everything you claimed is valid, but you missed some. The feedback lists You found: and Also valid (missed):.
  • Not quite (red) — at least one claim is wrong. The feedback lists Correct:, Incorrect: and Missed:.

Only a complete set counts as correct in your history. This setting is shared with the other recognition drills. - Ask the noun too — hides the hint and adds a Noun picker, so the form appears bare, as it would in a text. Pick the noun as well as the case and number. The picker offers the right noun among similar-looking nouns from your selection. If another noun you pick really has that form in that case and number, the answer counts as correct. The feedback card shows the noun's citation and meaning. This mode can't be combined with Multi-answer mode, and it switches off when you leave the drill.

Scoring. Each answer is either right or wrong; there is no half credit. The line at the top counts your answers, and the Incorrect answers switch, session length and noun choice work as in Decline the Noun. Each checked answer is recorded against the noun, in the same history the production drill uses. Skipped questions are not recorded.

Suggested workflow.

  1. Alternate with Decline the Noun: one production session, then one recognition session.
  2. If a form keeps catching you out, open Show all forms and see which other cells share its ending.
  3. Once the single-answer mode feels easy, try Multi-answer mode to practise finding every reading of a form, or Ask the noun too to practise meeting forms without a hint.
  4. Give the 3rd declension a focused session or two: select only that row in Select groups. The i-stem genitive plural in -ium (urbium, cīvium) is a common stumbling point.

docs.title: Selecting Declensions
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select noun groups decides which nouns can appear in Noun reference, Noun meaning, Decline the noun and Recognise the form. Declension is the only axis on this screen — there is no gender, textbook-chapter or frequency filter here. Level and topic are global: the level in the chip beside the flag (Scheme and level), the topics in Self Study → Select word scope.

The screen has one section, Declensions, with six rows:

  • 1st declension (-ae)
  • 2nd declension (-ī)
  • 3rd declension (-is)
  • 4th declension (-ūs)
  • 5th declension (-ēī)
  • Irregular

Each row shows how many nouns it contains. Tap a row to include or exclude that declension. The All / None button in the section header selects or clears every row at once.

The ⓘ button on a row opens a sheet about that declension: a short description, then the list of Nouns in this declension. Tap a noun in the list to open its detail screen.

The line at the top counts your selection and says how many of those nouns fall inside your level and your word scope (topics). When every row is on and nothing narrows them, all three numbers are the size of the catalogue. The drills and Noun reference use the in-scope nouns. The Select word scope row below it opens the scope screen, and says either All topics or Filtered by topic.

The Irregular row. It holds the two nouns whose paradigms are stored cell by cell rather than generated: vīs (force, strength) and Iuppiter (Jupiter). They are drilled like any other noun. The drills simply skip the cells these nouns don't have: vīs has no genitive or dative singular here, and Iuppiter has no plural.

Saving your selection. Your selection is saved when you leave the screen and stays until you change it. A fresh install starts with every row selected, Irregular included. If you clear every row, the drills show No nouns selected instead of a question until you select at least one declension.

Suggested starting sets.

  • 1st and 2nd declension only — the bulk of high-frequency vocabulary, and where every textbook begins.
  • Add the 3rd declension once you can produce 1st- and 2nd-declension forms reliably. It is the largest and most varied group, and it contains the i-stems (urbs, cīvis, mare) with their -ium genitive plural.
  • 4th and 5th declension last — they are the smallest groups.

docs.title: Tips for getting started with Latin
Tips for getting started with Latin
docs.text:
1. Decide what you're optimising for. If you're following a textbook (Wheelock, LLPSI), the catalogue carries no chapter tags, but you can make your own level scheme with a level per chapter (see Levels in the general guide). Otherwise, scope your pools by declension, adjective pattern and verb group, and use Select tenses to match what the chapter has introduced. Read the chapter in your textbook, then drill the same material here until it is automatic. If you're sight-reading classical texts, make the Sentence parser your main entry point and let what you look up drive your study.

  2. First declension first. Open Self Study → Nouns → Select groups and select the 1st declension only. Set Questions per session to 20 in Settings → Study. Before drilling, read the tables in Declension paradigms. Then run a few Decline the noun sessions in Type mode until the endings come without thinking.

  3. Add the 2nd declension once the 1st feels solid. The masculine -us, neuter -um and masculine -er nouns are the next chunk. Together the first two declensions give you over 350 nouns, which is where every textbook starts.

  4. Drill in both directions. Decline the noun takes you from the dictionary form to a requested case and number. Recognise the form goes the other way: from an inflected form to its case and number. The two drills train different skills, so use both.

  5. Start verbs with the 1st conjugation present. Open Self Study → Verbs. In Select groups choose only 1st conjugation (-āre), and in Select tenses choose only Praesens. Drill Produce the conjugation until amō, amās, amat, amāmus, amātis, amant is automatic.

  6. Adjectives only after declensions are reliable. Adjective agreement assumes you already know which case, number and gender each noun form is. Read Adjective patterns, then practise the forms. The Agreement drill combines everything, so use it once you can produce both noun and adjective forms on their own.

  7. Use the Sentence parser as your reading assistant. Whenever you meet Latin outside the app (Caesar, Vergil, the Vulgate, your homework), open Self Study → Look up (on the Mac, Look up in the sidebar), switch to Sentence, paste the line and tap Parse. Tap any word to see its analysis and open its full entry. It is the quickest way to check your reading.

  8. Try the reading texts. Open Self Study → Texts. Start with Villa in silva (difficulty 1) or the Pater Noster (difficulty 2). Every word is tappable, and the translation toggle and EN/NL picker let you check yourself as you go.

  9. Want a guided route? The Grammar lessons take you through the same ground in order: twelve lessons in four modules, from the first declensions and the verb's present and perfect systems to the passive, pronouns, participles and the subjunctive. Find them on the Home screen.

docs.title: Phrases
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Phrases hub collects Latin sentences of two kinds:

  • Set phrases: 22 fixed expressions such as salvē.
  • Example sentences: over 3,500 sentences, from the verbs' Tense Examples (over 1,800) and the nouns' examples (over 1,700). A tense example only appears when its tense is switched on in Select tenses.

The hub has these screens:

  • Phrases or sentences (Practice): tick the kinds you want. Each row shows a few sample sentences, and ⓘ shows more. Your level and topics also apply: a sentence takes its word's level and topic, and a tense example also needs its tense in your level.
  • Select tenses (Practice): the tenses the tense examples may use. This is the same tense choice as on the Verbs hub, so a change here changes the verb drills too.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Phrase reference: the selected sentences with their translations. Tap a sentence for its page: its level, for a tense example its tense (tap it for the tense's ⓘ), its topics, and the verb or noun it illustrates (tap it to open that word).
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Phrase meaning: flashcards for the translation of each sentence.
iPhoneiPadMac

This hub has no Theory page for Latin.

docs.title: Prepositions
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Every Latin preposition takes a fixed case, and you learn the case along with the word. The Prepositions hub is built around that. Open it from the Prepositions tile on the Self Study screen. The catalogue has 26 prepositions:

  • Accusative: ad, ante, apud, circā, contrā, extrā, īnfrā, inter, intrā, ob, per, post, praeter, propter, super, suprā, trāns
  • Ablative: ab, cum, dē, ex, prae, prō, sine
  • Both: in and sub. The case changes the meaning. With the accusative they express motion (in urbem, "into the city"; sub montem, "to the foot of the mountain"). With the ablative they express place where (in urbe, "in the city"; sub monte, "at the foot of the mountain").

docs.title: Practice: Select preposition groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Choose which governed case to practise: Accusativus, Ablativus or both. In and sub are included if either case is ticked. Tap ⓘ on a case to read about it and see its prepositions.

docs.title: Theory: Preposition grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This page covers the accusative group (motion and goal), the ablative group (source, means, rest), the in / sub meaning change, and how to study them.

docs.title: Study: Preposition reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This screen lists the selected prepositions with their translations, and each row is marked with its case (acc., abl., or both). Search by the Latin word or the translation. The detail screen for each one shows its Governed case, and its level and frequency. For in and sub, a second card, The case changes the meaning, gives the motion meaning and the place meaning.

docs.title: Practice: Case-government drill
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

You see a preposition with its translation, and you answer Which case does this preposition govern? by choosing Accusativus or Ablativus. In and sub each appear as two separate questions. The meaning is shown with the question ("into / onto — motion toward" or "in / on — place where"), and it decides the answer. After each answer, an explanation tells you whether the case is fixed for that word or chosen by the meaning.

docs.title: Practice: Preposition meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Flashcards for the meaning of each preposition.

docs.title: Pronouns and numerals
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Pronouns and numerals each have their own tile on the Self Study screen, next to Verbs, Nouns and Adjectives. Each opens a hub with the usual Theory, Study and Practice sections.

docs.title: Pronouns
docs.text:
Latin has twenty-four pronouns in five classes:

  • Personal: ego, tū, suī (reflexive)
  • Demonstrative: is, hic, ille, iste, ipse, īdem
  • Relative: quī, quīcumque
  • Interrogative: quis
  • Indefinite: aliquis, quīdam, quisque, quisquam, nēmō, and the -īus words alius, alter, uterque, ūllus, nūllus, tōtus, sōlus

Latin pronoun forms don't follow the regular declension patterns, so every form is stored individually rather than generated by the declension engine.

The Pronouns hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select pronoun groups: tick the classes you want to practise. Tap ⓘ on a class to read about it and see its pronouns. The hub shows how many of the twenty-four are selected.
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Pronoun classes (Theory): one card for each class, and a closing note on why the pronouns are irregular.
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Reference (Study) — opens Pronoun reference: the selected pronouns, grouped by class. Tap one to see its full table of case, number and gender (case and number only for ego, tū and suī, which have no gender).
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Pronoun meaning: flashcards for the meaning of each pronoun.
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Form drill (Practice): you see a pronoun and a case, number and gender (Genitivus · Singularis · Masculinum), and choose the right form from four. The three wrong options are other forms of the same pronoun (eī, eius, eum), because those are the ones you are most likely to confuse. The vocative is never asked.
iPhoneiPadMac

docs.title: Numerals
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Latin has 29 cardinal numbers: 1 to 20, the tens from 30 to 100, and mīlle. Ūnus, duo and trēs decline, and their detail screens show a full table. Ūnus has only singular columns, and duo and trēs only plural. The other 26 are indeclinable, and their detail screens show a card with the single form.

The Numerals hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select numeral groups: tick the ranges 1 – 10, 11 – 20, 21 – 100 and 1000 (mīlle). Tap ⓘ on a range to see its numerals.
  • Numeral system (Theory): the declinable 1, 2 and 3, the indeclinable 4 to 100, mīlle and mīlia, and the ordinals (prīmus, secundus, tertius…, which decline like bonus). The ordinals are explained on this page but are not in the numeral list.
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Reference (Study) — opens Numeral reference: the selected numerals in order of value. The three that decline are marked declined.
iPhoneiPadMac

iPhoneiPadMac

  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Numeral meaning: flashcards with the number in figures on the front and the Latin on the back.
iPhoneiPadMac

docs.title: Reading texts
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open Self Study → Texts (shown only when Latin is your learning language). It holds ten short passages of Latin, from a beginner's passage to unaltered Caesar and Cicero. Each is read with the same parser as the Sentence parser, so almost every word can be tapped, and each comes with English and Dutch translations.

Each row shows the title, the author and century, the difficulty as dots (out of 5) and the number of words. The list is sorted by difficulty; the sort button in the toolbar switches to Chronological.

Difficulty Title Author Topic 1 Villa in silva LinguaMorpha (a passage written for beginners) primer 2 Pater Noster Vulgate (Jerome), Matthew 6:9–13 prayer 2 Genesis 1.1–5 Vulgate (Jerome) religion 2 Iohannes 1.1–5 Vulgate (Jerome) religion 3 Catullus 5 (Vivamus, mea Lesbia, lines 1–6) Catullus poetry 3 Catullus 13 (Cenabis bene, lines 1–8) Catullus poetry 3 Cicero — de Amicitia §17 Cicero philosophy 3 Phaedrus — Lupus et Agnus Phaedrus fable 4 Caesar — Bellum Gallicum 1.1 Caesar history 4 Cicero — In Catilinam 1.1 Cicero history

Villa in silva and the Pater Noster are the easiest places to start. Caesar and In Catilinam are the hardest.

docs.title: Reading a passage
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Tap a passage to open it. The header gives the author and source, the century, the word count and the difficulty. The text follows line by line, and each numbered line has:

  • the Latin as word chips — each chip shows the word and the lemma of its most likely parse, with a badge if there are more parses. Words the parser doesn't know are marked unknown and outlined in orange;
  • the translation of that line, underneath;
  • Teacher note — on some lines, a yellow panel you tap to open. It explains a construction worth noticing, such as the jussive subjunctive sānctificētur in the first line of the Pater Noster. Not every line has one.

Two toolbar buttons control the translation. The speech-bubble button hides or shows it, so you can read the Latin on its own first. The EN / NL menu switches it between English and Nederlands; it starts in your app language. Every passage has both.

Tap a word to open Word details, which lists every possible parse with its lemma, form and translation, as in the Sentence parser. Unlike the sentence parser, this sheet doesn't open noun, adjective or verb pages. Read, close the sheet and carry on.

The Latin of the passages is written without macrons, as most printed texts are. The lemmas and forms in Word details, and the teacher notes, do use macrons.

If you touch and hold a word marked unknown, a Form not recognised message appears with that word. Its Report a problem button opens an e-mail with the form and the passage filled in, so the word can be added to the catalogue.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• After the first two declensions — Villa in silva is written for your first weeks.
  • As the step from drills to real text — the drills train forms one at a time; here you meet them in connected Latin, with translation and notes to fall back on.
  • Together with the sentence parser — read a passage here, then paste your own text into the Sentence parser and read it the same way.

docs.title: A. Latin verb conjugations
docs.text: Latin verbs fall into five textbook conjugation classes, plus the irregular verbs. In Select verb groups these are the six groups: 1st conjugation (-āre), 2nd conjugation (-ēre), 3rd conjugation (-ere), 3rd-iō conjugation, 4th conjugation (-īre) and Fully irregular.
