docs.title: 1st conjugation — -āre
docs.text: The stem ends in long -ā-, and almost all these verbs are regular: amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum; laudō, laudāre; vocō, vocāre.

docs.title: 2nd conjugation — -ēre
docs.text: The stem ends in long -ē-. The present system is regular, but perfect stems vary more: videō → vīdī, moneō → monuī, habeō → habuī. Examples: moneō, monēre; videō, vidēre; habeō, habēre.

docs.title: 3rd conjugation — -ere
docs.text: The infinitive ends in short -ere, and the stem vowel changes across the paradigm (regis, regit, regunt). Perfect stems vary widely: regō, regere, rēxī, rēctum; dūcō, dūcere, dūxī, ductum; agō, agere, ēgī, āctum. This is the largest group in the catalogue.

docs.title: 3rd-iō (3rd conjugation -iō type)
docs.text:
This is a mixed pattern. The first principal part ends in -iō, like the 4th conjugation, but the infinitive ends in short -ere, like the 3rd: capiō, capere, cēpī, captum; faciō, facere, fēcī, factum; iaciō, iacere, iēcī, iactum.

The i appears wherever the 4th conjugation has it before a vowel: capiō, capiunt, the imperfect capiēbam, the future capiam, capiēs, the participle capiēns. Elsewhere the verb behaves like the 3rd conjugation: capis, capit, capimus, capitis, capere, caperem.

docs.title: 4th conjugation — -īre
docs.text: The stem ends in long -ī-: audiō, audīre, audīvī, audītum; veniō, venīre, vēnī, ventum; sciō, scīre, scīvī, scītum.

docs.title: Irregular verbs
docs.text:
These verbs don't follow any of the regular classes, and the catalogue stores their irregular forms explicitly.

  • sum, esse, fuī, futūrus — to be.
  • possum, posse, potuī — to be able. A compound of pot- (from potis, "able") and sum.
  • eō, īre, iī, itum — to go.
  • ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum — to bring, to bear. Its perfect and supine come from different roots.
  • volō, velle, voluī — to want.
  • nōlō, nōlle, nōluī — not to want (nē + volō).
  • mālō, mālle, māluī — to prefer (magis + volō).
  • fīō, fierī, factus sum — to become, to be made. It serves as the passive of facere.

The Fully irregular group holds sum, possum, eō and fīō, together with compounds such as absum, abeō, redeō and trānseō. Ferō, volō, nōlō and mālō are filed under the 3rd conjugation, with their irregular forms stored.

Then there are the defective verbs. Each is filed under its conjugation, and the tenses it lacks show a dash:

  • meminī, meminisse — to remember. It has only perfect-system forms, with present meaning.
  • ōdī, ōdisse — to hate. Same pattern.
  • coepī, coepisse, coeptum — to have begun.

docs.title: B. Latin tense system
docs.text: The classical Latin tense system is built on two stems. The present stem comes from the infinitive, the second principal part (amā-re). The perfect stem is the third principal part minus its -ī (amāv-ī). Latin has six indicative tenses, four subjunctive tenses and two imperative tenses, plus the non-finite forms.

docs.title: Indicative — present system
docs.text:
These tenses are built on the present stem.

  • Praesens — amō, amās, amat, amāmus, amātis, amant — "I love / am loving".
  • Imperfectum — amābam, amābās, amābat… — "I was loving / used to love".
  • Futurum — amābō, amābis, amābit… in the 1st and 2nd conjugations; regam, regēs, reget… (and audiam, audiēs…) in the 3rd and 4th — "I will love".

The passives are formed directly from the same stem: amor, amāris, amātur… / amābar, amābāris… / amābor, amāberis….

docs.title: Indicative — perfect system
docs.text:
The active forms are built on the perfect stem. The passive forms combine the perfect participle with a form of esse.

  • Perfectum — amāvī, amāvistī, amāvit, amāvimus, amāvistis, amāvērunt — "I have loved / I loved". Passive: amātus sum.
  • Plusquamperfectum — amāveram, amāverās… — "I had loved". Passive: amātus eram.
  • Futurum Exactum — amāverō, amāveris… — "I will have loved". Passive: amātus erō.

docs.title: Coniunctivus
docs.text:
The subjunctive has four tenses, each in the active and the passive. It is used in subordinate clauses (purpose, result, indirect command, indirect question, conditions, fearing and more), and in main clauses with jussive, optative, deliberative or potential meaning.

  • Coniunctivus Praesens — amem, amēs, amet, amēmus, amētis, ament. Passive: amer, amēris….
  • Coniunctivus Imperfectum — amārem, amārēs, amāret… (the present infinitive plus personal endings). Passive: amārer, amārēris….
  • Coniunctivus Perfectum — amāverim, amāverīs…. Passive: amātus sim.
  • Coniunctivus Plusquamperfectum — amāvissem, amāvissēs…. Passive: amātus essem.

docs.title: Imperative
docs.text:
• Present — amā (singular), amāte (plural). This is the everyday "do this!".
  • Future — amātō (2nd and 3rd person singular), amātōte (2nd plural), amantō (3rd plural). It belongs to a formal register and appears in laws, prayers and maxims.

The passive forms are amāre and amāminī in the present, and amātor and amantor in the future.

docs.title: Non-finite forms
docs.text:
• Six infinitives: three tenses × two voices (amāre, amāvisse, amātūrus esse; amārī, amātus esse, amātum īrī).
  • Four participles: present active (amāns), perfect passive (amātus), future active (amātūrus), and future passive, also called the gerundive (amandus).
  • Gerund: the verbal noun, amandī, amandō, amandum, amandō.
  • Supine: the accusative in -um expresses purpose after verbs of motion (spectātum eō, "I go to watch"). The ablative in -ū expresses respect (mīrābile dictū, "wonderful to say").

You can turn any tense on or off in Select tenses.

docs.title: C. Latin declensions
docs.text: The five declensions are the main way to select Latin nouns. The genitive singular ending tells you the declension. You can often predict the gender from the declension and the ending, though not always, so every noun's gender is stored in the catalogue.

docs.title: First declension
docs.text:
The stem ends in -a-, and the genitive singular ends in -ae. Almost all these nouns are feminine. The exceptions are masculine nouns for men and their roles: agricola, nauta, poēta, pīrāta, scrība, aurīga.

Endings (singular / plural): nominative -a / -ae · genitive -ae / -ārum · dative -ae / -īs · accusative -am / -ās · ablative -ā / -īs. The vocative is the same as the nominative.

docs.title: Second declension
docs.text:
The stem ends in -o-, and the genitive singular ends in -ī. There are two main types:

  • Masculine -us (servus, dominus, amīcus), with a vocative singular in -e (serve!). Nouns in -er (puer, ager, magister) take the same endings, except that the nominative and vocative singular end in -er. Some keep the e in the other cases (puer, puerī), others drop it (ager, agrī); the genitive shows which.
  • Neuter -um (bellum, dōnum, oppidum). As with all neuters, the nominative and accusative are identical, and the nominative and accusative plural end in -a.

Deus has irregular plural forms (dī, deōrum, dīs), which the catalogue stores.

docs.title: Third declension
docs.text:
The stem ends in a consonant or in -i-, and the genitive singular ends in -is. Nouns of all three genders belong here. This is the most varied declension: you can't predict the nominative from the genitive, so learn both.

  • Consonant stems: rēx, rēgis; cōnsul, cōnsulis; pater, patris; corpus, corporis. Genitive plural in -um.
  • i-stems: urbs, urbis; cīvis, cīvis; mare, maris. The genitive plural ends in -ium (urbium). Neuters in -e, -al and -ar have the ablative singular in -ī and the nominative and accusative plural in -ia (marī, maria). Masculine and feminine i-stems can have the accusative plural in -īs as well as -ēs. A few nouns, such as turris and puppis, also have an accusative singular in -im and an ablative in -ī.

Nouns in -or are usually masculine. The exceptions arbor, soror and uxor are feminine, and the catalogue records them that way. Bōs, bovis has the irregular plurals boum and bōbus.

docs.title: Fourth declension
docs.text: The stem ends in -u-, and the genitive singular ends in -ūs. Most of these nouns are masculine. The best-known feminines are manus (hand) and domus (house). Domus borrows some second-declension forms, such as the ablative domō. The neuters cornū (horn) and genū (knee) end in -ū throughout the singular.

docs.title: Fifth declension
docs.text: The stem ends in -ē-. The genitive and dative singular end in -ēī after a vowel (diēī) and in -eī after a consonant (reī, fideī, speī). Almost all these nouns are feminine, except diēs (day), which is usually masculine. It is a small group; the catalogue has eight: rēs, diēs, fidēs, spēs, faciēs, glaciēs, aciēs, speciēs. Some have few plural forms: spēs and speciēs have no genitive, dative or ablative plural.

docs.title: Irregular nouns
docs.text: Two nouns have their whole paradigm stored by hand: vīs (force, power; plural vīrēs, strength) and Iuppiter (genitive Iovis). In the catalogue, vīs has no genitive or dative singular, and Iuppiter has no plural. You can drill both like any other noun. The drills use the stored forms and skip the missing ones.

docs.title: Plūrāle tantum
docs.text: Some nouns exist only in the plural. In the catalogue these are moenia (city walls), līberī (children), arma (weapons), castra (military camp), hīberna (winter quarters), īnsidiae (ambush), tenebrae (darkness), dīvitiae (riches), superī (the gods above) and māiōrēs (ancestors). Their singular forms are marked as missing, so the declension drills only ask for plural forms.

docs.title: D. Latin adjective patterns
docs.text: Latin adjectives follow five textbook patterns. Every adjective in the catalogue has a full case × number × gender paradigm.

docs.title: 1st/2nd-declension -us / -a / -um
docs.text: The masculine takes the 2nd-declension -us endings, the feminine the 1st-declension -a endings, and the neuter the 2nd-declension -um endings: bonus, bona, bonum; magnus, magna, magnum. This is by far the largest pattern: about two thirds of the adjectives in the catalogue.

docs.title: 1st/2nd-declension -er / -a / -um
docs.text:
The same endings as the -us pattern, but the masculine nominative singular ends in -er. There are two types:

  • Keeps the e in the other forms: miser, misera, miserum (genitive miserī); līber, lībera, līberum.
  • Drops the e: pulcher, pulchra, pulchrum; sacer, sacra, sacrum; noster, nostra, nostrum.

Each of these adjectives is stored with its genitive, which shows whether the e stays, so the app generates the right forms.

docs.title: 3rd-declension two-ending
docs.text:
The masculine and feminine share one form, and the neuter has another: fortis, forte; brevis, breve; facilis, facile; omnis, omne.

These adjectives follow the i-stem third declension: ablative singular in -ī, genitive plural in -ium, and neuter nominative and accusative plural in -ia.

docs.title: 3rd-declension one-ending
docs.text:
One nominative singular form serves all three genders, and the genitive shows the stem: ingēns (genitive ingentis), fēlīx (fēlīcis), audāx (audācis), sapiēns (sapientis), vetus (veteris), pār (paris).

The app always cites these adjectives with their genitive (ingēns, ingentis), so the stem is clear.

docs.title: 3rd-declension three-ending
docs.text: Here the masculine, feminine and neuter nominative singular all differ. This is the smallest group, with eight adjectives in the catalogue, including ācer, ācris, ācre; celer, celeris, celere; alacer, alacris, alacre; equester, equestris, equestre.

docs.title: Comparative and superlative
docs.text:
The app derives a comparative and a superlative for each adjective in the catalogue, and the Sentence parser recognises these forms.

  • Comparative: add -ior (masculine and feminine) or -ius (neuter) to the stem: altus → altior, altius; fortis → fortior, fortius. It declines like a 3rd-declension two-ending adjective, but with consonant-stem endings (ablative -e, genitive plural -um, neuter plural -a).
  • Superlative: the regular ending is -issimus, -issima, -issimum. Adjectives in -er take -rimus instead (miser → miserrimus, pulcher → pulcherrimus, ācer → ācerrimus). Six adjectives in -ilis take -limus: facilis → facillimus, and likewise difficilis, similis, dissimilis, gracilis, humilis.

docs.title: Irregular comparison
docs.text:
A few common adjectives use entirely different stems for the comparative and superlative:

Positive Comparative Superlative bonus melior, melius optimus magnus maior, maius maximus malus peior, peius pessimus parvus minor, minus minimus multus plūs plūrimus

The catalogue stores the irregular forms of bonus, magnus, malus and parvus explicitly rather than deriving them. It also stores the six superlatives in -illimus and the comparison of multus (plūs, plūrimus).

docs.title: Latin and speech
docs.text: Apple has never shipped a Latin voice. Instead of leaving Latin silent, LinguaMorpha reads it aloud with an Italian voice installed on your device. Italian spelling rules are closer to Latin than any other voice you are likely to have.

docs.title: How Latin speech works
docs.text:
• The app chooses the voice. Spanish and French each have a Voice row in their Settings tab where you pick the voice. The Latin tab has no such row. The app picks one of the Italian voices installed on your device, and you can't change which one.
  • Latin is read slowly. Latin always plays at about half the normal speed, and the Speed setting has no effect on it. The slower pace makes each syllable easier to follow.
  • No Italian voice, no sound. If no Italian voice is installed, the speaker button does nothing; the app never falls back to an English voice. The Listen option in the flashcard decks is then not offered for Latin either.
  • No pronouns. Latin conjugation rows are labelled 1 sg, 2 sg, 3 sg, 1 pl, 2 pl, 3 pl, and a table read aloud gives the bare forms. The Include pronoun switch that Spanish and French have is not offered for Latin.

docs.title: It is an approximation, not a Latin pronunciation
docs.text:
An Italian voice reading Latin is a rough guide, not the correct pronunciation. The app teaches Classical Latin, and Italian reading rules differ from it in ways you will hear:

  • c before e and i is read as ch, so Cicerō sounds like "CHEE-che-ro" instead of the classical "KIH-ke-roh". In Classical Latin, c is always hard.
  • v is read as English v, where Classical Latin has w: vīnum is "VEE-noom", not "WEE-noom".
  • Vowel length is not heard. Macrons don't change what the voice does, so ā and a sound alike. The slower speed helps you hear the syllables, but it can't add a distinction the voice doesn't make.

Use speech to get a feel for the shape and rhythm of a word, and to check that you're reading the right syllables. Don't use it as a model for pronouncing Latin: the macrons in the written form are the authority, and they are what the app checks you on (see Macron-accurate checking).

docs.title: Where the speaker appears
docs.text:
Latin speech is available on the screens Latin shares with the other languages: the meaning flashcards, the conjugation drills, the conjugation tables of a verb, and the example sentences under a verb's tenses.

There is no speaker on the declension tables.

docs.title: Getting the best out of it
docs.text: If Latin stays silent, install an Italian voice. On iPhone or iPad, go to Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices → Italian. On the Mac, go to System Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → System Voice → Manage Voices. Enhanced and Premium voices sound noticeably better than the standard ones.

docs.title: Verbs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Latin Verbs section covers over 600 verbs, with the full classical tense system: present and perfect systems, indicative, subjunctive and imperative, active and passive, plus the non-finite forms (six infinitives, four participles, gerund, supine). Open it from the Verbs tile on the Self Study screen. Like every topic hub, it has three sections: Theory, Study and Practice.

The verbs are filed in six verb groups:

  • 1st conjugation (-āre): amō, amāre; laudō, laudāre. Over 200 verbs.
  • 2nd conjugation (-ēre), with a long stem vowel: moneō, monēre; videō, vidēre.
  • 3rd conjugation (-ere), with a short stem vowel: regō, regere; dūcō, dūcere. The largest group, over 250 verbs.
  • 3rd-iō conjugation: capiō, capere; faciō, facere. A mixed pattern.
  • 4th conjugation (-īre): audiō, audīre; veniō, venīre.
  • Fully irregular: sum / esse, possum / posse, eō / īre, fīō / fierī, and compounds such as abesse and redīre.

ferō / ferre, volō / velle, nōlō / nōlle and mālō / mālle are filed under the 3rd conjugation. Their irregular forms (fers, fert; vīs, vult; velim) are stored one by one, and the tables mark them as irregular. Deponents (hortārī, loquī, patī) and defectives are not groups of their own; each is filed under its conjugation. The defectives meminisse, ōdisse and coepisse show a dash for the tenses they lack.

For the endings of each conjugation, see Appendix A. For the tenses, see Appendix B.

docs.title: Practice: Select verb groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select verb groups decides which verbs are in your drill pool. The rows are the six groups above, under two headings, Conjugations and Irregular, and each row shows how many verbs it holds. Tap ⓘ on a row to read about that group, or long-press a heading to read about the whole family. The hub row shows how many groups you have ticked ("5 of 6").

Verb group is the only filter on this screen. There is no textbook-chapter or frequency filter. Your level (the chip beside the flag) and your topics (Self Study → Select word scope) apply everywhere. If your topic scope removes every verb you picked, the hub shows a red warning at the top of Practice, above the selection rows.

docs.title: Practice: Select tenses
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select tenses turns individual tenses on or off. Latin has 36 of them, and the hub row shows how many are on ("12 of 36"). Two views are available:

  • By Section: the tenses grouped as Indicativus – Tempora Imperfecta, Indicativus – Tempora Perfecta, Coniunctivus, Imperativus, Imperativus Passivum, the three passive sections, Formae Non Finitae, Participia, and Gerundium et Supinum. Long-press a section heading for an explanation.
  • By Level: the same tenses grouped by the level at which each first appears.

Tap ⓘ on a tense to open the Tenses page at that tense, with its card open: when the tense is used, its endings table, how it is formed, and examples. It is the same page as Theory → Tenses, so the other tenses are one tap away. On iPhone and iPad it opens with a back button. On Mac it opens in a window of its own, which can stay open beside the list; another ⓘ moves it to the new tense. Use this screen to limit a drill to the tense you are learning, or to leave out tenses you haven't covered yet. The drills, the tables and the verb example sentences only show tenses that are switched on.

iPhoneiPadMac

docs.title: Theory: Conjugations and Tenses
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Conjugations explains the verb system. A short introduction sets out the tense system, then come the collapsible cards:

  • Reading principal parts: how amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum give you every form, and which tenses the present stem and the perfect stem build, with capiō as a worked example
  • one card for each of the five conjugations, plus Irregular and defective verbs
  • How irregularities are shown: the marks used in the tables

The conjugation tables use two marks. Red marks the part of a form you have to learn for this verb. When a whole form is red (esse, posse), it has no regular connection to any pattern. An underline marks the ending the pattern predicts, on regular and irregular forms alike. Latin has only one set of endings, so the blue mark used in other languages never appears in Latin tables.

iPhoneiPadMac

Tenses lists the tenses by section. Each one folds out into the explanation the ⓘ on Select tenses opens: when the tense is used, its endings, how it is formed, and examples.

iPhoneiPadMac

Regular patterns, at the bottom of the Conjugations page under To print, puts every tense's endings on printable pages, one page per stem (praesens, perfectum, supinum), each in the colour that stem has on the verb page, with the tenses grouped by mood and voice. It holds the regular endings only; an irregular verb's forms are on its own reference sheet.

docs.title: Study: Verb reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Verb reference lists every verb in your selection from A to Z. Search by the Latin infinitive or by the translation. Tap a verb to open its detail screen (see Inside a verb: the tabbed detail).

docs.title: Inside a verb: the tabbed detail
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The screen is titled with the verb's headword — amāre in the Dutch interface, amō in the English and Spanish ones (see How the app writes Latin). Under the title is the citation line with the principal parts in the same order (amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum; a deponent ends in secūtus sum) and the verb's group. For a verb with several distinct senses, Extended meaning, folded away, lists them, each with an example; it goes with the translations, so a scheme that shows none hides it too. Three tabs follow: Conjugation · Regularity · Reference sheet. The screen opens on Conjugation.

A compound that conjugates through another verb has a family note above the tabs: redīre belongs to the family of īre, with abīre, exīre, perīre and trānsīre. The note also says what the members share. Where every principal part is the prefix in front of the base's, every form is, as with īre. Where the prefix changed the root vowel, only the perfect comes from the base, and the present stem and the participle are the compound's own, as with efficere beside facere. On the base verb the note lists the members.

Conjugation shows the tables for the tenses you have selected. A By Tense / By Person / Filter picker switches between three views:

  • By Tense shows each tense as a full table.
  • By Person turns the tables around: one panel per person (1 sg, 2 sg, …) listing that person's form in every tense, with the tense name above each form. The mood and the stem (cad- from cadere, cecid- from cecidī) are named where they change, so you see where the perfect stem takes over. A dash marks a form the verb does not have, such as the passive of an intransitive verb.
  • Filter has chips for Modus, Tense, Stem (Praesens, Perfectum, Supinum) and Voice (Activum, Passivum), so you can narrow the forms down. For example, you can show only the tenses built on the perfect stem.
iPhoneiPadMac

In By Tense and By Person, the translations button in the toolbar shows a translation under every form. Every Latin verb has these translations. Where a verb has a second meaning, a ⇄ button switches all the translations to that meaning.

In By Tense a line under each tense's name says what the tense is for, and under the table is the verb's own sentence in that tense, with its translation, where the course has one. A verb without such sentences shows a generated one, marked auto and without translation, under the few tenses the generator covers. Each table's header has a book icon, which opens that tense's theory: when it is used, how it is formed, its endings. For a compound that takes the tense from its base, the theory says so first: abeō is ab- in front of eō, so it is eō that the endings table explains.

Only irregular tenses. The filter button in the toolbar shows only the tenses where this verb departs from its pattern. The choice is remembered across verbs, and per device. While it hides tenses, a note above the tables says so — "Only irregular tenses: 4 of 16 shown." — with Show all tenses to switch it off.

Why a tense departs. Under the table of a tense where the verb departs from its pattern is a fold-out, labelled with the verdict (Partly irregular, Regular endings, changed stem). Open, it gives the reason in a sentence, the stems the tense is built on (a stem to learn in amber), and for each form that departs the form the pattern predicts, struck through, beside the real one.

Regularity starts with a card of the verb's Level and, only when the verb is Deponent, Intransitive or has No passive, its Voice. Below it, Regularity lists the tenses in which the verb departs from the regular pattern, and only those. Each row gives a verdict (Regular endings, changed stem, Regular endings, learned form, Partly irregular, Irregular or No regular pattern) and the stems the tense is built on. A stem you have to memorise, such as ferre's tul- or capere's cēp-, is shown in amber. For the perfect system, that is the perfect stem taken from the third principal part. A last line names the tenses that follow the pattern; a verb with nothing to learn shows only Regular in all tenses. Tap a row to go to that tense on Conjugation, with its explanation open under the table.

The two colours answer different questions. Amber on Regularity names a whole stem to learn. Red in a conjugation table marks the letters of a single form that depart from the pattern.

iPhoneiPadMac

Reference sheet is a printable one-page PDF of the active voice. Its header shows the citation line (the principal parts, in the order of the interface language), the conjugation and any notes (Deponent, Active only, Defective, or which verb it is a compound of). Below that are the main non-finite forms and the Indicativus, Coniunctivus and Imperativus tables. On iPhone and iPad, share it from the share button. On the Mac, the share menu has Copy and Save as….

docs.title: Practice: Verb meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Flashcards for the verbs in your pool: turn the card and mark whether you knew the meaning. The book icon on a card opens the verb's conjugation.

docs.title: Practice: Produce the conjugation
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This is the production drill. The question names the verb and gives the Mood, Tense, Voice and Person on separate lines, so you see each part of the question separately. You give the form in one of two modes:

  • Type: type the form.
  • Pick: choose it from a wheel of up to ten options: the right form and forms that look like it.

For how macrons are checked, see Macron-accurate checking. Once your answer is graded, a book on the card opens the verb's table for that tense — in a window of its own on the Mac — and closes when you go on. If you type a real form of the wrong tense or person, the feedback tells you which form you produced. The gear button opens Production settings. There you can limit the drill to chosen values of Verb, Mood, Tense, Voice and Person. Leave a line empty to let it vary.

docs.title: Practice: Recognise the conjugation
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This is the recognition drill. You see a conjugated form and identify it. The gear button opens Recognition settings:

  • Picker style: Chips (the default) or Wheel.
  • Multi-answer mode: Latin forms are often ambiguous. With this mode off, any one correct analysis counts. With it on, you add each analysis with Add this analysis before checking, and only the complete set counts as a perfect answer.
  • Test me on: choose which of Verb, Mood, Tense, Voice and Person you are asked. The rest appear as hints above the form. Stem is always a hint. By default you are asked verb, tense and person.
  • Verb options: how many verbs the verb picker offers: 5, 10, 15 (the default), 25 or All. The extra choices are verbs that look like the right one.
iPhoneiPadMac

After you check, the feedback lists all the valid analyses of the form.

docs.title: Practice: Principal parts
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Flashcards for the principal parts. The front shows a perfect or a supine (tulī, āctum, cēpī), and you name the verb it belongs to. Turn the card for the full citation and the meaning, and mark whether you knew it.

The deck takes the verbs in your Select verb groups selection, but only those whose conjugation does not predict the perfect and the supine. amāre → amāvī, amātum follows the rule and is not asked; agere → ēgī, āctum and ferre → tulī, lātum are. That leaves most of the 3rd conjugation and the 3rd -iō, the irregular verbs, and the 1st, 2nd and 4th conjugation verbs that depart from their class. The line above the card shows how many verbs this round asks and how many the deck holds.

docs.title: Irregularity by tense
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Irregularity by tense is not a row of the Verbs hub: open it from Linguistic analysis → Irregularity by tense. It has one row per tense, with how many things there are to learn there (a family of verbs that share one stem counts once, and so does a verb on its own) and the share of its verbs that are not fully predictable. Opening a row lists them, and tapping a verb opens its page at that tense, with the explanation of why it departs open under the table. Practise then starts Produce the conjugation over exactly those verbs in that tense. Where other drills are about the tense, it is a menu that offers them too: Principal parts and Perfectum or imperfectum for the perfectum, Perfectum or imperfectum for the imperfectum, Indicativus or coniunctivus for the subjunctivus praesens. A tense with fewer than three offers no Practise button.

The filter. The filter button in the toolbar is on when the list opens: it shows the irregular verbs only. Switch it off (Show all verbs) and the list shows every verb in your level, from A to Z, each opening at that tense. Only the irregular verbs show the explanation of why they depart. Practise and the drills still work on the irregular verbs only.

The order menu sorts the irregular verbs:

  • By pattern: the verbs grouped by the pattern they follow. The list opens this way.
  • By reason: the verbs grouped under The stem differs, The ending differs, and The stem and the ending differ for a verb that departs in both. Each row shows the stem the verb takes in that tense, and for a family, how many more verbs share it (+ and a number). At the top, the box Fewer than the numbers suggest counts what there is to learn: a family of verbs that share one stem counts once, and so does a verb on its own.
  • Alphabetical: the verbs from A to Z.

With the filter off, the order menu is not shown. Cycle through randomly shows one verb's conjugation at a time and walks every verb on the list, as the list is shown.

docs.title: Practice: Perfectum or imperfectum
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This is a choice drill. You see an English sentence and a Latin sentence with a gap, and you choose between the perfect and the imperfect form of the verb. The bank has 36 sentences of three kinds:

  • sentences with a time marker (herī)
  • stories where one action is the background and another interrupts it
  • verbs whose meaning changes with the tense (tacēbat, "he was silent", against tacuit, "he fell silent")

After each answer, an explanation shows why that tense is right.

docs.title: Practice: Indicativus or coniunctivus
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This drill works the same way, but you choose the mood. It has 33 sentences. Most test clauses where the clause type decides the mood: purpose, result, indirect question, cum-clauses, relative clauses of characteristic, and unreal conditions. Others use the indicative correctly, so that you learn not to use the subjunctive everywhere.

The two choice drills and the other multiple-choice drills have fixed-length sessions. Set the length with Questions per session in Settings → Study. The Incorrect answers switch on the drill screen limits a session to the items you got wrong before.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
For learners new to Latin verbs:

  1. Select the 1st conjugation only, and switch on only the present indicative active (Praesens).
  2. Run Produce the conjugation in Type mode until the present comes without thinking.
  3. Add the Imperfectum and Futurum, still active and still 1st conjugation.
  4. Add the 2nd and 3rd conjugations. The stem vowel is what tells them apart.
  5. Add the perfect system (Perfectum, Plusquamperfectum, Futurum Exactum). Use each verb's Regularity tab and Reference sheet to learn its principal parts, and drill them with Principal parts.
  6. Add the passive once the active forms are solid. Most students slow down at the periphrastic perfect passive (amātus sum).
  7. Add the subjunctive last. Its forms are regular, but when to use it is a subject of its own. Indicativus or coniunctivus drills exactly that.

If you follow a textbook (Wheelock, Lingua Latina per se Illustrata), use Select tenses to switch on each tense as the book introduces it. The catalogue is not tagged by textbook chapter, so there is no chapter filter.

docs.title: Other Vocabulary
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Other Vocabulary tile holds single words that have no hub of their own. In Latin, these are the conjunctions (et, sed, nam, igitur, quamquam, …) and interjections (ō, ecce, heu, …), and a few words with no hub of their own: the verbs inquam, aiō, for, licet, decet and oportet, the pronouns nihil and quisquis, and necesse. Prepositions have their own hub (see Prepositions).

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select word groups: tick the categories you want. Tap ⓘ on a category to see its words. Your level also applies. Topics do not.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Word reference: the selected words with their translations.
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Word meaning: flashcards for the meaning of each word.
iPhoneiPadMac

This hub has no Theory page for Latin.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Every course is organised in levels. A level scheme says at which level each thing first appears — words, tenses and the other grammar, drills and theory — and your level decides how much of that you see. Levels add up: at the third level you see everything of the first three. The standard schemes of Spanish and French name their levels after CEFR, A1 to C2; Latin's has six levels of its own.

docs.title: Your level
docs.text:
Your current level, such as A1, is shown in one chip with the course's flag and the scheme in use: in the toolbar on iPhone and iPad, at the top of the sidebar on the Mac. A new install starts at the first level, and so does a scheme you have not used before. Tap or click the chip for Scheme and level (a window of its own on the Mac). It has three sections:

  • Learner — who is studying; see Learners below.
  • Scheme — the courses, the one you study ticked. Tap a course to fold out its schemes; choosing a scheme of another course switches to that course. A lock marks the schemes of a course you have not unlocked, and they open the store. Tap the scheme in use to fold out its levels: All levels first — no level: everything shows, as in a course without a scheme, except what the scheme leaves out with Not shown — then the levels where something starts. Choose one to change what the app shows; the top level shows everything the scheme shows at all.
  • Level — the three switches below, offered only at a level, not at All levels.

The switches:

  • Assign items — for your own scheme: set, on each item as you walk through the app, the level at which it first appears (see Assigning items in the app). A built-in scheme cannot be changed, so it is not offered there.
  • Show levels — puts a small chip with its level on every item, read-only.
  • Only new at this level — the meaning decks hold only the words your level adds, not those of the levels below, and the reference lists open showing only what is new at your level. Above each list a control switches between New at A2 (n), Up to A2 and All levels, which adds the words of higher levels; a choice with nothing in it is left out, and searching looks through everything. A sparkle beside your level shows that it is on.

Changing your level shows and hides; it deletes nothing. Your answers are kept per item and count again when an item comes back.

Your level applies to Self Study: its hubs, drills, reference lists and theory. A theory page leaves out the cards above your level; Also later levels at the top brings them back, with their level beside them, and does the same for the tenses on a verb's page. Practice Sets follow it too: a set whose tenses or most of whose words lie above your level is kept off the list (Also later levels at the top shows them; it is the same setting as on the theory pages, and it is kept), and a set's words are trimmed to your level on its page. Grammar lessons follow the same level, but only mark what lies above it: a lesson above your level is dimmed, and a module that lies wholly above it says Above this level; every lesson stays open. At All levels nothing is above.

docs.title: Learners
docs.text:
Several people can study on one device, each as a learner. The Learner section of Scheme and level lists them, the active one ticked; tap another to switch to them. Add learner adds one by name. Touch and hold a learner (right-click on the Mac) for Rename and Delete; deleting says how many answers go with them, and when the last one goes a new, empty Default learner takes their place. The first learner is called Default until you rename it.

Each learner has their own progress, scheme and level; everything else, such as the settings, your own schemes and the practice sets, is shared. Once there are several, the chip shows the active learner's name before the flag. You cannot switch learner during a drill: finish it first.

docs.title: Level schemes
docs.text:
Open the dialog from the Level schemes row in the course tab of Settings, which shows the scheme in use. It has two columns, one above the other on iPhone:

  • Scheme — the course's built-in schemes, each marked with a lock, the standard one first; then your own schemes. A checkmark marks the scheme in use. Selecting a scheme shows its levels; it does not switch to it.
  • Levels — the selected scheme's levels, each with how many items start there and of what kind, and a Not shown row for what the scheme leaves out. The line under the list names the level that holds everything the scheme does not name.

Every action is on a menu: right-click on the Mac, touch and hold on iPhone and iPad. The line at the bottom of the dialog says so.

docs.title: Working with schemes
docs.text:
A scheme's menu offers:

  • Use — makes it the scheme in use.
  • Duplicate… — copies it under a new name, with its levels and which item is on which level; the copy becomes the scheme in use. This is how you start from a built-in scheme.
  • Export… — saves the scheme as a file, to keep or to give to someone.
  • Summary as PDF… — what starts at each level, as a PDF to save, share or print.
  • Rename…, Place words…, Options… and Delete… — your own schemes only. Delete… removes the scheme from this device; export it first if you want to keep it.
  • New… and Import… — on the empty space under the list too.

New… asks for a name, the levels, and under Start with how to begin: Everything on the first level, after which you assign items in the app, or Take over “…” for an existing scheme, choosing under Where the levels go which new level each of its levels becomes.

Import… reads a scheme file. A file for another course, one that does not fit this course, one that is too large, or one that is not a level file at all is refused with a sentence saying why. A scheme you already have asks before the file replaces it. After an import the app says how many levels arrived and what did not match: names this course does not know are ignored, and words the file does not mention follow the scheme's word rule or sit on the level that holds everything unnamed.

docs.title: Opening a level
docs.text: Select a level to see its items by name, grouped by kind — verbs, nouns, tenses, drills and so on. ‹ Levels goes back. In your own scheme, an item's menu offers Move to another level, or — to leave it out; on the Mac, ⌘-click or ⇧-click selects several items first.

docs.title: Changing the levels
docs.text: In your own scheme, a level's menu offers Rename…, Insert level before…, Insert level after…, Move up, Move down and Delete…. A new level starts empty, and moving a level takes its items along. Deleting an empty level just removes it; deleting one that holds items — or the level that holds everything unnamed — asks where they go: to another level, or to —, where they are not shown at any level.

docs.title: Placing words
docs.text:
Place words… on your own scheme puts whole word types on the levels in one go. For Verbs, Nouns, Adjectives and Adverbs choose:

  • Unchanged — leave the type as it is.
  • By frequency — the most frequent words on the first level, and each next level half as many again. Frequency is measured in a corpus of the language; a word without a measured value is placed by its frequency band.
  • All on the lowest level.
  • Not placed — the words of that type are not shown at any level.

Each row says how many words the type has and how it is placed now. Preview shows how many words of each type each level would get. Apply asks first, because it replaces the placements you made by hand for those types.

The choice is kept with the scheme. Words added to the app later follow it: a new word goes to the level whose words are as frequent as it is, and no word already placed moves.

docs.title: Scheme options
docs.text:
Options… on your own scheme holds the switches that are not about levels:

  • Show translations — off for a learner who already speaks the language: the word lists, the drills and the guides show no translation. The meaning drills are then pointless; hide them on the Levels side.
  • Tense names — as courses for learners name them, or as the language's own schools do. Only for a course that has both traditions. Every table, drill and guide follows the choice.
  • App language — the app language the scheme sets, once, when it is chosen; Leave as it is sets none. The learner can change it afterwards in Settings.
  • Unnamed items at — the level that holds everything the scheme does not name: a word added to the app later, a drill with no level set.

The built-in schemes keep their own settings; duplicate one to change them.

docs.title: Assigning items in the app
docs.text: With Assign items on, every item carries a chip with its level — word rows, tenses, drills, theory, topics — and items above your level are dimmed rather than hidden. Tap a chip to choose the item's level: its own level and the ones next to it, Other levels for the rest, and Not shown to leave it out. A pencil beside your level reminds you that assigning is on; switch it off in Scheme and level.

docs.title: Level and word scope
docs.text: The level decides what exists in Self Study. Select word scope narrows it further by topic, and each hub's selection rows by group. See Choosing what is in play.

docs.title: The main screen
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

When you open the app you land on the main screen. On iPhone and iPad it is the screen titled LinguaMorpha; on the Mac it is a window with a sidebar on the left and the chosen area on the right. From here you choose how to study and reach the global tools.

On iPhone and iPad, while the Open the app on this page switch on the Getting started page is on, the app opens on Getting started first. Switch it off when you no longer need it; the page stays on the main screen. On the Mac the same page is Home, and the app always opens there.

docs.title: On iPhone and iPad
docs.text:
At the top is the trial banner (see The platform shape) and, when there is one, the update line (see Updates and ratings below), then a Getting started row, then large cards. Which cards you see depends on the course you are studying:

  • Grammar lessons — step-by-step lessons in a fixed order.
  • Theory — the grammar of the course in one place, by word type. See Theory.
  • Practice Sets — ready-made sessions you run as a unit. The card says how many sets the course has and what kinds of practice they cover. You can build your own, and share sets with another learner.
  • Self Study — you decide which verbs, nouns, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, numerals, phrases and other vocabulary are in play, and which drill to run. See Self Study.
  • Tests — every test for your level, by word type, each with the theory one tap away. See Tests.
  • Linguistic analysis — explore the catalogue's structure and export it.

If the course is locked (the trial is over and you have not bought it), the cards open the store instead.

Toolbar, left side

  • The chip — the flag of the course you are studying, the scheme in use and your level in it, such as A1; with more than one learner, the learner's name comes first. Tap it for Scheme and level, where you choose the learner, the course and its scheme, and the level; see Levels.
  • The chart icon — opens My Progress.

Toolbar, right side

  • Unlock — opens the store: each course with its price (or Owned), Unlock all languages, Restore Previous Purchase, and Redeem Code for an offer code you have received.
  • The ⋯ menu — Getting started, Help (with This screen, the User Guide and the guide for the course you are studying), Settings and About.

The Look up button

The round magnifying glass at the bottom right is on every screen, not only this one. It opens Look up over the screen you are on; swipe it away and you are back where you were. On an iPad with a keyboard, ⇧⌘F does the same. It is hidden while a drill is running: a drill that asks for a form while the answer is one lookup away measures nothing.

docs.title: On the Mac
docs.text:
The sidebar replaces the cards and the toolbar icons. From top to bottom:

  • Look up a form — a search field: type any form and the right-hand pane shows what it is (see Look up). Clear the field and you are back where you were.
  • The chip — the course's flag, the scheme in use and your level, with the learner's name when there are several. Click it for the Scheme and level window; see Levels. Everything below follows it.
  • Home — the start page, where the app opens: a card for each way to study. ⇧⌘H brings you back to it from anywhere, and so does the back chevron at the top of every section: Back, Back, … always ends on Home.
  • Study — Grammar lessons, Theory, Practice Sets, Self Study and Tests; Grammar lessons and Practice Sets where the course has them.
  • Tools — Linguistic analysis, Traps (Spanish) and My Progress.
  • Help — User Guide and the guide for the course you are studying. The guides open in the right-hand pane.
  • At the foot, the update line when there is one (see Updates and ratings below), the trial countdown while the trial runs, and the Unlock button (Purchases once you own everything).

From any screen, Edit ▸ Look up… (⇧⌘F) opens Look up in a window of its own beside the main window, starting on an empty field — handy for looking up while you read. ⌘F goes to the search field of the screen you are on, or to the sidebar's Look up field on a screen without one. Look up is not offered while a drill is running.

Settings and About are in the LinguaMorpha menu rather than the sidebar; see On the Mac.

docs.title: Updates and ratings
docs.text:
A newer version. About once a day the app asks the App Store which version it has. When that is newer than the one you are running, a line says so — Version 1.1.0 is in the App Store — with Update, which opens the App Store page, and ✕, which hides it until an even newer version appears. The App Store usually updates apps by itself; the line is for when that is switched off. Only the version number counts, so a line appears once per release, not for every build.

A rating. Now and then, at the end of a round that went well, the app may ask you to rate it, in Apple's own window. It asks only after you have used it for a while — at least a week, several sessions on different days and of different kinds, and a good look around the app — at most once per version and not more than about three times a year. Apple decides whether the window actually appears, and you can simply close it.

docs.title: Conventions used throughout the app
docs.text:
Help on every screen. Screens explain themselves: tap the labelled Help button at the top of a hub, or the ? in the toolbar, for a short help sheet about that screen. Many menu rows offer a second way in: press and hold a row (about half a second) and you get a help sheet about that single row instead of the whole screen. A quick tap always does the row's normal thing.

Reporting a problem. Press and hold a Help button or ? to start an email about that screen, with the app version and the screen's name already in the subject. Add a screenshot if you can.

Detail views. Many screens show words in a list. Tapping a word opens its detail view — translation, forms, level, topics and example sentences, where the course has them.

Going back. The ‹ arrow at the top left takes you back one step, to the screen you came from. On the Mac, choosing a sidebar row jumps straight to that area.

docs.title: Nouns
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Spanish course has over 1,600 nouns. Every noun has its article, its plural (where it has one), a translation and three example sentences. The Nouns hub is where you practise the parts of noun vocabulary that cause the most mistakes: gender, plurals, and the nouns whose form or meaning changes with the article.

Open Self Study → Nouns to reach the hub. It has three sections:

  • Theory — Noun grammar: gender rules, the exceptions, the nouns that take both articles, the nouns with one article for both sexes, and plurals. See Noun grammar.
  • Study — Reference (Noun reference): browse the full noun catalogue. See Noun reference.
  • Practice — Select groups (Select noun groups): choose the kinds of noun to practise. See Select noun groups. Then the drills:
  • Meaning (Noun meaning) — flashcards: recall what each noun means. See Noun meaning.
  • Pick the correct article — choose el or la for each noun. See Pick the correct article.
  • Singular / Plural — form the plural (or the singular) of the selected nouns. See Singular / Plural.
  • Alternate gender pairs — give the masculine or feminine form of a noun. See Alternate gender pairs.
  • Meaning changes with gender — flashcards for the nouns whose meaning depends on the article (el papa / la papa). See Meaning changes with gender.
  • One article for both sexes — sentences with a noun of fixed gender used for a man or a woman: choose the article or adjective. See One article for both sexes.

The line under the hub title shows how many nouns your selection gives you, out of the whole catalogue. The Select groups row shows how many of the 22 groups you have ticked; the count turns red when none are ticked. Touch and hold a drill row for a short explanation of that drill, or use the Help button at the top of the hub.

Which drills follow your selection. Noun meaning, Pick the correct article and Singular / Plural use the nouns in your selected groups, narrowed by your level and the topics you set in Self Study → Select word scope. Alternate gender pairs and One article for both sexes use their own fixed set of nouns and ignore your selection and level. Meaning changes with gender holds the meaning-changers within your level and ignores your noun selection and topics. Noun reference always lists the whole catalogue.

A recommended workflow

  1. In Select groups, start with Regular and the two predictable-suffix groups, and set your level to A1 in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag). Set Questions per session to 20 in Settings → Study.
  2. Run Meaning until the core vocabulary feels solid.
  3. Add Pick the correct article to fix el and la in memory.
  4. Move on to Singular / Plural once the meanings and articles are secure.
  5. Leave Alternate gender pairs and Meaning changes with gender until later — both assume you already know the ordinary gender of a noun.

docs.title: Nouns whose meaning changes with the article
Nouns whose meaning changes with the article
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

These nouns are explained in the last cards of Noun grammar, which also opens as a sheet from the ? button in the Alternate gender pairs drill (tap Done to close it). Two cards belong together:

  • Different meaning by article — one word with two unrelated meanings, where only the article tells you which is meant.
  • Same word, different article — one word used for both genders with the same meaning (el / la dentista, el / la estudiante). Only the article changes.

Read side by side, the two cards show the contrast: in the first the meanings differ, in the second they don't.

These are the nouns whose meaning changes with the article:

Noun el la capital capital (money) capital (city) coma coma comma cometa comet kite corte cut court (royal) cura priest cure cólera cholera anger, wrath disco record, disc nightclub editorial editorial (opinion piece) publishing house frente front (military, weather) forehead orden order (arrangement) order (command) papa Pope potato pendiente earring slope

These lists always show the whole catalogue, whatever you have selected.

Why this matters. You usually meet a noun with one gender, so a noun that takes either article is disorienting. Both sentences below are grammatical, but they say different things:

  • Hay un orden — there is an order (a sequence).
  • Hay una orden — there is an order (someone has given a command).

To practise these nouns, use Meaning changes with gender.

docs.title: Pick the correct article
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Pick the correct article is a quick drill that tests one thing: el or la? There is no typing and no self-grading, just two buttons.

How it works

  1. A noun appears without its article.
  2. Tap el or la at the bottom of the screen.
  3. The card flashes green or red and turns over. The back shows the noun with its correct article (in green if you were right, red if not) and its translation. For a noun that takes either article, the back says both are accepted, and either answer counts as correct.
  4. After about two seconds the card turns back and the next noun appears.

The speaker button on the card reads the noun aloud.

Which nouns appear. The drill uses the nouns in your selection that take an article and have a gender. It leaves out nouns of more than one word and nouns ending in -s. When your selection contains gender traps (nouns whose ending points to the wrong gender, such as mano or día), about seven cards in ten are drawn from them.

The session

  • Each noun appears once per session. A session asks the number of questions set in Questions per session (Settings → Study). The nouns are picked from your selection based on your answer history and your Learning pace.
  • The Incorrect answers switch at the top limits the session to nouns whose article you have got wrong before.
  • The line at the top shows your score so far and how many candidate cards your selection gives.
  • At the end, tap New session to start again.

Every answer is recorded against the noun, so nouns you get wrong come back more often in later sessions.

Tips

  • Run this drill alongside Noun meaning, not before it. Knowing the article of a noun whose meaning you don't know is of little use.
  • If you find yourself guessing, read Noun grammar first: most nouns follow predictable patterns.
  • It works well with a narrow word scope. Right after a Noun meaning session on one topic, run this drill on the same topic to fix both the meaning and the gender.
  • For nouns whose meaning changes with the article, use Meaning changes with gender instead.

docs.title: Alternate gender pairs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Alternate gender pairs asks for the other gender of a noun: given el abogado, what is the feminine? Given la tía, what is the masculine?

How a card works

  1. The card shows a noun with its article and translation. The instruction above it says Give the feminine form or Give the masculine form.
  2. Say the answer, with its article, and tap the card to turn it.
  3. Grade yourself: swipe right if you were right and left if not. On the Mac, and with VoiceOver on, use the Wrong and Correct buttons.

The answer side shows the other form with its article and translation. Some cards add a note:

  • Same word, different article (el / la dentista): The word doesn't change — only the article.
  • Nouns whose meaning changes (el / la capital): The meaning changes with gender. The two translations show the difference.
  • Trick cards: about one card in five is a noun with only one gender. The right answer is that there is no other form. The answer side shows "—" and a note saying the noun is masculine (or feminine) only, with no opposite-gender form. These cards make sure you read the noun rather than assume there is always a pair.

Which nouns appear. This drill does not follow your selection. It uses every noun in the catalogue that has both a masculine and a feminine form, plus a limited number of common single-gender nouns for the trick cards. Nouns used only in the plural and nouns without an article are left out.

The session. A session asks the number of questions set in Questions per session (Settings → Study), picked based on your answer history and your Learning pace. A card you mark wrong can come back later in the same session. The Incorrect answers switch limits the session to nouns you have got wrong here before. Every answer is recorded against the noun.

Help. The ? button at the top opens the Noun grammar screen as a sheet, so you can check a rule mid-session. Tap Done to return to the drill.

When to use it. Once you know the ordinary gender of the nouns. Look at Standard pairs and Same word, different article in Noun grammar first.

docs.title: Meaning changes with gender
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Meaning changes with gender is a flashcard deck for the nouns whose meaning depends on the article: el papa is the Pope, la papa is a potato; el capital is money, la capital is a city. The full list is in Nouns whose meaning changes with the article.

Each noun gives two cards, one per article. Each card has one correct answer: el cura is the priest, la cura is the cure.

The deck works exactly like Noun meaning: choose a direction, tap the card to turn it, then swipe (or use Wrong and Correct). The Incorrect answers and Listen switches work the same way too.

  • Spanish → your language: you see la frente and answer "forehead", not "front", which would be el frente.
  • Your language → Spanish: you see "capital (money)" and must answer el capital, not la capital and not just capital.

Which nouns appear. The deck is closed: it holds the nouns of this list that are within your level and ignores your noun selection and topics, so you do not need to select them first. Answers are recorded like Noun meaning answers.

The same nouns are also in Traps, in the Meaning-changers reference and the same Meaning changes with gender drill (see Traps).

docs.title: Noun reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Noun reference is a browse-only list: nothing is tested and nothing is recorded. It lists the whole noun catalogue, not just your selection. Use it to check a translation before a session, or to look up a noun you got wrong.

The list is alphabetical with a search field. Search finds a noun by its Spanish form (masculine, feminine or plural) or by its translation. Each row shows:

  • the noun with its article (la casa)
  • its translation in your display language

A masculine/feminine pair such as tío / tía appears as two separate rows. So does a noun whose meaning changes with the article: el capital (capital (money)) and la capital (capital (city)) are two rows, each with its own meaning.

The noun's detail screen

Tap a noun to open its detail screen. It shows:

  • the noun with its article and its translation
  • the singular and the plural, each with its article (el lápiz · los lápices); a noun with one form for both genders shows el/la and los/las
  • notes on anything unusual — for example a gender trap, a look-alike word, or a noun used only in the plural
  • its Level, its Topics and its Groups. Tap a group to read about it.
  • Examples: three Spanish sentences, each with a translation in your display language and a speaker button to hear it
  • the book icon in the toolbar, for online dictionaries (see External dictionary lookups)

Noun reference or Noun meaning?

  • Noun reference is for warming up and looking things up. Glance over the words before a session, or check one you got wrong.
  • Noun meaning is the drill. Every answer there is recorded.

docs.title: Noun meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Noun meaning is a flashcard drill for noun vocabulary. A card shows a noun or its translation; you recall the other side, turn the card, and say whether you knew it.

How a card works

  1. Choose a direction at the top of the screen:
  2. Spanish → your language — you see the noun with its article (la casa) and recall the translation. This is recognition, the easier direction.
  3. Your language → Spanish — you see the translation and recall the noun, with its article. This is recall, the harder direction.
  4. Mixed (⇄) — each card picks a direction at random. Use this once both directions feel comfortable.
  5. Tap the card to turn it.
  6. Grade yourself. On iPhone and iPad, swipe the card right if you knew it and left if you didn't. On the Mac, and on iPhone and iPad with VoiceOver on, use the Wrong and Correct buttons instead. The next card follows automatically.

A masculine/feminine pair gives two cards: el tío and la tía are asked separately. So does a noun whose meaning changes with the article (el capital, la capital). Where a noun has something unusual about it, such as a gender trap or a noun used only in the plural, a short note appears on the answer side.

Listening and audio. The speaker button in the corner of the card reads aloud the side you are looking at. If your device has a Spanish voice, a Listen switch appears at the top: with it on, the Spanish side of a card is spoken instead of shown. Tap the large speaker to hear it again, then turn the card to see the answer and the spelling. Listen is hidden in the your language → Spanish direction. For better audio, see Setting up Spanish speech.

The session

  • The cards are drawn at random from your selection. A session asks the number of questions set in Questions per session (Settings → Study).
  • A card you mark wrong stays in the deck and can come back later in the same session.
  • The Incorrect answers switch at the top limits the session to nouns you have got wrong before. When a noun comes right, it drops out. If you have no wrong answers yet, the app says so and turns the switch off.
  • The line above the card shows your score so far ("7 out of 9 correct").
  • After seven correct answers in a row, the app offers to end the session: choose Stop — session complete or Continue.
  • At the end, Session complete appears. Tap New session to start another. Under it, To look at again names the nouns you got wrong; tap one for its page.

Every answer is recorded against the noun and counts towards your progress.

docs.title: Noun grammar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article (el or la) must match. Gender cannot always be predicted, but the ending of a word is a reliable first clue. Noun grammar (in the Theory section of the hub) sets out the rules, then the exceptions. It also shows how to form the plural.

How the screen works. Each section is a card that opens and closes when you tap its heading. The first card is open when you arrive. Expand all opens every card at once. The cards are labelled with their level, and Look up finds them too. Inside the cards on endings, tap a rule to show its examples. The examples come from the app's noun catalogue, most common first, with their translations. Only single-word nouns that take an article are used as examples. A rule shows six; when it has more, a line under them says how many — "42 more in Reference" — and opens every noun the rule covers as a list.

The cards, in order

  • Usually masculine — ends in -o (el libro); ends in -or, -ón, -és (el color, el avión); ends in -ma of Greek origin (el problema, el tema, el sistema).
  • Usually feminine — ends in -a (la casa); ends in -ción / -sión (la canción, la decisión); ends in -dad / -tad / -tud (la ciudad, la libertad, la juventud); ends in -umbre (la costumbre).
  • Standard pairs — a masculine and a feminine that are two forms of the same noun, usually differing in the final vowel: el tío · la tía.
  • Forming plurals — a table of the plural rules: -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant, -z → -ces. After a stressed vowel + -n or -s, the plural adds -es and the accent drops (la canción, las canciones). Words in -en gain an accent (el joven, los jóvenes). After an unstressed vowel + -s, nothing changes (el lunes, los lunes). The article goes plural too: el → los, la → las, el agua → las aguas. See Plural formation.
  • Watch out — common exceptions — -o nouns that are feminine (la mano, la foto, la radio) and -a nouns that are masculine (el día, el mapa, and the Greek -ma nouns such as el problema, el programa, el clima).
  • Special case: el with feminine nouns — feminine nouns that begin with a stressed a- or ha- take el in the singular to avoid the clash of sounds with la: el agua → las aguas, el arma → las armas, el hacha → las hachas, el alma → las almas. They are still feminine, so adjectives agree in the feminine (el agua fría).
  • Look-alike pairs — these are not gender pairs. They are two separate words that happen to differ only in the final vowel: el puerto (port) and la puerta (door). The -a word is not the feminine of the -o word.
  • Different meaning by article — one word, two meanings, and only the article tells them apart (el capital / la capital). See Nouns whose meaning changes with the article.
  • Same word, different article — nouns with one form for both genders and the same meaning, most often those ending in -ista or -nte: el / la artista, el / la estudiante.
  • One article for both sexes — nouns for people with one fixed gender, whoever they refer to: la persona, la víctima, el personaje. A table shows each with a man and a woman, and the adjective follows the noun: Juan es una persona simpática. See One article for both sexes.

When the rule isn't enough. For nouns where the ending does not decide the gender — mainly nouns ending in -e or in a consonant (el coche, la calle, el árbol, la flor) — you have to learn the article with the word. Noun meaning always shows a noun with its article, so the gender is part of what you learn from the start.

docs.title: One article for both sexes
docs.text:
Some nouns for people have one fixed gender, whoever they refer to. Persona, víctima, celebridad and criatura are always feminine; personaje, individuo and bebé are always masculine. So a man is una persona, and a woman can be el personaje principal. The article, and an adjective next to the noun, follow the noun, not the person. The One article for both sexes card of Noun grammar explains them, and the group of the same name in Select noun groups holds them.

One article for both sexes practises them in sentences. It works like the other choice drills (see The choice drills): the card shows the sentence in your language and the Spanish sentence with a gap. You choose between two words:

Juan is a very kind person. Spanish: Juan es ___ persona muy amable.

The three kinds of sentence.

  • Feminine word, a man meant — the gap is the article, and the man in the sentence pulls you towards the masculine: Juan es una persona muy amable, Juan fue la víctima del accidente, Las tres víctimas eran hombres.
  • Masculine word, a woman meant — the same trap the other way round: María es un personaje interesante, Ana es el personaje principal de la película.
  • The adjective follows the noun — the gap is an adjective right next to the noun, and it agrees with the noun: Juan es una persona muy simpática, Luis y Pablo son personas muy generosas. The drill only asks for adjectives next to the noun.

After you answer, a card names the kind of sentence and explains why ("Why una?").

Which sentences appear. The deck is fixed and ignores your noun selection. Each of the three kinds is recorded separately, so the kind you keep missing comes back more often.

docs.title: Plural formation
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The rules are on the Forming plurals card of Noun grammar. The app also has the Plural formation and Plural class sections of Select noun groups (each group's ⓘ sheet explains its pattern and lists its nouns), the singular and plural on every noun's detail screen, and the Singular / Plural drill. The rules are also gathered here for reference.

Spanish forms the plural by adding -s or -es to the singular. Which one depends on how the singular ends.

Singular ends in… Plural Examples an unstressed vowel, or stressed -á, -é, -ó add -s libro → libros, casa → casas, café → cafés a consonant (other than -s after an unstressed syllable) add -es flor → flores, mes → meses, ciudad → ciudades -z change z to c and add -es luz → luces, vez → veces, lápiz → lápices

Stress and written accents. Adding -es adds a syllable, but the stress stays on the same syllable. So a written accent can appear or disappear in the plural:

  • examen → exámenes, joven → jóvenes — the accent appears, because the stress is now on the third syllable from the end.
  • canción → canciones, avión → aviones — the accent disappears, because the stress now falls on the second syllable from the end of a word ending in -s, which needs no accent.

The Accent shift in plural group collects the nouns where this happens.

Unchanged in the plural. Nouns that end in -s or -x after an unstressed syllable keep the same form; only the article changes:

  • days of the week: el lunes → los lunes, el martes → los martes
  • many compounds: el paraguas → los paraguas, el cumpleaños → los cumpleaños
  • words such as la crisis → las crisis

The Invariable singular/plural group collects these nouns.

Nouns with only one number. Some nouns are used only in the singular (mass nouns such as la leche) and some only in the plural (los pantalones, las gafas). They are in the Mass / uncountable and Plurale tantum groups.

To practise the rules, use Singular / Plural.

docs.title: Select noun groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select noun groups decides which nouns can appear in Noun meaning, Pick the correct article and Singular / Plural. Nouns are grouped by their grammatical character, not by vocabulary. Level and topic are global for every word type: the level in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag), the topics in Self Study → Select word scope. There is no frequency filter in Self Study.

A noun can belong to several groups at once. Lápiz, for example, is in Plural -z → -ces, and canción is in both Predictable feminine suffix and Accent shift in plural. A group filter therefore gives you a focused set of nouns for exactly the pattern you want to practise. A noun is in your selection when any of its groups is ticked.

The 22 groups are arranged in six sections:

  • Basic — Regular: nouns with no special gender, plural or learning quirk. Most everyday vocabulary is here.
  • Gender patterns — Predictable feminine suffix (-a, and the reliable -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -umbre), Predictable masculine suffix (-o, and -or, -aje, -ón, -án, -ín), Gender trap (the gender contradicts the ending: la mano, el día), Greek -ma masculines (el problema, el idioma) and Stressed-á feminines (feminine nouns that take el in the singular: el agua, las aguas).
  • Gender pairs — M/F pair (el tío / la tía), Heteronymous pair (a different word for each gender: el padre / la madre), Look-alike pair (two separate words that differ only in the final vowel: el puerto / la puerta), Same word, different article (one form for both genders: el / la dentista), One article for both sexes (one article whoever is meant: la persona, el personaje) and Different meaning by article (el capital / la capital).
  • Plural class — Invariable singular/plural (el lunes / los lunes), Mass / uncountable, Plurale tantum (only used in the plural: los pantalones), Collective (a plural that covers both members of a pair: los tíos) and Compound (el paraguas).
  • Plural formation — Plural -z → -ces (lápiz → lápices), Accent shift in plural (canción → canciones), Plural consonant + -es and Stem-change plural.
  • Traps — False cognate: words that look like a word in your own language but mean something else.

Using the screen

  • Tap a group's row to include or exclude it. Each row shows how many nouns it contains.
  • Tap ⓘ on a row to open the group's info sheet: what the group covers, an example, and the nouns that belong to it.
  • All and None at the top select or clear every group at once.
  • An unticked group can show a note such as "12 still in scope via Regular": those nouns are already in your selection through another group you have ticked.
  • The line at the top shows how many groups you have ticked and how many nouns that gives you within your word scope. The Select word scope row below it takes you to the topic filter.
  • If you leave the screen with no group ticked, the app warns you that every noun drill will be empty. Choose Stay and select or Go back anyway.

Selection and session size

These are two separate things:

  • Your selection is the set of nouns that can appear in a drill — the result of the groups and scope above. It might hold 200 nouns.
  • Your session size is how many questions one session asks: Questions per session in Settings → Study (10, 20, 30, 50, or ∞ to keep going until you stop).

The drills that follow your selection all use the same selection, so a change here applies to each of them.

docs.title: Singular / Plural
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Singular / Plural is a flashcard drill for number. It uses the nouns in your selection that have an article and a plural.

How a card works

  1. The card shows a noun with its article and its translation. The instruction above it says what to do: Give the plural (the card shows la canción) or Give the singular (the card shows las canciones). The direction is chosen at random for each card.
  2. Say the answer to yourself — article included — and tap the card to turn it.
  3. Grade yourself: swipe right if you were right and left if not. On the Mac, and with VoiceOver on, use the Wrong and Correct buttons.

The speaker button reads aloud the side you are looking at.

Special cards

  • Invariable nouns (el lunes, los lunes): the answer side notes Singular and plural are identical.
  • Plural-only nouns (los pantalones): the card always shows the plural and asks for the singular. The answer is "—", with the note Always plural — no singular form.
  • Collective plurals (los tíos): the answer shows both singulars, el tío / la tía.

Mass nouns, which have no plural, and nouns without an article are left out.

What the drill covers. Depending on your selection, you meet:

  • vowel endings: libro → libros
  • consonant endings: flor → flores, mes → meses
  • -z → -ces: luz → luces, lápiz → lápices
  • accent shifts: examen → exámenes, canción → canciones
  • unchanged plurals: el lunes → los lunes, el paraguas → los paraguas

To drill one pattern, select only its group under Plural formation in Select groups.

The session. A session asks the number of questions set in Questions per session (Settings → Study). The nouns are picked from your selection based on your answer history and your Learning pace. A card you mark wrong can come back later in the same session. The Incorrect answers switch limits the session to nouns you have got wrong here before. At the end, tap New session. Every answer is recorded against the noun.

Tips

  • Read Plural formation first. The drill is there to make the rules automatic, not to teach them.
  • The accent-shift cases (examen → exámenes) are the most useful part. Most learners pick up -s / -es / -ces quickly but misspell the accented forms.

docs.title: Numerals
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Numerals hub from the Numerals tile on the Self Study screen. The Spanish catalogue has 65 numerals of five kinds:

Kind Examples Numerals Cardinal uno, dos, tres … cien, mil, millón 39 Ordinal primero … décimo 10 Collective par, docena, decena, centena 8 Multiplicative doble, triple, cuádruple 4 Fractional medio, tercio, cuarto, quinto 4

The badge under the title shows how many numerals your selected kinds contain. Your level decides whether the hub appears, not which numerals it holds, and the topics in Select word scope do not narrow it.

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select numeral groups: tick the kinds you want. Tap ⓘ on a kind for an explanation and its numerals.
  • Numeral grammar (Theory): the five kinds, then shortening, agreement of the hundreds, the y between tens and units, and how numbers are written.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Numeral reference: the selected numerals.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Numeral meaning.
  • Shortening drill and Agreement drill (Practice).

docs.title: Numeral grammar
docs.text:
• Shortening (apocope): uno becomes un before a masculine noun (un libro), also at the end of a larger number (veintiún libros, treinta y un libros). The feminine keeps its full form: veintiuna casas. Ciento becomes cien before any noun (cien libros, cien casas) and before mil. Primero and tercero become primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun: el primer día, but la primera vez.
  • Agreement of the hundreds: 200 to 900 change for gender: doscientos libros, doscientas casas. This also applies inside larger numbers: doscientas cincuenta casas. Ordinals change like adjectives: primero, primera, primeros, primeras.
  • The y connector: y stands only between tens and units from 31 to 99: treinta y uno. 16 to 29 are written as one word (dieciséis, veintidós), and there is no y after the hundreds: doscientos cincuenta.
  • Written conventions: Spanish writes a decimal comma (3,14) and uses a point or a space to group thousands. Dates are written 31 de diciembre de 2024.

The kinds each have their own section. Collectives take de: una docena de huevos. Fractions above ten use -avo: un onceavo. Medio changes for gender: media hora.

docs.title: Numeral reference
docs.text: The selected numerals, grouped by kind, with a search field. Tap a kind heading to open or close it. The search also finds a numeral by its value, so 12 finds doce. The picker at the top sorts By value or Alphabetical. A numeral with forms or a short form is shown with them, such as uno, -a, -os, -as (un). Tap a numeral to open its page. It shows the value and, where there is one, the short form used before a masculine singular noun.

docs.title: Numeral meaning
docs.text: Flashcards for the meaning of each numeral. The card shows the numeral as it appears in the reference, short form included, and you recall the translation (one, hundred). The speaker reads only the numeral itself. See Word meaning for how the flashcards work.

docs.title: Shortening drill
docs.text: This drill uses uno, veintiuno, ciento, primero and tercero. You see a short phrase with a gap, its gender-and-number tag and a gloss — ___ libro, veintiún ___ años — and choose between the short form and the full form, as in the adjectives' Shortening drill.
