The phrases cycle through the frames where the rule applies and where it does not: before a masculine singular noun (un, veintiún, primer), before a feminine (una, primera), before a plural. For ciento the choice is ciento or cien, and before a noun it is always cien (cien casas). See How the choice drills work under Adjectives.

docs.title: Agreement drill
docs.text: This drill uses the numerals that change for gender: the hundreds, the ordinals, uno and veintiuno. You see an English sentence, such as "There are 200 houses." or "It is the third page.", and a Spanish sentence with a gap: Hay ___ casas. or Es la ___ página. Choose the right form (doscientas, tercera). A Dutch display language gives the sentence in Dutch.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Start with only the Cardinal kind.
  2. Run Meaning until the number words are familiar.
  3. Add the Ordinal kind, then the Shortening drill and the Agreement drill.

docs.title: Phrases
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Phrases hub from the Phrases tile on the Self Study screen. The badge under the title ("… of … phrases") shows how many phrases your selection leaves. The phrases are of two kinds:

  1. Set phrases: over 270 fixed expressions that you learn as a whole: greetings and social phrases (buenos días, mucho gusto, de nada), time expressions (de vez en cuando, a veces) and connecting phrases (a pesar de, sin embargo, por lo menos). Some are built around a verb (darse cuenta de, echar de menos).
  2. Example sentences: about 25,000 sentences written for the verbs and nouns, each one practised as a phrase: Soy de España, pero vivo en Holanda. Every sentence records the tenses it uses and the verbs in it, and only counts when its tenses are switched on in Select tenses. If you study the present and the pretérito indefinido, you practise the sentences that use only those. Add the subjunctive and the sentences that use it are added.

You can practise every example sentence you see in the app.

The hub has these screens:

  • Phrases or sentences (Practice): choose which kinds count.
  • Select tenses (Practice): the tenses the sentences may use.
  • Phrases catalogue (Theory): how the pool is built and how to study it.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Phrase reference: the selected phrases.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Phrase meaning: flashcards.

Phrases work best alongside the Verbs and Nouns hubs, not instead of them. They add the ready-made phrases you need in a real conversation. For single words that have no hub, see Other Vocabulary.

docs.title: Phrases or sentences
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This screen chooses which of the two kinds count: Set phrases and Example sentences. Tap a kind to switch it on or off; tick both for both. Each row shows its size and a few samples. Tap ⓘ for a short explanation with more examples.

The line at the top shows how many phrases you selected and how many are left after the rest of your scope. The phrases in the pool are also narrowed by:

  • Select tenses: a sentence only counts when every tense it uses is selected. With only the present selected, El abogado defendió a su cliente stays out, because defendió is an indefinido. A verb's tense example is the exception: it needs only the tense it was written for, so Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría counts when the condicional is selected; its other tense, the imperfecto de subjuntivo, only has to be within your level. This is the same tense choice as on the Verbs hub, and the Select tenses row in this hub opens it: a change here changes the verb drills too.
  • Your level and Select word scope: a sentence counts when its word and every tense it uses are within your level, and it takes its word's topic. Its level is the latest of these: with abogado at A1 and the indefinido at A2, the sentence is at A2. A sentence with no verb (Un café solo, por favor) follows its word alone.

The choice of kinds changes the pool the most. Set phrases alone is a small, focused pool. With Example sentences on, thousands of sentences are included. Topics are useful here too: going on a trip? Limit Select word scope to Travel and Social.

Learn set phrases as a whole. Don't translate de vez en cuando word by word.

docs.title: Phrase reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A list of the phrases in your selection with their translations, in alphabetical order, with an A–Z index and a search field. The search matches the phrase or its translation. Nothing is recorded here. Use it to look something up or to look through a set before you drill it.

  • Touch and hold a row to hear the phrase.
  • The button in the toolbar hides or shows the translations (Hide translation / Show translation), so you can test yourself on the list.
  • Tap a phrase to open its page. A set phrase shows its translation and type (Expression or Verbal expression), its Level, Frequency and Topics, and the book icon in the toolbar for online dictionaries.
  • An example sentence's page is marked Example sentence and shows what the sentence is made of:
  • Level: the sentence's level, with where it comes from: A2 — abogado A1 · Pretérito Indefinido A2.
  • Tenses: each tense the sentence uses. Tap one to open its ⓘ.
  • Topics: its word's topic.
  • Illustrates: the verb or noun the sentence was written for. Tap it to open that word.
  • Verbs in the sentence: every verb form with its infinitive and tense (defendió — defender · Pretérito Indefinido). Tap one to open the verb.

A good routine: look through the set in Phrase reference for a minute, then start Phrase meaning.

docs.title: Phrase meaning
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the meaning of the selected phrases. It works like every meaning deck (see Word meaning). The phrase is on the card and you recall its translation, or the other way round. The deck holds the same phrases as Phrase reference: the kinds you chose, and only the sentences whose tenses you selected.

On a card with an example sentence built on a verb, the verb appears as a chip on the Spanish side. Tap the chip to open that verb.

The speaker button is especially useful here. Hearing a whole phrase such as de vez en cuando helps you remember its rhythm.

docs.title: Practice Sets
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A practice set is a ready-made session you run as a unit: a body of content — verbs, nouns, adjectives, other vocabulary, phrases, in any mix — together with the exercises to run over it. Open Practice Sets from its card on the main screen, or from Study in the Mac sidebar. It appears for every course that has sets; the header says how many there are.

The sets that come with the app and the sets you build are the same kind of thing: every set is yours to run, edit, rename or delete.

docs.title: The library
docs.text:
Sets are grouped into folders. Tap a folder heading to open or close it; a folder with more than three sets starts closed. Depending on the course, the app supplies:

  • Topics — vocabulary grouped by theme.
  • By level — sets by CEFR level, from beginner (A1) to advanced (C2), verbs and nouns separately.
  • Essential Verbs — the core verbs through one tense per set, plus review sets per level.
  • My Practice Sets — where new sets go by default. It starts with one example, Example - 5 verbs, 2 tenses, to show what a set looks like.

Which folders and sets a course has is described in the course guide.

Managing sets. Every row carries a ⋯ at its right-hand edge: on a set it offers Edit, Rename, Duplicate and Delete, on a folder Rename and Delete (with every set in it). A long press on the row opens the same menu, and on the Mac so does a right-click. Deleting always asks first.

docs.title: Running a set
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Tap a set to open it. The screen shows the set's name and description, its exercises under Practice, the Tenses covered (for verb sets), then the content, one section per word class:

  • Verbs — tap a verb for its conjugation, limited to the set's tenses. Cycle through randomly at the top of the list steps through the verbs for you.
  • Nouns and Adjectives — tap one for its detail screen.
  • Adverbs, Prepositions, Words and Phrases — read through the pairs.

Each word list shows its first five entries; Show all under the list opens the rest.

The exercises come first: under Practice are the set's drills — for example Verb meaning, Verb conjugation, Verb recognition, Noun meaning or Mixed meaning (the meaning of every word in the set); in Latin, a set with nouns also offers Decline the noun, the declension drill over exactly the set's nouns, and the Agreement drill, which matches an adjective to them; a Spanish or French set that contains adjectives offers the Agreement drill over those adjectives. Tap one to start it. Every answer feeds the same adaptive engine as the rest of the app and shows up in My Progress.

iPhoneiPadMac

Cycle through randomly shows one verb's conjugation at a time, in shuffled order. Next moves on and Previous goes back; every verb comes round once before the order is reshuffled, and a counter shows how many you have seen. There is no score — stop whenever you like.

docs.title: Building your own
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Tap New (the +) to build a set by describing it rather than picking every word. A bar at the top shows how many items match as you go.

  1. Name — give the set a name.
  2. Folder — choose a folder, or New folder… to make one.
  3. Word types — switch on the word classes the set draws from.
  4. Specific words — optionally pick individual verbs, nouns, words or phrases. The level and frequency then follow from the words you chose. In the verb and noun pickers, the filter menu at the top left picks many at once: By Topic, or By Grammar with the same groups as Select verb groups and Select noun groups. Tick groups and tap Apply; with words already chosen, it asks whether to replace them, add to them (OR) or keep the overlap (AND). Every group can be ticked, whatever your level. On the Mac these screens open as a sheet.
  5. Level and Frequency — narrow to CEFR levels and to how common the words are. All and None set every chip at once.
  6. Topics — narrow to themes; leave it empty for every topic.
  7. Refine by type — narrow a word class by its own groupings (verb groups, for example). Leave a row on All to keep everything.
  8. Exercises — switch on the drills to run. The choice follows the word types: verbs offer Verb meaning, Verb conjugation and Verb recognition; nouns Noun meaning, adjectives Adjective meaning, other words Word meaning and phrases Phrase meaning; every set can have Mixed meaning.
  9. Tenses — greyed out until conjugation or recognition is on; then pick at least one.
  10. Review words — untick any matching word you do not want. Your removals stick; new words that match the description still join the set later.

Tap Save. It stays unavailable until the set has a name, at least one word type, at least one exercise, at least one matching item and, where needed, a tense.

Because the set is saved as a description, it keeps up with the catalogue. Edit on such a set opens the same screen, filled in.

iPhoneiPadMac

A set that is a fixed list of words — the example set, for instance — opens in Edit Practice Set instead: its name, its folder, the words in the set per word class, the Activities to run, and the Tenses when a verb drill is on.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Reports in the toolbar shows how your sets are going. All Practice Sets gives the total number of sessions and correct answers; under Per Practice Set, each set shows its sessions and correct answers, or Not attempted yet. Only answers given inside a set count here.

iPhoneiPadMac

Tap a set for its Recipe progress: All-time on this Practice Set gives each item's accuracy across all your sessions with the set, and Past sessions lists your recent sessions with their scores.

docs.title: Sharing: export and import
docs.text: Practice sets can be written to a file, so you can move your library between devices or give a few sets to someone else. There are two kinds of transfer, kept apart on purpose. Your study history is separate again (see Settings), so sets and progress move independently.

docs.title: Full backup — your whole library
docs.text:
Use this to move everything between your own devices, or to keep a safety copy.

On iPhone and iPad, tap Import or Export in the toolbar:

  • Export Full Backup… writes your whole library, for every course, to one file (LinguaMorpha Practice Sets followed by the date and time) and opens the share sheet — AirDrop it, send it or save it to Files.
  • Import Full Backup… reads a backup. Nothing changes until you confirm.
iPhoneiPadMac

The Review Import screen covers only the course you are studying; sets for other courses in the file are ignored. It sorts the sets into:

  • Already identical — nothing to do.
  • Only in the file — Add them (on by default).
  • Changed on both sides — for each, Replace, Skip or Keep both (which adds the file's version under a dated name). The default is whichever version was saved later.
  • Only on this device — sets missing from the file. You can Delete them, but this is off by default: a set missing from the file may simply be newer than the file.

Tap Apply to carry it out. Sets are matched by identity, so importing your own backup again updates sets in place instead of duplicating them.

On the Mac, the same pair is File → Practice Sets → Import… and Export… (⌘I / ⌘E).

docs.title: Sharing individual sets
docs.text:
Use this to send a set or two to someone else without disturbing either library.

iPhoneiPadMac

  • Export Practice Sets… (in the same menu) opens Share Practice Sets: tick the sets to send, or Select All, and tap Share. One set is written as LinguaMorpha Practice Set — ‹name›, several as LinguaMorpha Shared Practice Sets; then the share sheet opens.
  • Import Practice Sets… reads a shared file.
iPhoneiPadMac

Import Shared Sets shows what the file holds for the course you are studying. New sets are listed under Add; a set with the same name as one of yours is listed separately, and for each you choose Rename (the default — both are kept), Overwrite or Skip. Tap Import. Nothing already in your library is deleted.

On the Mac these are File → Practice Sets → Share Selected… and Import Shared….

docs.title: A recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Start from a set at your level to see the shape.
  2. Build your own set around what you are working on this week — a tense, a topic, a handful of tricky words.
  3. Keep a full backup to carry your library between your devices; share single sets with a study partner, and import the ones they send you.

docs.title: Prepositions
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Prepositions hub from the Prepositions tile on the Self Study screen. Prepositions do not change form, so this hub is about use: por or para, en, a or de, and the fixed combinations prepositions appear in. The Spanish catalogue has 36 prepositions: 18 simple ones (a, de, en, por) and 18 compound ones (a causa de, cerca de, delante de).

The badge under the title shows how many prepositions your selected senses contain. Your level decides whether the hub appears, not which prepositions it holds, and the topics in Select word scope do not narrow it.

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select preposition groups: tick the senses you want.
  • Preposition grammar (Theory).
  • Reference (Study) — opens Preposition reference: the selected prepositions.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Preposition meaning.
  • Contrast drill (Practice).

docs.title: Select preposition groups
docs.text: Every preposition has one or more of seven senses: Location, Motion, Time, Cause, Purpose, Manner and Topic. Most have several: por is both cause and motion. A preposition is included when at least one of its senses is ticked. Tap ⓘ on a sense for an explanation and its prepositions.

docs.title: Preposition grammar
docs.text:
• por vs para: both often translate as "for". Por looks back at a cause: reason (lo hago por ti), duration (por dos horas), exchange (por diez euros), the agent of a passive (escrito por García Márquez) and movement through a place (por el parque). Para looks forward to a goal: purpose (para aprender), recipient (es para ti), deadline (para mañana), destination (salgo para Madrid) and opinion (para mí).
  • en / a / de: en for where something is, a for where something goes, de for where something comes from.
  • Contractions: del, al: a + el becomes al and de + el becomes del. This does not happen with él (de él) or with El in a name (a El Salvador).
  • Verb + preposition collocations: verbs that take a fixed preposition, such as pensar en, soñar con and acordarse de.
  • Idiomatic prep phrases: fixed expressions such as a pesar de and por lo tanto.

docs.title: Preposition reference
docs.text: The selected prepositions in two sections, Simple and Compound, with a search field. Tap a heading to open or close it. Tap a preposition to open its page, with the cards Senses, Often confused with, Verb collocations and Idiomatic phrases.

docs.title: Preposition meaning
docs.text: Flashcards for the meaning of each preposition. See Word meaning for how the flashcards work.

docs.title: Contrast drill
docs.text:
You see an English sentence and a Spanish sentence with a gap: "I studied for two hours." and Estudié ___ dos horas. Choose the preposition. The options are por and para, or en, a and de, sometimes with con. Most questions are about por and para. Many sentences change a word each time (another object, price or city), so the same question does not always look the same.

After you answer, a card names the sense being tested (such as Duration or Recipient) and explains Why por?, and for por, para, en, a and de a Read more in Theory link opens the matching section of Preposition grammar. Your results are recorded per preposition and sense, so por for a cause and por for a duration are tracked separately. The drill only asks about por, para, en, a and de, and only when they are in your selection. See How the choice drills work under Adjectives.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Tick the senses you want to work on.
  2. Run Meaning to learn the prepositions.
  3. Spend most of your time on the Contrast drill. The por / para split is where most of the difficulty is.

docs.title: Reading your progress
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

My Progress shows what you have practised and how well it went, for the current learner and the course you are studying. On iPhone and iPad, open it from the chart icon at the top left of the main screen; on the Mac, choose My Progress under Tools in the sidebar.

Everything here is worked out on your device from the answers already stored. Nothing is uploaded.

The screen answers four questions, top to bottom: what to practise next, what you know, where you lose points, and how it goes over time. Until you have answered anything, a line says there is no study data yet.

docs.title: The top of the screen
docs.text:
When and how often. The day you started, how many days you have been active and, when you have one, your current streak.

Recent activity. A practice grid for one calendar month, one square per day: the darker the square, the more answers you gave that day. The ‹ and › arrows page through the months, back as far as your first recorded answer; Today jumps back to the current month. Under the grid, a count of the active days in that month and a less … more colour key.

This and lower levels / Whole course. When you study at a level (chosen in Scheme and level), a switch decides what the figures below count against: your level and the levels below it, or the whole course. Under it, the level and the scheme it belongs to. Without a level the switch is not shown and everything counts against the whole course.

Toolbar. The ? explains the screen. The share icon makes a PDF of it (see PDF export).

docs.title: Practise next
docs.text:
The one thing most worth your time. The app looks at your conjugation answers per tense, per person and per verb group, and names the weakest one that has at least 20 answers behind it and is below 80% correct — Your weak spot is the Pretérito Indefinido — 64 % correct. Tap it to drill exactly that: the tense, or the verbs of the group. Only tenses at your level are considered.

When nothing qualifies, a line says so: either you have not practised verbs yet, or everything you have answered often enough is above the bar.

Weakest words. Below it, up to six words at your level that you have answered at least three times and get right less than 80% of the time, weakest first, with each word's correct rate and number of attempts. Tap a verb to drill its conjugation; Practise all drills every verb on the list. Other words are shown for information only.

docs.title: What I know
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Which words you can actually claim. For each category — Verb meaning, Verb conjugation, Noun meaning, Other vocabulary and Phrases (the set phrases; the example sentences are practice, not words to know) — a bar splits the words at your level into three parts:

  • known — your answers show you know it: about six correct in a row, more if picked or self-checked;
  • learning — practised, but the answers do not show it yet;
  • not seen — never practised in this category.

The split by category is deliberate. Knowing what poder means and being able to conjugate it are different skills on the same word, so they are counted separately: one number averaging the two would hide exactly the gap you want to see.

Tap a category for the words behind it: Known, best first, and Still learning, weakest first, each with its accuracy and how often you answered it, plus a count of the words Not seen yet.

iPhoneiPadMac

Verb conjugation opens a screen of its own, with two views: By verb — for each verb, how many of the tenses you have practised it in are known — and By tense — for each tense, how many of the verbs you have practised in it are known. Beside each row, your accuracy and the number of answers; it is green when everything behind the row is known. Tap a row for the tenses of that verb, or the verbs of that tense, each known or not by the same rule as above.

iPhoneiPadMac

Under the categories, Tenses practised and Verb groups met count how many of the tenses and verb groups at your level you have practised. Tenses practised opens Verb conjugation by tense: the tenses you have practised, with what you know in each, and under Not practised yet the tenses at your level you have not. Verb groups met lists the verb groups at your level, each ticked once you have conjugated one of its verbs — translating a verb does not meet its group — with your accuracy and the number of answers. Groups you met above your level are listed apart, under Above this level, and are not counted until you switch to Whole course.

docs.title: Where I lose points
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Your correct rate, split three ways. Each row shows the percentage — green from 80%, orange from 50%, red below — and the number of answers behind it.

  • By exercise — per type of question (word meaning, article / gender, singular / plural, conjugation, …).
  • By person — conjugation questions only, per grammatical person.
  • By verb group — conjugation questions only, per verb group. A verb in several groups counts towards each.

Per tense is under What I know › Verb conjugation › By tense, with what you know in each tense beside your accuracy.

These views are diagnostic: they show where you lose points, so you know where to focus.

docs.title: Over time
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Charts of how your activity and results change. The switch at the top shows the last 30 days or All of your history; the arrows under it page back through earlier periods, and Today returns to the latest.

  • Daily activity — answers per day as bars, and that day's accuracy as a line.
  • Words known — how many words you know, over time.

"Known" means the same here as everywhere in the app. A word counts only when your record makes it reasonably certain that you get it right at least 60% of the time — about six correct answers in a row, more if you picked from a list or checked yourself, not a lucky three. The caption under the chart quotes the figure and how many answers the chart rests on.

Use it to answer am I getting better? — and to spot stretches where accuracy dips, often a sign that you have widened your selection too quickly.

docs.title: PDF export
docs.text: The share icon at the top of My Progress makes a Progress report PDF: the screen on paper, in the same order and counted against the same level or the whole course. A cover with the course, what the figures count against, the day you started, active days and streak; then Practise next, What I know, Where I lose points and Over time. It is offered to the share sheet, so you can save it, keep it as a record or send it to a teacher. It is generated on your device and uploaded nowhere. The icon is greyed out until you have answered something.

docs.title: When to check it
docs.text:
You do not need My Progress every day. Good moments to look are:

  • after a week or two of steady practice, when the grid and the charts start telling a story;
  • when you feel stuck — Practise next names the weak spot and the weakest words, Where I lose points the categories;
  • before widening your selection — check in What I know that the current material has stuck;
  • when you have a specific suspicion ("I'm fine on -ar verbs and lost on -ir") — check it under Where I lose points, by verb group, rather than guessing.

docs.title: Pronouns
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open the Pronouns hub from the Pronouns tile on the Self Study screen. The Spanish catalogue has 50 pronouns in six classes:

Class Examples Pronouns Personal yo, tú, él, nosotros 12 Demonstrative este, ese, aquel 3 Possessive nuestro, mío, tuyo 8 Relative que, quien, cuyo 4 Interrogative qué, quién, cuál, dónde, cuándo 14 Indefinite alguien, algo, todo, alguno 9

The badge under the title shows how many pronouns your selected classes contain. Your level decides whether the hub appears, not which pronouns it holds, and the topics in Select word scope do not narrow it.

The hub has these screens:

  • Select groups (Practice) — opens Select pronoun groups: tick the classes you want. Tap ⓘ on a class for an explanation and its pronouns.
  • Pronoun grammar (Theory): the six classes, where object pronouns go, and regional differences. The tables on this page are built from the same catalogue the drills use.
  • Reference (Study) — opens Pronoun reference: the selected pronouns.
  • Meaning (Practice) — opens Pronoun meaning.
  • Agreement drill, Which pronoun? and Two pronouns at once (Practice).

docs.title: Pronoun grammar
docs.text:
• Personal pronouns have five slots: subject, direct object, indirect object, reflexive, and the form used after a preposition. Me covers the direct object, indirect object and reflexive of yo. After a preposition you use mí and ti, and con combines with them into conmigo and contigo.
  • Demonstratives have three distances: este (near me), ese (near you), aquel (far from both). Each has four forms. The neuter forms esto, eso, aquello refer to an idea or situation.
  • Possessives have a short form before the noun (mi, tu, su, which only change for number; nuestro and vuestro also change for gender) and a full form after the noun or with an article (un amigo mío, el mío).
  • Relatives join clauses: que for people and things, quien only for people, el cual in more formal writing, and cuyo, which agrees with the thing possessed: el autor cuyos libros leí.
  • Interrogatives carry a written accent: qué asks, que joins. The accent stays in indirect questions: No sé dónde está.
  • Indefinites: some never change (alguien, nadie, algo, nada). Others have four forms (alguno, ninguno, todo, otro). Alguno and ninguno shorten to algún and ningún before a masculine singular noun. A negative word after the verb needs no before it: No veo a nadie.
  • Position and pronoun order: an object pronoun goes before a conjugated verb (te veo) and is attached to an infinitive, a gerund or an affirmative command (verte, viéndote, dímelo). With a verb plus an infinitive or gerund, either position works: te quiero ver or quiero verte. The indirect object comes before the direct object: me lo dio. When both are third person, le or les becomes se: se lo dio.
  • Regional variation: Spain uses vosotros for informal "you" plural. Latin America uses ustedes for all plural "you". Some countries use vos instead of tú. The hub includes vosotros but not vos.

docs.title: Pronoun reference
docs.text: The selected pronouns, grouped by class, with a search field. Tap a class heading to open or close it. Tap a pronoun to open its page. A personal pronoun shows its Five syntactic slots: Subject, Direct object, Indirect object, Reflexive and Prepositional. A pronoun that changes for gender and number shows its Four-form agreement. Other pronouns are marked Invariant.

docs.title: Pronoun meaning
docs.text: Flashcards for the meaning of each pronoun. See Word meaning for how the flashcards work.

docs.title: Agreement drill
docs.text: This drill uses the pronouns that have four forms: the demonstratives, the possessives nuestro, vuestro, mío, tuyo, suyo, the relative cuyo, the interrogative cuánto, and alguno, ninguno, todo, otro. You see a noun with its gender and number, such as hermanas (sisters (f.pl)), and pick the form of the pronoun that agrees with it. The drill never asks for a form that Spanish does not use: ninguno is only asked with a singular noun. See How the choice drills work under Adjectives.

docs.title: Which pronoun?
docs.text: This drill needs the Personal class. It has 16 fixed sentences. Each shows an English sentence with the pronoun in bold, such as "We see her.", a label (Direct object slot, Indirect object slot or Reflexive slot) and a Spanish sentence with a gap before the verb: Nosotros ___ vemos. Choose the pronoun from four options (la). The drill tests which object pronoun fits, not where it goes; every gap is before the conjugated verb. For the position rules, see Pronoun grammar. Your results are recorded per sentence, not per pronoun.

docs.title: Two pronouns at once
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

This drill also needs the Personal class. It has 24 fixed sentences — every indirect form (me te se nos os) with every direct form (lo la los las) — and asks one gap at a time.

Spanish puts the indirect object first and the direct object second, and that order forces a change: two third-person pronouns cannot both begin with l-, so le lo is impossible and the indirect le (or les) becomes se. Se lo di, never le lo di.

The first question asks the indirect object, with le among the four options — it is the form you will want to pick, and picking it is the mistake the drill exists to correct. The second question asks the direct object with your first answer already standing in the sentence, so Él ___ ___ da. has become Él se ___ da. and the order is there to read. Third-person sentences come up most often, because they are the ones where the substitution happens.

The explanation waits until both slots are answered: it covers the whole sentence, so showing it after the first question would give the second away. Right and wrong are still marked on each answer. It links to Pronoun grammar. Results are recorded per sentence and per slot, so having the order but not the substitution shows up as weakness on the first question alone.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
1. Start with only the Personal class.
  2. Run Meaning until the forms are familiar.
  3. Add Which pronoun? for the object pronouns.
  4. Add the demonstrative and possessive classes and practise them with the Agreement drill.
  5. Add Two pronouns at once once single object pronouns are secure.

docs.title: Choosing what is in play
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

One screen decides which words Self Study draws on, for every word type at once: Select word scope. Open it from Self Study → Select word scope, the row under the Self Study card. Its second line says which state you are in: All topics, or Filtered by topic. The selection pickers that show an in-scope count have a Select word scope row that leads here too.

This is the screen people most often look for in the wrong place. The individual pickers do something narrower: Select verb groups picks conjugation patterns, Select noun groups picks noun groups, Select word groups ticks grammatical categories. Anything that narrows which words exist, for every word type at once, lives here.

docs.title: The banner
docs.text:
At the top a banner shows the current state and how much of the catalogue gets through, for example 812 of 2540 items in scope (32%):

  • Filter active — topics are narrowing the catalogue.
  • No topics selected or All topics selected — no filter — nothing is being filtered.

docs.title: Level
docs.text: Not on this screen. Your level is chosen in Scheme and level, from the chip with the flag, and decides which words exist at all; this screen narrows within it. See Levels.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
A tree of 29 topic tags, listed alphabetically. Tap a tag to include or exclude it. Tags with subgroups expand, so you can take Food → Drinks without the rest of the kitchen; a partly-ticked tag shows a dash. Expand and Collapse open or close every tag at once, and Search topics… jumps to the first tag or subgroup whose name contains what you type.

Before committing to a tag, tap its ⓘ (on the Mac it opens in a window of its own). It explains what the topic covers and lists how many verbs, nouns, adjectives, phrases and so on it holds; tap a word class to see the words themselves. A tag's name rarely tells you how big it is.

All ticks every topic; None clears them. Either way nothing is filtered — they are the quick way back to everything.

A word can be in more than one topic — enfermero is under both Professions and Treatment — and then counts in each; its page lists them all. Topics this course has no words in are hidden: Show empty, beside Expand and Collapse, shows them dimmed, and Hide empty hides them again.

docs.title: How the two combine
docs.text: Level and topic are an intersection: a word has to pass both. Level A2 with Travel ticked gives you the travel words of that level — not everything at that level plus everything about travel. Within the topic tree, selections add up: three topics ticked means words from any of the three.

docs.title: What it touches, and what it doesn't
docs.text:
It governs every Self Study word pool, in both the reference lists and the drills.

It does not govern Grammar lessons or Practice Sets, which bring their own fixed word lists. A practice set built around Food keeps working whatever your scope says.

It does not delete anything. Scope is a view, not an edit. Filtering a word out only hides it; your history for it is kept and counts again when the word returns.

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text: Frequency is not something you filter on here. Within your scope, words you have not seen yet are introduced lowest level first and, within a level, most frequent first.

docs.title: Self Study
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Self Study screen is where you pick a word type to practise. Each word type opens its own hub with Theory, Study and Practice sections, so meaning practice and grammar drills live together in one place (see The Theory / Study / Practice pattern).

At the top is a card titled Self Study, naming the course you are studying, with a Help button. Under it is the Select word scope row, which sets the topics every hub below draws on; its second line reads All topics or Filtered by topic. See Choosing what is in play.

The word-type cards follow. A card appears only when the course has content for it and your level has reached that word type:

  1. Verbs — conjugations, meanings, and translations.
  2. Nouns — gender, plurals, meanings, and translations.
  3. Adjectives — declension paradigms across all three genders in Latin; agreement, shortening, comparison and adverb derivation in Spanish; agreement across gender and number in French.
  4. Adverbs — derived and lexical adverbs (-mente in Spanish, -ment in French, -ē / -iter / -nter in Latin).
  5. Pronouns — personal, demonstrative, relative, and interrogative.
  6. Prepositions — in Spanish por / para, en / a / de, collocations and idioms; in French spatial, temporal and grammatical relations; in Latin which case each preposition governs.
  7. Numerals — cardinal numbers, with a focus that shifts by course: in Latin the three that decline against the invariant rest, in Spanish shortening and hundreds agreement, in French 1 to 100 including the vigesimal pattern.
  8. Other Vocabulary — conjunctions, articles, determiners, interjections and other single-word vocabulary.
  9. Phrases — set phrases and common expressions.

On iPhone and iPad a Tools section follows:

  • Look up — look up any conjugation, plural or vocabulary item. See Look up.
  • Traps (Spanish) — false friends, meaning-changers, gender traps and ser/estar shifts. Closed decks, each scored on its own; they do not follow your word scope.

On the Mac, Look up is the search field at the top of the sidebar, and Traps is under Tools.

In Latin, a Texts card comes last, at the bottom of the screen: passages to read with every word parsed. The Latin course guide covers it.

Toolbar. The filter icon opens Selection, an overview of the word types with how many items each type's own picker leaves in, shown as in / total — green when everything is included, red when nothing is. Tap a row with a chevron to change that selection; rows without one have nothing to choose. These counts reflect each type's own picker only; level and topics are set under Select word scope, and the filter icon is filled while that filter is active. On iPhone and iPad the chip at the left opens Scheme and level.

If you would rather have the app decide what to study next, use Grammar lessons instead.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Settings holds the preferences that apply everywhere in the app: languages, appearance, session size, pace and grading, speech, dictionaries and your study data.

  • iPhone and iPad — tap ⋯ at the top right of the main screen and choose Settings. Done closes it, and ? explains it.
  • Mac — a window of its own: LinguaMorpha → Settings… or ⌘,.

There are four tabs: General, Study, a tab named after the course you are studying (Spanish, French or Latin) with that course's own settings, and Progress. On iPhone and iPad the tabs are a switch at the top; on the Mac they are icons along the top of the window.

Settings and the selection rows are different things. Settings are app-wide preferences. The selection rows at the top of each hub’s Practice section are where you choose which words, groups or tenses are in play; it lives in the hub, not here.

docs.title: Languages
docs.text:
• App language — English, Dutch or Spanish. It sets the language of the app's menus, labels and help, and the language translations are shown in. The language you are studying is not offered — a translation into it would only repeat the word — and a note says so. The App language applies to every learner on the device.

The course is not chosen here but in Scheme and level, by choosing one of its schemes (see Levels).

On the Mac the menu bar is built when the app starts, so after changing App language the app offers Restart Now or Later; the rest of the app switches at once.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text: • Appearance — System, Dark or Light. System follows your device.

docs.title: Hints (iPhone and iPad)
docs.text: • Show swipe hints again — replays the swipe hint on the flashcard drills, the one that shows which way to swipe for knew it and didn't.

docs.title: Study
docs.text:
• Questions per session — how many questions a session asks: 10, 20 (the default), 30, 50, or ∞ (keep going until you stop). It applies to every drill.
  • Learning pace — Relaxed, Balanced (the default) or Intensive: the mix of words you have already seen and new words in each session. Relaxed leans on review, Intensive on new material, Balanced splits evenly. See Adaptive learning — how it works.
  • Auto-advance after correct answer — on by default. After a correct answer the drill moves to the next question by itself; a wrong answer always waits for Next, so you can read the correction. A choice drill that explains every answer (the agreement, shortening, preposition and pronoun drills) never advances by itself: Next, or Return, moves on once you have read the explanation.
  • Auto-advance after — shown while auto-advance is on: how long the drill waits first, 1 s, 2 s (the default), 3 s or 5 s.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: • Exact spelling — off by default. Then a typed answer with a wrong or missing accent (Spanish, French) or long mark (Latin) counts as correct, with a note that shows the right spelling; in Spanish, so does a small typo in a verb form. French and Latin forgive only accents and long marks, not typos. The exception is an answer that spells another form of the same word — the note under the switch gives an example in the course you study — which is wrong, because it is a different form. With Exact spelling on, only the exact spelling counts. It applies where you type: Produce the conjugation, and in Latin also Decline the noun and Decline the adjective. A picked answer is always graded on the exact form. One setting for all courses.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text: • Level schemes — opens the level-schemes dialog; the row shows the scheme in use. See Levels.

docs.title: Spanish and French
docs.text:
Voice & Conjugation

  • Voice — the speech voice for the course's language. On iPhone and iPad the row shows the current voice and opens a screen with the voice list and the Speed slider. On the Mac the voice menu and the slider sit directly in the tab.
  • Speed — how fast forms are spoken, from Slowest to Fastest. One speed applies to every course.
  • Include pronoun — speaks the pronoun (yo / tú / él…, je / tu / il…) in front of each spoken conjugation. On by default.

Dictionary services

The pages of verbs, nouns, phrases and other words have a book icon in the toolbar; tap it for a menu of online dictionaries:

  • Linguee — example sentences from real translated texts.
  • WordReference — bilingual entries with usage notes.
  • Reverso — translations in context and conjugation tables.
  • RAE — the Real Academia Española's dictionary (Spanish only).

Tap a switch to choose which dictionaries the menu offers. All four are on at first, and the sites are free to use; once you know which ones you reach for, switch off the rest to keep the menu short. With none on, the book disappears.

The French tab offers the same switches without RAE, and the choices are shared: a dictionary switched off on one tab is off on the other. Latin has no dictionary row. On iPhone and iPad a dictionary opens in a browser sheet inside the app; on the Mac it opens in your web browser.

docs.title: Latin
docs.text: Latin has no Voice row and no dictionaries; see Setting up speech.

docs.title: Progress
docs.text:
The tab is headed Progress of and the name of the current learner: everything on it, except the last row, is about that learner.

  • Study History — the learner's record of sessions and answers, from every course. Export writes a dated folder of CSV files with every session and answer: keep it as a backup, open it in Numbers or Excel, or import it on another device. Import reads such a folder, or the files inside it; the answers are added to what is already there, nothing is replaced or removed, and importing the same export twice changes nothing. Only your own history can be imported: an export made under another Apple Account is refused, and for an export that does not say whose it is, the app asks Whose history is this? before going on. An export of another learner on this device asks first too (Another learner's history). Practice sets are not included — they have their own export (see Practice Sets).
iPhoneiPadMac

  • Reset Progress — deletes the current learner's recorded answers, in every course. Reset verb, noun, word or phrase progress on its own, or Reset all progress to delete every answer and session. Each asks for confirmation. Your word selections, settings, scheme and level are not affected.
  • Erase all data and settings — deletes every learner's progress, all settings, schemes and levels, and the dictionary choices, and returns the app to its first-launch state, with the welcome screens. It asks for confirmation and cannot be undone.
iPhoneiPadMac

docs.title: Voice and speed
docs.text:
LinguaMorpha speaks with the voices that Apple installs on your device (see Setting up speech). To choose one:

  1. Open Settings and switch to the tab for your course.
  2. On iPhone and iPad, tap Voice. The list shows every installed voice for the language, each with its flag and Apple's quality label — Standard, Enhanced or Premium. Voices for the course's main region come first, then the other regions, best quality first. On the Mac, choose from the Voice menu.
  3. Pick a voice.
  4. Drag Speed to taste.

If no voice is installed for the language, the screen says so and tells you where to download one.

docs.title: Spanish module
docs.text:
The Spanish module covers over 1,200 verbs in sixteen tenses, over 1,600 nouns, and the smaller word classes around them.

The ways to study it are described under Ways to study in the User Guide. This guide describes what is in the course, word type by word type.

Each word type has its own tile on Self Study, and each tile opens a hub with the same Theory / Study / Practice sections as the rest of the app. Level and topic are not set per hub. Your level is chosen in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag), the topics in Self Study → Select word scope, and every hub draws on both. There is no frequency filter in Self Study.

  • Verbs — over 1,200 verbs in 23 verb groups, conjugated in sixteen tenses and forms: the indicative, subjunctive and imperative, and the gerundio. Choose verb groups and tenses, read the theory, look up any verb's full conjugation, then drill meanings, production, recognition and the choice drills. See Verbs.
  • Nouns — over 1,600 nouns: gender, plurals, meanings and translations. See Nouns.
  • Adjectives — over 290 adjectives: agreement, shortening, comparison and adverb derivation.
  • Adverbs — over 230 adverbs, derived (-mente) and lexical.
  • Pronouns — around fifty pronouns: personal, demonstrative, possessive, relative, interrogative and indefinite.
  • Prepositions — over 30 prepositions, taught by usage: por / para, en / a / de, collocations and idioms.
  • Numerals — cardinal numbers and their relatives, with shortening (un, cien) and agreement in the hundreds.
  • Other Vocabulary — the remaining single words: conjunctions, articles, determiners and interjections.
  • Phrases — over 270 curated set phrases, plus the example sentences from the verb and noun catalogues. See Words and phrases.

Some features exist only in the Spanish course:

  • Traps — curated decks of things that actively mislead a learner: false friends, nouns whose ending lies about their gender, nouns whose meaning changes with the article, and adjectives whose meaning changes with ser or estar. On iPhone and iPad it is a card under Tools on Self Study; on the Mac it is in the sidebar. See Traps.
  • Spanish verb drills — the form drills from Past participle (Participio) to Stem changes (Presente) drill the forms where Spanish irregularity concentrates, and Ser or estar, Gustar and verbs like it, Ir a, tener que, acabar de and Which past tense? (Perfecto / Indefinido) are choice drills no other course has. See The choice drills.
  • Setting up Spanish speech — how to get a natural Spanish voice for the app to speak with.

docs.title: Level schemes
docs.text:
The Spanish course has two level schemes. Choose one in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag); the schemes themselves are under Level schemes in the course tab of Settings (see Level schemes in the User Guide).

  • CEFR — the standard scheme, for someone learning Spanish as a foreign language: six levels, A1 to C2, with translations in your app language.
  • Escuela — for a Spanish-speaking pupil following Lengua castellana at school. Its levels are the school years, 3.º de Primaria to 2.º de ESO. Choosing it sets the app language to Spanish, shows no translations, names the tenses as Spanish schools do (pretérito perfecto simple for the indefinido), and leaves out what is meant for foreign learners: the meaning drills, Traps, Linguistic analysis, the theme lessons and the false friends. 1.º de ESO completes the conjugation (the imperfect and compound subjunctive); 2.º de ESO adds the drills on periphrasis and aspect and the rarest words. The scheme ends there: from 3.º de ESO on, the subject is syntax, text types and literature, which the app does not teach.

docs.title: The choice drills
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Most Spanish drills ask you to produce or recognise a form. The choice drills ask you to make a choice: which verb, tense, mood, preposition or pronoun a sentence needs, or which form of a word goes with a noun. That is where knowing the forms stops being enough.

Where to find them.

  • Verbs — Ser or estar, Gustar and verbs like it (me gusta, me gustan, les gusta), Ir a, tener que, acabar de, Which past tense? (perfecto or indefinido), Preterite or imperfect and Indicative or subjunctive, at the end of the Practice section.
  • Prepositions — Contrast drill: the right preposition for the sentence (por or para, en, a or de).
  • Pronouns — Which pronoun? (the pronoun a slot needs: direct object, indirect object or reflexive), Two pronouns at once (se lo, not le lo) and Agreement drill.
  • Adjectives — Agreement drill, Shortening drill (bueno → buen, grande → gran) and Comparisons (más, tan, mejor).
  • Numerals — Shortening drill (uno → un, primero → primer) and Agreement drill (doscientos / doscientas, primero / primera).
  • Nouns — One article for both sexes: the article or adjective a noun of fixed gender needs (Juan es una persona amable).
  • Traps — Ser or estar, limited to the adjectives whose meaning changes with the verb.

What the screen shows. At the top, the Incorrect answers switch, then "Question 3 of 10" and the running "Score: 2 / 2". Below that, the instruction ("Choose the tense", "Which form of bueno goes with this noun?") and a card with the material. The card comes in two kinds:

  • A sentence — in the sentence drills (the verb drills, Contrast drill, Which pronoun?, Two pronouns at once, Comparisons, the numeral Agreement drill and One article for both sexes), the card shows the sentence in your own language, then the Spanish sentence with a gap. Each is labelled with its language. The option you tap fills the gap, so you can read the whole sentence.
  • A word — in the agreement and shortening drills for adjectives and pronouns and the numeral Shortening drill, the card shows a noun (or a short phrase) with its gender and number, e.g. ciudad (f.sg), and its meaning.

Below the card are the options. Tap one: the right answer turns green with a tick, and a wrong pick turns red with a cross. Then tap Next, or See results after the last question.

The explanation. After you answer, a card explains the answer: "Why es?", with a short explanation of the rule. In the verb drills, the Contrast drill, Comparisons and One article for both sexes it starts with a small coloured label naming the rule at work: Location of an event, Backdrop, Doubt / denial. It tells you which rule a mistake belongs to. The label comes only after the answer, because naming the rule would give the answer away. Which pronoun? names the slot (Direct object slot) under your-language sentence instead, since the slot is part of the question. In the Contrast drill it can end with a Read more in Theory link to the matching part of the prepositions Theory.

Your display language. The sentence in your language, the rule label and the explanation are all shown in your display language. If you switch the display language during a drill, the card is redrawn in the new language. The Spanish sentence and the options stay in Spanish.

The session. A session is a fixed number of questions, set in Settings → Study → Questions per session; with ∞, a session has up to 50 questions, or as many as the drill has. At the end, Session complete appears with a New session button. The questions are picked based on your answer history and your Learning pace, so rules you keep missing come back more often. Incorrect answers limits the session to questions you have got wrong before. Ser or estar, Preterite or imperfect and Indicative or subjunctive also appear in guided lessons, where a session is always ten questions.

What's recorded. Every answer is recorded on your device. The grammar drills record the rule, not a word: Ser or estar records each rule for each verb, and the other verb drills and Comparisons record each principle. Those answers never count towards your vocabulary figures. The agreement and shortening drills record against the adjective, pronoun or numeral.

Reporting a sentence. Tap Help (the question-mark button) to read about the drill. Press and hold it to report a sentence that reads wrong; the report names the screen it came from.

docs.title: Tips for getting started with Spanish
Tips for getting started with Spanish
docs.text:
1. Set up speech first. Install an Enhanced or Premium Spanish voice in Apple's settings, then choose it in LinguaMorpha under Settings → Spanish → Voice. Standard voices sound robotic, and the better voices make a real difference. See Setting up Spanish speech.

  2. Start with A1 nouns. Choose A1 in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag). Set Questions per session to 20 in Settings → Study. Then open Nouns and run a few Meaning sessions until the basic vocabulary feels solid.

  3. Add verbs gradually. Once the A1 nouns feel comfortable, open Self Study → Verbs. In Select groups, choose only Regular. In Select tenses, choose only Presente. Run Produce the conjugation until the regular present tense is automatic, before you touch anything irregular.

  4. Use the conjugation tables actively. Before you drill, open Reference on the verbs hub, tap a verb you are about to practise and look at its Conjugation tab. Red marks the parts of a form that depart from the regular pattern. Once you understand the pattern, the drill sticks faster.

  5. Broaden in steps. Move your level up to A2. Add verb groups one at a time, for example e→ie, then o→ue. Add one tense at a time: Pretérito Indefinido is the most important after Presente. Never widen your selection so far that sessions feel overwhelming.

  6. Check your progress. Tap the chart icon at the top of the main screen (on the Mac, choose My Progress under Tools in the sidebar). Practise next names your weak spot, and Weakest words lists the words you have practised often enough to rank and still get wrong most. Tap a verb there to drill just that verb, or tap Practise all N to drill all the verbs in the list.

docs.title: A. Spanish verb groups
docs.text:
LinguaMorpha sorts Spanish verbs into groups by how they conjugate or how they are used. The groups decide what you drill (Self Study → Verbs → Select groups) and appear as coloured badges on each verb. A verb can belong to more than one group: tener is in Irregular yo: -go, e→ie, Strong preterite and Irregular future stem.

Select verb groups has two views. By Section shows the groups below, in nine families. By regularity sorts verbs by how many things they ask you to remember beyond the regular endings. Each row shows how many verbs it holds, and the ⓘ button opens an explanation with the verbs in that group.

The last three families — reflexive, impersonal and gusto-type, and stative verbs — change no ending. They describe how the verb is used in a sentence, so a verb in one of them can also be Regular.

docs.title: Regular
docs.text: The verb takes the standard endings for its infinitive type (-ar, -er, -ir), with no stem change, no spelling shift and no irregular form anywhere, including the participle and the gerund. Hablar, comer and vivir are the models. A reflexive verb that conjugates regularly, such as lavarse, counts as regular too.

docs.title: Stem-changing verbs
docs.text: The stem vowel changes when it carries the stress. In the present that means yo, tú, él and ellos, but not nosotros or vosotros, where the stress falls on the ending. The present subjunctive changes in the same four persons (piense, pensemos). Stem-changing -ir verbs also change nosotros and vosotros there (pidamos, durmamos), as well as the él and ellos forms of the preterite (pidió, durmieron) and the gerund (pidiendo). In the picker these groups are listed by the change alone.

docs.title: e→ie
docs.text: pensar → pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, pensáis, piensan. The most common stem change. It occurs in all three verb types: pensar, querer, preferir.

docs.title: o→ue
docs.text: poder → puedo; dormir → duermo. It also occurs in -ar, -er and -ir verbs.

docs.title: e→i
docs.text: pedir → pido. Only in -ir verbs.

docs.title: u→ue
docs.text: jugar → juego. Jugar is the member.

docs.title: i→ie
docs.text: adquirir → adquiero.

docs.title: Accent shift í/ú
docs.text: Some -iar and -uar verbs stress the stem vowel and mark it with a written accent instead of changing it: enviar → envío, envías, envía, enviamos, enviáis, envían; actuar → actúo. Again, nosotros and vosotros stay unaccented.

docs.title: Yo-form irregularities
docs.text: The yo form of the present is irregular, and the other persons of the present are not. The present subjunctive is built on the yo form, so there the change runs through every person: tengo → tenga, conozco → conozca.

docs.title: Irregular yo: -go
docs.text: A g appears before the -o of the present yo form: tener → tengo, poner → pongo, salir → salgo, hacer → hago, decir → digo, traer → traigo, caer → caigo, oír → oigo. The present subjunctive is built on that form, so the g runs through all its persons: tenga, tengamos.

docs.title: Irregular yo: -zco
docs.text: Verbs ending in a vowel + -cer or -cir have -zco in the present yo form: conocer → conozco, parecer → parezco, producir → produzco. The other persons of the present are regular. The present subjunctive keeps the zc: conozca.

docs.title: Consonant + -cer/-cir: c → z
docs.text: When a consonant comes before -cer or -cir, the yo form is a plain spelling change instead: vencer → venzo, ejercer → ejerzo. The z runs through the present subjunctive: venza.

docs.title: Spelling shift -ger/-gir
docs.text: To keep the soft sound, g is written j before a and o: escoger → escojo, proteger → protejo, dirigir → dirijo. The same shift appears in every person of the present subjunctive (escoja). The preterite is not affected: escogí, escogió.

docs.title: Verbs ending in -guir
docs.text: The silent u is dropped before o and a: seguir → sigo, distinguir → distingo. The present subjunctive drops it too: siga.

docs.title: Spelling-change verbs
docs.text: A letter changes in some forms so that the pronunciation stays the same. There is nothing to memorise per verb: recognise the ending and the rule applies.

docs.title: Y-insertion
docs.text: When the stem ends in a vowel, an unstressed i between vowels is written y. This happens in the él and ellos forms of the preterite and in the gerund: leer → leyó, leyeron, leyendo. Other examples are creer, oír and caer. The imperfect subjunctive inherits the y: leyera.

docs.title: Verbs ending in -uir
docs.text: A y is inserted before the ending in the present, except in nosotros and vosotros: construir → construyo, construyes, construye, construimos, construís, construyen. These verbs also take the preterite and gerund y: construyó, construyendo.

docs.title: Spelling shift -car/-gar/-zar
docs.text: To keep the consonant's sound before e, the yo form of the preterite changes its spelling: buscar → busqué, llegar → llegué, empezar → empecé. The present subjunctive has the same shift in every person: busque, llegue, empiece.

docs.title: An irregular stem in one tense
docs.text: One tense, or the participle, has a stem of its own. Learn that stem and you know the tense.

docs.title: Strong preterite
docs.text: These verbs use a different stem in the preterite, with endings that carry no written accent: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. Examples: estar → estuve, poder → pude, venir → vine, hacer → hice (él hizo), querer → quise, tener → tuve, andar → anduve. When the stem ends in j, the ellos ending is -eron: decir → dijeron, traer → trajeron, conducir → condujeron. Compounds follow their base verb: obtener → obtuve, componer → compuse. The imperfect subjunctive is built on the same stem: tuviera, dijera.

docs.title: Irregular participle
docs.text: The verb is regular in every simple tense, but its past participle has to be learned: abrir → abierto, escribir → escrito, romper → roto. Every compound tense uses that participle: he abierto, había escrito.

docs.title: Irregular future stem
docs.text: The future and the conditional are built on the whole infinitive. These verbs replace it with a shortened stem, and the endings stay regular. One stem covers both tenses: tener → tendré, tendría. Other examples: poner → pondr-, salir → saldr-, venir → vendr-, haber → habr-, saber → sabr-, poder → podr-, querer → querr-, decir → dir-, hacer → har-.

docs.title: Irregular
docs.text: A verb lands here when it is irregular in a way none of the other groups names. The group includes the verbs whose forms follow no rule across whole tenses: ser (soy, era, fui), ir (voy, iba, fui), estar (estoy, estás), dar (doy, di), haber (he, has, ha) and ver (veo, veía). A verb with only one irregular corner, such as a yo form, a participle or a future stem, is filed in that group instead. So tener, hacer and poder are not in Irregular.

docs.title: Reflexive
docs.text: The verb is used with a reflexive pronoun that agrees with the subject: me, te, se, nos, os, se. It conjugates exactly like the same verb without the pronoun: lavarse is a regular -ar verb, acostarse an o→ue verb, vestirse an e→i verb. The pronoun goes before a conjugated verb (me lavo) and is attached to an infinitive, a gerund or an affirmative command (lavarse, lavándose, ¡lávate!). Some verbs change meaning with the pronoun: dormir (to sleep) and dormirse (to fall asleep).

docs.title: Impersonal
docs.text: Weather verbs and hay have no one doing the action. They are used only in the third-person singular, in every tense: llover → llueve, nevar → nieva, granizar, lloviznar, and hay (había, habrá).

docs.title: Me gusta pattern
docs.text: The thing that pleases is the subject, and the person is an indirect object pronoun. Me gusta el libro literally means "the book pleases me", and the verb agrees with the thing: me gustan los libros. Other members include encantar, interesar, molestar, doler, faltar and parecer.

docs.title: Stative
docs.text: The verb describes a state rather than an action, so it is not normally used in the progressive: sé, not estoy sabiendo. Members include saber, conocer, tener, querer, poder and deber. The me gusta verbs are in this group too.

docs.title: B. Spanish verb tenses
docs.text:
LinguaMorpha conjugates sixteen Spanish tenses and forms. You choose them in Self Study → Verbs → Select tenses, and they are listed below in the order that screen shows them (By Section). By Level sorts the same tenses by the level at which each first appears in the scheme you use:

Level Tenses A1 Presente A2 Pretérito Perfecto, Pretérito Indefinido, Pretérito Imperfecto, Gerundio, Imperativo Afirmativo B1 Futuro, Condicional, Pluscuamperfecto, Presente de Subjuntivo, Imperativo Negativo B2 Futuro Perfecto, Condicional Perfecto, Imperfecto de Subjuntivo, Pretérito Perfecto Subjuntivo, Pluscuamperfecto Subjuntivo

Six of the tenses are compound: a form of haber plus the past participle. That is why the participle drill under Verbs feeds all six.

docs.title: Presente
docs.text: The foundation of the language: habitual actions, general truths, scheduled future events. Endings for -ar: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. For -er: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. For -ir: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en.

docs.title: Pretérito Indefinido
docs.text: The standard narrative past: completed actions, specific past events, sequences of events. Endings for -ar: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. For -er and -ir: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. This is the most irregular tense in Spanish; see Strong preterite in Appendix A.

docs.title: Pretérito Imperfecto
docs.text: Ongoing situations, habits, background description, and an action that is interrupted by another. Endings for -ar: -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban. For -er and -ir: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. Only three verbs are irregular: ser → era, ir → iba, ver → veía.

docs.title: Futuro
docs.text: Actions that will happen, predictions and promises. The endings are added to the whole infinitive, the same for all verb types: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. Some verbs use a shortened stem: tener → tendré, hacer → haré (see Irregular future stem in Appendix A). The future also expresses probability in the present: ¿Dónde estará María? — Where could María be?

docs.title: Condicional
docs.text: What would happen under certain conditions, polite requests and suggestions. Like the future, it is built on the infinitive, with the same irregular stems (tendría, haría). Endings: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían.

docs.title: Pretérito Perfecto
docs.text: Past actions connected to the present. Formed with haber in the present (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) plus the past participle. He perdido las llaves — I have lost my keys (and still don't have them). It is used especially in Spain; much of Latin America uses the Indefinido in the same situations.

docs.title: Pluscuamperfecto
docs.text: Actions completed before another past event: the background layer of a story, and reported speech in the past. Formed with haber in the imperfect (había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían) plus the past participle. Ya habíamos comido cuando llegó — We had already eaten when he arrived.

docs.title: Futuro Perfecto
docs.text: Actions that will be finished before a moment in the future. Formed with haber in the future (habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habréis, habrán) plus the past participle. Habré terminado para las ocho — I will have finished by eight. It also expresses probability about the past, just as the simple future does about the present: Habrá salido — He must have left.

docs.title: Condicional Perfecto
docs.text: What would have happened under different circumstances: hypothetical pasts, regrets, missed chances. Formed with haber in the conditional (habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían) plus the past participle. Habría hablado, pero no tuve tiempo — I would have spoken, but I didn't have time. It is the result clause of an unreal past condition, whose si clause takes the Pluscuamperfecto Subjuntivo.

docs.title: Presente de Subjuntivo
docs.text: Built on the yo form of the present indicative, with the opposite ending vowel: hablar → hable, comer → coma, vivir → viva, tener → tenga. Used after expressions of doubt, emotion, wish and denial: Quiero que estudies — I want you to study.

docs.title: Imperfecto de Subjuntivo
docs.text: Built on the ellos form of the Indefinido: hablaron → hablara, tuvieron → tuviera. Used when the main verb is in the past, and in unreal si clauses: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría — If I had money, I would travel. Spanish also has an equivalent set of forms in -se (hablase); the app shows the -ra forms.

docs.title: Pretérito Perfecto Subjuntivo
docs.text: Haber in the present subjunctive (haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayáis, hayan) plus the past participle. A completed action in a context that requires the subjunctive: Espero que hayas comido — I hope you have eaten; No creo que lo hayas entendido — I don't think you have understood it.

docs.title: Pluscuamperfecto Subjuntivo
docs.text: Haber in the imperfect subjunctive (hubiera, hubieras, hubiera, hubiéramos, hubierais, hubieran) plus the past participle. The -se set (hubiese…) exists too; the app uses hubiera. Used for hypothetical pasts and unreal conditions: Si hubiera estudiado, habría aprobado — If I had studied, I would have passed; Ojalá hubiera venido — If only he had come. Its result clause takes the Condicional Perfecto.

docs.title: Imperativo
docs.text: Commands. There is no yo form, so the app shows five persons.

docs.title: Imperativo Afirmativo
docs.text: Tú uses the él form of the present (¡Habla!), and vosotros replaces the -r of the infinitive with -d (¡Hablad!). The other persons use the present subjunctive (hable, hablemos, hablen). Several common verbs have a short irregular tú form: tener → ten, poner → pon, salir → sal, hacer → haz, decir → di, venir → ven.

docs.title: Imperativo Negativo
docs.text: No plus the present subjunctive, in every person: ¡No hables! — Don't speak! ¡No habléis!

docs.title: Gerundio
docs.text: Actions in progress, and the progressive forms built on them. -ar verbs take -ando (hablando); -er and -ir verbs take -iendo (comiendo, viviendo). The app conjugates it as the progressive (estoy hablando … están hablando), so the table shows all six persons even though the gerund itself is a single form. It is irregular where the stem changes (decir → diciendo, pedir → pidiendo, dormir → durmiendo) and where a vowel comes before the ending (leer → leyendo, oír → oyendo, construir → construyendo). Verbs in the Stative group are not normally used in the progressive.

docs.title: Setting up Spanish speech
docs.text: iPhoneiPadMac

docs.title: Why this matters (Spanish)
docs.text:
The voices are Apple's, not LinguaMorpha's. The app speaks through the text-to-speech engine built into iOS, iPadOS and macOS. It can only use voices already installed on your device. It has no voices of its own and cannot improve Apple's.

Apple offers Spanish voices at three quality levels: Standard, Enhanced and Premium. Standard voices sound robotic. Enhanced and Premium voices sound far more natural and are strongly recommended for language learning. They are free, and once you download one, every app on the device can use it.

docs.title: Downloading a better Spanish voice
docs.text:
You do this in Apple's settings, not in LinguaMorpha:

  1. On iPhone or iPad, open the Settings app and go to Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices → Spanish. On the Mac, open System Settings and go to Accessibility → Spoken Content → System Voice → Manage Voices.
  2. Choose the region whose accent you want to learn (Spain, Mexico, and so on).
  3. Download a voice marked Enhanced or Premium. These are large downloads, so use Wi-Fi.

Apple sometimes moves these settings between OS versions. If the path above doesn't match your device, search its settings for "Voices".

docs.title: Choosing the voice and speed in LinguaMorpha
docs.text:
• iPhone and iPad — open the ⋯ menu on the Home screen, choose Settings, and switch to the Spanish tab. Under Voice & Conjugation, tap Voice. The Spanish Voice screen lists the voices, and below them is the Speaking Speed slider, from Slowest to Fastest.
  • Mac — open LinguaMorpha's Settings and choose the Spanish tab. The Voice menu and the Speed slider are right there.

Only voices already installed on your device appear. Each one shows its region's flag, its name and its quality (Premium, Enhanced or Standard). Voices for Spain come first, then other regions, with the best quality first in each group. Until you choose a voice, the app uses the best-quality voice for Spain on your device. If no Spanish voice is installed, the screen tells you where to download one.

Speed is one setting for all spoken languages; Latin is the exception and always plays at its own slower pace. The slider goes slightly faster than normal at the top end. On the Mac, the speed starts a little slower than on iPhone and iPad, because Mac voices speak faster.

Include pronoun, in the same section, adds yo / tú / él… before each form when a conjugation table is read aloud. It is on by default.

LinguaMorpha reads the Spanish side with the voice you choose here. The English or Dutch side of a flashcard is read by your device's standard voice for that language.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Tests page holds every test for your level on one page: the level in the chip with the flag (on the Mac, at the top of the sidebar). Change the level there and the page follows; at All levels it shows everything. It is a way to find out what you already know, rather than a place to learn something new.

Vocabulary comes first: one Meaning test that mixes the words of every type up to your level — verbs, nouns, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, other vocabulary and set phrases. Pronouns and numerals keep a meaning test of their own under their word type.

Below it, each word type lists its tests, in the order of Self Study, as they stand at your level. A test appears at the level where its subject is taught and stays in every level after it: a tense's test appears at the level that brings the tense in.

The book button beside a test opens the theory of its word type, for when a test shows you are not there yet. A round with less than 70% correct also ends with Review the theory, which opens the same page.

Your level's words. Vocabulary, Produce the conjugation, Recognise the conjugation, the noun and adjective tests and, in Spanish, the verb-form tests (participio, gerundio, indefinido, future stem, subjunctive stems, short tú, stem and spelling changes) ask every word and every tense up to your level, whatever you have selected in Self Study. The other tests use your Self Study selection, as they do in the hubs.

Only new at this level, in Scheme and level, narrows the tests to what your level adds: Vocabulary asks the words new at your level, the conjugation tests ask every verb you know in the tenses new at your level, the Spanish form tests ask the new verbs, and the noun and adjective tests the new nouns and adjectives.

Answers count like any other drill's, in My Progress and in the adaptive engine.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Theory page lists every theory page of the course in one place, by word type in the order of Self Study: under Verbs the verb groups and the tenses (the sheets to print are at the bottom of the verb groups page); under Nouns the gender and plural rules; and so on through adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, numerals, other vocabulary and phrases. Each row opens the same page the word type's hub opens from its Theory section — this is the reading order, the hub is the place beside the drills. A page whose cards lie above your level still opens, but leaves those cards out; Also later levels at the top brings them back, with their level beside them.

On a theory page, tap a card to open or close it; Expand all opens every card at once. With a keyboard, on the Mac and the iPad, ⌘← closes the open card and scrolls back to its heading. With no card open, it closes the open family, such as Indicativo – tiempos simples on the Tenses page; with Expand all on, it closes everything. ⌘→ reopens the card that ⌘← just closed. Both keys also work in a theory page opened in a window of its own.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Most of the app is a catalogue: everything there is to know about a word class, filtered down to what you want to work on. Traps is the opposite. It holds small, closed, curated decks of things that actively mislead a learner:

  • False friends — Spanish words that look or sound like a word in your language and mean something else.
  • Meaning changes with gender — nouns that are one word with two unrelated meanings, where only el or la tells you which is meant.
  • Gender traps — nouns whose ending points to the wrong gender: el problema, la mano.
  • Ser/estar shifts — adjectives whose meaning depends on the verb: es listo is clever, está listo is ready.

Where to find it. On iPhone and iPad, open Self Study and tap Traps under Tools. On the Mac, choose Traps in the Tools section of the sidebar. Traps exists in the Spanish course and, with one deck so far, in the French course; Latin has none.

The decks sit together because they have the same shape, not the same cause. Each is a fixed set that brings its own words: you don't select anything first, and Select word scope doesn't narrow them. Your level does: each deck holds the entries within your level. So the hub has no selection rows, only Theory, Study and Practice. The line under the hub title shows how many entries each of the four decks holds for you.

The false-friend flashcards keep their own record, so getting sensible wrong there doesn't count against the adjective in the adjective drills. The other three drills record your answers the same way as the ordinary drills they are built on. A gender-trap card counts as an article answer for that noun, a meaning-change card as a noun-meaning answer, and a ser/estar shift question as a ser/estar answer.

docs.title: About traps
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Theory row opens About traps. It explains why these words are collected, and the one thing you can't work out from the decks themselves:

A false friend is a fact about the language you already speak. A meaning-changer is a fact about Spanish.

Embarazada is only a trap if your language has embarrassed in it. El capital and la capital catch everyone equally. The page also explains why the meaning-changers are drilled as two cards each, and suggests an order of work: read the list first, then drill.

docs.title: False friends reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The whole false-friend deck on one page, grouped under Nouns, Verbs, Adjectives and Adverbs, with a search field. Each row shows three things:

  • the Spanish word (nouns with their article: el nombre),
  • what it really means,
  • what it is mistaken for, and the Spanish word that does mean that: not "number" — that is número.

The deck depends on your display language. A false friend has to resemble a word in the language you already speak, so the app shows only the entries that are traps for you. The deck holds 42 entries: 25 nouns, 10 verbs, 5 adjectives and 2 adverbs. With English as display language all 42 apply to you. With Dutch 19 do, because the other 23 are no trap for a Dutch speaker. Sensible catches an English speaker (Spanish sensible means sensitive), but Dutch sensibel already means sensitive. El nombre catches both: it means name, and the Spanish for number is número. Your level narrows the deck further, and the line at the top shows how many entries are left for you.

docs.title: False friends flashcards
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The False friends drill turns the same deck into flashcards: translate the word, then flip the card. The back shows the answer and a short note:

  • Looks like "…" — the word it is mistaken for,
  • "…" is … — the Spanish word that does mean that,
  • a line explaining where the resemblance comes from.
