A session draws from the deck, based on your answer history and your Learning pace, up to your Questions per session (Settings → Study). The switch at the top sets the direction: Spanish → your language, or the other way round.

docs.title: Meaning-changers reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

These nouns carry two unrelated meanings that only the article separates. The reference shows each noun within your level once, with an el line and a la line:

Noun With el With la capital money, capital capital city coma coma comma cometa comet kite corte cut court (royal) cura priest cure cólera cholera anger, wrath disco record, disc nightclub, disco editorial editorial (opinion piece) publishing house frente front (military, weather) forehead orden order (arrangement) order (command) papa Pope potato (Latin America; Spain says la patata) pendiente earring slope

Hay un orden and hay una orden are both grammatical, but only one of them means what you intended. That is why these nouns are worth drilling as a group rather than meeting them one at a time.

This is not the same as a noun with two genders. El dentista and la dentista are one word for one job, and the article only tells you who is meant. El papa and la papa are two different words that happen to share a spelling.

The list comes from the noun catalogue, so these are the same nouns that carry the Different meaning by article group under Nouns.

docs.title: Meaning changes with gender
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The flashcard drill for the meaning-changers. Each noun becomes two cards, one per article (el papa → Pope, la papa → potato), because a single card for el/la papa would have no one right answer. The deck holds the meaning-changers within your level, whatever your noun selection. The same drill also appears on the Nouns hub.

docs.title: Gender traps reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Spanish noun endings usually predict the gender: -a, -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad and -umbre are typically feminine, -o masculine. This deck holds every catalogue noun that ending gets wrong:

  • the Greek-derived -ma masculines: el problema, el idioma, el clima, el sistema, el tema,
  • other masculines in -a: el día, el mapa, el planeta, el tranvía,
  • feminines in -o, most of them shortened words: la mano, la foto, la moto, la radio.

The list has two sections: Looks feminine, is masculine (el) and Looks masculine, is feminine (la). Every word is shown with its article, because the article is what you are learning. Reading each section in one go makes the patterns visible: the -ma words cluster, and so do the shortened feminines.

The deck is built from the noun catalogue, so a new noun with a misleading ending joins it automatically. Nouns that take both genders and multi-word nouns are left out.

Stressed-á feminines are not traps. El agua and el aula take el in the singular for the sake of sound, but they are feminine (las aguas, el agua fría), and they follow a rule rather than break one. They have their own group under Nouns, Stressed-á feminines.

docs.title: Gender traps drill
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Gender traps drill is the familiar el/la article drill, limited to exactly this deck. In the ordinary drill, most nouns in your selection follow the ending rule. Here every card is one where the rule gives the wrong answer, and each session asks all of them.

docs.title: Ser/estar shifts reference
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Twelve adjectives mean one thing with ser and another with estar. The reference shows each adjective with a ser line and an estar line:

Adjective With ser With estar aburrido boring bored abierto open-minded, sociable open (right now) atento courteous, considerate paying attention bueno good (character) tasty; recovered despierto sharp, alert by nature awake interesado self-interested interested (in) listo clever ready malo bad, wicked ill; (food) off rico wealthy delicious seguro safe, reliable certain, sure verde green (colour) unripe vivo sharp, quick-witted alive

This is the sharpest of the four hazards. With a false friend you use the wrong word. Here you say a perfectly grammatical sentence that means something else: es interesada is an insult, está interesada is a plain fact. The deck keeps to systematic shifts and leaves out idioms such as estar católico.

docs.title: Ser or estar (shift drill)
docs.text: The Ser or estar row under Traps opens the ser/estar drill, limited to these twelve adjectives. Each question gives an English sentence and a Spanish sentence with a gap (El profesor ___ aburrido.). You choose the right form of ser or estar. Each adjective is asked in both directions (The teacher is boring / The teacher is bored), so the English sentence is your only clue. After you answer, a short explanation shows the two meanings. The number of questions comes from Questions per session. The open Ser or estar drill under Verbs keeps its full set of sentences and includes these as well.

docs.title: Working through the decks
docs.text:
1. Read About traps once. The difference between a false friend and a meaning-changer is what makes the rest make sense.
  2. Read the False friends reference, including the "that is …" part of each row. The Spanish word you were actually looking for is what makes the pair stick.
  3. Run the False friends flashcards until the deck feels comfortable.
  4. Do the same for the meaning-changers: read the pairs side by side, then drill Meaning changes with gender.
  5. Browse the Gender traps reference section by section, then run the Gender traps drill.
  6. Read the Ser/estar shifts reference, then run Ser or estar.
  7. Come back from time to time. A trap stays tempting long after you have learned it, and these decks are small enough to finish, unlike the noun catalogue.

The trap entries and their notes are written as teaching material and are still waiting to be checked by someone who knows both languages well.

docs.title: Flashcard sessions
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

All flashcard screens in the app work the same way, whether you are practising verb meanings, noun vocabulary or everyday expressions.

docs.title: The controls at the top
docs.text:
• Direction — three flag buttons: the target language → your language, your language → the target language, or a random mix of both in the same session. Fixed-direction decks, such as singular and plural, have no direction picker.
  • Incorrect answers — a switch that limits the session to cards you have previously got wrong and not yet recovered. If you have none, the app says so and switches it off. In this mode the session ends as soon as nothing incorrect is left.
  • Listen — on decks that can speak, when a voice for the language is installed, a switch that plays the question instead of showing it. Tap the large speaker to hear it again, then turn the card to see the spelling. It is not offered when the question is in your own language.

Under them, a bar shows how far through the deck you are, with Score: X / Y beside it for how many you have right so far, and a line shows how many candidate cards your selection produces.

Session size and learning pace are not set here: they are Questions per session and Learning pace in Settings → Study, and apply to every drill.

docs.title: Answering
docs.text:
A word or phrase appears on the card. Think of the answer, then tap the card to turn it over. Then grade yourself:

  • Swipe the card — right if you knew it, left if you did not. The next card appears straight away. On iPhone and iPad the first few times a short animation shows the gesture; tap its ✕ to stop it.
  • Tap a button — Wrong or Correct. The card flashes, then the next one appears. On the Mac these buttons are always under the card (swiping still works on a trackpad); on iPhone and iPad they appear when VoiceOver is on, since swiping is the main route there.

A speaker icon on the card plays the side you are looking at, where the course has speech. On verb cards a book icon shows the verb's conjugation.

docs.title: How a session runs
docs.text:
A session draws a set of cards from your pool and asks as many questions as it drew. A card you get right is put aside; a card you get wrong stays in the deck and can come round again, but never twice in a row. After seven correct answers in a row the app asks whether to stop and count the session as complete, or continue.

At the end the card area reads Session complete; the score stays where it was. Tap New session to draw the next batch. Every drill ends the same way, cards or not.

Under it, To look at again names the words you got wrong in the round — up to five, with their meaning, and how many more there were. Tap one for its page; a verb opens at the tense you missed. Practise incorrect answers starts a new round with the Incorrect answers switch on: every word you have got wrong and not yet recovered, these among them. A miss on a rule rather than a word — ser or estar, the reason for an article — counts in the score but has no word to name.

docs.title: Tips for getting started
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The Getting started page — a row near the top of the main screen and an item in the ⋯ menu on iPhone and iPad, and Home at the top of the Mac sidebar — says which way in suits you: a card for each of Grammar lessons, Theory, Practice Sets, Self Study and Tests, each opening with the question that makes it yours. Until you first change your level, it also explains what the level does. A few tips that apply whatever you are studying:

  • You start at the lowest level. A new install begins at the first level, A1, and Self Study then shows only what belongs to it; the rest waits. Move up in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag) when this level feels easy, or choose All levels to see everything. If something seems to be missing, it is most likely above your level. Practice Sets follow your level too; in Grammar lessons every lesson stays open, and those above your level are dimmed. See Levels.
  • New to the language? Start with Grammar lessons, where the course has them: they run in order, so you never have to decide what comes next.
  • Know what needs work? Go to Practice Sets and launch a set instead of setting anything up.
  • Want to choose for yourself? Go to Self Study. Start narrow: stay at a low level, tick one or two topics under Select word scope, and widen only when the words start to feel easy.
  • Set up each hub once. Open the selection rows at the top of a hub's Practice section and choose what suits your level; the app remembers your choices.
  • Read the Theory before the Drills. A few minutes with the pattern first makes the drills stick.
  • Little and often. Prefer short, frequent sessions to occasional long ones — the adaptive engine keeps bringing back your weakest words.
  • Use Incorrect answers. Now and then, switch it on in a drill to work only on what you got wrong.
  • Ask the screen. When something is unclear, tap Help or ?.

Course-specific tips are in the course guide.

docs.title: The Theory / Study / Practice pattern
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Every word-type hub in Self Study — Verbs, Nouns, Adjectives, Adverbs, Pronouns, Prepositions, Numerals, Other Vocabulary, Phrases — follows the same pattern. At the top is a card with the hub's name, a short description, often a count of what is in play (for verbs, n of m verbs), and a Help button. Below it are up to three sections:

  • Theory — explanations: grammar prose, paradigms, how the catalogue is organised. No drills, no tests; just read until the pattern makes sense. The same pages, from every hub, are listed together under Theory in the Study section.
  • Study — the reference: browse the items in your pool with their translations, and open any one for its full forms. Nothing is recorded here.
  • Practice — choose which kinds are in play: verb groups and tenses, noun groups, adjective groups, word groups and so on (Select groups, and on the verbs hub also Select tenses). Each row shows how many you have chosen (12 of 40), in red when nothing is chosen. The picker it opens shows a running count of what your choice matches — and, where it applies, how many of those survive your word scope ("· 250 in scope"), with a Select word scope row to change that. So the pool a hub works from is what passes both your choice in these rows and the level and topics you set under Select word scope. Then the drills: flashcard decks and graded drills. Every answer is recorded and feeds the adaptive engine.

The Spanish Traps hub follows the same pattern without the selection rows: its decks are closed, so there is nothing to choose.

If your choice of verb groups has verbs but your word scope removes all of them, a red banner in the Practice section, above the selection rows, says so.

Opening a verb. Tapping a verb opens a tabbed detail screen — Conjugation · Regularity · Reference sheet — with the verb's translation beside the infinitive in the header. It opens on Conjugation: the tables for the tenses you have selected, each with a speaker button, a line saying what the tense is for and the verb's own sentence in that tense, and a toolbar button that shows a translation under every form. A By Tense / By Person picker turns the tables around: one panel per tense, or one per person with that person's form in every tense; Latin adds Filter. Regularity starts with a card of facts about how the verb is built, and answers a different question: where this verb departs from the regular pattern. It lists only those tenses, each with a verdict (Regular endings, changed stem, Regular endings, learned form, Partly irregular, Irregular or No regular pattern) and the stem it is built on, and names the regular tenses in one closing line. Tap a tense to see it on Conjugation with its explanation open. Reference sheet, where the course has one, is a one-page PDF of the verb; share or save it from the share button (on the Mac, Copy or Save as…).

The colours answer different questions. On the Regularity tab a stem you have to memorise is shown in amber; in the conjugation table the letters of a form that depart from the pattern are shown in red. A tense can therefore read Regular endings, changed stem — the endings hold, the stem does not — which is the ordinary case for a tense built on a stem of its own.

Word pool vs session size. Your word pool is the full set of items eligible to appear (defined by the selection rows and your word scope). Your session size is how many questions a single sitting asks: Questions per session in Settings → Study — 10, 20, 30, 50 or ∞ (until you stop). Each session the app draws from your pool, mixing words you have not seen yet with ones you find hard, in the proportion set by Learning pace.

Always check the selection rows before starting a drill. If nothing is selected, the drill has nothing to ask.

docs.title: Look up
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Look up is the place to go when you read or hear a form and want to know what it is. It can be opened from anywhere:

  • iPhone and iPad — the round magnifying glass at the bottom right of every screen opens it over the screen you are on, or ⇧⌘F on an iPad keyboard. It is also under Tools on the Self Study screen.
  • Mac — type in the Look up a form field at the top of the sidebar, and the right-hand pane shows Look up; clear the field to go back. Edit ▸ Look up… (⇧⌘F) opens it in a window of its own beside the main window instead, on an empty field each time.

Not during a drill: while a drill is running the button is hidden and the menu item greyed out, and a Look up window left open says so instead of answering.

It has two modes. Word mode looks up a single form in the course you are studying. Sentence mode, in Latin only, parses a whole sentence and labels every word; the Latin course guide covers it. In the other courses there is no mode picker: the screen is Word mode.

docs.title: Word mode
docs.text:
Type at least two characters. The search runs as you type and matches every entry that starts with what you typed:

  • Case is ignored — DAR finds dar.
  • Accents and macrons are optional — dio finds dió, amico finds amīcō. If you do type an accent, it counts: dió no longer matches dio.
  • Prefixes work — trab finds trabajar and its conjugated forms.
  • Meanings work too — a word in your app language, or in English, finds entries with a translation that contains a word starting with it. The matched meaning is shown on the row.

Results are grouped under Verbs, Nouns, Adjectives, Adverbs, Phrases and Other vocabulary, each with a count. Within a group, form matches come before meaning matches, and a very short query shows only the first hundred or so results. Each row shows:

  • the form, with the part you typed highlighted, and the word it comes from when that is different (one written form often belongs to more than one word, or is several forms of one word, so expect several rows);
  • its translation;
  • its grammatical description — tense and person, case and number, gender.

Verb and noun rows have a chevron and open the word's detail screen: a verb opens at the tense of the matched form, and a noun highlights the matched form in its table. Other rows are for reading only.

Theory. The theory pages are searched too: every card of every hub's Theory row, by its title and its text — gustar finds the card on me gusta, hubiera the pluscuamperfecto de subjuntivo. When forms and cards both match, a switch at the top chooses between Forms (n) and Theory (n), Forms first; when only cards match, they are shown straight away. A card's row names the card and the sentence that matched; tap it to open the page at that card.

If nothing starts with what you typed, the screen falls back to headwords spelled like it — a letter slipped, a form written from memory: tiner finds tener, ablar finds hablar — under the notice No exact match — these are spelled similarly. When no headword is a slip away, conjugated forms are tried the same way: huce finds hice, hace, hube and huye, each with its tense and person. These rows are approximate, so nothing in them is highlighted as the match, and expressions are left out of this fallback. Only when that too finds nothing does the screen say No matches. Switching course clears the search.

docs.title: On the Mac
docs.text: LinguaMorpha on the Mac is the same app, but it puts its controls where a Mac user expects them.

docs.title: The window
docs.text: A sidebar replaces the cards and toolbar icons of the iPhone: the Look up a form field and the chip with the flag and your level at the top, then Home, Study, Tools and Help, with the trial countdown and Unlock at the foot (see The main screen). Choosing a row shows that area on the right.

docs.title: The menus
docs.text:
LinguaMorpha

  • About LinguaMorpha — opens the About window.
  • Unlock… — opens the store.
  • Settings… (⌘,) — opens the Settings window. See Settings.

File

  • Practice Sets — Import… (⌘I) and Export… (⌘E) for a full backup, and Share Selected… and Import Shared… for sending sets to someone else. See Sharing: export and import. These work wherever you are in the app.

Study history is exported and imported in Settings → Progress, as on the iPhone.

Edit

  • Find (⌘F) — puts the cursor in the search field of the screen you are on, or in the sidebar's Look up a form field when the screen has none.
  • Look up… (⇧⌘F) — opens Look up in a window of its own. See Look up.

Study

  • Home (⇧⌘H) — back to the start page from anywhere.
  • The courses, with a tick by the one you are studying. ⌘1, ⌘2 and ⌘3 switch between them in the order listed.
  • Previous lesson (⌘[) and Next lesson (⌘]) — in a lesson, go to the lesson before or after it on the path; greyed out elsewhere.

Help

  • User Guide (⌘?) — opens the guide in its own window, which you can keep open beside the app.

The menu bar follows your App language. Because macOS builds it when the app starts, changing App language offers to restart the app.

docs.title: Working differently from the iPhone
docs.text:
• Settings is a separate window, with General, Study, your course and Progress as tabs along the top, and the voice menu and speed slider directly in the course tab.
  • Row actions are on the ⋯ at the end of the row, and on the right-click menu: a practice set offers Edit, Rename, Duplicate and Delete, a folder Rename and Delete.
  • Grading buttons always sit under the flashcard.
  • Lesson exercises open in a sheet over the lesson.
  • Import and export of practice sets are in the File menu rather than on the screens.
  • A verb's reference sheet has a share menu with Copy and Save as… (⌘S) to save it as a PDF.
  • Dictionary lookups open in your web browser.
  • Swipe hints are not shown, so Settings has no Show swipe hints again row.

docs.title: A. Adaptive learning — how it works
docs.text: LinguaMorpha keeps every answer you give and uses that history to decide which words appear in each session. The aim is to spend your time where it matters: on words you have not met yet, and on words you keep getting wrong.

docs.title: What gets recorded
docs.text: For every answer the app stores the word and its word type, the kind of question (meaning, conjugation, article, and so on), whether you were right, and the date and time — for conjugation questions also the tense and person. It is kept in a database on your device and never leaves it, unless you export it yourself.

docs.title: How each session pool is built
docs.text:
The words for a session are chosen in this order:

1. Words you got wrong last time. A word you answered incorrectly is flagged, and flagged words go to the front of the next session. Answering it correctly removes the flag.

2. New words and review words, in the mix set by Learning pace. The remaining places are shared between:

  • new words — words with no history yet. Verbs and nouns come in order of importance: a combination of CEFR level and frequency, so common A1 words come first and rare C2 words last;
  • review words — words you have met before, weakest first. A word's correct rate decides its place, adjusted for how recently you saw it: a word from yesterday drops back behind a similar word you last saw a fortnight ago, so the review rotates instead of showing the same cards every morning. A recent sighting never pushes a well-known word ahead of one you cannot do.

If there are not enough words of one kind, the other fills the gap, so a session is always full as long as your selection has enough words. In the session, new words come before review words.

docs.title: What this means in practice
docs.text:
• Early on, sessions are mostly new words, introduced in order of importance.
  • As your vocabulary grows, sessions shift towards reviewing words you already know, concentrating on the ones you find hardest.
  • A word you keep answering correctly moves back in the queue and appears less often.
  • Once you have met every word in your selection, there are no new words left: every session is review, whatever the pace.

docs.title: Session pool stability
docs.text: The pool is worked out once and kept. If you leave a session halfway and come back, you see the same words, not a fresh shuffle. It is worked out again when your word selection, session size or learning pace changes, when you start a new session, or when you reset your progress.

docs.title: Learning Pace
docs.text:
Learning pace in Settings → Study sets the share of review words among the places left after the flagged words:

  • Relaxed — about 80% review, 20% new. Good for consolidating what you know.
  • Balanced — half and half. The default; steady progress.
  • Intensive — about 20% review, 80% new. More demanding, but your vocabulary grows faster.

docs.title: B. Setting up speech
docs.text: LinguaMorpha reads forms aloud with Apple's speech synthesis, which is built into iOS, iPadOS and macOS. The voices belong to the system, not to the app: LinguaMorpha bundles none and can only use what is installed on your device. Good sound therefore takes a one-time setup: download a better voice for the language you study, then choose it in the app (see Voice and speed under Settings).

docs.title: Downloading a better voice
docs.text:
Apple offers most languages in three qualities: Standard, Enhanced and Premium. The Enhanced and Premium voices sound much better than the default. If you are unsure, choose an Enhanced voice.

  • iPhone and iPad — Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices, then the language.
  • Mac — System Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → System Voice → Manage Voices.

Where a language has regional variants, choose the accent you prefer. Once the download has finished, the voice appears in LinguaMorpha's voice list.

docs.title: When nothing is installed
docs.text: If no voice is installed for the language, the voice screen says so and shows where to download one. The flashcards' Listen switch is not offered until the app can speak the language.

docs.title: Latin
docs.text:
No system has a Latin voice. LinguaMorpha reads Latin with an Italian voice it chooses itself, at a slower fixed speed, so there is no Voice row for Latin. An Enhanced Italian voice improves it. The course guide has the details.

For which voices to download for your course, see the course guide.

docs.title: C. CEFR levels
docs.text:
CEFR stands for the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, an internationally recognised scale for describing language ability, divided into six levels.

Level Label What it means A1 Beginner Understand and use very basic everyday expressions and simple phrases. A2 Elementary Communicate about familiar topics — family, shopping, local geography. B1 Intermediate Handle most situations while travelling; describe experiences and plans. B2 Upper Intermediate Understand complex text on concrete and abstract topics. C1 Advanced Express ideas fluently and spontaneously. C2 Mastery Understand virtually everything heard or read.

docs.title: How LinguaMorpha uses them
docs.text:
Every verb and noun, and most other words, carries a CEFR level. You meet the levels in several places:

  • Your level — the standard schemes of Spanish and French name their levels after CEFR; the level you choose in Scheme and level decides what Self Study shows. Another scheme names its own levels — school years, gymnasium classes — and the words keep their CEFR tag under it. See Levels.
  • New words — among words you have not met yet, lower levels come first (see Adaptive learning — how it works).
  • Practice Sets — the By level sets, and the Level filter when you build a set.
  • Grammar lessons — each lesson shows its level.
  • My Progress — This and lower levels counts against your level and the ones below it, which in the standard Spanish and French schemes are these six.

Most learners starting from scratch will find CEFR A1 and A2 enough for the first few months.

A level describes the word, not you. Some languages have no official CEFR scale — Latin, for one — so their levels are an approximate mapping onto a standard teaching sequence; the course guide explains how.

docs.title: Verbs
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Open Self Study → Verbs to reach the verbs hub, the control centre for verb practice. The header at the top shows how many verbs your current selection gives you out of the whole catalogue. Its Help button explains the hub and what each drill asks of you, and a long press on any row (on the Mac, click and hold) explains that row.

If your verb groups select verbs but your level and topics remove all of them, a warning at the top of Practice says so: "No verbs match once your topic scope is applied." Widen your topics or clear the topic filter to get the verbs back.

The hub has three sections.

Theory

  • Verb groups — the families the verbs fall into: the regular pattern, the stem changes, the yo irregulars, the spelling changes, the strong preterites and the verbs no pattern explains. Each group opens with its explanation, a worked example and a list of its verbs. Read this before choosing groups: Select verb groups is only as useful as your sense of what the groups are. The page ends with Beyond the groups — the compound families (contener is tener) and how the tables mark irregular forms — and To print, with Regular patterns and Irregular patterns.
  • Tenses — an overview of how the three moods and the tenses divide the work and of where the irregular forms come from (five sources, which the other tenses inherit), then one card per tense in four groups: Indicativo, Subjuntivo, Imperativo and Formas no personales. Each card says how the tense is formed and which few patterns its irregular forms follow. The ⓘ beside a tense elsewhere in the app opens this page at that tense's card.
iPhoneiPadMac

Study

  • Reference (Verb reference) — every verb in your selection, each with its translation; tap a verb for its conjugation, regularity and reference sheet. See Verb reference and Conjugation tables.

Practice

  • Select groups (Select verb groups) — pick the conjugation patterns to drill, and so which verbs are in your pool. The badge shows how many of the 23 groups are ticked, e.g. "23 of 23", and turns red at zero. See Select verb groups.

  • Select tenses — pick which of the sixteen tenses to study, e.g. "16 of 16". See Select tenses.

  • Meaning — Recall what each verb means

  • Produce the conjugation — Type or pick the correct verb form
  • Recognise the conjugation — Identify verb, tense, and person from a conjugated form
  • Past participle (Participio) — Recall the participio of irregular verbs
  • Gerund (Gerundio) — Recall the gerundio / present progressive form
  • Preterite (Indefinido) — Recall the simple past (indefinido) form
  • Future stem (Futuro / Condicional) — Recall the stem the futuro and the condicional share
  • Yo-form stem (Presente / Subjuntivo) — Build the subjunctive on the yo form: tengo → tenga
  • Preterite stem (Indefinido / Imperfecto de subjuntivo) — Build the imperfect subjunctive on the indefinido: tuvieron → tuviera
  • Short tú commands (Imperativo) — The eight short commands and their negatives: ten / no tengas
  • -ir stem change (Indefinido / Gerundio / Subjuntivo) — The -ir stem change outside the presente: pidió, pidiendo, pidamos
  • Spelling changes (Indefinido / Subjuntivo) — -car, -gar, -zar keep their sound: busqué, busque
  • Stem changes (Presente) — The whole presente of a stem-changing verb: quiero … queremos
  • Ser or estar — Choose the right verb for the sentence
  • Gustar and verbs like it — Choose the form and the pronoun: me gusta, me gustan, les gusta
  • Ir a, tener que, acabar de — Choose the construction the meaning needs
  • Which past tense? (Perfecto / Indefinido) — Choose the past the sentence needs
  • Preterite or imperfect (Indefinido / Imperfecto) — Choose which past tense the situation needs
  • Indicative or subjunctive (Indicativo / Subjuntivo) — Choose the mood the sentence requires

Most have a section of their own further on; Gustar and verbs like it, Ir a, tener que, acabar de and Which past tense? are described under The choice drills.

docs.title: Studying verbs goes in three steps
docs.text:
1. Choose what to study. In Select groups, tick the patterns you want — start with Regular and a stem change or two rather than all 23. In Select tenses, narrow to the tenses you are learning; the conjugation tables and the drills show only those. Level and topic come from Scheme and level (the chip with the flag) and from Self Study → Select word scope.
  2. Study. Read Verb groups and Tenses under Theory, then open verbs in Reference to see their tables before you drill them.
  3. Drill. Warm up with Meaning so you know what the verbs mean, then move to Produce the conjugation and Recognise the conjugation. Use Past participle, Gerund and Preterite for the forms where the irregulars concentrate, and the choice drills once the forms are secure.

docs.title: The three verb families
docs.text:
Every Spanish verb belongs to one of three families, determined by the ending of its infinitive. The conjugation endings differ for each.

  • -ar verbs (hablar, trabajar, estudiar) — by far the most common family.
  • -er verbs (comer, beber, aprender) — the second family.
  • -ir verbs (vivir, escribir, subir) — the third.

The stem is everything that remains after you remove the -ar/-er/-ir ending. Endings are added to the stem to produce each conjugated form. Regular -er and -ir verbs share most of their endings; in the present tense they differ only in the nosotros and vosotros forms (comemos, coméis against vivimos, vivís).

The infinitive type also determines the regular past participle: -ar verbs add -ado (hablado), -er and -ir verbs add -ido (comido, vivido). The gerundio follows the same split: -ar verbs add -ando (hablando), -er and -ir verbs add -iendo (comiendo, viviendo). Verbs such as escribir (escrito) and leer (leyendo) depart from this, and the conjugation tables mark them.

See Appendix A for the full Spanish verb-group taxonomy and Appendix B for the tense overview.

docs.title: Preterite or imperfect (Indefinido / Imperfecto)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Spanish has two simple past tenses, the indefinido and the imperfecto. The choice between them is not about when something happened but about how you look at it: as a completed event, or as something ongoing, habitual or in the background. The conjugation drills tell you which tense to use; this drill asks you to choose it. It works like the other choice drills (see The choice drills).

How a question looks. Under the instruction "Choose the tense", the card shows the sentence in your language, and below it the Spanish sentence with a gap. The two options are the same verb in the indefinido and in the imperfecto (comí / comía). After you answer, a card names the principle at work and explains the choice.

The three kinds of question.

  • A time marker points the way. Ayer, anoche, el año pasado, de repente and a counted number of times (tres veces) go with the indefinido (Completed event). Siempre, todos los días, de niño and English "used to" go with the imperfecto (Habitual / ongoing). Descriptions, the weather, clock time and age in the past take the imperfecto (Description). These markers are useful, but they are only part of the deck, so that you can't score by spotting adverbs.
  • A scene and an interruption. Mientras leía, sonó el teléfono. The imperfecto sets the scene (Backdrop); the indefinido is the event that cuts into it (Interruption), and a series of events is told in the indefinido (Chain of events). A period with clear limits is still a completed event: Viví en Madrid durante tres años takes the indefinido (Closed duration).
  • The verb changes meaning (Meaning changes). A few verbs mean something different in each tense. The Spanish sentence is the same for both options, so the sentence in your language is your only clue:
Indefinido Imperfecto conocí — I met conocía — I knew supe — I found out sabía — I knew quiso — he tried quería — he wanted no quiso — he refused no quería — he didn't want to pude — I managed to podía — I was able to tuve — I got, received tenía — I had hubo — there was (it took place) había — there was (it existed)

What's recorded. Each principle is recorded separately, so a principle you keep missing, such as Backdrop, comes back more often.

docs.title: Produce the conjugation
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The production drill. You get a verb, a tense and a person, and you give the conjugated form. This is the drill that turns the conjugation tables into something you can do.

How a question looks. The card reads "Type the correct form for" (or "Pick the correct form for"), then the infinitive in large type, then two rows: Tense and Person.

Type the correct form for tener Tense: Pretérito Indefinido Person: yo

The questions come from the verbs and tenses in your selection (Select groups and Select tenses in the Verbs hub). Narrowing the selection is how you work on one thing: one tense across many verbs, or one verb group in a single tense.

The two icons on the card.

  • The book appears once your answer is graded. It opens the verb's table for the tense that was asked — in a sheet on iPhone and iPad, in a window of its own on the Mac that you can move aside — and closes when you go on to the next question.
  • The speaker pronounces the infinitive.

Type and Pick. Switch with the Type / Pick control above the card. You can switch at any time; the current answer is cleared when you do.

  • Type — type the form and tap Check (or press Return, or tap the arrow in the field). Tapping Check with an empty field moves on to a new question.
  • Pick — choose the form from a wheel of up to ten options, then tap Check. The wrong options are the same verb in other persons and in your other selected tenses, forms of similar-looking verbs from your selection, and the form the verb would have if it were regular. When the answer is more than one word (he hablado, estoy hablando), most options share the auxiliary, so you have to judge the participle or gerund itself.

Feedback. After Check, a feedback card appears and the button becomes Next.

  • Correct (green) — shows the verb's translation.
  • Accent: … (green) — right letters, but an accent is missing, extra or in the wrong place. This counts as correct; the card shows the correct spelling.
  • Typo: … (green) — the ending is exact and the stem is one letter off (two for words of eight letters or more). This counts as correct. A slip in the ending, a missing stem change, or a wrong auxiliary or reflexive pronoun is not treated as a typo.
  • The answer is … (red) — wrong. If what you gave is a real form of some verb, the card also says what it was ("You picked tuvo — Pretérito Indefinido, él") and shows two tables: the tense your answer belongs to, with your form in red, and the tense that was asked, with the right form in blue. Otherwise it shows only the table with the right form.

Accent and Typo apply only in Type mode and only while Exact spelling is off (Settings → Study → Grading; off by default). They never apply when what you typed is another form of the same verb: hablo for habló is a different person and tense, so it is wrong. With Exact spelling on, only the exact form counts.

The spellings recommended by the Real Academia since 2010 (rio, criais) count as plain correct, with no correction.

Skip. The Skip button always moves to a new question without recording anything.

Production settings. The gear button opens Production settings, where you can restrict the drill to chosen values of Verb, Tense and Person. Leave an axis empty to let it vary freely; Clear all restrictions undoes them all.

The session. The line at the top counts your answers ("7 out of 9 correct"), and the bar under it shows your success rate. The Incorrect answers switch limits the session to questions you have got wrong before. A session ends after the number of questions set in Settings → Study → Questions per session. The verbs are picked from your selection, based on your answer history and your Learning pace. After seven correct answers in a row the app offers to stop there: Continue or Stop — session complete.

What's recorded. Every checked answer is recorded on your device. Accent and typo answers count as correct. Skipped questions are not recorded.

Suggested workflow.

  1. Start in Pick mode while a tense is new.
  2. Switch to Type once the endings look familiar: Pick lets you eliminate options, Type makes you recall the form.
  3. Alternate sessions with Recognise the conjugation. Here you produce a form; there you name the form you are given.

docs.title: Conjugation tables
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Tap any verb in Verb reference to open its detail screen. The same screen opens from a verb group's list of verbs, from Look up, and from the verb lists behind the ⓘ buttons on Select verb groups.

The header

Above the tabs you see what the verb means and what kind of verb it is:

  • the translation of the infinitive (on the Mac, beside the infinitive in the title bar);
  • Extended meaning, folded away — for a verb with several distinct senses, a numbered list of them. It goes with the translations: a scheme that shows none hides it too;
  • a regularity line — Regular, Mostly regular or Irregular, with a count such as "2 things beyond the pattern", or "No pattern explains this verb" for verbs like ser;
  • the group badges — see Verb group badges and info sheets below — and the verb's level;
  • notes such as "Stative verb — not normally used in the progressive (estar + gerundio)." or "Impersonal — typically used only in the third person singular.";
  • for a verb built on another — contener on tener, producir on conducir — a family note: "Belongs to the family of tener, with …" and the other members. Where the verb departs from its base the note says so, form by form: bendecir keeps its future, conditional, imperative and participle regular (bendeciré, not bendiré; he bendecido, not he bendicho). On the base verb the note lists the members, and adds "Learn this verb and you have them all" when none of them departs.

Below that, three tabs: Conjugation · Regularity · Reference sheet. The screen opens on Conjugation.

Conjugation

The Conjugation tab starts with the Gerundio and Participio, each marked irregular where it is. Below them comes one table per tense — the tenses of your level; if your level has none, the tab tells you so. When your level leaves tenses out, Also later levels (n) above the tables brings them in: the same setting as on the theory pages and Practice Sets, and it is kept. Each table lists the persons with their forms. Under the tense's name a line says what the tense is for, and under the table is the verb's own sentence in that tense, with its translation and a speaker button. On its header, the book icon opens that tense's theory — what it is for, its endings, examples — and the speaker icon reads the whole tense aloud.

By Tense / By Person. A picker above the tables switches the view. By Tense shows one table per tense, as above. By Person turns them around: one panel per person — yo, tú, … — listing that person's form in every tense, with the tense name above each form, so you can follow how one person's ending changes from tense to tense. The mood is named where it changes. The speaker on a panel reads that person through all the tenses. The choice is remembered across verbs.

Only irregular tenses. The filter button in the toolbar shows only the tenses where this verb departs from the pattern. The choice is remembered across verbs, and per device. While it hides tenses, a note above the tables says so — "Only irregular tenses: 4 of 16 shown." — with Show all tenses to switch it off.

Why a tense departs. Under the table of a tense where the verb departs is a fold-out, labelled with the verdict — Partly irregular, Regular endings, changed stem. Open, it gives the reason in a sentence, the stems the tense is built on (a stem to learn in amber), and for each person that departs the form the pattern predicts, struck through, beside the real one: ~~teno~~ tengo, ~~tenes~~ tienes.

Where a verb has authored translations, a toolbar button shows a translation under every conjugated form. For verbs with a second meaning, a second button switches all the translations on the page to that meaning. The book icon in the toolbar looks the verb up in online dictionaries.

For gustar-type verbs the tables also show The me gusta use — the forms that agree with the thing liked — beside the forms With an ordinary subject, each with its own example sentence.

The conjugation colour code

iPhoneiPadMac

Irregular forms are colour-coded so you can see at a glance exactly where a verb departs from the regular pattern, and by how much.

  • No colour — regular. The form is stem plus the standard ending. The ending is underlined: that is the part the pattern predicts.
  • Red partial highlight — something changed within the form. Only the part that departs is red; the rest stays in the normal colour, and a regular ending is still underlined. For example:
  • Stem changes: the changed vowel is red. Poder (o→ue) shows puedo, puedes, puede with ue in red, while podemos and podéis have no highlight because their stem does not change.
  • Yo-form irregularities: only the inserted letters are red — the g of tengo, the z of conozco.
  • Y-insertion: the inserted y is red — leyó, construyo — and the rest of the regular ending after it stays underlined: the -ó of leyó.
  • Spelling shifts: the adjusted letters are red, as in jugué — a red u beside an underlined -é.
  • Accent shift: the accented í or ú is red — envío, and leíste, where the accent falls on the ending and the rest of it, -ste, is underlined.
  • Irregular future and conditional stem: the shortened stem is red — tendr- in tendré and tendría — and the ordinary endings after it are not.
  • Full red — completely irregular. The whole form is red when it has no systematic connection to the regular pattern and must be learned as a whole: soy, eres, es and voy, vas, va, the imperfect era and iba, and irregular participles such as dicho and hecho, which are red in every compound tense.
  • Red stem + blue ending — strong preterite. Strong preterites get two colours because there are two things to learn. The irregular stem is red (estuv-, pud-, vin-), and the ending is blue: strong preterites share their own ending set (-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron), which differs from the regular preterite and carries no written accent. Blue is used for nothing else.

Regularity

Regularity answers one question: where does this verb depart from the regular pattern? It lists only the tenses where it does, in the usual tense order. Each row has a coloured dot and a verdict — Regular endings, changed stem, Regular endings, learned form, Partly irregular, Irregular or No regular pattern — and under a partly irregular tense the persons that depart.

Under each tense is the stem it is built on. A stem you have to learn is in amber; so is a single form that carries a whole tense, such as the participle dicho for the compound tenses. That is why decir's pretérito indefinido reads Regular endings, changed stem: the endings are the ordinary strong-preterite set, and the amber stem dij- is the thing to learn. The two colours answer different questions: amber on Regularity names a whole stem or form to memorise, and red on Conjugation marks the letters of one form that departed.

A last line names the tenses that follow the pattern (Regular in the other tenses: …); a verb with nothing to learn shows only Regular in all tenses. Tap a tense to go to it on Conjugation, with its explanation open under the table.

Reference sheet

iPhoneiPadMac

Reference sheet is a one-page printable PDF of the verb's forms. On iPhone and iPad, the share button sends, saves or prints it; on the Mac, the toolbar menu offers Copy and Save as….

Regular patterns

iPhoneiPadMac

Regular patterns, at the bottom of the Verb groups page under To print, is the other printable page: the regular endings of all sixteen tenses at once, for -ar, -er and -ir. What a cell holds follows how the tense is built — the ending itself for a simple tense, haber's six forms with the participle noted under the table for a compound one, stem + ending for the imperfecto de subjuntivo, and the formation rule per person for the imperative, which borrows its forms rather than having endings of its own.

It is the regular pattern only. A verb with a stem change, an irregular yo form or a strong preterite takes these same endings; its own Reference sheet shows what they attach to, with the irregular material marked. The tables are the ones on each tense's card on the Tenses page — one tense at a time there, all sixteen here.

Irregular patterns

iPhoneiPadMac

Irregular patterns, beside it under To print, is its companion: that one shows the regular endings, this one where the irregular forms come from. It prints every tense's Formation block — the few patterns its irregular forms follow, each a sentence and a short table — in tense order, the same text as the tense cards. A block that several tenses share, such as the participle list of the six compound tenses, is printed once; the later tenses point back to it. It runs to several pages.

Verb group badges and info sheets

iPhoneiPadMac

The badges in the header name the groups the verb belongs to — for example Stem change e→ie, Irregular yo: -go or Reflexive. They are coloured by family: grey for Regular, red for stem changes, blue for yo-form and spelling changes, orange for an irregular stem in one tense and for the verbs that fit no pattern, purple for reflexive, impersonal, gustar-type and stative verbs.

Tap a badge to open the group's information sheet: a plain-language explanation of the pattern, a note on which persons it affects where that applies, a worked example table, and Browse all verbs with the number of verbs in the group. The same sheet opens from the ⓘ on Select verb groups and from Verb groups under Theory.

In the Browse all verbs list a verb family is one row: the base verb, with +N for the verbs built on it and its -se form — volver +3 stands for devolver, envolver and volverse. Tap the row to see the family; a verb without a family opens its page directly. Search still finds every member: devolver shows the volver row.

Tip: In Produce the conjugation and Recognise the conjugation, once your answer is graded a book icon on the card shows the verb's table for that tense — useful right after a wrong answer.

docs.title: Future stem (Futuro / Condicional)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the one stem the futuro and the condicional are both built on.

The endings of these two tenses are the same for every verb in the language, without a single exception: -é -ás -á -emos -éis -án for the futuro, -ía -ías -ía -íamos -íais -ían for the condicional. For most verbs the stem is the infinitive itself (hablar → hablaré, hablaría). Fifty-one verbs use a stem of their own, and that stem is the whole of what there is to learn — which is why one drill covers both tenses.

They fall into three families:

  • A d takes the place of the vowel — tener → tendré, poner → pondré, venir → vendré, salir → saldré, valer → valdré. With their compounds (mantener, suponer, convenir, …) these five roots account for thirty-eight of the fifty-one.
  • The vowel drops — haber → habré, poder → podré, saber → sabré, caber → cabré, querer → querré, and hay → habrá.
  • A stem of its own — decir → diré and hacer → haré, with contradecir, desdecir, deshacer, rehacer and satisfacer.

Two forms per card. The front shows the infinitive under the instruction "Give the yo forms of the futuro and the condicional". Tap the card to turn it: the back shows the Futuro and the Condicional yo form, one under the other, with the verb's translation. The irregular stem is coloured as in the conjugation tables (see The conjugation colour code).

The book opens the verb's conjugation, showing the futuro and the condicional. The speaker reads the infinitive on the front and both forms on the back.

Grading. On iPhone and iPad, swipe right if you knew both forms and left if you didn't. On the Mac, and with VoiceOver, use the Wrong and Correct buttons. The card then moves on by itself.

How the deck is built. Every verb in your selection that carries its own future stem. About one card in five is a regular verb — twenty irregulars bring five — drawn afresh each time you open the drill, so you have to decide whether the verb departs at all. For a regular verb the back is the infinitive with the endings. The line under the progress bar shows how many of the deck this round holds. If your selection has none, the screen offers Edit your verb selection or Use every verb (just for this drill).

The session. The Incorrect answers switch, session length, answer count and end of the session work as in Verb meaning. Each graded card is recorded twice on your device: once for the futuro and once for the condicional.

docs.title: Gerund (Gerundio)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the gerundio, the -ndo form used in the progressive (estoy hablando).

The gerundio is regular for most verbs: -ar verbs take -ando (hablando), -er and -ir verbs take -iendo (comiendo, viviendo). The irregular ones are a small set worth knowing by heart:

  • the -ir stem-changers, which raise the stem vowel: decir → diciendo, pedir → pidiendo, dormir → durmiendo;
  • verbs whose stem ends in a vowel, which take -yendo: leer → leyendo, oír → oyendo, ir → yendo;
  • a few more, such as poder → pudiendo.

The card. The front shows the infinitive under the instruction "Give the gerundio". Tap the card to turn it: the back shows the gerundio and the verb's translation. The part of the gerundio that departs from the regular pattern is coloured as in the conjugation tables (see The conjugation colour code), e.g. the u in durmiendo. The book opens the verb's full conjugation; the speaker reads the infinitive on the front and the gerundio on the back.

Grading. On iPhone and iPad, swipe right if you knew it and left if you didn't. On the Mac, and with VoiceOver, use the Wrong and Correct buttons. The card then moves on by itself.

How the deck is built. Every verb in your selection with an irregular gerundio is in the deck. About one card in five is a regular verb — twenty irregulars bring five — drawn afresh each time you open the drill, so you have to decide whether the verb departs at all. The line under the progress bar shows how many of the deck this round holds. If your selection has no irregular gerundios, the screen offers Edit your verb selection or Use every verb (just for this drill).

The session. The Incorrect answers switch, session length, answer count and end of the session work as in Verb meaning. Each graded card is recorded on your device against the verb.

docs.title: Preterite (Indefinido)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the pretérito indefinido, the tense where Spanish keeps many of its irregular forms.

The hardest group is the strong preterites: verbs whose indefinido is built on a different stem, with their own endings that carry no written accent. Tener → tuve, tuvo; poder → pude, pudo; decir → dije, dijo; hacer → hice, hizo; venir → vine, vino. Ser and ir share fui, fue.

Two forms per card. The front shows the infinitive under the instruction "Give the yo and él forms of the indefinido". Tap the card to turn it: the back shows the yo and the él form, one under the other, with the verb's translation. Together the two forms show the new stem and the unaccented endings, and those are what make a verb a strong preterite.

The forms are coloured as in the conjugation tables (see The conjugation colour code). An irregular stem is red. An ending that is the regular one is underlined. The special endings of a strong preterite (tuve, tuvo) are blue.

The book opens the verb's conjugation, showing the indefinido only. The speaker reads the infinitive on the front, and both forms on the back.

Grading. On iPhone and iPad, swipe right if you knew both forms and left if you didn't. On the Mac, and with VoiceOver, use the Wrong and Correct buttons. The card then moves on by itself.

How the deck is built. Every verb in your selection whose yo or él form is irregular in the indefinido is in the deck. About one card in five is a regular verb — twenty irregulars bring five — drawn afresh each time you open the drill, so you have to decide whether the verb departs at all. The line under the progress bar shows the mix. If your selection has none, the screen offers Edit your verb selection or Use every verb (just for this drill).

The session. The Incorrect answers switch, session length, answer count and end of the session work as in Verb meaning. Each graded card is recorded twice on your device: once for the yo form and once for the él form.

docs.title: -ir stem change (Indefinido / Gerundio / Subjuntivo)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

An -ir verb that changes its stem in the presente changes it in three more places, one step only — e → i, o → u: the third person of the indefinido (pidió, durmió), the gerundio (pidiendo, durmiendo), and nosotros and vosotros of the presente de subjuntivo (pidamos, durmamos).

The card. The back shows one form of each: the él form of the Pretérito Indefinido, the Gerundio, and the nosotros form of the Presente de Subjuntivo, each labelled. The book opens the verb's conjugation at those three.

The deck. Every -ir verb in your selection with a stem change. The stem-changing verbs in -ar and -er keep their stem outside the presente, so they are not in it. About one card in five is a regular verb — twenty irregulars bring five — drawn afresh each time you open the drill, so you have to decide whether the verb departs at all.

Grading and the session work as in Future stem (Futuro / Condicional), and each graded card is recorded once for every form on its back.

docs.title: Irregularity by tense
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The verbs that break the pattern, tense by tense: the screen Irregularity by tense under Linguistic analysis, and the list behind each tense card's Irregular verbs on the Tenses page. It is described here, with the verbs, because it is where the drills for a single tense start.

One row per tense: how many things there are to learn there — a family of verbs that share one stem counts once, and so does a verb on its own — and the share of its verbs that are not fully predictable. Tenses that hold exactly the same verbs are folded into one row, and the row says what they share — the six compound tenses share one participle, the futuro and the condicional share one stem. A cap beside the number means there is a drill behind the row.

Opening a row lists those verbs, grouped under the patterns the tense's Formation card names — for the indefinido Strong preterite (u-stem), Vowel change in the 3rd person singular and plural, i → y in the 3rd person singular and plural and so on — with the number of verbs beside each heading. Every heading is open; tap one to close it. The headings name the visible change, so the same pattern has the same name in every tense: the presente de subjuntivo and the imperativo afirmativo share their headings, and above the imperative's list a line says why — apart from tú and vosotros (di, haz, pon; hablad), the affirmative imperative takes its forms from the present subjunctive.

The order menu in the toolbar sorts the list three ways:

  • By pattern — the patterns of the Formation card, as above. The list opens this way.
  • By reason — why each verb departs: The stem differs, The ending differs, and The stem and the ending differ for a verb that has both (pon has lost its ending, ponga has a different stem). For the compound tenses there are also the written accent (caído) and Regular where the family is not (bendecido). Each row shows the stem the verb takes in that tense, such as pondr-, and beside it the size of its family, such as +16. At the top, the box Fewer than the numbers suggest says how much there is to learn: in the futuro, for example, 51 verbs depart, but that is 13 things to learn — 6 families that share one stem, plus 7 verbs on their own.
  • Alphabetical — every verb from A to Z.

The filter button in the toolbar is on when the screen opens: the list shows only the irregular verbs. Switch it off (Show all verbs) and the list shows every verb in your level, from A to Z, each opening at that tense. Only the irregular verbs show the explanation of why they depart. With the filter off, the order menu is hidden. Practise and the drills always work on the irregular verbs, with about one regular verb in five mixed in.

From there:

  • tapping a verb opens its page at that tense, with the explanation of why it departs open under the table (for a folded row, at the first of its tenses, with what they share above the tabs);
  • Practise starts the drill — Past participle, Gerund, Preterite or Future stem where Spanish has one for that tense, and otherwise Produce the conjugation over the verbs on the list, mixed the same way. Where the list falls under more than one heading, the menu's One pattern offers each heading on its own. Where other drills are about the tense as well, Practise is a menu: that drill first, then the others — for the indefinido Preterite stem, -ir stem change, Spelling changes and the two past-tense choices;
  • Cycle through randomly shows one verb's conjugation at a time, and walks every verb on the list as it is shown.

What the list shows.

  • The rows follow the order of the tenses in the app.
  • A tense needs at least three irregular verbs before the cap appears; the row itself is always there, because a census that hides a tense with two is not a census.
  • The verbs come from the whole catalogue, not from your verb selection.

The first time you open the screen it scans the catalogue, which takes a moment ("Scanning the catalogue…").

docs.title: Indicative or subjunctive (Indicativo / Subjuntivo)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Spanish uses the subjunctive in many places where English does not. The app conjugates all four subjunctive tenses for over 1,200 verbs; this drill asks when one is needed. It works like the other choice drills (see The choice drills).

How a question looks. Under the instruction "Choose the mood", the card shows the sentence in your language, and below it the Spanish sentence with a gap. The two options are the same verb in the indicative and in the subjunctive (viene / venga). After you answer, a card names the trigger at work (Belief, Doubt / denial, Volition, Emotion, Purpose…) and explains the choice.

A que is not a trigger. About a third of the answers in this drill are the indicative, on purpose. A drill where the answer is always the subjunctive only teaches you to spot que. The questions are built from minimal pairs: the same sentence with one thing changed, and a different mood.

Indicative Subjunctive Creo que viene No creo que venga Es verdad que está No es verdad que esté Cuando llego, ceno Cuando llegue, cenaré Aunque es caro (I know it is) Aunque sea caro (even if it is) Busco el piso que tiene … Busco un piso que tenga …

What moves the mood is negation, the future, and whether the thing referred to is known.

The trigger classes.

  • Always subjunctive: wanting and asking (quiero que, pide que), emotion (me alegro de que), doubt and denial (dudo que, no creo que), value judgements (es importante que), and the conjunctions para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que.
  • Always indicative: assertions — creo que, es verdad que, es evidente que, está claro que.
  • It depends: cuando (has it happened, or is it still to come?), aunque (although it is, or even if it were?), and relative clauses (a known thing, or any thing that fits?).

Emotion is the tricky class. Me alegro de que estés aquí: you really are here, and it is still the subjunctive, because the clause is not being asserted but reacted to. A rule of thumb based on "uncertainty" breaks down here.

What's recorded. Each trigger class is recorded separately, so a class you keep missing comes back more often.

docs.title: Past participle (Participio)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

A flashcard deck for the past participle, the form used in the compound tenses (he hablado) and as an adjective (la puerta cerrada).

Regular participles end in -ado (-ar verbs) or -ido (-er and -ir verbs). About a dozen common verbs have their own: decir → dicho, hacer → hecho, poner → puesto, ver → visto, escribir → escrito, volver → vuelto, morir → muerto, abrir → abierto, romper → roto. Their compounds take the same form (descubrir → descubierto, deshacer → deshecho).

The card. The front shows the infinitive under the instruction "Give the participio". Tap the card to turn it: the back shows the participle and the verb's translation. The book opens the verb's full conjugation; the speaker reads the infinitive on the front and the participle on the back.

Grading. On iPhone and iPad, swipe right if you knew it and left if you didn't. On the Mac, and with VoiceOver, use the Wrong and Correct buttons. The card then moves on by itself.

How the deck is built. Every verb in your selection with an irregular participle is in the deck. About one card in five is a regular verb — twenty irregulars bring five — drawn afresh each time you open the drill, so you have to decide whether the verb departs at all. The line under the progress bar shows how many of the deck this round holds. Each session then takes its cards from this deck, up to Questions per session, based on your answer history and your Learning pace.

If none of your selected verbs has an irregular participle, the screen says so and offers two ways out: Edit your verb selection, or Use every verb (just for this drill).

The session. The Incorrect answers switch, the answer count, the seven-in-a-row prompt and the end of the session work as in Verb meaning. Each graded card is recorded on your device against the verb.

docs.title: Preterite stem (Indefinido / Imperfecto de subjuntivo)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The imperfecto de subjuntivo is built on the ellos form of the indefinido — drop -ron, add -ra — so every irregularity of the indefinido carries over: tuvieron → tuviera, pidieron → pidiera, leyeron → leyera, fueron → fuera.

The card. The back shows the ellos form of the Pretérito Indefinido and the yo form of the Imperfecto de Subjuntivo, each labelled with its tense and person. The book opens the verb's conjugation at those two tenses.

The deck. Every verb in your selection whose ellos form in the indefinido is irregular: the strong preterites, the -ir verbs whose vowel changes in the third person, the verbs that write a y, and those with forms of their own. Verbs that only change their spelling in the yo form (busqué) are not in it: their ellos form is regular. About one card in five is a regular verb — twenty irregulars bring five — drawn afresh each time you open the drill, so you have to decide whether the verb departs at all.

Grading and the session work as in Future stem (Futuro / Condicional), and each graded card is recorded once for every form on its back.

docs.title: Recognise the conjugation
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

The recognition drill, the reverse of Produce the conjugation. You see a conjugated form and say what it is: which verb, which tense and which person.

How a question looks. The form is shown in large type, with a speaker that pronounces it. Once you have checked, a book appears beside the form: it opens the table of the form's tense for its verb — in a window of its own on the Mac — and closes when you go on. Below the form are three pickers, VERB, TENSE and PERSON.

  • VERB offers the right verb among similar-looking verbs, chosen by spelling, so sentir and sentar, poder and poner appear together. The similar verbs come from the whole catalogue, not only from your selection.
  • TENSE offers the tenses you have selected in Select tenses.
  • PERSON offers all six persons.

The form is always a real form of a verb in your selection. Reflexive verbs are shown with their pronoun (os habéis buscado), so they can't be confused with the plain verb.

The action button changes with what you have done:

  • Skip — nothing picked yet. Moves to a new question without recording anything.
  • Check — all three pickers set. The button is disabled while only some of them are set.
  • Next — after checking.

Ambiguous forms. Some forms have more than one reading. Hablara is both the yo and the él/ella form of the imperfect subjunctive, and vivimos is both present and preterite. Any valid reading counts as correct. After a correct answer the feedback says Correct and lists Other valid analyses:, each with its table. After a wrong one it names what was wrong (Wrong tense, Wrong person, or just Wrong when more than one pick is off), then shows Your answer: (the table your picks point to, in red) and then the Valid analyses: (in blue).

Recognition settings. The gear button opens the settings:

  • Picker style — Chips (the default) or Wheel. Wheels take more room but are easier to scroll; chips are denser.
  • Multi-answer mode — instead of naming one reading, you collect every reading the form has. Set the pickers and tap Add this analysis for each one; your claims are listed and can be removed. Check then grades the whole set, and only the complete set counts as fully correct.
  • Test me on — switch Verb, Tense and Person on or off. A dimension you switch off is shown as a hint above the form, so you can start with the tense alone and add person and verb later. At least one must stay on.
  • Verb options (shown while Verb is tested) — how many verbs the VERB picker offers: 5, 10, 15 (the default), 25 or All. It applies from the next question.

The session. The line at the top counts your answers ("7 / 9 correct"), with a bar showing your success rate. The Incorrect answers switch, the session length and the choice of verbs work as in Produce the conjugation. Each checked answer is recorded on your device; skipped questions are not.

When to use it. Recognition is the drill for reading: when you can produce the common forms but stumble over them in a text, or when you want to test your sense of tense without a prompt that gives it away. If it feels too hard, run Produce the conjugation in Pick mode first, then come back.

docs.title: Select tenses
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select tenses chooses which of the sixteen tenses you study. The choice applies everywhere verbs are practised: the conjugation tables show only the selected tenses, the example sentence under each tense on a verb's page follows it, and the conjugation drills ask only about those tenses.

The banner shows how many tenses are active, e.g. "16 of 16". Tap a row to include or exclude that tense. Each section header has an All / None button, and All | None at the top right selects or clears every tense at once. If you leave the screen with nothing selected, the app warns you — "No tenses selected".

By Section

The tenses are grouped by mood:

  • Indicativo – Tiempos Simples — Presente, Pretérito Indefinido, Pretérito Imperfecto, Futuro, Condicional.
  • Indicativo – Tiempos Compuestos — Pretérito Perfecto, Pluscuamperfecto, Futuro Perfecto, Condicional Perfecto.
  • Subjuntivo – Tiempos Simples — Presente de Subjuntivo, Imperfecto de Subjuntivo.
  • Subjuntivo – Tiempos Compuestos — Pretérito Perfecto Subjuntivo, Pluscuamperfecto Subjuntivo.
  • Imperativo — Imperativo Afirmativo, Imperativo Negativo.
  • Formas no Personales — Gerundio. (The infinitive and the past participle appear on every verb, but the gerundio is the only one you select here.)

Long-press a section header (on the Mac, click and hold) to read what that group of tenses is for.

By Level

The second view groups the same tenses by the level at which each first appears in the scheme you use:

Level Tenses A1 Presente A2 Pretérito Perfecto, Pretérito Indefinido, Pretérito Imperfecto, Gerundio, Imperativo Afirmativo B1 Futuro, Condicional, Pluscuamperfecto, Presente de Subjuntivo, Imperativo Negativo B2 Futuro Perfecto, Condicional Perfecto, Imperfecto de Subjuntivo, Pretérito Perfecto Subjuntivo, Pluscuamperfecto Subjuntivo

The ⓘ on each tense

iPhoneiPadMac

Every tense row has an ⓘ. It opens the Tenses page — the same page as Tenses under Theory on the verbs hub — at that tense, with its card open. The other tenses are one tap away. On iPhone and iPad the page opens with a back button. On the Mac it opens in a window of its own, which can stay open beside the list; tap another ⓘ and the window moves to that tense. The same ⓘ is beside the tenses of a lesson, in the tense picker of your own practice set, and on a word's page.

The tense's card has:

  • an overview and when the tense is used;
  • the endings, with an example conjugation;
  • Formation: how the tense is built, and where its irregular forms come from. The point is that the irregularity is smaller than it looks: a handful of patterns and a few verbs of their own. Each pattern is a sentence and a short table in aligned columns — infinitive, then the form or stem it produces — so the change can be read down a column: tener · tendr- · tendré. A table headed yo shows the yo form;
  • example sentences;
  • Irregular verbs (N), which opens the tense's irregular verbs grouped by those same patterns (see Irregularity by tense).

Tip: Start with Presente alone, or with the simple indicative tenses. Add the others one at a time — Pretérito Indefinido is usually the next one worth learning.

docs.title: Select verb groups
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Select verb groups chooses which verbs you practise, by their grammatical character rather than one by one. The screen does not set level or topic: those are global. Your level is in Scheme and level (the chip with the flag), and the Select word scope row near the top takes you to the topics (its second line says All topics or Filtered by topic).

The banner at the top keeps a running count of what you have chosen, e.g. "23 of 23 groups · … · 212 in scope", with the number of selected verbs in the middle: how many groups are ticked, how many verbs those groups cover in the whole catalogue, and how many of those are left within your level and word scope. The last number is what the drills draw from.

Tap a row to tick or untick it. Each row shows how many verbs are in the group, and its ⓘ opens the group's explanation (see Verb group badges and info sheets under Conjugation tables). Each section header has an All / None button, and All | None at the top right ticks or clears every group at once. Long-press a family header (on the Mac, click and hold) for an explanation of the whole family. A family of one group, such as Fully regular, has none: the row's ⓘ covers it.

A verb usually belongs to more than one group, and it is in your pool when any of its groups is ticked. Lavarse, for example, is both Regular and Reflexive, so ticking Regular alone already includes it.

If you leave the screen with nothing ticked, the app warns you — "No verb groups selected" — and offers Stay and select or Go back anyway.

By Section

The first view lists the 23 groups under nine families — the same families, in the same order, as the Verb groups page under Theory:

Family Groups Fully regular Regular Stem-changing verbs e→ie, o→ue, e→i, u→ue, i→ie, Accent shift í/ú Yo-form irregularities Irregular yo: -go, Irregular yo: -zco, Consonant + -cer/-cir: c → z, Spelling shift -ger/-gir, Verbs ending in -guir Spelling-change verbs Verbs ending in -uir, Y-insertion, Spelling shift -car/-gar/-zar An irregular stem in one tense Strong preterite, Irregular participle, Irregular future stem Irregulars that fit no pattern Irregular Reflexive verbs Reflexive Impersonal and gusto-type verbs Impersonal, Me gusta pattern Stative verbs Stative

Stem-changing verbs holds the five vowel changes plus Accent shift í/ú — verbs like enviar, confiar, actuar and continuar, whose stem vowel takes a written accent where the spoken stress falls on it (envío, actúe). Nosotros and vosotros keep the stress on the ending and take no accent (enviamos).

An irregular stem in one tense holds the strong preterite (tener → tuve), the shortened future stem (tener → tendré, tendría) and the irregular participle (abrir → abierto): each is one stem to learn for one tense. Irregular is for the verbs no pattern explains, such as ser and ir.

The last three families are different in kind: none of their groups changes an ending. They describe how the verb is built into a sentence — with a reflexive pronoun, only in the third person, with the me gusta construction, or (stative) not in the progressive.

By regularity

iPhoneiPadMac

The second view asks a different question: not which pattern, but how many. It lists flat rows — No exceptions, 1 exception, 2 exceptions and so on — and a last row, Not classifiable, for the verbs no pattern accounts for. Each row is labelled Regular, Mostly regular (one or two exceptions) or Irregular.

Tick 2 exceptions and you get every verb that asks you to remember two things beyond its endings, whichever two they are: almorzar is o→ue and a -zar spelling shift, salir takes -go and a shortened future stem, and both are 2.

iPhoneiPadMac

Each row's ⓘ explains the row and lists its verbs, each with a mark for every exception it has and a legend underneath, so you can see what the number is made of before you commit to it. Tap a verb there to open it.

Ticks in the two views add up: a verb is in your pool if it matches a ticked group or a ticked exception count.

Seeing which verbs you ended up with

This screen chooses patterns; it does not list the verbs they match. To see the resulting pool, open Reference on the verbs hub.

docs.title: Ser or estar
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac

Spanish has two verbs for to be, ser and estar, where English and Dutch have one. The conjugation is soon automatic; the choice stays hard for years. This drill asks only which of the two a sentence needs. It works like the other choice drills (see The choice drills).

How a question looks. Under the instruction "Choose ser or estar", the card shows the sentence in your language, and below it the Spanish sentence with a gap:

My mother is tired. Spanish: Mi madre ___ cansada.

The two options are already conjugated in the person and tense the sentence needs — es / está, soy / estoy, son / están, era / estaba — so you also have to recognise the forms. The option you tap fills the gap. After you answer, a card names the rule at work, such as Identity, Location, Condition or Meaning changes, and explains why ("Why está?"); read it even when you were right.

The rules in the deck.

  • Ser — identity and profession (Mi hermana es médica), origin (Soy neerlandés), material and possession (La mesa es de madera, Ese libro es mío), time and dates (Son las tres, Hoy es lunes), and impersonal expressions (Es importante estudiar).
  • Estar — where a person or thing is (Las llaves están en la mesa), a passing condition (La sopa está fría), the result of a change (La ventana está abierta, and also Mi abuelo está muerto), and fixed expressions (Estoy de acuerdo).
  • The location of an event — events take ser even for "where": La fiesta es en mi casa, but La casa está en la calle Mayor. If you could say "takes place" instead of "is", use ser.
  • Meaning changes — adjectives whose meaning depends on the verb. The Spanish sentence is the same for both, so the sentence in your language is your only clue: es aburrido (boring) / está aburrido (bored), es listo (clever) / está listo (ready), es rico (wealthy) / está rico (delicious), es verde (green) / está verde (unripe), es malo (wicked) / está malo (ill), and also vivo, abierto, bueno, despierto, atento, seguro and interesado.
  • In the past — the same choice with era and estaba: the rule doesn't change with the tense.

What's recorded. Each rule is recorded separately (ser for identity is one entry, ser for events another), so a rule you keep missing comes back more often.

The Ser or estar deck under Traps is this same drill, limited to the Meaning changes sentences.

docs.title: Short tú commands (Imperativo)
docs.text:
iPhoneiPadMac
